courses.title: AIXI
courses.subtitle: Universal artificial intelligence: induction, planning and the limits of the ideal agent
courses.author: Lilith Learning Lab
courses.description: A 12-chapter course on AIXI, Marcus Hutter's mathematical definition of an ideal reinforcement learning agent. Based on Hutter's Universal Algorithmic Intelligence survey, the Monte-Carlo AIXI paper by Veness and colleagues, Legg and Hutter's universal intelligence paper, and Leike, Hutter and Orseau on computability and bad priors. Covers the agent-environment cycle, expectimax, Bayesian mixtures, Kolmogorov complexity, Solomonoff induction, the AIXI equation, horizons, optimality, incomputability and AIXItl, MC-AIXI-CTW and critiques. Python labs run on the built-in MicroPython engine. The toy programs are teaching miniatures, not code from the papers.

outline.title: What is AIXI?
outline.summary: AIXI is a mathematical definition of an ideal reinforcement learning agent, proposed by Marcus Hutter in 2000. It is not a program you can run. It answers a thought experiment: how would you act if you had unlimited computing power and no knowledge of your world? It joins two ideas. Solomonoff induction predicts what comes next by weighing every computable explanation of the past, simple ones more heavily. Expectimax planning then picks the action with the highest expected total reward under those predictions. The course builds both halves in small Python programs, then the real approximations and the serious criticisms.
keyPoints: AIXI was proposed by Marcus Hutter in 2000; the main results are in his 2005 book Universal Artificial Intelligence.
It acts in an unknown but computable environment and tries to maximize total reward.
Prediction comes from a Solomonoff-style mixture; action comes from expectimax.
There are no free parameters except the choice of universal Turing machine and the horizon.
AIXI is incomputable, so it is a gold standard to approximate, not a program to run.
It does not model itself as part of the world: that is its biggest conceptual limit.

outline.title: The agent-environment cycle
outline.summary: The formal setting is simple. Time runs in steps. At step t the agent picks an action a_t from a finite set and the environment replies with a percept, an observation o_t and a reward r_t. Everything seen so far is the history. A policy maps each history to an action. An environment maps each history and action to a distribution over percepts. There is no assumption that the world is Markov: the reply may depend on the whole past. The environment must be chronological: its reply at step t cannot depend on actions the agent has not taken yet. This sounds obvious but needs stating when everything is written as functions on strings.
keyPoints: A step is an action followed by a percept (observation, reward).
A history is the list of all action-percept pairs so far.
A policy turns a history into an action; an environment turns a history and action into a percept distribution.
No Markov assumption: the whole history may matter.
Chronological environments cannot see future actions.
Total reward over a horizon is the quantity the agent wants to maximize.

outline.title: Planning with a known model: expectimax
outline.summary: Suppose the agent knows the environment exactly. Then choosing actions is a planning problem. Draw a tree: at agent nodes pick the best action, at chance nodes average over the environment's replies, and add up rewards along the way. This is expectimax. The value of a history is the expected total reward the best policy can still collect. The recursion is: value is the maximum over actions of the expected, over percepts, of reward plus the value of the longer history. The tree grows exponentially with the horizon, which is the first reason AIXI cannot be run. The second is that the environment is not known, which is where Solomonoff induction comes in.
keyPoints: With a known environment, optimal action is a search problem.
Max over actions, expectation over percepts, sum of rewards.
V(h) = max_a sum_x P(x | h a) [ r(x) + V(h a x) ] with V = 0 at the horizon.
The search tree has (actions x percepts)^horizon leaves.
AIXI uses this same recursion, with the true environment replaced by a mixture.
Sampling approximations such as UCT avoid expanding the whole tree.

outline.title: Bayesian mixtures and prediction
outline.summary: When the environment is unknown, a Bayesian keeps several candidates, each with a prior weight. As data arrives, candidates that predicted it badly lose weight. To predict, average the candidates' predictions using the current weights. The mixture has a remarkable property. It assigns every observed sequence at least its prior weight times the probability that the true candidate gave it. So it can never do much worse than the best candidate, and the extra cost is at most the log of one over that candidate's weight. AIXI uses the largest sensible class, all computable environments, and a particular prior, which is the topic of the next chapters.
keyPoints: Bayes rule: new weight is proportional to old weight times likelihood.
Mixture probability xi(x) = sum of w_i times nu_i(x).
Dominance: xi(x) >= w_i nu_i(x) for each i.
Hence the log-loss of the mixture exceeds the best member's by at most ln(1/w_i).
For deterministic hypotheses, the mixture's mistakes are bounded by the log of one over the true hypothesis's weight in bits.
A class containing the truth with positive prior weight is called a grain of truth.

outline.title: Kolmogorov complexity and the universal prior
outline.summary: The Kolmogorov complexity of a string is the length of the shortest program that prints it on a fixed universal computer. A string with a pattern has a short program. A random string has no program much shorter than itself. Changing the computer changes the complexity by at most a constant, so the notion is meaningful. But no program can compute it exactly. The universal prior gives a string the total weight of all programs that produce it, each program counting two to the power of minus its length. This is Occam's razor written as arithmetic.
keyPoints: K(x) is the length of the shortest program printing x.
The reference machine matters only up to an additive constant (invariance theorem).
K is not computable.
Prefix-free programs obey the Kraft inequality, so 2^-length can be read as probabilities.
M(x) is the sum of 2^-length(p) over programs whose output starts with x.
Shorter explanations get exponentially more weight.

outline.title: Solomonoff induction
outline.summary: Solomonoff induction predicts the next symbol by the ratio M of x followed by a symbol, to M of x. It is the Bayesian mixture of chapter 4 over every computable hypothesis, with weights from the universal prior. Its signature result is a bound on total error. If the data comes from any computable source mu, the predictions converge to mu's own, and the total prediction error, however long the sequence, is bounded by a constant proportional to K of mu. The result is strong and rare: one predictor that works for every computable world. The price is that M itself is incomputable.
keyPoints: Prediction is a ratio: M(x a) / M(x).
M is a mixture over all computable environments with weights 2^-K.
Dominance: M(x) >= c 2^-K(mu) mu(x).
Hence total prediction error on mu-data is bounded by a multiple of K(mu).
For a deterministic computable sequence the number of wrong predictions is bounded by a multiple of K.
M is only lower semicomputable, so Solomonoff induction cannot be run exactly.

outline.title: The AIXI equation
outline.summary: The AIXI equation puts the pieces together. A program q stands for an environment: given the agent's actions, it outputs the percepts. Each q consistent with the history so far is weighted by two to the minus its length. The agent takes the action with the highest weighted expected total reward. Written in full, a maximum over the next action alternates with sums over the next percept, all the way to the horizon, with the reward sum multiplying a weighted count of the consistent programs. On a small finite class of environments the same computation is easy to carry out. The practice section builds it and the app lets you watch it work.
keyPoints: a_k = argmax_{a_k} sum_{o_k r_k} ... max_{a_m} sum_{o_m r_m} [r_k + ... + r_m] sum_{q: U(q, a_1..a_m) = o_1 r_1 .. o_m r_m} 2^-length(q).
The inner sum is the Solomonoff-style weight of all environments producing that future.
The only parameters are the reference machine U and the horizon m.
In a finite class: weight each consistent environment, expand the tree, take the best action.
Deterministic consistent environments are eliminated as soon as their reply differs from the percept seen.
Computing the real thing needs all programs, including those that never halt.

outline.title: Horizons and discounting
outline.summary: The AIXI equation sums reward up to a horizon m. How far ahead should the agent look? Too short and it is greedy. Too long and the sums may not converge, or, in a patient universe, the agent may keep postponing. Discounting replaces a hard cutoff with weights on the steps. Geometric discounting makes the near future matter much more than the far future. Hutter's survey also discusses harmonic discounting, whose horizon grows as the agent ages. None of these choices is neutral: the discount shapes how much the agent explores, and chapter 12 shows prior and discount can interact badly.
keyPoints: A finite lifetime m is simplest but the agent must know m.
Geometric discounting: effective horizon about log(1/eps) / log(1/gamma).
Harmonic discounting: tail after step t is about 1/t, so the horizon grows linearly with age.
With no discounting and an infinite life, delaying rewards forever can look optimal.
Hutter notes immortal agents are lazy.
The choice of discount is part of the problem specification, not a detail.

outline.title: Optimality and universal intelligence
outline.summary: Hutter argued that AIXI is optimal in several senses. A policy is Pareto optimal if no other policy does at least as well in every environment and strictly better in one. Balanced Pareto optimality uses a weighted sum over environments. Legg and Hutter turned the weighted sum into a definition of machine intelligence: an agent's universal intelligence is its expected reward in each computable environment, weighted by two to the minus the environment's complexity. AIXI maximizes it by construction. Chapter 12 shows that these notions depend heavily on the choice of prior and reference machine, so read them as results about a particular setup.
keyPoints: Pareto optimality is a weak requirement: no policy dominates.
Balanced Pareto optimality maximizes the weighted sum of values.
Upsilon(pi) = sum_mu 2^-K(mu) V(pi, mu), with total reward at most 1 in each environment.
AIXI attains the maximum Upsilon, relative to its prior.
Random agents score low; specialist agents such as a chess program score very low.
Later work found these claims are subjective: they depend on the prior.

outline.title: Incomputability and AIXItl
outline.summary: AIXI looks at every program, including ones that never halt, so it is not computable. The limits can be pinned down in the arithmetical hierarchy: Leike and Hutter show planning in general computable environments is hard even in principle. Hutter's own response was AIXItl: restrict attention to policies of length at most l that run at most t steps per cycle. It is computable but its running time is of the order t times two to the l, and it is useless in practice. Two ideas help to see why: Levin search shares time among programs in proportion to two to the minus their length, and a speed prior, proposed by Schmidhuber, penalizes slow programs as well as long ones.
keyPoints: Exact AIXI is incomputable: it needs to know which programs halt.
AIXItl is computable with a cost of about t * 2^l per cycle.
Levin search allocates time 2^-length to each program.
Leike and Hutter: finding an optimal policy is Pi_2-hard and finding an epsilon-optimal one is undecidable in general semicomputable environments.
By default AIXI is not even limit computable, but a limit-computable epsilon-optimal variant exists.
Schmidhuber's speed prior replaces M to give an approximable alternative.

outline.title: Monte Carlo AIXI with context tree weighting
outline.summary: Veness, Ng, Hutter, Uther and Silver built the first computationally feasible AIXI approximation. It replaces the mixture over all programs with a mixture over prediction suffix trees, computed exactly by context tree weighting, and replaces the exact expectimax with a Monte Carlo tree search. The KT estimator predicts the next bit from counts of zeros and ones. A context tree uses KT estimators at the leaves and mixes over all tree depths. The prior favors small trees, an Occam's razor for context models. The agent, called MC-AIXI-CTW, learned small stochastic and partially observable games, including a version of Pac-Man.
keyPoints: MC-AIXI-CTW is a direct approximation of AIXI: CTW for learning, rho-UCT for planning.
A CTW node mixes its own KT estimate and the product of its children's weighted estimates, equally.
The prior over trees is 2^-(code length of the tree), preferring small trees.
rho-UCT picks actions with an upper confidence bound and samples percepts from the model.
It is a principled approximation, not a scaled-up success on large problems.

outline.title: Critiques, bad priors and what comes next
outline.summary: AIXI treats itself as outside the world: it can't be damaged or modified by its environment because that possibility is not in its model. It also depends on the choice of universal Turing machine, which sets the prior. Orseau showed AIXI is not asymptotically optimal in all computable environments. Leike and Hutter then showed that unlucky or adversarial choices of the machine can make AIXI misbehave drastically, and that Legg-Hutter intelligence and balanced Pareto optimality are subjective. Remedies include more exploration, such as Thompson sampling, which restores asymptotic optimality, and models that embed the agent in the world.
keyPoints: AIXI's agent is outside its environment: it cannot represent being modified or destroyed.
The prior depends on the reference machine and that choice can be made adversarially.
Leike and Hutter: every policy is Pareto optimal in the class of all computable environments.
Dogmatic prior: AIXI keeps following a chosen computable policy as long as its expected reward is not near zero.
Orseau: AIXI is not asymptotically optimal in all computable environments.
Thompson sampling is asymptotically optimal in general environments (Leike and colleagues, 2016).

courses.title: AlphaGo
courses.subtitle: Deep neural networks and tree search for the game of Go
courses.author: Lilith Learning Lab
courses.description: A 12-chapter course on AlphaGo, the DeepMind program that beat a professional Go player and then Lee Sedol. Based on the 2016 Nature paper by Silver, Huang and colleagues and public accounts of the Fan Hui and Lee Sedol matches. Covers the rules of Go, Monte Carlo tree search before AlphaGo, the 48-plane input and the policy network, supervised learning from expert games, the fast rollout policy, policy-gradient self-play, the value network, the search with PUCT and mixed evaluation, hardware and Elo, a tic-tac-toe miniature, and the matches, successors and criticism. Python labs run on the built-in MicroPython engine. DeepMind did not release the code; the labs are teaching miniatures.

outline.title: What is AlphaGo?
outline.summary: AlphaGo is the DeepMind program that became the first to beat a professional Go player on a full board without handicap. It did so in October 2015 against the European champion Fan Hui, and in March 2016 it beat Lee Sedol, one of the world's top players, four games to one. Its idea is to combine Monte Carlo tree search with deep neural networks. A policy network suggests promising moves, which cuts the breadth of the search. A value network judges positions, which cuts its depth. The networks were trained in stages: first to imitate human experts, then improved by self-play. This course builds each piece in small Python programs.
keyPoints: AlphaGo was published in Nature on 28 January 2016 by Silver, Huang and colleagues at DeepMind.
It beat the European champion Fan Hui 5-0 in October 2015, the first win over a professional on a full board without handicap.
It beat Lee Sedol 4-1 in March 2016.
Four learned components: a fast rollout policy, an SL policy network, an RL policy network and a value network.
Policy networks cut the breadth of the search; the value network cuts its depth.
Later versions (Master, Zero) and AlphaZero removed the human data.

outline.title: The game of Go
outline.summary: Go is played on a 19 by 19 grid. Black and White alternate placing a stone on an empty point. Connected stones of one colour form a group, and the empty points next to a group are its liberties. A group with no liberties is captured and removed. A move that repeats an earlier position is not allowed; this is the ko rule. At the end the players count area: a player's stones plus the empty points surrounded only by their stones. White receives komi, here 7.5 points, because Black moves first. The rules fit on a page, but a typical position has about two hundred and fifty legal moves and a game lasts about a hundred and fifty moves.
keyPoints: Players alternate; Black moves first.
A group is captured when it has no liberties.
Suicide moves are generally forbidden and positions may not repeat (ko).
Chinese area scoring counts stones and surrounded empty points; the Lee Sedol match used a 7.5 komi.
Go's branching factor is about 250 and its depth about 150, versus about 35 and 80 for chess.
Evaluating a Go position is hard because the board has no simple material count.

outline.title: Before AlphaGo: search and Monte Carlo
outline.summary: Chess programs search deeply with alpha-beta and a hand-written evaluation. In Go that approach stalled: the tree is too wide and no one could write a good evaluation. Programs stayed weak amateurs. Progress came from Monte Carlo methods. To judge a position, play many random games from it and count the wins. Monte Carlo tree search builds a tree and spends more simulations on moves that look promising, with a bandit rule such as UCT choosing which to explore. By 2015 the strongest programs, such as Crazy Stone and Zen, used MCTS and reached strong amateur level. AlphaGo's contribution was to guide that search with learned networks.
keyPoints: Hand-written evaluation functions for Go never reached strong play.
Monte Carlo rollouts estimate a position by the win rate of random games played from it.
MCTS repeats selection, expansion, simulation and backup.
UCT selects the child with the best average plus an exploration bonus that shrinks with visits.
The strongest programs before AlphaGo reached about five-dan amateur level.
Rollouts are noisy and need many simulations.

outline.title: Looking at the board: features and policy networks
outline.summary: A neural network cannot read a board directly. AlphaGo turns each position into a stack of 19 by 19 binary planes: where the black, white and empty stones are, how recently each move was played, how many liberties each group has, and so on. The paper lists 48 such planes. A convolutional network turns the planes into a probability for every point of the board. A final softmax makes the numbers positive and sum to one. Illegal moves are given probability zero by a mask before the numbers are renormalized. This chapter builds the encodings and the softmax in code. The training comes in the next chapters.
keyPoints: The policy network input is 48 binary 19 by 19 planes; the value network adds a plane for the player's colour.
Planes include stone colour (3), turns since a move was played (8), liberties (8), capture size (8), self-atari size (8), liberties after move (8), ladder capture and escape, and sensibleness.
The output is a probability for each of 361 points.
Softmax: p_i = exp(z_i) / sum_j exp(z_j).
Illegal moves are masked out and the rest renormalized.
In search, the paper uses a softmax temperature of 0.67 on the SL policy network for priors.

outline.title: Learning from experts: the SL policy network
outline.summary: The first training stage is plain supervised learning. Take positions from games played by strong humans on the KGS Go Server, and train the network to give high probability to the move the expert actually played. The training signal is the log likelihood of the human move: the weights are nudged in the direction that makes that move more probable. In the paper, a 13-layer network trained on 30 million positions predicted the expert move 57.0 percent of the time, against 44.4 percent for the previous best. The labs write the loss, its gradient and a full tiny training loop for a linear softmax model.
keyPoints: The SL policy network is trained to maximize the log likelihood of the human move.
Update: delta sigma is proportional to the gradient of log p_sigma(a | s) with respect to sigma.
For softmax outputs, the gradient of -log p_a with respect to the logits is p - onehot(a).
The paper: 13 layers, 30 million positions, 57.0 percent accuracy (55.7 percent from raw board and history only).
The earlier state of the art was 44.4 percent.
A stronger accuracy gave much stronger play, though the network was slower to evaluate.

outline.title: Speed: the rollout and tree policies
outline.summary: The deep network is slow: several milliseconds per position. A Monte Carlo rollout needs a move at every step of a game that may last 150 moves. So AlphaGo trains a second, much smaller policy for rollouts: a linear softmax over small pattern features. It picks a move in about 2 microseconds, about 1,500 times faster than the SL policy network, at the cost of accuracy: 24.2 percent against 57.0 percent. A similar linear policy, the tree policy, supplies provisional priors for new tree nodes until the network has finished evaluating them.
keyPoints: The rollout policy p_pi is a linear softmax of small pattern features.
It reached 24.2 percent accuracy and takes about 2 microseconds per action.
It ran about 1,000 simulations per second per CPU thread on an empty board.
The SL policy network takes about 3 ms, roughly 1,500 times slower.
The tree policy p_tau is similar to the rollout policy with more features.
Fast and weak is the right tool when you need millions of moves.

outline.title: Getting better: policy gradient self-play
outline.summary: Imitation copies the experts' moves; it does not directly optimize winning. The second stage fixes that. The RL policy network starts as a copy of the SL network and plays games against earlier versions of itself, adjusting its weights to win. The update is the policy gradient. After a game, every move played is made more likely if the game was won and less likely if it was lost: the weights move in the direction of the gradient of log p, multiplied by plus one or minus one. The result was strong. The RL policy network won more than 80 percent of games against the SL network, and 85 percent against Pachi with no search at all.
keyPoints: The RL network is initialized to the SL weights (rho = sigma).
It plays against randomly selected earlier iterations, to avoid overfitting to the current self.
Update: delta rho is proportional to (d log p_rho(a_t | s_t) / d rho) times z_t.
The reward is +1 for a win and -1 for a loss; zero for all other steps.
Training used 10,000 mini-batches of 128 games on 50 GPUs for a day.
The RL network beat the SL network over 80 percent of the time and Pachi 85 percent without search.

outline.title: Judging positions: the value network
outline.summary: The value network estimates the outcome of the game from a position: a single number between minus one and one. It is a deep network like the policy network, with one scalar output, and it takes an extra input plane saying whose turn it is. Training it needed care. Positions from a single game are strongly correlated, and early attempts that used all positions from human games memorized the games and failed on new ones. The fix was to generate 30 million positions, each from a different self-play game, and to regress them on the game outcomes. The result approached the accuracy of Monte Carlo rollouts with the RL policy, with about 15,000 times less computation.
keyPoints: v_theta(s) predicts the game outcome from position s.
Trained by regression with mean squared error on (s, z) pairs.
30 million positions, each from a separate self-play game of the RL network.
Training on KGS human games overfit: test error 0.37 against training error 0.19.
With the self-play data: training MSE 0.226 and test MSE 0.234.
One evaluation approaches the accuracy of RL-policy rollouts at about 15,000 times less compute.

outline.title: The search: policy and value inside MCTS
outline.summary: AlphaGo's search is Monte Carlo tree search with a twist: the networks guide it. Each edge of the tree stores a prior probability P from the SL policy network, a visit count N, and an average value Q. Selection picks the move with the highest Q plus a bonus u that is large for moves with a big prior and few visits. When a leaf is reached it is expanded, then evaluated two ways: by the value network, and by a fast rollout. The two are mixed with weight one half each. After the search the program plays the most visited move, not the one with the highest Q.
keyPoints: Selection: a_t = argmax over a of Q(s_t, a) + u(s_t, a).
u = c_puct * P * sqrt(sum_b N(s, b)) / (1 + N(s, a)) with c_puct = 5 in the paper.
Leaf value: V = (1 - lambda) v_theta + lambda z, with lambda = 0.5.
Backup: N += 1 and Q becomes the mean of all V in the subtree.
A leaf is expanded when its edge has been visited 40 times (threshold n_thr = 40).
At the end, play the most visited move; resign if the win estimate falls below 10 percent.

outline.title: Engineering and strength: hardware, Elo, scaling
outline.summary: Strength in Go is measured with the Elo rating: a difference of 400 points means the stronger side is expected to win about 91 percent of the time. The paper's table gives a single-machine AlphaGo about 2,890 and the distributed version about 3,140, against 1,929 for Crazy Stone. The distributed version used 1,202 CPUs and 176 GPUs in the match against Fan Hui. The paper also ran a tournament in which the single-machine version, with 48 CPUs and 8 GPUs, won 494 of its 495 games against other Go programs. The search ran asynchronously: many threads walk the tree at once, while the networks are evaluated on GPUs in a batch behind them.
keyPoints: Elo: expected score = 1 / (1 + 10^(-d/400)); 400 points is about 91 percent.
Single machine: 40 search threads, 48 CPUs, 8 GPUs, Elo about 2,890.
Distributed: 40 search threads, 1,202 CPUs, 176 GPUs, Elo about 3,140.
Against other programs the single machine won 494 of 495 games with 5 seconds per move.
Distributed AlphaGo beat the single-machine version 77 percent of the time.
Mixed evaluation beat value-only and rollout-only versions.

outline.title: Capstone: a miniature AlphaGo
outline.summary: This chapter puts the pieces together on tic-tac-toe, small enough to run in a lab. The prior comes from a hand-made rule instead of a policy network, the value network is a stub that always says zero, and the rollouts use a tiny random generator. Everything else follows the paper: PUCT selection with constant five, a leaf value mixing value and rollout, a sign flip in backup and the most-visited move at the end. It is a teaching miniature, not DeepMind's program. Its purpose is to show that the loop of chapter 9 is short to write. Build it in steps: result detection, prior, rollout, then the full search.
keyPoints: Selection uses Q + 5 * P * sqrt(sum N) / (1 + N).
A new leaf is evaluated as 0.5 * v + 0.5 * z with v = 0 here.
z is the outcome of a random rollout from the leaf's player-to-move view.
Values flip sign each level going up.
Terminal positions are scored exactly: -1 for the player to move who has lost, 0 for a draw.
The move with most visits is chosen.

outline.title: Matches, successors and criticism
outline.summary: The first AlphaGo, later called Fan, beat Fan Hui 5-0 in October 2015. A stronger version, Lee, beat Lee Sedol four games to one in March 2016. Lee won game four after a move, number 78, that the program had not anticipated. Master, an updated version, won 60 straight online games in late December 2016 and early January 2017, and in May 2017 beat Ke Jie 3-0. AlphaGo Zero then learned Go from self-play alone, without human games, and beat the Lee version 100-0. Critics pointed to the huge computing cost, the reliance on human data in the first versions, and the narrowness of Go as a test of intelligence.
keyPoints: October 2015: AlphaGo beat Fan Hui, a 2-dan professional, 5-0.
March 2016: AlphaGo beat Lee Sedol 4-1; all games ended by resignation; Chinese rules with 7.5 komi.
Lee won game four by resignation at move 180, his move 78 was unanticipated by the program.
Master won 60 online games without a loss and beat Ke Jie 3-0 in May 2017.
AlphaGo Zero beat the Lee version 100-0 and later versions without human data.
AlphaZero extended the Zero method to chess and shogi.

courses.title: AlphaZero
courses.subtitle: Self-play, tree search and learning without human knowledge
courses.author: Lilith Learning Lab
courses.description: A 12-chapter course on AlphaZero, the DeepMind algorithm that learns chess, shogi and Go from self-play with only the rules. Based on the AlphaZero preprint and Science paper by Silver and colleagues, the AlphaGo Zero Nature paper and reports on the matches and the debate that followed. Covers game search, Monte Carlo tree search, the policy and value network, PUCT, exploration noise and temperature, self-play data, the loss and training, differences from AlphaGo Zero, results and criticism, a working tic-tac-toe search and successors such as MuZero. Python labs run on the built-in MicroPython engine. The original program was never released; the capstone is a teaching miniature.

outline.title: What is AlphaZero?
outline.summary: AlphaZero is a reinforcement learning algorithm from DeepMind that learns board games from scratch. It starts from random play and is given nothing but the rules. It plays against itself, and in its first paper it reached superhuman strength in chess, shogi and Go. Its core is a loop. A neural network guides a Monte Carlo tree search. The search picks moves and plays games against itself. The finished games become training data that improve the network, which makes the next search better. The course builds every piece in small Python programs: game search, tree search, the network's outputs, the loss, the training loop and a tiny working search for tic-tac-toe.
keyPoints: AlphaZero is a general version of AlphaGo Zero.
It uses only the rules of the game: no opening books, no human games, no hand-written evaluation.
One network f(s) = (p, v) gives move probabilities and a value.
MCTS guided by the network chooses moves; the search results train the network.
The same algorithm and hyperparameters were used for chess, shogi and Go, except the exploration noise.
The program was never released; the papers describe the algorithm.

outline.title: Games, search and classical engines
outline.summary: The games AlphaZero plays are two-player, zero-sum, perfect-information games: players alternate, one's gain is the other's loss, and nothing is hidden. They can be drawn as a game tree whose root is the current position and whose edges are legal moves. Minimax searches the tree assuming both sides play best. Negamax is the same idea written with one function by flipping the sign at each level. Alpha-beta pruning skips branches that cannot change the result. Full trees are far too big for chess, so classical engines search to a limited depth and score the leaves with a handwritten evaluation function. Replacing that function with a learned one is the main idea AlphaZero builds on.
keyPoints: Perfect-information two-player zero-sum games can be searched as trees.
Negamax: value(s) = max over moves of -value(child); terminal win = +1 for the winner's side.
Alpha-beta gives the same value as minimax with fewer nodes if moves are well ordered.
Chess programs before AlphaZero used alpha-beta with handwritten evaluation and many tricks.
Shogi is harder than chess: bigger board and captured pieces can be dropped back.
Stockfish later adopted a small neural evaluation, so the contrast is no longer absolute.

outline.title: Monte Carlo tree search
outline.summary: Monte Carlo tree search grows a tree one simulation at a time. Each simulation walks down the tree choosing promising moves, adds a new node, evaluates it and passes the result back up. Over many simulations the statistics at the root point to the best move. The classic choice rule comes from multi-armed bandits: try moves with a high average reward, but also moves tried rarely. UCB1 adds an exploration bonus that shrinks as a move is visited more. Classic MCTS evaluates a new node by playing random moves to the end of the game. AlphaZero keeps the same four phases but replaces the random rollout with the network's value.
keyPoints: Four phases: selection, expansion, evaluation (or simulation), backup.
Each node stores visit counts and a mean value.
UCB1 score: mean + c * sqrt(ln(parent visits) / visits).
Unvisited moves are tried first.
Classic MCTS uses random rollouts; AlphaZero uses a learned value instead.
The root's visit counts are the output of the search.

outline.title: The policy and value network
outline.summary: AlphaZero's network takes a board position and returns two things: a probability for every possible move (the policy) and one number estimating the outcome (the value). One shared body of convolutional layers feeds two output heads. The policy is produced with a softmax over all moves, then illegal moves are zeroed out and the rest renormalized. For chess, moves are encoded as 73 planes of 8 by 8 squares: for each from-square, 56 queen-style moves, 8 knight moves and 9 underpromotions. Early in training the network knows nothing, so p is nearly uniform and v is near zero. Everything it later knows comes from self-play.
keyPoints: (p, v) = f_theta(s).
Softmax: p_i = exp(x_i) / sum_j exp(x_j).
Illegal moves are masked out and the policy renormalized.
Chess input: 119 planes of 8x8 (8 steps of piece history plus constant planes).
Chess output: 8 x 8 x 73 = 4,672 move slots.
Value target z is -1 for a loss, 0 for a draw, +1 for a win.

outline.title: MCTS guided by the network (PUCT)
outline.summary: Each edge of the search tree stores a visit count N, a total value W, a mean value Q equal to W over N, and a prior probability P from the network. Selection picks the edge with the largest Q plus U, where U is an exploration bonus proportional to the prior and shrinking with visits. When a simulation reaches a leaf, the network evaluates it. Its policy becomes the priors of the new edges and its value is backed up along the path, with the sign flipped at every level since the players alternate. No random rollout is used. After many simulations the root visit counts form a probability distribution over moves. That distribution is the search's answer, and it is also the training target for the policy.
keyPoints: Selection: a = argmax over moves of Q(s,a) + U(s,a).
U(s,a) = c * P(s,a) * sqrt(sum_b N(s,b)) / (1 + N(s,a)).
Leaf: (p, v) = f(s); store p as priors, back up v.
Backup: N += 1, W += v, Q = W / N, with the sign flipped at each level.
In the AlphaZero pseudocode c is c_init + log((1 + N + c_base) / c_base), with c_init = 1.25 and c_base = 19652.
Training used 800 simulations per move.

outline.title: Exploration: noise and temperature
outline.summary: If a program always plays its single best move, it may play the same game forever and learn nothing new. AlphaZero adds randomness in two places: noise on the root priors, and sampling the played move from the visit counts. The Dirichlet noise mixes a random probability vector into the network's priors at the root. Its concentration is scaled inversely to the typical number of legal moves: 0.3 for chess, 0.15 for shogi, 0.03 for Go. This was the only game-specific hyperparameter. Temperature controls how sharply the visit counts are turned into move probabilities. At temperature one, moves are chosen in proportion to visits. As it approaches zero, the most-visited move is always chosen.
keyPoints: Root prior with noise: P = (1 - eps) * p + eps * eta, eta ~ Dirichlet(alpha).
alpha is 0.3 (chess), 0.15 (shogi), 0.03 (Go): inversely related to move counts.
Move choice: pi(a) proportional to N(a)^(1/tau).
AlphaGo Zero: tau = 1 for the first 30 moves of a game, then tau near 0.
In evaluation matches the most-visited move is played.
Noise and temperature affect the move played, not the learning rule.

outline.title: Self-play and training data
outline.summary: A self-play game gives one training example per position played: the position s, the search probabilities pi that were used to choose the move, and the final outcome z of the game. The outcome is the same game result, but seen from the side of whoever was to move in that position. So if the first player wins, z is plus one for every position where the first player was to move and minus one for the others. A draw gives zero for all. Go has eightfold symmetry, which AlphaGo Zero used to multiply its data. Chess and shogi are not symmetric, so AlphaZero does not augment its data or transform positions during search.
keyPoints: Each position in a game yields (s_t, pi_t, z_t).
z_t = +1 if the player to move at t eventually wins, -1 if loses, 0 for a draw.
pi_t comes from the visit counts, not from the move actually played.
Games end by the rules of the game; Go also ends after 722 moves.
AlphaGo Zero used the symmetries of Go; AlphaZero does not augment data.
Positions are drawn from recent games to train the network.

outline.title: The loss function and training
outline.summary: The network is trained on the self-play records to make two predictions: the value v should match the game outcome z, and the policy p should match the search probabilities pi. A third term penalizes large weights. The loss is the sum of a squared error on the value, a cross-entropy between pi and p, and an L2 regularization term. It is minimized with mini-batch gradient descent on batches of positions. This works as policy iteration. The search improves on the raw policy, the network is trained to imitate the improved policy, and the improved network makes the next search stronger.
keyPoints: l = (z - v)^2 - pi . log p + c ||theta||^2.
The value target z is -1, 0 or +1.
The policy target pi is the MCTS visit distribution.
AlphaZero used mini-batches of 4,096 positions for 700 thousand steps.
The learning rate was 0.2, dropped to 0.02, then 0.002, then 0.0002.
Search = policy improvement; game outcome = policy evaluation.

outline.title: From AlphaGo Zero to AlphaZero
outline.summary: AlphaZero is described in its paper as a more generic version of AlphaGo Zero. It differs in several places. Gone is the evaluation step in which a newly trained network had to beat the best player by a 55 percent margin before it could generate self-play games. Instead a single network is updated continually and always generates the games. AlphaZero also optimizes the expected outcome including draws, uses no symmetry augmentation, and uses the same hyperparameters across games without per-game tuning, except for the exploration noise. The published training used thousands of first-generation TPUs for self-play and 64 second-generation TPUs for learning. The training lasted 9, 12 and 34 hours for chess, shogi and Go.
keyPoints: AlphaGo Zero: a new network must win by about 55 percent to replace the best player.
AlphaZero: one network, always the latest, generates self-play.
AlphaGo Zero estimated win probability; AlphaZero the expected outcome.
No symmetry augmentation or board transformation in AlphaZero.
No per-game hyperparameter tuning; only the Dirichlet noise scale differs.
Chess: 9 h, 44 million games; shogi: 12 h, 24 million; Go: 34 h, 21 million.

outline.title: Results, Elo and the debate
outline.summary: In the 2017 preprint AlphaZero played a 100-game match against Stockfish 8 and scored 28 wins, 72 draws and no losses. It also beat Elmo in shogi and a 3-day AlphaGo Zero in Go. The result was criticized for the settings: Stockfish had 64 threads and only 1 GB of hash memory, one minute per move, and no opening book or tablebases. The Science paper in 2018 reported a new 1000-game match under tournament-style conditions, 3 hours plus 15 seconds per move with 44 threads, 32 GB hash and tablebases, against a Stockfish 9 development version: 155 wins, 839 draws and 6 losses. AlphaZero ran on four TPUs and a 44-core CPU. Elo turns a match score into a rating difference. The 1000-game score of about 57 percent is around 52 Elo, a clear but not enormous edge, on very different hardware. Some experts judged that a later Stockfish version might have matched it.
keyPoints: 2017 chess match: +28 =72 -0 vs Stockfish 8, one minute per move.
2018 chess match: +155 =839 -6 vs Stockfish 9 dev, 3 hours + 15 s per move.
Shogi vs Elmo: 90 wins, 2 draws, 8 losses in the first paper's two 50-game sets.
Go: 60 to 40 over a 3-day AlphaGo Zero in two 50-game sets.
Positions per second: AlphaZero about 80,000 in chess; Stockfish about 70 million.
Elo difference = 400 log10(s / (1 - s)) for score s.

outline.title: Build a tiny AlphaZero search
outline.summary: The capstone is a working AlphaZero-style search for tic-tac-toe, with the network stubbed out: every legal move gets the same prior, and every non-terminal leaf has value zero. What remains is the machinery of the previous chapters: tree, PUCT selection, expansion, backup with sign flips and terminal results from the rules. Even with a know-nothing network, the search finds forced wins and blocks, because real results at terminal positions flow back up the tree. Visit counts concentrate on the right move. A trained network would supply better priors and values and make the search reach further for the same number of simulations.
keyPoints: Each node: legal moves, priors P (uniform), visit counts N, total values W.
Simulation: select by PUCT, recurse on the child, back up the negated value.
Unknown leaf: create its node, return value 0 (the stub network).
Finished game: win = +1 for the player who moved last, seen as -1 by the mover now.
Result: the list of root visit counts.
More simulations sharpen the counts.

outline.title: Successors, limits and open questions
outline.summary: AlphaZero was not released, but its papers were detailed enough for the community to rebuild it. Leela Zero followed AlphaGo Zero for Go and Leela Chess Zero followed AlphaZero for chess, both powered by volunteers who donate computing time for self-play. KataGo and others extended the idea. MuZero, also from DeepMind, drops the requirement that the rules are given: it learns a model of the environment and plans with it, so the same approach covers video games as well as board games. Gumbel variants of AlphaZero and MuZero change the search to guarantee policy improvement even with few simulations. The limits are real. AlphaZero needs a perfect and fast simulator of the game rules, perfect information, and a lot of compute. The strongest-claims about generality refer to this class of games.
keyPoints: Leela Zero (Go, from 2017) and Leela Chess Zero (chess, from 2018) reproduced the methods with volunteer compute.
By 2020 Lc0 had reached the strength of AlphaZero's published results, according to a University of Alberta paper.
MuZero does not need the rules; AlphaZero does.
Later research showed AlphaZero does not guarantee policy improvement without evaluating all root actions.
AlphaZero covers perfect-information, two-player, zero-sum games with a known simulator.
The original program and training code were never published.

courses.title: Art Theory
courses.subtitle: Elements, colour, composition, perspective, light and a tour of movements, with Python labs and two interactive tools
courses.author: Lilith Learning Lab
courses.description: A beginner-friendly course in art theory: the elements of art and principles of design, colour basics and harmonies, composition with the rule of thirds and the golden ratio, perspective and depth, light and shadow, and a quick tour of art movements from the Renaissance to the present. Python labs turn colour, composition and perspective into numbers, and two interactive tools let you pick colour harmonies and try composition grids.

outline.title: Learning to see: what art theory is for
outline.summary: Art theory gives names to what you see and a way to talk about why a picture works. It does not tell you what to make, but it gives you tools to choose with. Most theory splits into elements, the building blocks (line, shape, form, space, value, texture, colour), and principles, the ways to arrange them (balance, contrast, emphasis, rhythm, unity). The best way to learn is to look closely, name what you see, and try small studies.
keyPoints: Elements are the ingredients; principles are the recipe.
Describe before you judge.
Compare works to see choices.
Small studies beat big plans.
Rules are tools, not laws.

outline.title: The elements of art
outline.summary: Line is a mark between two points; it can be straight, curved, thick, thin, actual or implied. Shape is a flat area enclosed by a line or a colour change. Form is a shape with depth. Space is the area around and inside things, both positive (the subject) and negative (the empty area). Value is how light or dark something is. Texture is the feel of a surface, real or drawn. Colour is the seventh element and has its own chapters. Each element can be used in a drawing to build mood and meaning.
keyPoints: Line: straight, curved, thick, thin, implied.
Shape is 2D; form is 3D.
Negative space shapes the subject.
Value: white to black in steps.
Texture can be real or implied.

outline.title: Colour basics
outline.summary: Every colour has three properties: hue (which colour it is), saturation (how vivid) and value (how light). Changing one gives a tint, shade or tone of the same hue. The traditional primaries are red, yellow and blue. Mixing two gives a secondary (orange, green, violet), and mixing a primary with a neighbouring secondary gives a tertiary. Screens use red, green and blue light; printers use cyan, magenta, yellow and black ink. Warm colours (reds, oranges, yellows) seem to come forward, and cool colours (blues, greens) seem to recede.
keyPoints: Hue, saturation, value.
Tint = + white. Shade = + black. Tone = + grey.
Primaries: RYB (paint), RGB (light), CMY (ink).
Warm advances; cool recedes.
Opposites on the wheel are complementary.

outline.title: Colour harmony and palettes
outline.summary: Colour harmonies are ways of picking colours that sit well together, found by distances on the colour wheel. Complementary uses opposites, analogous uses neighbours, triadic uses three evenly spaced, and split-complementary uses one hue and the two next to its opposite. A palette is a limited set of colours for one work. Limiting the palette gives unity. Contrast matters too: colours with similar values read poorly together, even if the hues contrast.
keyPoints: Complementary: hue + 180 degrees.
Analogous: hue +/- 30 degrees.
Triadic: hue + 120 and + 240.
60-30-10: dominant, secondary, accent.
Value contrast matters more than hue contrast for legibility.

outline.title: Principles of design
outline.summary: The principles of design are ways of organising the elements. Balance spreads visual weight. Contrast sets differences against each other. Emphasis creates a focal point. Movement leads the eye. Rhythm and pattern repeat things. Proportion relates sizes. Unity makes it all feel like one piece. Balance can be symmetrical (mirror-like), asymmetrical (different things of equal weight) or radial (around a centre). Good design balances unity with variety: enough sameness to feel whole, enough difference to stay interesting.
keyPoints: Balance: symmetrical, asymmetrical, radial.
Emphasis: one thing should lead.
Movement follows lines, edges and gaze.
Rhythm: regular, random, flowing, progressive.
Unity with variety.

outline.title: Composition: arranging the picture
outline.summary: Composition is how you place things inside the frame. A simple guide is the rule of thirds: divide the frame into a three by three grid, and place the subject on a line or where two lines meet. The golden ratio, about 1.618, is another old guide. Dividing a length in golden proportion puts the dividing point about 0.618 of the way along. Leading lines, framing and negative space help guide the eye. None of these are laws. They give a starting point and a reason, and good work often bends them.
keyPoints: Thirds: lines at 1/3 and 2/3 across and down.
Golden section: 0.618 of the length.
Leading lines lead to the focal point.
Centred = stable; off-centre = dynamic.
Give a moving subject space to move into.

outline.title: Perspective and space
outline.summary: Perspective is the art of showing three-dimensional space on a flat surface. The horizon line is your eye level. Parallel lines that go away from you seem to meet at a vanishing point on the horizon. One-point perspective has a single vanishing point, as when looking straight down a road. Two-point perspective shows a building corner, with two vanishing points. Without lines, depth also comes from overlap, size, position and atmospheric perspective, where far things become lighter, bluer and less sharp.
keyPoints: Horizon = your eye level.
Parallel lines meet at a vanishing point.
One-point: straight-on. Two-point: corner view.
Far objects: smaller, higher, lighter, bluer.
Overlap shows what is in front.

outline.title: Light, shadow and value
outline.summary: Light is what lets us see form. On a rounded object lit from one side, the surface goes from highlight through light and halftone to a core shadow, then a touch of reflected light at the edge, and finally a cast shadow on the ground. A value scale of five to nine steps from white to black helps judge values. Most strong drawings simplify the many values they see into three or four main groups. Chiaroscuro, light and dark contrast, was used by painters such as Caravaggio and Rembrandt to give drama and depth.
keyPoints: Order on a sphere: highlight, light, halftone, core shadow, reflected light.
Cast shadow is darkest near the object.
Light direction decides every value.
Simplify to 3 or 4 value groups.
Squint to see the big pattern.

outline.title: Art movements: a quick tour
outline.summary: Art movements are groups of artists who shared ideas in a time and place. Knowing the main ones shows how the elements and principles have been used differently. The Renaissance perfected perspective and anatomy. The Baroque added drama with light. Impressionism painted fleeting light and colour. Cubism showed objects from many viewpoints, and abstract art dropped the subject altogether. A timeline is a map. Place each artist or movement on it, and you start to see how one idea led to the next.
keyPoints: Renaissance: perspective, proportion, realism.
Baroque: drama, movement, chiaroscuro.
Impressionism: light, colour, outdoors.
Cubism: many viewpoints, flattened space.
Abstract: form and colour for their own sake.

outline.title: Critique and a practice routine
outline.summary: Skill grows by looking carefully and making many small studies. A daily routine of ten to twenty minutes beats an occasional long session. Before a large piece, make several small thumbnail sketches to try different compositions quickly. Use reference, and then change it to make it your own. Finish by looking at your own work as a critic. Describe, analyse, interpret, judge, and then pick one thing to try next.
keyPoints: Ten minutes a day beats once a month.
Thumbnails first, big piece after.
One skill per study.
Copy to learn, then create.
Keep dated work to see progress.

courses.title: Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach, Condensed
courses.subtitle: Agents, search, logic, probability, learning and more, with Python labs
courses.author: Lilith Learning Lab
courses.description: A condensed course based on the structure of Russell and Norvig's Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach (4th edition), written in original words: rational agents, search and games, constraint satisfaction, logic and planning, probability and Bayesian networks, temporal models, decisions and MDPs, game theory, machine learning, neural networks and reinforcement learning, and applications and ethics. Theory plus Python labs.

outline.title: What AI is: rational agents
outline.summary: Artificial intelligence is the study of building agents: things that perceive an environment and act in it. This course follows the structure of the textbook Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach by Russell and Norvig, condensed and re-explained in original words. The central idea is the rational agent. It picks the action that is expected to give the best score on a performance measure, given what it has perceived so far. Rationality is not perfection. The agent cannot know what it could not perceive. It is judged on expected, not lucky, outcomes.
keyPoints: An agent maps percept sequences to actions.
Rational means best expected performance, not omniscient.
Describe a task with PEAS before designing the agent.
Environments differ: observable or not, deterministic or not, episodic or sequential, static or dynamic.
Agent types: simple reflex, model-based, goal-based, utility-based, learning.
The standard model: optimise a fixed objective. Its danger is a wrong objective.

outline.title: Solving problems by search
outline.summary: A problem-solving agent looks ahead. It models the world as states and actions, then searches for a sequence of actions leading to a goal. Uninformed methods use only the problem definition: breadth-first, uniform-cost, depth-first and iterative deepening. Informed methods use a heuristic estimate of the remaining cost. A star search combines the cost so far with that estimate and is optimal when the estimate never overestimates. The labs write breadth-first search and A star on a small graph.
keyPoints: Define a problem by initial state, actions, transition model, goal test and path cost.
BFS is complete and finds the fewest steps, but uses O(b^d) memory.
Uniform-cost search expands the cheapest frontier node first.
Depth-first uses little memory but may not find the best path.
A* orders by f = g + h; optimal if h is admissible (and consistent for graph search).
Heuristics come from relaxed problems.

outline.title: Beyond classical search: local search and games
outline.summary: Some problems have no meaningful path, only a good final state. Local search keeps a single state and improves it step by step. Hill climbing can get stuck on a local maximum; random restarts and simulated annealing help. In two-player games, minimax chooses the move that is best assuming the opponent also plays best. Alpha-beta pruning skips branches that cannot change the decision. Monte Carlo tree search, used in Go programs, chooses moves by many random playouts. The labs compute a minimax value and a hill climb.
keyPoints: Local search uses little memory and suits optimisation.
Hill climbing: local maxima, ridges and plateaus.
Simulated annealing accepts a worse move with probability exp(delta/T).
Minimax value: max at our turns, min at the opponent's.
Alpha-beta can double the reachable depth with good move ordering.
MCTS balances exploring and exploiting with random rollouts.

outline.title: Constraint satisfaction
outline.summary: A constraint satisfaction problem, or CSP, is defined by variables, the values each may take, and constraints on which combinations are allowed. Map colouring, scheduling and Sudoku are classic examples. Because constraints expose structure, a CSP solver can do much better than blind search. Backtracking assigns variables one at a time and undoes a choice when a constraint fails. Propagation, such as forward checking and arc consistency, removes impossible values early. The labs write a constraint check and a backtracking colour solver.
keyPoints: CSP = variables + domains + constraints.
Backtracking is depth-first search over partial assignments.
Forward checking removes values that a new assignment rules out.
Arc consistency propagates constraints between variable pairs.
Order heuristics: MRV, degree, least-constraining value.
A tree-shaped constraint graph can be solved in linear time.

outline.title: Logical agents: propositional logic
outline.summary: A knowledge-based agent keeps sentences in a knowledge base and uses inference to decide what to do. Propositional logic has symbols that are true or false, combined with not, and, or, implies and if and only if. A sentence is entailed by the knowledge base if it is true in every model where the knowledge base is true. Inference algorithms are sound if they derive only entailed sentences and complete if they derive all of them. Resolution is sound and complete for propositional logic. The labs evaluate sentences and test entailment by enumerating models.
keyPoints: Syntax defines sentences; semantics defines their truth in a model.
Entailment: KB entails a iff KB and not a is unsatisfiable.
Model checking is exponential in the number of symbols.
Resolution proves entailment by deriving the empty clause.
Horn clauses admit forward and backward chaining in linear time.
Modern SAT solvers handle millions of clauses (DPLL, clause learning).

outline.title: First-order logic and inference
outline.summary: Propositional logic cannot say that all humans are mortal without listing every human. First-order logic adds objects, relations, functions and quantifiers, so general facts are stated once. Inference uses unification: finding a substitution that makes two expressions identical. With unification, rules can be chained forward or backward, and resolution works on clauses with variables. The labs write a small unifier and a term matcher.
keyPoints: Use implies with for-all and and with there-exists.
Not-for-all x P is the same as there-exists x not P.
Unification finds the most general substitution.
The occur check stops a variable from binding to a term containing it.
FOL entailment is semi-decidable.
Prolog uses backward chaining on Horn clauses.

outline.title: Planning and knowledge representation
outline.summary: Classical planning finds a sequence of actions that turns an initial state into a goal in a deterministic, fully observable world. States are sets of facts. Each action has preconditions and effects that add and delete facts. A planner can search forward from the start, backward from the goal, or use heuristics from relaxed problems. Hierarchical task networks plan with high-level tasks refined into primitive steps, and are the practical choice in many applications. Knowledge representation organises the world into categories with inheritance, and supports default reasoning that can be withdrawn.
keyPoints: A planning problem = initial state, actions, goal.
An action applies if its preconditions are a subset of the state.
Applying: remove the delete list, add the add list.
Forward search is simple; heuristics make it practical.
The delete-relaxation ignores deletions to estimate distance.
Nonmonotonic reasoning lets conclusions be withdrawn.

outline.title: Uncertainty: probability and Bayes' rule
outline.summary: An agent rarely knows the whole truth. Probability theory gives it a language for degrees of belief. Combined with utility it yields decision theory. From a full joint distribution any query can be answered by summing matching entries and dividing. Bayes' rule reverses a conditional: it turns the chance of symptoms given a disease into the chance of the disease given symptoms. The labs compute posteriors and a naive Bayes score.
keyPoints: Probabilities lie in 0..1 and sum to 1 over possible worlds.
P(a or b) = P(a) + P(b) - P(a and b).
Bayes: P(h | e) = P(e | h) P(h) / P(e).
Ignoring the base rate causes many errors.
Full joint tables grow as 2^n.
Naive Bayes: P(cause, e1..en) = P(cause) times the product of P(ei | cause).

outline.title: Bayesian networks
outline.summary: A Bayesian network shows how variables depend on one another. Each node is a variable with a table giving its probability conditioned on its parents. The network represents the full joint compactly as a product of those local tables. To answer a query, sum over the hidden variables. Variable elimination does this efficiently. For networks that are too large, sampling methods approximate the answer. The labs compute a joint probability and answer a query by enumeration.
keyPoints: The joint is the product of P(X | parents(X)).
A network with n Boolean nodes and at most k parents needs n times 2^k numbers.
Enumeration sums the joint over hidden variables.
A node is independent of non-descendants given its parents.
Exact inference is hard in general; easy on trees.
Likelihood weighting and Gibbs sampling approximate.

outline.title: Reasoning over time
outline.summary: Worlds change, and an agent must track hidden state over time from noisy observations. Temporal models assume the state depends on a bounded past (the Markov assumption) and each observation depends only on the current state. Filtering computes the belief about the present from all evidence so far, and can be updated recursively in constant time per step. Hidden Markov models, Kalman filters and particle filters are the main tools. The labs write one step of a prediction and a filtering update.
keyPoints: Markov assumption: the present depends on a bounded past.
Sensor assumption: observation depends on the current state only.
Filtering update: predict, then weight by the evidence, then normalise.
Smoothing uses future evidence to improve past estimates.
Kalman filters: linear dynamics with Gaussian noise.
Particle filters: propagate, weight, resample.

outline.title: Making decisions: utility and MDPs
outline.summary: A rational agent chooses the action with the highest expected utility: the sum over outcomes of probability times utility. Utility of money is usually concave, which explains risk aversion. When decisions come in sequence, we use a Markov decision process: states, actions, a transition model and rewards. The solution is a policy that gives an action for each state. Value iteration computes it by repeatedly applying the Bellman update. The labs write expected utility and value iteration.
keyPoints: Maximise expected utility.
A concave utility of money means risk aversion.
A policy, not a plan, is the solution when outcomes are uncertain.
Value iteration repeats the Bellman update until values settle.
Policy iteration alternates evaluating and improving a policy.
A POMDP is an MDP with hidden state: plan over belief states.

outline.title: Multiple agents and game theory
outline.summary: When several agents act, each one's best choice depends on the others. Game theory studies this. A Nash equilibrium is a set of strategies where no player gains by changing alone. The prisoner's dilemma shows that individually rational choices can leave everyone worse off. Mechanism design flips the question: choose the rules so that self-interested agents produce a good result. A Vickrey auction makes honest bidding the best strategy. The labs find equilibria and run an auction.
keyPoints: Normal form: a table of payoffs.
Dominant strategies are the simplest solution.
Not every game has a pure Nash equilibrium; mixed strategies always exist.
In the prisoner's dilemma defection is dominant, yet cooperation pays more.
Vickrey: bidding your true value is dominant.
Social choice: Arrow's theorem limits fair voting.

outline.title: Learning from examples
outline.summary: Learning lets an agent improve from data. In supervised learning the data are input-output pairs and the aim is a function that predicts well on new inputs. The main danger is overfitting: a model that fits noise in the training data. Decision trees split on the attribute with the highest information gain. Linear models fit a line or plane by minimising squared error, using a formula or gradient descent. Nearest neighbours predict from the closest examples. Ensembles such as random forests combine many models. The labs compute entropy, nearest neighbours and a gradient step.
keyPoints: Hold out data to measure generalisation.
Bias-variance trade-off: simple models underfit, complex ones overfit.
Entropy H = minus the sum of p log2 p.
Decision trees choose the split with the largest information gain.
Linear regression: minimise squared error; gradient descent updates w by minus alpha times the gradient.
Bagging averages models; boosting trains them in sequence.

outline.title: Neural networks and reinforcement learning
outline.summary: Neural networks stack layers of simple units. Each unit takes a weighted sum of its inputs and applies a nonlinearity such as ReLU. Back-propagation applies the chain rule backward to get the gradient of the loss for every weight. Convolutional networks suit images, sharing small filters across positions. Transformers use attention and power modern language models. Reinforcement learning learns from rewards, not labelled answers: Q-learning estimates the value of each action in each state by temporal-difference updates. The labs write a small forward pass, a softmax and a Q-learning update.
keyPoints: A unit: output = activation(w . x + b).
Without nonlinear activations, many layers collapse into one linear map.
Training: forward pass, loss, back-propagation, weight update.
Regularisers: dropout, weight decay, data augmentation.
Q-learning: Q(s,a) += alpha (r + gamma max Q(s',a') - Q(s,a)).
Explore with epsilon-greedy; exploit by taking the best known action.

outline.title: Language, perception, robots and the future of AI
outline.summary: Natural language processing starts with language models: probability distributions over word sequences. Simple n-gram models count short sequences. Neural models trained on huge text collections now generate fluent text, though they can still state falsehoods confidently. Computer vision recovers scene properties from images, using edges, motion, stereo and, above all, deep networks for recognition. Robots perceive, plan in a space of joint configurations, and control motors with feedback. AI also raises questions about fairness, privacy, safety and control. The textbook's closing view is that machines should be uncertain about human preferences, so they stay open to correction.
keyPoints: Smoothing stops unseen n-grams getting zero probability.
Parsing assigns a grammatical structure; ambiguity is the main difficulty.
Image classification, detection and segmentation use convolutional or transformer networks.
Depth from stereo = focal length times baseline divided by disparity.
Motion planning in configuration space; controllers such as PID close the loop.
Fairness definitions can conflict when base rates differ.

courses.title: Bible Languages: Biblical Hebrew, Koine Greek and Latin
courses.subtitle: Alphabets, grammar, core vocabulary, everyday phrases and how to translate between the three, with flashcards and an interlinear reader
courses.author: Lilith Learning Lab
courses.description: A beginner-friendly course in the three languages of the Bible. Learn the Hebrew alphabet and vowels, the Greek alphabet and cases, and Latin nouns and verbs; build a core vocabulary of 45 words and 16 phrases side by side with memory hooks; read thirteen parallel passages with an interlinear reader; and practise translating between the languages with spaced-repetition flashcards and Python labs.

outline.title: Three languages, one library
outline.summary: The Bible was written mostly in Hebrew, with a little Aramaic, and the New Testament in Koine Greek. Early Greek and Latin translations, the Septuagint and the Vulgate, shaped the church for a thousand years and still hold many of its words. The three languages work differently. Hebrew builds words from three-letter roots and reads right to left. Greek and Latin both use endings (cases) to show who does what to whom, so word order is flexible. This course teaches the alphabets and sounds, the grammar, the core vocabulary side by side, common phrases, and how to translate between the three, with memory tools in every chapter.
keyPoints: Hebrew: right to left, consonants first, roots of three letters.
Greek: 24 letters, five cases, three genders, flexible word order.
Latin: no alphabet to learn, six cases, no articles, verb at the end.
A Greek or Latin ending tells you the job of the word; Hebrew uses small words and word order.
You learn fastest by short daily sessions, not long rare ones.
Link every new word to something you know: an English word, a picture or a story.

outline.title: Hebrew: the alphabet
outline.summary: Hebrew has 22 letters, all of them consonants, written and read from right to left. Five letters change shape at the end of a word. Letters double as numbers, so every word has a numeric value, called gematria. A few letters sound alike (tet (ט) and tav (ת), kaf (כ) and qof (ק)). Learning each one with a picture-name and a sound makes them stick. The labs match letters to sounds and compute gematria in Python.
keyPoints: 22 letters, no capitals, read right to left.
Final forms: kaf ך, mem ם, nun ן, pe ף, tsade ץ.
Alef (א) and ayin (ע) are silent carriers of a vowel; chet (ח) is a rough h.
Vav ו and yod י can be vowel letters as well as consonants.
Values: alef (א) 1 to yod (י) 10, then 20, 30 ... 90, then 100 to 400 (qof (ק), resh (ר), shin (ש), tav (ת)).

outline.title: Hebrew: vowels and reading
outline.summary: Early Hebrew wrote only consonants. Later scribes added little dots and dashes, the niqqud (נִקּוּד), to show vowels. With them a beginner can read any word aloud. There are five vowel sounds in several shapes, plus the half-vowel shva (◌ְ) and the dot called dagesh (◌ּ). Every syllable has exactly one vowel. The labs match vowel signs to sounds and ask you to read real words.
keyPoints: Vowel signs sit below, above or inside the consonant.
ַ patach (◌ַ) and ָ kamets (◌ָ) sound like ah; ֵ tsere (◌ֵ) and ֶ segol (◌ֶ) like eh.
ִ hiriq (◌ִ) is ee, ֹ holam (◌ֹ) is oh, ֻ kubbuts (◌ֻ) and וּ shureq (וּ) are oo.
ְ shva (◌ְ) at the start of a word is a quick e; between syllables it is silent.
Most words are stressed on the last syllable.

outline.title: Hebrew grammar: nouns, articles and sentences
outline.summary: Hebrew nouns are masculine or feminine and singular, plural or dual. The plural usually ends in -im for masculine and -ot for feminine, and pairs of things use the dual -ayim. There is one article, ha- (הַ), meaning 'the'. There is no word for 'a'. The verb 'is' is usually left out: 'The man good' means 'the man is good'. Two nouns joined together, as in 'house of the king', form a construct chain. Small words are attached to the front: ve- (וְ) and, be- (בְּ) in, le- (לְ) to or for, min (מִן) from. Pronouns can attach to the end: -i my, -kha your, -o his.
keyPoints: Masculine plural -im: melekh (מֶלֶךְ), melakhim (מְלָכִים) (kings).
Feminine often ends in -ah; plural -ot: torah (תּוֹרָה), torot (תּוֹרוֹת).
Dual -ayim: yad hand, yadayim (יָדַיִם) two hands; mayim (מַיִם), shamayim (שָׁמַיִם).
Definite: ha- (הַ) plus the noun, ha-melekh (הַמֶּלֶךְ) = the king. No word for 'a'.
Present 'is' is not written: ha-ish tov (הָאִישׁ טוֹב) means the man is good.
Construct: bet melekh (בֵּית מֶלֶךְ) = house of a king; devar adonai (דְּבַר יְהוָה) = word of the LORD.

outline.title: Hebrew grammar: verbs, roots and pronouns
outline.summary: Hebrew verbs are built on roots of three consonants. Vowel patterns and prefixes turn the root into a tense or a stem. The two basic tenses are the perfect (completed) and the imperfect (incomplete). Seven stems, called binyanim, give the basic, intensive, causative and reflexive meanings of the same root. Pronoun endings attach to nouns (my, your) and to prepositions. The lab builds the perfect paradigm from a root in Python.
keyPoints: Root k-t-v: katav (כָּתַב) wrote, ktav (כְּתָב) writing, mikhtav (מִכְתָּב) letter, sofer (סוֹפֵר) scribe.
Perfect suffixes: -ti I, -ta you (m), - he, -ah she, -nu we, -u they.
Imperfect prefixes: e- I, ti- you, yi- he, ni- we.
Seven binyanim: Qal, Niphal, Piel, Pual, Hiphil, Hophal, Hitpael.
Vayomer (וַיֹּאמֶר) = and he said: vav plus imperfect tells a story in sequence.
Pronouns: ani (אֲנִי) I, atah (אַתָּה) you, hu he, hi she, anachnu (אֲנַחְנוּ) we, hem they.

outline.title: Greek: the alphabet and sounds
outline.summary: Greek has 24 letters, each with a capital and a small form, and it reads left to right. You already know many of them from mathematics: alpha (Α α), beta (Β β), pi (Π π), sigma (Σ σ ς), omega (Ω ω). Words that begin with a vowel carry a breathing mark: smooth (no h) or rough (an h sound). Marks above the word show stress and are learned with each word. Diphthongs like ou and ai give single sounds. The labs match letters and compute isopsephy, the Greek counterpart of gematria.
keyPoints: 24 letters: alpha (Α α) to omega (Ω ω), left to right.
Final sigma ς appears only at the end of a word.
Rough breathing ῾ means an h before the vowel; smooth ᾿ means none.
Diphthongs: ai, ei, oi, au, eu, ou.
Gamma (Γ γ) before gamma, kappa (Κ κ), xi (Ξ ξ) or chi (Χ χ) sounds like n: aggelos is angelos.
Every word of two or more syllables carries an accent.

outline.title: Greek grammar: nouns, articles and cases
outline.summary: Greek nouns have gender (masculine, feminine, neuter), number and one of five cases. The case, not the position, shows the role: nominative for the subject, accusative for the object, genitive for 'of', dative for 'to or for' and vocative for calling out. The article (the) changes with the noun, and it agrees in gender, number and case. Prepositions take certain cases, and the case changes the meaning. The labs match case to function and build the endings of a typical noun.
keyPoints: Five cases: nominative, genitive, dative, accusative, vocative.
Article (nominative): ho (ὁ) masculine, he feminine, to neuter; ton (τόν), ten, to in the accusative.
Second declension masculine: logos (λόγος), logou (λόγου), logo (λόγῳ), logon (λόγον).
First declension feminine: agape (ἀγάπη), agapes (ἀγάπης), agape, agapen (ἀγάπην).
Plural nominative: logoi (λόγοι), agapai (ἀγάπαι).
Word order is flexible because endings show roles.

outline.title: Greek grammar: verbs
outline.summary: A Greek verb shows tense, voice, mood, person and number. Tense in Greek is as much about the kind of action (ongoing, simple, completed) as about time. The regular present active has endings -ō, -eis, -ei, -omen, -ete, -ousi. Past tenses add an augment (e-) at the front. Voice can be active, middle or passive. The verb 'to be' is irregular. The lab conjugates the present of regular verbs.
keyPoints: Present active of luo (λύω): luo, lueis (λύεις), luei (λύει), luomen (λύομεν), luete (λύετε), luousi (λύουσι).
Imperfect: eluon (ἔλυον), ongoing past; aorist: eluse (ἔλυσε), simple past.
Future: luso (λύσω); perfect: leluka, a past act with present result.
Voices: active, middle, passive. Moods: indicative, subjunctive, optative, imperative.
Eimi (εἰμί), to be: eimi, ei, esti (ἐστί), esmen (ἐσμέν), este (ἐστέ), eisi (εἰσί).
The verb form shows the person, so the subject pronoun is often left out.

outline.title: Latin: sounds, nouns and cases
outline.summary: Latin uses the same letters as English, so you can start reading at once. The Church pronounces them softly (ci as chi) and the classical way is harder (ci as ki); this course uses the Church reading. Latin has no word for 'the' or 'a'. Nouns have gender and number and six cases: nominative, genitive, dative, accusative, ablative and vocative. Five declensions group the nouns by their endings. Adjectives agree with their noun in gender, number and case. The verb tends to come last. The labs decline the first declension and match cases to their functions.
keyPoints: Church sounds: c before e or i is 'ch'; ae and oe are 'e'; gn is 'ny'; j and i are 'y'.
No articles: puella means girl, a girl or the girl.
Six cases: nom, gen, dat, acc, abl, voc.
First declension (puella): -a -ae -ae -am -a; plural -ae -arum -is -as -is.
Second declension (dominus): -us -i -o -um -o; voc -e.
Stress: the next-to-last syllable if it is long or closed, otherwise the one before it.

outline.title: Latin grammar: verbs
outline.summary: Latin verbs belong to four conjugations, told apart by the vowel before -re in the infinitive: amare, monere, regere, audire. Personal endings -o, -s, -t, -mus, -tis, -nt show the person, so the pronoun is not needed. Each verb is listed with four principal parts from which every form can be built. The tenses include the present, imperfect, future and perfect. The verb sum, to be, is irregular and common. The lab conjugates a first-conjugation verb in Python.
keyPoints: Present of amo: amo, amas, amat, amamus, amatis, amant.
Four conjugations: amare, monere, regere, audire.
Sum: sum, es, est, sumus, estis, sunt; imperfect eram, erat; perfect fui.
Perfect endings: -i, -isti, -it, -imus, -istis, -erunt.
Principal parts of amo: amo, amare, amavi, amatum.
Imperative: ama! (love!), audi! (hear!).

outline.title: Comparing the three: pronouns, numbers and 'to be'
outline.summary: The same ideas are expressed in different ways in the three languages. This chapter lays them side by side: pronouns, numbers 1 to 10, the verb 'to be', questions and negatives. Hebrew has one article and no case endings, Greek has an article and five cases, and Latin has no article and six cases. Seeing the contrasts makes each language easier to remember. The labs ask you to match the same word across the three languages.
keyPoints: I: ani (אֲנִי), ego (ἐγώ), ego; you: atah (אַתָּה), su, tu; we: anachnu (אֲנַחְנוּ), hemeis (ἡμεῖς), nos.
To be: Hebrew leaves it out in the present, Greek eimi (εἰμί), Latin sum.
No/not: lo, ou(k) or me, non.
Question words: who mi, tis, quis; what mah, ti, quid; where eifo (אֵיפֹה), pou, ubi.
Numbers 1 to 10 side by side are below.
An article tells definiteness; Latin relies on context.

outline.title: Core vocabulary I: nouns in three languages
outline.summary: Thirty common nouns, each in Hebrew, Greek and Latin, with a memory hook. Many of them became English words through Greek and Latin, which makes them easy to remember. The flashcard lab uses Leitner boxes: you move up a box when you know a card and back to box 1 when you miss it. You can choose any direction, such as English to Hebrew or Greek to Latin, so that you can translate between the languages directly. Three matching labs drill the words in groups.
keyPoints: Learn 5 words at a time and revisit them tomorrow.
Say each word aloud with its English hook.
Greek and Latin give English hundreds of words; Hebrew gives shalom (שָׁלוֹם), amen, sabbath.
Reverse the direction once you know a card.
Review every day, a little, instead of once a week for a long time.

outline.title: Core vocabulary II: verbs and adjectives
