outline.summary: Fifteen of the most frequent verbs and adjectives in the Bible, in all three languages: say, see, hear, go, come, give, know, be, do, write, love, live, good, great and one. Verbs change form: in Hebrew by root and pattern, in Greek and Latin by ending. We list the dictionary form of each (Hebrew past he-form, Greek 'I' form, Latin 'I' form) and drill them with flashcards. The lab matches verbs across the languages and uses the cards.
keyPoints: Hebrew lists a verb by its 3rd masculine singular perfect: amar, he said.
Greek and Latin list the 'I' form: lego, dico; Latin also gives the infinitive.
Frequent verbs are often irregular: sum, eo, do, facio.
Good and great are adjectives and agree with their nouns.
Learn a verb with a sample phrase: audi, Israel; ho theos agape estin (ὁ θεὸς ἀγάπη ἐστίν).

outline.title: Conversational phrases
outline.summary: Sixteen useful phrases: greetings, thanks, yes and no, asking a name, asking where, and a few blessings. Each is given in Hebrew, Greek and Latin so you can say it in whichever language you like. Most of these phrases are formed from the vocabulary and grammar you have seen. Hebrew and Greek greetings were wishes of peace and joy. Latin greetings wish health. The flashcard lab includes a Phrases deck. Go through it in both directions.
keyPoints: Shalom (שָׁלוֹם), chaire (χαῖρε), salve open a conversation.
Shalom (שָׁלוֹם) aleichem, eirene (εἰρήνη) hymin, pax vobis: peace be with you.
Toda (תּוֹדָה), eucharisto (εὐχαριστῶ), gratias: thank you.
Mah shimkha, ti onoma (ὄνομα) soi, quod nomen tibi est: what is your name?
Te amo, agapo se (ἀγαπῶ σε), ani (אֲנִי) ohev otkha: I love you.
Barukh elohim (אֱלֹהִים), eulogetos ho (ὁ) theos (θεός), benedictus Deus: blessed be God.

outline.title: Reading with an interlinear
outline.summary: An interlinear shows the original word, its sound, and a gloss, one under the other. It lets you read real verses before you know the whole grammar. The reader lab holds thirteen passages: Genesis 1:1 in Hebrew, Greek and Latin, John 1:1 in Greek and Latin, Genesis 1:3, the Shema, Psalm 23:1, 1 John 4:8 and the Pater (πατήρ) Noster. Tap a word to see its sound and meaning, then show the smooth translation and the grammar notes. You learn the most by comparing: the same verse in three languages.
keyPoints: Read the original aloud before you look at the gloss.
Tap each word: sound, then meaning.
Find the verb first, then the subject, then the object.
Compare the same verse in two languages.
Parse the endings you know: case for nouns, person for verbs.

outline.title: Translating and remembering
outline.summary: A reliable method for translating a sentence: find the verb, find the subject, use the endings to work out the roles, gloss each word literally, then smooth into good English. The same steps work for Hebrew, Greek and Latin. Translating between the languages teaches you quickly, because you compare structures: the same idea turns up with different grammar. Cognates and hooks help you remember, and spaced repetition makes it last. The labs include a Leitner scheduler in Python and a translation exercise.
keyPoints: Method: verb, subject, object, endings, literal gloss, smooth English.
Compare the same sentence in three languages to see the structure.
Use hooks: connect to English words, pictures and stories.
Space your reviews: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 days.
Say words aloud, and write them by hand.
Use the words in your own sentences.

courses.title: Commodore 64 Programming: BASIC, Assembly, C and the Hardware
courses.subtitle: From the memory map to sprites, sound, tape, disk and the user port, with a real C64 emulator in every lab
courses.author: Lilith Learning Lab
courses.description: A condensed, original course on programming the Commodore 64. It covers the chips and memory map, BASIC V2, 6510 assembly, C with cc65, VIC-II sprites, SID sound, interrupts, joysticks and keyboard, the user port, tape and disk, with labs that run on an emulated C64 inside the app, so no real hardware is needed. Credits: the labs reuse the WebAssembly C64 emulator core from floooh/chips (zlib licence) as packaged by 8bitworkshop (GPL-3.0), the Open ROMs generic ROM image, and the cc65 toolchain (zlib licence). The course text is original.

outline.title: Meet the Commodore 64
outline.summary: The Commodore 64 is an 8-bit home computer from 1982. It was cheap, it had real graphics and sound chips, and it sold in the millions. Its heart is a 6510 processor with 64 KB of RAM. Three custom chips do the rest: VIC-II for video, SID for sound and two CIAs for timers and ports. This course teaches the machine, from BASIC down to chips, tape, disk and the user port, and every lab runs on a real emulator inside the app.
keyPoints: 8-bit CPU at about 1 MHz, 16-bit addresses.
64 KB RAM plus 20 KB ROM (BASIC, KERNAL, characters).
40 by 25 text, 320 by 200 pixels, 16 colours, 8 sprites.
SID: three voices, four waveforms.
PAL machines run at 985248 Hz, NTSC at 1022727 Hz.

outline.title: Tools, files and the Studio
outline.summary: You do not need real hardware. An emulator runs C64 programs on any device, and the labs in this course use one built into the app. Programs travel as files. A PRG file is two bytes of load address followed by the program. Disks and tapes have image formats too. This chapter ends with a first lab: assemble a tiny program and watch it change the screen colours.
keyPoints: A PRG's first two bytes are the load address, low byte first.
BASIC programs load at $0801.
A SYS line at $0801 starts machine code.
An emulator is the safest way to try things.
A D64 holds 35 tracks of 256-byte sectors.

outline.title: BASIC V2
outline.summary: Turn the C64 on and you are in BASIC V2. It is slow but friendly, and its PEEK and POKE commands reach every chip. Programs are numbered lines. The computer runs them in order, jumping with GOTO and GOSUB. Every example in this chapter can be typed straight into a real C64 or an emulator such as VICE. The labs in this course use assembly and C, which run on a real C64 emulator.
keyPoints: Lines run in number order.
Variable names use only the first two letters.
Text variables end with $, whole numbers with %.
POKE 53280,0 makes the border black.
BASIC V2 has no sound or graphics commands: use POKE.

outline.title: Memory map and banking
outline.summary: The CPU can address only 64 KB, yet there is also 20 KB of ROM and a set of chips. They share addresses with RAM. Three bits in the processor port at address 1 choose what the CPU sees at $A000, $D000 and $E000. Reads see the ROM or chip, but writes always reach the RAM underneath.
keyPoints: $0000-$00FF zero page; $0100-$01FF stack.
$0400 screen; $0801 BASIC; $C000 free RAM.
$A000 BASIC ROM; $D000 I/O or characters; $E000 KERNAL.
Bit 0 LORAM, bit 1 HIRAM, bit 2 CHAREN.
Writes to a ROM address go to the RAM below.

outline.title: Screen, characters and colour
outline.summary: The text screen is 40 columns by 25 rows. Each cell is one byte in screen RAM and one colour nibble in colour RAM. To put a letter on screen you store its screen code in memory. No drawing routine is needed. Screen codes are not the same as PETSCII, the numbers you use with PRINT and CHR$.
keyPoints: Cell address = $0400 + row*40 + column.
Colour address = $D800 + row*40 + column.
Screen code 1 is A; 32 is a space.
Colours 0-15: black, white, red, cyan, purple, green, blue, yellow...
Border $D020, background $D021.

outline.title: 6510 assembly I: registers and flags
outline.summary: Machine code runs thousands of times faster than BASIC. You write it as assembly: short names for each instruction. The 6510 has three working registers, A, X and Y, a stack pointer, a program counter and a status register of flags. The lab assembles your code, loads it into the emulated C64 and runs it.
keyPoints: LDA #5 loads the number 5; LDA $D020 loads the byte at that address.
STA stores A. INX and DEX change X by one.
Flags: Z zero, C carry, N negative, V overflow.
BNE branches if the zero flag is clear.
A branch reaches -128 to +127 bytes.

outline.title: 6510 assembly II: KERNAL, stack and patterns
outline.summary: Real programs call subroutines. JSR jumps to one and RTS returns, with the return address kept on the stack. The KERNAL gives you ready-made routines at fixed addresses, such as CHROUT at $FFD2 to print a character. Every instruction takes a known number of clock cycles, so you can count how long a loop lasts.
keyPoints: JSR pushes the return address minus one, high byte first.
RTS pulls it and adds one.
The stack grows downward from $01FF.
CHROUT is at $FFD2, GETIN at $FFE4.
DEX is 2 cycles; BNE is 3 if taken, 2 if not.

outline.title: C on the C64 with cc65
outline.summary: You can write C for the 6502. The cc65 toolchain compiles it to assembly, assembles it and links a PRG file that starts with a BASIC stub. The code is small and sometimes surprising: an int is 16 bits and floating point is not built in. The lab runs cc65 inside the app, so you can build C with no installation.
keyPoints: cc65 turns C into 6502 assembly.
int is 16 bits, char is 8 bits, long is 32.
POKE(addr, value) writes memory.
Programs start at $0801 with a SYS stub.
Avoid deep recursion and big stack arrays.

outline.title: VIC-II graphics and sprites
outline.summary: The VIC-II reads memory by itself and builds the picture. Programs change it by writing to registers at $D000. A sprite is a movable image, 24 pixels wide and 21 high, stored as 63 bytes. There are eight of them. The chip sees only 16 KB at a time, chosen by two bits on CIA 2.
keyPoints: Sprite data: 3 bytes per row, 21 rows = 63 bytes.
Pointer value = data address / 64 (at $07F8-$07FF).
$D015 turns sprites on, one bit each.
$D000/$D001 are sprite 0 X and Y; $D027 its colour.
VIC bank = 3 minus the low two bits of $DD00.

outline.title: SID sound
outline.summary: The SID chip has three voices. Each has a waveform, a frequency and an envelope, and a master volume controls the whole chip. Registers start at $D400, seven per voice. A note starts when you set the gate bit and ends when you clear it. Pitch is a 16-bit number, and it depends on the clock, so PAL and NTSC machines differ slightly.
keyPoints: Voice 1 is $D400-$D406; add 7 for voice 2 and 14 for voice 3.
Control bits: $10 triangle, $20 saw, $40 pulse, $80 noise, plus $01 gate.
$D418 sets volume 0-15.
freq register = Hz x 2^24 / clock.
Clock: 985248 Hz (PAL), 1022727 Hz (NTSC).

outline.title: Interrupts and the CIA chips
outline.summary: An interrupt stops the program, runs a handler, and then carries on. The C64 uses them for the keyboard, the clock and your own timing. The VIC-II can raise an interrupt at any screen line, so you can change colours or sprites mid-frame. The CIA chips have timers and handle ports, the keyboard and joysticks.
keyPoints: The system IRQ runs 60 or 50 times a second from a CIA timer.
Change $0314/$0315 to hook the IRQ.
Raster line goes in $D012 and bit 7 of $D011.
Enable the raster IRQ with $D01A; acknowledge with $D019.
CIA 1 is at $DC00, CIA 2 at $DD00.

outline.title: Controllers: joysticks, paddles and keys
outline.summary: A joystick has five switches. Each is a bit in a CIA register, and a bit reads 0 when the switch is pressed. The keyboard is a grid of 8 rows by 8 columns that the CIA scans. Paddles are knobs read as voltages through the SID's analogue inputs.
keyPoints: Port 2 at $DC00; port 1 at $DC01.
Bit 0 up, 1 down, 2 left, 3 right, 4 fire; 0 means pressed.
Keyboard: write a column pattern to $DC00, read the rows at $DC01.
Paddle values come from $D419 and $D41A.
Port 1 can confuse the keyboard scan.

outline.title: The user port
outline.summary: The user port is the edge connector at the back. It gives you eight data pins you can drive or read yourself, plus power and control lines. Each data pin is an input or an output, chosen by a bit in the data direction register. Hobbyists used it for modems, printers, sensors and home-made hardware.
keyPoints: PB0-PB7 are read and written at $DD01.
$DD03 is the direction register: bit 1 = output.
Reading gives output bits for output pins and the outside voltage for input pins.
The pins are 5 V TTL, not RS-232 voltages.
A pin can drive only a few milliamps.

outline.title: The tape drive
outline.summary: The Datassette stores programs on an ordinary cassette. Data is written as pulses of three lengths. Each bit is a pair of pulses. A long and a medium pulse mark the start of every byte, and an odd-parity bit follows the eight data bits. The processor port controls the motor, the sense switch and the write line.
keyPoints: Pulses: short, medium, long.
Bit 0 = short then medium; bit 1 = medium then short.
Byte marker = long then medium; end-of-data = long then short.
Data bits go lowest bit first, then odd parity.
Checksum = XOR of the data bytes.

outline.title: The 1541 disk drive
outline.summary: The 1541 floppy drive stores 35 tracks. Outer tracks are longer, so they hold more sectors. Each sector is 256 bytes: two bytes link to the next block and 254 hold data. Track 18 is special. It holds the block availability map and the directory.
keyPoints: 683 blocks in total; 664 free on a new disk.
A sector holds 254 data bytes after a 2-byte link.
BAM at 18/0, directory from 18/1.
A directory entry is 32 bytes.

outline.title: Projects and next steps
outline.summary: You now know the memory map, the screen, assembly, C, graphics, sound, interrupts, input and storage. The best way forward is to build something small: a sprite you move, a tune you play, a raster effect. The lab below starts you off with a joystick-controlled sprite.
keyPoints: Game loop: input, update, draw, wait.
Keep your code in $C000 or after BASIC's stub.
Test small steps in the emulator.
Use frames, not delays, to time things.
Share D64 or PRG files.

outline.title: Demo coding
outline.summary: A demo is a program with no purpose except to impress: moving graphics, effects and music, squeezed out of old hardware by tricks its designers never planned for. Making them is called demo coding, and it grew into the demoscene. A few ideas build almost every C64 effect: change a register at an exact raster line, use a precomputed sine table for smooth motion, move text with the hardware scroll register, and drive everything from a raster interrupt that fires once per frame. This chapter walks through those ideas with working labs in assembly and C, and ends with a plan for a small demo of your own.
keyPoints: A PAL frame is 19656 cycles; a raster line is 63.
Do the heavy work in tables, not in the effect loop.
Time effects to the raster beam, not to delay loops.
Music is played by calling a player routine once per frame.
Start simple: one effect, then another, then join them into parts.

courses.title: Compiler Design
courses.subtitle: Theory and practice, with Python labs
courses.author: Lilith Learning Lab
courses.description: A 17-chapter course based on the Tutorialspoint Compiler Design tutorial: compiler architecture and phases, lexical analysis, regular expressions, finite automata, syntax analysis, top-down and bottom-up parsing, error recovery, semantic analysis, runtime environments, symbol tables, intermediate code, code generation and optimization. Python labs run on the built-in MicroPython engine; each lab builds a small working version of a compiler component. Known errors in the source tutorial are corrected and flagged in the lessons.

outline.title: Overview of compilers
outline.summary: A compiler translates code written in one language into another language without changing the meaning. It is also expected to make the target code efficient in time and space. Compiler design covers translation, error detection and recovery. The front end is lexical, syntax and semantic analysis; the back end is code generation and optimization. A whole language processing system has more parts: a preprocessor, the compiler, an assembler, a linker and a loader. Related tools are the interpreter, the cross-compiler and the source-to-source compiler.
keyPoints: A compiler must preserve the meaning of the program.
A compiler reads the whole program; an interpreter works statement by statement.
The interpreter stops at the first error; a compiler keeps reading and reports many.
Source goes through preprocessor, compiler, assembler, linker and loader.
The linker resolves references between separately compiled modules.
A cross-compiler runs on platform A and targets platform B.

outline.title: Compiler architecture
outline.summary: A compiler splits into two parts. The analysis phase, the front end, reads the source, divides it into core parts and checks for lexical, grammar and syntax errors. It produces an intermediate representation and a symbol table. The synthesis phase, the back end, generates the target program from the intermediate representation and the symbol table. A pass is one traversal of the entire program. A phase is a distinguishable stage that takes input from the previous stage and yields output for the next. A pass can contain more than one phase.
keyPoints: Front end = analysis; back end = synthesis.
The front end depends on the source language, the back end on the target machine.
The intermediate representation and symbol table link the two parts.
A pass traverses the whole program; a phase is one stage.
A pass may contain several phases.

outline.title: Phases of a compiler
outline.summary: Compilation is a sequence of phases. Each takes input from the previous phase, has its own representation of the program and feeds the next. The phases are lexical analysis, syntax analysis, semantic analysis, intermediate code generation, code optimization and code generation. The lexical analyzer turns characters into tokens. The parser turns tokens into a parse tree. The semantic analyzer checks the rules of the language. The code generators then produce, improve and finally map code to the target machine. The symbol table is a data structure maintained through all phases. It stores identifier names with their types and supports scope management.
keyPoints: Phases: lexical, syntax, semantic, intermediate code, optimization, code generation.
A token is <token-name, attribute-value>.
The parser checks that the token arrangement fits the grammar.
The semantic analyzer checks types and declarations.
Intermediate code is machine independent, so optimization can be shared.
The symbol table is used throughout.

outline.title: Lexical analysis
outline.summary: Lexical analysis is the first phase. It takes the preprocessed source, removes whitespace and comments, and breaks it into tokens. An invalid token is a lexical error. It works closely with the syntax analyzer, which asks for tokens when it needs them. A lexeme is the matched text. A pattern, written as a regular expression, says which lexemes make a valid token. Keywords, constants, identifiers, strings, numbers, operators and punctuation are all tokens. An alphabet is a finite set of symbols, a string a finite sequence of them, and a language a set of strings. When scanning is ambiguous the longest match wins, and reserved words beat identifiers.
keyPoints: The lexer removes whitespace and comments and reports invalid tokens.
int value = 100; has the tokens int, value, =, 100 and ;.
Patterns are regular expressions; lexemes are the matched text.
Longest match: intvalue is one identifier, not int followed by value.
Keywords have priority over identifiers.
The length of a string is its number of symbols; the empty string has length zero.

outline.title: Regular expressions
outline.summary: The lexical analyzer must recognize a finite set of valid lexemes of the language. Regular expressions define patterns for strings of symbols. The grammar they define is a regular grammar and the language is a regular language. Operations on languages are union, concatenation and Kleene closure. A regular expression built with them denotes a language. The star has the highest precedence, then concatenation, and union has the lowest. All are left associative. Shorthands such as plus, question mark and character ranges are common. Tokens like identifiers and decimal numbers are written with them: letter followed by letters or digits, and an optional sign followed by one or more digits.
keyPoints: Operations: union, concatenation, Kleene closure.
Precedence: star, then concatenation, then union.
x* is zero or more; x+ is one or more; x? is zero or one.
Identifier = letter (letter | digit)*.
Decimal = (sign)? (digit)+.
Finite automata verify the expressions.

outline.title: Finite automata
outline.summary: A finite automaton is a state machine that takes a string of symbols and changes state for each symbol. It is a recognizer for regular expressions. If the whole input is processed and the automaton is in a final state, the string is accepted as a valid token. It consists of a finite set of states, a finite input alphabet, one start state, a set of final states and a transition function that maps a state and a symbol to a state. A lexer built on automata implements the longest match rule by running as far as it can and remembering the last point at which it was in a final state.
keyPoints: The model: Q, the alphabet, q0, the final states and delta.
delta maps Q times the alphabet to Q.
Accept the input if it is consumed and the state is final.
Transitions can loop back to the same state.
The automaton for three binary digits ending in 1 has four steps.
Longest match: keep going, remember the last accepting position.

outline.title: Syntax analysis
outline.summary: Syntax analysis, or parsing, is the second phase. A lexer cannot check balanced parentheses because regular expressions are too weak, so the parser uses a context-free grammar, recognized by push-down automata. A grammar has non-terminals, terminals, productions and a start symbol. A derivation replaces non-terminals step by step, left-most or right-most; a parse tree depicts it. A grammar with two parse trees for one string is ambiguous, which is fixed with precedence and associativity or a rewrite. Top-down parsers need grammars without left recursion and with common prefixes factored out. FIRST and FOLLOW sets are the ingredients of parsing tables. Syntax analysis cannot check declarations or types; the semantic analyzer does.
keyPoints: Regular expressions cannot match balanced tokens; context-free grammars can.
Left-most derivation replaces the left-most non-terminal; right-most replaces the right-most.
Ambiguity: remove it by precedence, associativity or rewriting.
Left recursion: A becomes beta A' and A' becomes alpha A' or epsilon.
Left factoring: pull out the common prefix.
FIRST and FOLLOW feed the parsing table.
The parser cannot check declarations, initialization or types.

outline.title: Types of parsing
outline.summary: Parsers follow the production rules of a context-free grammar. How the rules are applied divides parsing into two kinds: top-down and bottom-up. Top-down parsing starts from the start symbol and tries to transform it into the input, building the tree from the root. A common form is recursive descent, which can need backtracking: if one production fails, the parser restarts with another production of the same non-terminal. Bottom-up parsing starts from the input symbols and builds the tree up to the start symbol, by finding right sides in the input and replacing them with left sides.
keyPoints: The two kinds: top-down and bottom-up.
Top-down starts at the start symbol and expands it.
Bottom-up starts at the input and reduces to the start symbol.
Recursive descent may need backtracking.
Backtracking may process the input more than once.

outline.title: Top-down parsing
outline.summary: Top-down parsing builds the tree from the root toward the leaves. A recursive descent parser uses procedures for each terminal and non-terminal, and may need backtracking unless the grammar is left factored. A predictive parser is a recursive descent parser that predicts which production to use, using a look-ahead pointer, and never backtracks. It accepts only LL(k) grammars. It can be table driven: a stack and a parsing table decide each step. In LL(k) the first L is for left-to-right input, the second for a left-most derivation, and k is the number of look-ahead symbols. Usually k is 1.
keyPoints: Recursive descent has a procedure for each non-terminal.
A predictive parser picks the production from the look-ahead alone.
LL(1): scan Left to right, Left-most derivation, 1 look-ahead.
The table-driven parser uses a stack and table M[X, a].
Pop a non-terminal, push its right side in reverse; pop a matching terminal.
A non-LL(1) grammar is usually not LL(k) either.

outline.title: Bottom-up parsing
outline.summary: Bottom-up parsing starts from the leaves and works upward to the root: it starts with a sentence and applies productions in reverse to reach the start symbol. Shift-reduce parsing has two steps. A shift moves the next input symbol onto the stack. A reduce, when the top of the stack holds a handle (a complete right side), pops it and pushes the left-side non-terminal. The LR parser is a non-recursive shift-reduce parser. It reads input left to right and builds a right-most derivation in reverse. Three constructions are common: SLR(1), LR(1) and LALR(1), trading table size against the class of grammars they handle.
keyPoints: Shift pushes an input symbol; reduce pops a handle and pushes the left side.
Bottom-up parsing runs a right-most derivation backwards.
LR uses action and goto tables.
SLR(1) is simplest; LR(1) most powerful; LALR(1) in between.
LL expands non-terminals and builds top-down; LR reduces and builds bottom-up.
LR can handle a larger class of grammars than LL.

outline.title: Error recovery and ASTs
outline.summary: A parser should detect and report errors and then carry on parsing. Errors arise at several stages: lexical (a misspelled identifier), syntactic (a missing semicolon or unbalanced parenthesis), semantic (an incompatible assignment) and logical (unreachable code, an infinite loop). Four recovery strategies: panic mode skips input up to a delimiter such as a semicolon; statement mode makes a local correction; error productions add known mistakes to the grammar; global correction finds the closest correct program but is too expensive in practice. Parse trees contain more detail than later phases need. An abstract syntax tree hides single-child chains and punctuation, leaving only the operators and operands.
keyPoints: Errors: lexical, syntactical, semantical, logical.
Panic mode is the simplest and cannot loop forever.
Statement mode can loop if a correction is wrong.
Error productions describe expected mistakes.
Global correction is too costly for practice.
ASTs are smaller than parse trees and easier for later phases.

outline.title: Semantic analysis
outline.summary: A parse tree alone does not say how to evaluate or interpret anything. Semantics give meaning to the constructs: grammar plus semantic rules is a syntax directed definition. Semantic analysis checks scope resolution, type checking and array bounds, and reports semantic errors such as type mismatch and undeclared variables. An attribute grammar attaches attributes to non-terminals. Synthesized attributes take their values from child nodes; inherited attributes take theirs from the parent or siblings. An S-attributed definition uses only synthesized attributes and is evaluated bottom-up. An L-attributed definition also allows inherited attributes, but never from right siblings, and is evaluated depth-first and left to right. Every S-attributed definition is L-attributed.
keyPoints: CFG + semantic rules = syntax directed definition.
Tasks: scope resolution, type checking, array-bound checking.
Errors: type mismatch, undeclared variable, redeclaration, out-of-scope access, parameter mismatch.
Synthesized: from children. Inherited: from parent and siblings.
S-attributed: bottom-up. L-attributed: depth-first, left to right.
S-attributed implies L-attributed.

outline.title: Runtime environment
outline.summary: A program needs memory and a mapping from names to locations at run time. The runtime environment is the state of the target machine, and the runtime support system handles memory allocation and de-allocation while the program runs. Each procedure execution is an activation with an activation record on the control stack, holding temporaries, local data, machine status, links, parameters and the return value. The sequence of activations forms an activation tree. Code is allocated statically, procedure activations on a stack and dynamic data on a heap. Parameters are passed by value, by reference, by copy-restore or by name. They differ in whether the callee can change the caller's variable and when.
keyPoints: Activation records live on the control stack.
The call order gives a depth-first activation tree.
Static: code, global data. Stack: procedure calls. Heap: dynamic data.
Stack and heap sit at opposite ends of memory and grow toward each other.
r-value is a value; l-value is a location. 7 = x + y is an l-value error.
Value does not change the caller; reference does; copy-restore does at the end; name substitutes text.

outline.title: Symbol table
outline.summary: The symbol table stores information about names: variables, functions, objects, classes and interfaces. It is used by both the analysis and the synthesis parts of the compiler. It serves to store names in one place, to check that a variable is declared, to type check, and to resolve scope. It is a linear table or, most often, a hash table. Each entry holds the symbol name, type and attributes. The two operations are insert, used mostly by the analysis phase, and lookup, which returns 0 when the symbol is absent. For scope, tables are arranged in a hierarchy, and lookup searches the current scope first and then the parent scopes.
keyPoints: Entry format: symbol name, type, attribute.
static int interest is stored as interest, int, static.
Implementation choices: linear list, binary search tree, hash table. Hash tables are most common.
insert is used mostly by the analysis phase.
lookup checks existence, prior declaration, scope, initialization and duplicates.
Scope lookup: current table first, then parents, up to the global table.

outline.title: Intermediate code generation
outline.summary: Intermediate code lets one analysis front end serve many machines: only the synthesis part changes with the target. It also makes it easier to apply optimizations that are independent of the machine. It can be high level, close to the source, or low level, close to the machine, and language specific (Java byte code) or language independent (three-address code). Three-address code has at most three addresses per instruction and is stored as quadruples, triples or indirect triples. Declarations allocate memory to names consecutively, using an offset that starts at zero and grows by each name's width, and enter the name, type and offset into the symbol table.
keyPoints: IR saves writing a full compiler for each machine.
Analysis stays the same; only synthesis changes per target.
Three-address code assumes unlimited registers.
Quadruples have a result field; triples use positions; indirect triples use pointers.
Triples are hard to reorder; indirect triples fix that.
Declarations: offset = offset + width.

outline.title: Code generation
outline.summary: Code generation is the final phase. It produces object code in a lower-level language such as assembly, which must carry the exact meaning of the source and be efficient in CPU and memory. A directed acyclic graph shows how values flow among the statements of a basic block and exposes shared sub-expressions. Peephole optimization improves a small window of code: redundant instructions, unreachable code, jumps to jumps, algebraic simplifications and strength reduction. A code generator has to select instructions, allocate registers and order instructions. It uses a register descriptor and an address descriptor, and a function getReg picks the register for each result.
keyPoints: The object code must keep the meaning and be efficient.
A DAG shows shared sub-expressions in a basic block.
Peephole: redundant loads, unreachable code, jumps to jumps, algebraic simplification, strength reduction.
x * 2 can become x << 1.
The code generator selects instructions, allocates registers and orders instructions.
Descriptors are updated as code is generated.

outline.title: Code optimization
outline.summary: Optimization transforms a program so that it uses fewer resources and runs faster, while keeping the meaning, and without slowing the compiler too much. It can be done by the user, on the intermediate code, and on the target code. Machine-independent optimization works on intermediate code, with no registers or absolute addresses. Machine-dependent optimization uses registers and the memory hierarchy. Basic blocks and the control flow graph structure the program for analysis. Loops get special attention: moving invariant code out, working with induction variables, and strength reduction. Dead code, partially dead code and partially redundant expressions are removed or moved.
keyPoints: Rules: keep the meaning; speed up; be fast itself.
Levels: user code, intermediate code, target code.
Leaders start basic blocks: the first statement, branch targets and statements after a branch.
Loop optimizations: invariant code, induction analysis, strength reduction.
Dead code: unreachable or unused result.
Code motion removes partial redundancy.

courses.title: Computer Vision
courses.subtitle: From pixels and filters to CNNs, detectors and vision transformers, classical and modern, with Python labs and playgrounds
courses.author: Lilith Learning Lab
courses.description: A hands-on course in computer vision covering both classical and modern techniques: images as data and colour spaces; convolution, blurring and the median filter; Sobel, Canny and Hough; keypoints, descriptors, RANSAC and homographies; thresholding, morphology and connected components; camera geometry, calibration and stereo depth; HOG, Haar cascades, bags of visual words and SVMs; convolutional networks, ResNet and transfer learning; detection with IoU and non-maximum suppression, YOLO and Mask R-CNN, and segmentation with U-Net; and vision transformers, CLIP, SAM and diffusion with a look at bias and responsible use. Every chapter has Python labs verified in the built-in interpreter, plus a convolution playground and an IoU and NMS lab.

outline.title: Images as data
outline.summary: A digital image is a grid of pixels. A grayscale pixel is one number, usually 0 to 255; a colour pixel has three channels, red, green and blue. In code, an image is an array with a shape such as height by width by 3. Computer vision asks a machine to extract meaning from such arrays: what is in the picture, where, how far, how it moves. It splits into classical methods, built from hand-designed filters and geometry, and modern methods that learn their filters from data. Simple operations already do useful work: converting to gray, adjusting brightness, flipping, resizing and counting intensities in a histogram.
keyPoints: Image = array of shape (H, W) or (H, W, 3).
Histogram: count per intensity.
Brightness: add and clip to 0..255.
Index as img[row][col].

outline.title: Filtering and convolution
outline.summary: A filter replaces each pixel by a weighted sum of its neighbours. The weights form a small grid called a kernel, and sliding it over the image is convolution (or its twin, correlation). A box blur averages; a Gaussian blur weights nearer pixels more and blurs without blocky artefacts; sharpening subtracts a blur from the original to boost detail. A median filter, which is not linear, removes isolated speckles without smearing edges. Many kernels are separable: a 2D Gaussian is the product of two 1D ones, which cuts the work from k squared to 2k per pixel.
keyPoints: out[r][c] = sum k[i][j] img[r+i][c+j].
Blur kernels sum to 1.
Edge kernels sum to 0.
Gaussian sigma sets the blur size.
Median removes salt and pepper noise.

outline.title: Edges, gradients and lines
outline.summary: An edge is a place where brightness changes quickly. The gradient of an image points in the direction of fastest increase and its length measures how fast; edges are where the gradient magnitude is large. The Sobel kernels estimate the horizontal and vertical derivatives. The Canny detector smooths, finds the gradient, thins edges to one pixel by non-maximum suppression and links them with two thresholds. The Hough transform finds lines by letting every edge pixel vote for all the lines that could pass through it; real lines collect many votes.
keyPoints: Magnitude = sqrt(Gx^2 + Gy^2).
Direction = atan2(Gy, Gx).
Canny: blur, gradient, thin, threshold.
Line: rho = x cos(theta) + y sin(theta).
Smooth first or noise explodes.

outline.title: Features, matching and geometry of images
outline.summary: To recognise a place or stitch photos we need points that can be found again from another view. Corners are good: the image changes in every direction around them. The Harris detector scores this with the structure tensor. A descriptor summarises the patch around a keypoint as a vector. SIFT uses gradient histograms; ORB uses a binary string compared with Hamming distance. Matching finds nearest descriptors and a ratio test removes ambiguous ones. RANSAC fits a model, such as a homography, to many noisy matches by repeatedly fitting to random minimal sets and keeping the model with the most inliers.
keyPoints: Harris: R = det(M) - k trace(M)^2.
ORB descriptor: bits; compare with Hamming distance.
Ratio test: d1 < 0.75 d2.
RANSAC: sample, fit, count inliers, repeat.
Homography: (x, y, 1) -> H (x, y, 1).

outline.title: Segmentation, morphology and regions
outline.summary: Segmentation divides an image into meaningful regions. The simplest method is thresholding: pixels above a value are foreground. Otsu's method picks the threshold that best separates the two groups of the histogram. Morphological operations clean up binary masks: erosion shrinks shapes and removes specks, dilation grows them and fills holes, and opening and closing combine the two. Connected component labelling counts and measures blobs. Clustering colours with k-means and the watershed algorithm are other classical ways to segment.
keyPoints: mask = img > t.
Opening = erode then dilate (removes specks).
Closing = dilate then erode (fills holes).
Connectivity: 4 or 8 neighbours.
Otsu: maximise between-class variance.

outline.title: Cameras, geometry and depth
outline.summary: The pinhole model projects a 3D point (X, Y, Z) to the image at (f X / Z, f Y / Z): farther things appear smaller. Intrinsic parameters (focal length, principal point) describe the camera; extrinsics give its position and rotation. Real lenses distort straight lines; calibration with a checkerboard estimates the parameters so we can undo it. Two cameras a baseline B apart see the same point shifted by a disparity d; depth is Z = f B / d. Closer objects have larger disparity.
keyPoints: u = f X / Z + cx; v = f Y / Z + cy.
Depth Z = f B / d.
Field of view = 2 atan(W / (2 f)).
Calibrate with a checkerboard.
Homogeneous coordinates make projection a matrix product.

outline.title: Classical recognition: HOG, Haar and bags of features
outline.summary: Before deep learning, recognition was a pipeline: extract hand-designed features, then train a classifier. HOG (histogram of oriented gradients) describes shape by local gradient directions and, with a linear SVM, detected pedestrians. Viola and Jones detected faces in real time using Haar features (differences of rectangle sums) computed instantly from an integral image, and a cascade that rejects most windows early. Bag of visual words clusters local descriptors into a vocabulary and describes an image by the histogram of words, then classifies the histogram.
keyPoints: Rectangle sum = I(D) - I(B) - I(C) + I(A).
HOG: cells of 8x8, 9 orientation bins.
Sliding window x image pyramid = detector.
SVM: sign(w.x + b).
Bag of words: histogram of cluster ids.

outline.title: Convolutional neural networks
outline.summary: A convolutional neural network stacks learned convolution layers with non-linearities and pooling. Early layers learn edges, middle layers textures and parts, late layers whole objects. AlexNet's win in the 2012 ImageNet contest started the deep learning era. VGG, Inception and ResNet followed; ResNet's skip connections made very deep networks trainable. Instead of training from scratch, you usually start from a network pretrained on ImageNet and fine-tune it on your own data: transfer learning.
keyPoints: Output size = (W - K + 2P) / S + 1.
Params per conv layer = K*K*Cin*Cout + Cout.
Max pool 2x2 halves width and height.
ResNet: y = F(x) + x.
Fine-tune: freeze early layers, train the head.

outline.title: Detection, segmentation and tracking
outline.summary: Detection finds what and where: a box and a class for every object. Intersection over union (IoU) measures how well two boxes overlap, and non-maximum suppression removes duplicate detections of the same object. R-CNN families propose regions then classify them; YOLO and SSD predict boxes in a single pass and run in real time. Mask R-CNN adds a mask per object (instance segmentation). Semantic segmentation labels every pixel; encoder-decoder networks such as U-Net downsample to understand and upsample to localise.
keyPoints: IoU = intersection / (A + B - intersection).
NMS: sort by score, keep, drop IoU > threshold.
Match if IoU >= 0.5.
YOLO: grid cells predict boxes.
U-Net: encoder, decoder, skip links.

outline.title: Vision transformers, foundation models and responsible vision
outline.summary: The Vision Transformer (ViT) cuts an image into patches, treats each as a token, adds position information and applies self-attention so every patch can relate to every other. With enough data it matches or beats CNNs. Foundation models are trained on huge data and reused for many tasks. CLIP learns to match images with captions, enabling zero-shot classification by comparing an image with text prompts. SAM segments any object from a click or a box. Diffusion models generate images by learning to remove noise step by step. These powerful tools also raise issues of bias, privacy, surveillance and misinformation.
keyPoints: Patches: (H/P) x (W/P) tokens.
Attention = softmax(Q K^T / sqrt(d)) V.
CLIP: cosine similarity of image and text embeddings.
Diffusion: x_t = sqrt(a) x_0 + sqrt(1 - a) noise.
Audit performance across groups.

courses.title: Control Theory
courses.subtitle: Feedback, stability, PID, frequency methods and state space, with runnable Python labs and a PID tuner
courses.author: Lilith Learning Lab
courses.description: A hands-on introduction to classical and modern control: feedback and the control problem, modelling with differential equations and Euler simulation, first and second-order responses with damping and overshoot, transfer functions, poles and Routh-Hurwitz stability, PID design with anti-windup, root locus and Bode margins, state-space models with pole placement, controllability and observers, and digital implementation including delay, sampling and feedforward. Every chapter has Python labs verified in the built-in interpreter, and two interactive labs let you move poles around the s-plane and tune a PID loop live.

outline.title: Feedback and the control problem
outline.summary: Control theory is the study of making systems behave as we want. A plant (a motor, a room, a rocket) is driven by an input, and we want its output to follow a target called the setpoint. An open-loop controller sends a fixed command and hopes. A closed-loop (feedback) controller measures the output, forms the error between setpoint and measurement, and corrects it continuously. Feedback fights disturbances and uncertainty, but a badly designed loop can oscillate or go unstable.
keyPoints: e = r - y.
Closed loop: sense, compare, act, repeat.
Feedback rejects disturbances.
Too much gain can destabilise a loop.
Goals: stability, accuracy, speed, robustness.

outline.title: Modelling dynamic systems
outline.summary: To control a system we need a model: equations for how it changes. Most are differential equations such as dx/dt = f(x, u). A first-order system, like a cooling cup or a charging capacitor, moves toward its final value exponentially. Its time constant tau is the time to cover about 63 percent of the gap. We can simulate any model on a computer by stepping through time: Euler's method updates x by the rate times a small time step.
keyPoints: tau dy/dt + y = K u.
Step response: y(t) = K (1 - e^(-t/tau)).
After 3 tau: 95 percent. After 5 tau: 99 percent.
Euler: x[k+1] = x[k] + dt f(x[k], u[k]).
Smaller dt means better accuracy.

outline.title: Second-order systems: damping and overshoot
outline.summary: Many systems, such as a mass on a spring, a pendulum or a motor with inertia, behave as second-order systems, described by a natural frequency wn and a damping ratio zeta. With little damping (zeta below 1) the response overshoots and rings. At zeta equal to 1 it is critically damped. Above 1 it is overdamped and slow. Specifications such as percent overshoot and settling time translate directly into zeta and wn.
keyPoints: y'' + 2 zeta wn y' + wn^2 y = wn^2 u.
Overshoot = exp(-pi zeta / sqrt(1 - zeta^2)).
Settling (2 percent) is about 4 / (zeta wn).
zeta < 1 underdamped; = 1 critical; > 1 over.
Poles: -zeta wn plus or minus i wn sqrt(1 - zeta^2).

outline.title: Transfer functions and stability
outline.summary: The Laplace transform replaces differentiation by multiplication by s. A linear system then becomes a transfer function G(s) = Y(s) / U(s), a ratio of polynomials in s. The roots of the denominator are the poles. A continuous-time system is stable when all poles have negative real parts, lying in the left half of the s-plane. Routh-Hurwitz checks stability from the coefficients alone, without finding the roots. Closing a loop changes the poles, which is how feedback reshapes behaviour.
keyPoints: G(s) = K / (tau s + 1).
Closed loop: T = L / (1 + L).
Characteristic equation: 1 + L(s) = 0.
Stable iff all poles have Re < 0.
Second order: stable iff all coefficients positive.

outline.title: PID control
outline.summary: The PID controller computes its command from three terms: proportional to the error now, integral of the error so far, and derivative of the error's rate of change. Proportional control alone often leaves a steady-state error. The integral term removes it by acting until the error is exactly zero. The derivative term damps oscillation by reacting to the trend. Practical PID needs care: limit the output, stop the integrator winding up when saturated, and filter the derivative to avoid amplifying noise.
keyPoints: u = Kp e + Ki integral(e) + Kd de/dt.
Discrete: I += e dt; D = (e - e_prev) / dt.
Raise Kp: faster, more overshoot.
Raise Ki: removes offset, more oscillation.
Raise Kd: damps, amplifies noise.

outline.title: Root locus and frequency response
outline.summary: Root locus shows how the closed-loop poles move as a gain k grows from zero to infinity, giving a picture of when the loop becomes unstable. Frequency response describes how a system treats sine inputs. A Bode plot draws gain and phase against frequency. Margins measure how close the loop is to instability. Gain margin and phase margin are safety distances. A phase margin of 45 to 60 degrees usually means a well-damped loop.
keyPoints: |G(iw)| and angle G(iw).
dB = 20 log10 |G|.
Phase margin = 180 + phase at crossover.
Gain margin = 1 / |L| at phase -180.
Bandwidth sets speed of response.

outline.title: State space and state feedback
outline.summary: State-space models write a system as x' = A x + B u and y = C x, handling many inputs and outputs and giving direct access to internal variables. State feedback u = -K x changes the closed-loop matrix to A - B K. If the system is controllable, K can place the closed-loop poles anywhere we like. If we cannot measure all states, an observer estimates them from the outputs. A controller plus an observer is the basis of modern control, including the Kalman filter.
keyPoints: x' = A x + B u.
u = -K x gives x' = (A - B K) x.
Poles = eigenvalues of A - BK.
Controllable if [B, AB, ...] has full rank.
Kalman filter: the optimal observer.

outline.title: Digital control and practical design
outline.summary: Controllers run on computers at a fixed sample time T. A zero-order hold keeps each command constant between samples. The model and the PID must be discretised. Sampling and computation add delay, which eats phase margin, so a good rule is to sample 10 to 20 times faster than the closed-loop bandwidth. Real designs deal with actuator limits, sensor noise, dead zones, delays and modelling errors. Robustness means still working when the plant is not exactly as modelled.
keyPoints: Sample 10 to 20 times faster than bandwidth.
Delay costs phase: w T radians.
Always limit actuator commands.
Feedforward plus feedback is best.
Test with model error.

courses.title: Curry-Howard-Lambek
courses.subtitle: Computational trinitarianism: logic, programs and categories
courses.author: Lilith Learning Lab
courses.description: A course on the three-way correspondence between logic, programming languages and category theory, usually called computational trinitarianism. It builds from natural deduction and the simply typed lambda calculus to cartesian closed categories, then dependent types, proof assistants and the wider family of correspondences. Math uses LaTeX. Lean examples were checked against Lean 4; other code is illustrative.

outline.title: Three views of one idea
outline.summary: Logic, programming and category theory look like three separate subjects, but they describe the same structure in three vocabularies. A proposition is a type, a proof is a program, and both are an object and a morphism in a category. The first link is the Curry-Howard correspondence between proofs and programs. The second is the Lambek correspondence between typed programs and categories. Together they are often called the Curry-Howard-Lambek correspondence, or computational trinitarianism, a slogan associated with Robert Harper. Why care? Each view brings tools to the others. Logic gives you a way to say what a program means. Programming gives a proof something you can run. Category theory gives the common language that shows the three are the same shape.
keyPoints: Three views: logic (propositions, proofs), programs (types, terms), categories (objects, morphisms).
Curry-Howard: a proof of A implies B is a function from proofs of A to proofs of B.
Lambek: a typed program is an arrow between objects in a cartesian closed category.
The correspondence is exact for constructive (intuitionistic) logic, not for classical logic out of the box.
This is the idea behind proof assistants such as Lean, Rocq and Agda.
You do not need advanced math to start: every idea in this course is introduced with small examples.

outline.title: Logic and natural deduction
outline.summary: Natural deduction is a way to write proofs as trees of small rules. Each logical connective has an introduction rule, which says how to prove it, and an elimination rule, which says how to use it. A judgment has the form Gamma proves A: from the assumptions in Gamma we can conclude A. Proving an implication means assuming the premise and proving the conclusion; that assumption is then discharged. The Brouwer-Heyting-Kolmogorov, or BHK, reading explains the rules constructively: a proof of A and B is a pair of proofs, a proof of A implies B is a method turning proofs of A into proofs of B, and there is no proof of false.
keyPoints: Propositions: atoms, true, false, and, or, implies. Negation of A is A implies false.
Every connective has an introduction rule and an elimination rule.
Implication introduction discharges an assumption.
Or elimination is proof by cases.
BHK: and is a pair, implies is a function, or is a tagged choice, false has no proof.
A proof tree is a data structure, and that is why it can later be read as a program.

outline.title: The simply typed lambda calculus
outline.summary: The lambda calculus is the smallest programming language: variables, functions written with lambda, and application. The simply typed version gives every term a type built from base types and function arrows. Three typing rules do everything: a variable has the type its context gives it, a lambda abstraction has a function type, and applying a function of type A to B to an argument of type A gives type B. Computation is beta reduction, which substitutes the argument into the body. Well-typed terms in this calculus always finish computing. That strong normalization property is the computational reflection of logical consistency, which we use in chapter 5.
keyPoints: Terms: variables, lambda abstractions, applications.
Types: base types and A to B, where the arrow is right associative.
Typing judgment: Gamma proves M has type A.
Beta: applying lambda x. M to N reduces to M with x replaced by N.
Well-typed terms cannot loop; the untyped lambda calculus can.
The identity has type A to A. The constant function K has type A to B to A.

outline.title: Propositions as types
outline.summary: Extend the lambda calculus with pairs, tagged sums, a unit type and an empty type, and every rule of natural deduction has a matching program construct. Implication becomes the function type, and becomes the pair type, or becomes the sum type, true becomes unit and false becomes the empty type. A proposition is provable exactly when its type has a closed program, we say the type is inhabited. Writing the program is writing the proof, and type checking is proof checking. Currying is the first famous example: the proposition A and B implies C is equivalent to A implies B implies C, and the two functions curry and uncurry are the proofs of each direction.
keyPoints: A and B is the pair type; its introduction is making a pair and its eliminations are fst and snd.
A or B is the sum type; its introductions are inl and inr, and its elimination is case.
A implies B is the function type; introduction is lambda, elimination is application.
True is the unit type with one value. False is the empty type with none.
Not A is the function type A to empty. A proof of a negation is a program that turns any A into a contradiction.
Provable means inhabited. Type checking is proof checking.

outline.title: Computation is proof simplification
outline.summary: A proof can contain a detour: you build a conjunction with and introduction and immediately take it apart with and elimination. Simplifying that detour away is the proof-theoretic twin of a beta reduction in a program. Running a program corresponds to normalizing a proof, and a normal proof is a program that has finished computing. Gentzen's cut elimination theorem is the same idea for his sequent calculus. Strong normalization of the simply typed lambda calculus shows that every well-typed program terminates, and as a bonus that the logic is consistent: there is no closed normal term of the empty type, so false cannot be proved.
keyPoints: A beta redex is a proof detour; reducing it removes the detour.
Normalization of a proof is evaluation of a program.
Well-typed terms of the simply typed lambda calculus always terminate.
Consistency follows: a closed proof of false would normalize to a closed normal term of the empty type, and there is none.
Type safety is progress plus preservation: well-typed programs do not get stuck.
Confluence says the normal form does not depend on the order of reduction.

outline.title: Constructive and classical logic
outline.summary: Constructive, or intuitionistic, logic is the logic that matches programs: to prove something exists you must be able to build it. It rejects the law of excluded middle, A or not A, as a general principle, because that law gives no way to decide which side holds. Classical logic adds excluded middle, or equivalently double negation elimination or Peirce's law. None of these has a program in the pure typed lambda calculus. Remarkably, Griffin discovered in 1990 that the type of Peirce's law is exactly the type of the call with current continuation operator, so control operators give classical logic a computational meaning. Classical logic is not lost: the double negation translation maps classical statements to intuitionistic ones, so constructive proofs can still carry classical reasoning, at the price of weaker conclusions.
keyPoints: Intuitionistic logic matches pure typed programs; classical logic needs more.
A to not not A is provable constructively. Not not A to A is not.
Excluded middle, double negation elimination and Peirce's law are equivalent over intuitionistic logic.
A constructive proof of an exists statement yields a witness.
call/cc has the type of Peirce's law, so classical reasoning means control effects.
Classical logic can be embedded into intuitionistic logic by a double negation translation.

outline.title: Categories: objects, arrows and composition
outline.summary: A category is a collection of objects and arrows between them. Arrows compose, composition is associative, and each object has an identity arrow that changes nothing. That is the whole definition. Many things are categories: sets and functions, a preorder where there is an arrow when one element is below another, a monoid with a single object, and, most importantly for us, a logic whose objects are propositions and whose arrows are proofs of entailment. An isomorphism is an arrow with a two-sided inverse. Category theory studies structure through arrows, not through what the objects are made of, which is exactly the right level to compare logic and programming.
keyPoints: Category: objects, morphisms, composition, identities.
Laws: (h after g) after f equals h after (g after f); id after f equals f equals f after id.
Examples: Set (sets and functions), preorders, monoids, types and programs.
A proof system is a category: objects are propositions, arrows are proofs of A entails B.
Isomorphic objects are interchangeable for every purpose the category cares about.
A functor preserves structure; later it maps syntax to meaning.

outline.title: Products, sums and exponentials
outline.summary: Products, coproducts and exponentials are characterized by universal properties: each is the best object with a given set of arrows, unique up to isomorphism. They are the category-theory versions of pairs, sums and function types. A product A x B has two projections and a pairing operation. A coproduct A + B has two injections and a case operation. An exponential B to the A has an evaluation arrow and a currying operation, which turns arrows out of C x A into arrows C to B to the A. A category with a terminal object, binary products and exponentials is called cartesian closed. Adding an initial object and coproducts makes it bicartesian closed. This is the structure needed to interpret the typed lambda calculus.
keyPoints: Product: arrows into A x B correspond to pairs of arrows into A and into B.
Coproduct: arrows out of A + B correspond to pairs of arrows out of A and out of B.
Exponential: arrows C x A to B correspond to arrows C to B to the A (currying).
Terminal is the empty product and initial is the empty coproduct.
Cartesian closed: terminal object, products, exponentials. These model simply typed lambda calculus.
In finite sets the sizes obey: product is multiplication, coproduct is addition, exponential is power.

outline.title: The Lambek correspondence
outline.summary: The Lambek correspondence reads the typed lambda calculus inside any cartesian closed category. Each type is an object, each context is a product of objects, and each term of type B in context Gamma is an arrow from the context to B. Lambda abstraction becomes currying, application becomes the evaluation arrow, and pairs become the pairing arrow. The beta and eta equations of the calculus become exactly the universal property laws of products and exponentials. Going the other way, the syntax of the calculus itself forms a cartesian closed category, so the lambda calculus is the internal language of such categories. Proofs, programs and arrows are three descriptions of the same structure, which is the slogan computational trinitarianism.
keyPoints: Types are objects. A context x1:A1, ..., xn:An is the product A1 x ... x An.
A term Gamma proves M : B is an arrow from the context to B.
Lambda is currying, application is evaluation, pairs are pairing.
Beta and eta equal the universal-property equations.
Taking sets and functions as the category gives the standard set-theoretic semantics.
Posetal case: propositions as objects, entailment as arrows, a Heyting algebra.

outline.title: Dependent types and quantifiers
outline.summary: When a type can depend on a value, propositions can talk about values too. A dependent function type, or Pi type, matches the universal quantifier. A dependent pair type, or Sigma type, matches the existential quantifier. Equality becomes an identity type whose proofs are built from reflexivity. Proof by induction is the same thing as writing a recursive function. A vector type that records its length in the type makes some bugs impossible, such as taking the head of an empty list. This is Martin-Lof type theory and the logic of Lean, Rocq and Agda. The correspondence is the same, one dimension up: propositions about values are types that depend on values.
keyPoints: For all x in A, P(x) is the Pi type: a function giving a proof of P(x) for each x.
There exists x in A with P(x) is the Sigma type: a witness plus a proof about it.
Equality is an inductive type whose constructor is reflexivity.
Induction on the natural numbers is a recursive function.
Indexing a vector by its length lets the type checker reject head of the empty vector.
Dependent types are what make programs and proofs live in one language.

outline.title: Proof assistants in practice
outline.summary: A proof assistant is a programming language whose type checker is a proof checker. You state a theorem as a type, build a term of that type, and the kernel verifies it. Lean, Rocq and Agda are well-known examples. You can write proofs directly as terms, as in earlier chapters, or use tactics, small commands that build the term step by step. Either way the kernel checks the final term, so a tactic bug cannot sneak in a wrong proof. Proof assistants have been used for verified compilers, operating system kernels and large libraries of mathematics. You can ask which axioms a proof depends on, which shows whether it used classical logic.
keyPoints: A theorem is a type, a proof is a term of that type, the kernel is the checker.
Term mode is the Curry-Howard correspondence written directly.
Tactics build terms; only the kernel is trusted.
#check shows a type, #eval runs a program, #print axioms lists assumptions.
Lean, Rocq and Agda are constructive by default.
A proof that depends on classical axioms is visible through #print axioms.

outline.title: Beyond the triangle
outline.summary: The correspondence is a pattern, not a single theorem. Change the logic and you change the programming language and the categories. Linear logic, where assumptions must be used exactly once, matches linear types and symmetric monoidal closed categories. Moggi showed that monads model computational effects such as state, exceptions and input and output. Homotopy type theory reads types as spaces and equalities as paths, and adds the univalence axiom. Categorical quantum mechanics uses categories with extra structure to describe quantum processes. You now have the core triangle. The best next steps are to try a proof assistant, to read a category theory text for programmers, and to write your own small type checker.
keyPoints: Change the logic, and the types and categories change with it.
Linear logic: use each assumption exactly once. Linear types and monoidal categories match.
Rust-style ownership is closely related to affine and linear types.
Monads package effects. Effects are not part of the pure correspondence.
Homotopy type theory: types are spaces, equalities are paths.
Next steps: use Lean, read about categories, implement a small type checker.

courses.title: Data Science and Machine Learning
courses.subtitle: NumPy, pandas, Matplotlib, scikit-learn and Keras from first principles, with Python labs and four interactive playgrounds
courses.author: Lilith Learning Lab
courses.description: A first course in data science and machine learning in the order you meet the tools: the data science workflow; NumPy arrays and vectorised thinking; pandas tables, filtering, groupby, missing data and merging; Matplotlib and exploratory data analysis; preparing data with encoding, scaling and train-test splits; linear regression and the scikit-learn estimator pattern; classification with logistic regression, k-nearest neighbours, decision trees and precision and recall; overfitting, cross-validation and tuning; clustering with k-means and PCA; neural networks and Keras; and a project workflow with fairness checks. Lessons show real library code; the Python labs rebuild each idea in plain Python so you understand what the libraries do. Four live labs let you explore plots, regression, k-NN boundaries and train a small neural network.

outline.title: What data science is, and the tools
outline.summary: Data science is the practice of asking questions of data and answering them with statistics, programming and judgement. Machine learning is the part where a program learns a pattern from examples instead of being given rules. A typical project follows a loop: ask a question, collect data, clean it, explore it, build a model, evaluate it honestly, and communicate. Most of the time goes into data, not models. Python's toolkit is layered. NumPy gives fast arrays, pandas gives tables, Matplotlib draws charts, scikit-learn gives classic machine learning, and Keras gives neural networks.
keyPoints: Question, data, clean, explore, model, evaluate, communicate.
Supervised: features X and labels y.
Regression predicts numbers; classification predicts categories.
Unsupervised: clustering, dimension reduction.
The tools: NumPy, pandas, Matplotlib, scikit-learn, Keras.

outline.title: NumPy: arrays and vectorised thinking
outline.summary: A NumPy array stores numbers of one type in a compact block, so operations on whole arrays run in fast compiled code. Its shape tells how many rows, columns and so on. Vectorisation means writing a * 2 or a + b instead of a loop. Broadcasting lets arrays of different shapes combine, for example adding a row of column means to every row. Reductions such as sum, mean and std collapse an axis. Boolean masks select elements that meet a condition.
keyPoints: a.shape, a.reshape(2, 3).
a + b, a * 2, a ** 2 act element by element.
a.mean(axis=0) averages each column.
a[a > 0] keeps positive entries.

outline.title: pandas: tables of data
outline.summary: A pandas DataFrame is a table with named columns, and a Series is a single column. You load data with read_csv, look with head and info, and select with square brackets. Filtering uses conditions such as df[df.age > 30]. Groupby splits the table by a category, applies a summary such as mean to each group, and combines the answer. Real data has missing values, shown as NaN. You can drop rows, or fill the gaps with a mean, a median or a constant. Merge joins two tables on a shared key column.
keyPoints: df['col'] is a Series; df[['a', 'b']] a DataFrame.
df[df.price > 100] filters rows.
df.groupby('city')['price'].mean().
df.isna().sum() counts missing values.
pd.merge(a, b, on='id').

outline.title: Matplotlib and exploring data
outline.summary: Exploratory data analysis (EDA) means looking at the data before modelling. Matplotlib draws the basic charts: line plots for trends, scatter plots for relationships between two variables, histograms for distributions and bar charts for categories. Summary numbers complement plots: the mean and median, the standard deviation, quartiles and the correlation coefficient between two variables. Outliers, skewed distributions and surprises found now save trouble later. Always plot before you model.
keyPoints: plt.plot(x, y); plt.scatter(x, y); plt.hist(x, bins=10).
Always label axes and add a title.
r = covariance / (sd_x sd_y).
IQR = Q3 - Q1.
Correlation is not causation.

outline.title: Preparing data for models
outline.summary: Models need numbers, in sensible ranges, with no gaps. Preparation fills or removes missing values, converts categories to numbers (one-hot encoding), and scales features so large-valued columns do not dominate. Before anything is fitted, split the data into a training set to learn from and a test set held back for an honest score. Data leakage is when information from outside the training data sneaks in, such as scaling with statistics from the test set. It gives scores that are too good to be true. Pipelines keep every step inside training.
keyPoints: X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2, random_state=0).
Fit the scaler on training data only.
One-hot: one column per category.
Impute with the training median.
Pipeline = preprocessing + model.

outline.title: Linear regression and the scikit-learn way
outline.summary: Linear regression predicts a number as a weighted sum of features plus an intercept. Least squares picks the weights that minimise the sum of squared errors between predictions and true values. Every scikit-learn model follows the same pattern: create the model, call fit on training data, call predict on new data, and call score to evaluate. The quality of a regression is measured by mean squared error (average squared mistake) and R squared (the fraction of variation explained, up to 1).
keyPoints: model = LinearRegression(); model.fit(X_train, y_train).
y_pred = model.predict(X_test).
slope = cov(x, y) / var(x); intercept = mean_y - slope mean_x.
MSE = mean((y - y_pred)^2).
R2 = 1 - SSE / SST.

outline.title: Classification: logistic regression, k-NN and trees
outline.summary: A classifier predicts a category. Logistic regression computes a weighted sum, passes it through the sigmoid function to get a probability between 0 and 1, and predicts the class if that exceeds a threshold. k-nearest neighbours predicts by letting the k closest training points vote. Decision trees ask a sequence of yes/no questions about features, choosing questions that best separate the classes. Accuracy is not enough. The confusion matrix and the measures precision, recall and F1 show what kinds of mistakes a model makes, which matters when classes are imbalanced.
keyPoints: LogisticRegression().fit(X, y).
precision = TP / (TP + FP).
recall = TP / (TP + FN).

outline.title: Overfitting, validation and tuning
outline.summary: A model that scores perfectly on its training data may just have memorised it. Overfitting means fitting the noise, so performance on new data is poor. Underfitting means the model is too simple to capture the pattern. To choose settings (hyperparameters) such as k in k-NN, use cross-validation: split the training data into folds, train on all but one, score on the held-out fold, and average. Keep the test set untouched until the end. Always compare against a baseline, such as predicting the mean or the most common class. A fancy model that barely beats the baseline is not worth deploying.
keyPoints: Training score high, validation low = overfit.
Both low = underfit.
cross_val_score(model, X, y, cv=5).
GridSearchCV tries parameter combinations.
Touch the test set once.

outline.title: Unsupervised learning: clustering and PCA
outline.summary: Unsupervised learning looks for structure without labels. Clustering groups similar items: customers, documents, genes. k-means alternates between assigning each point to its nearest centre and moving each centre to the mean of its points. Principal component analysis (PCA) finds the directions along which the data varies most and re-expresses the data in those directions, so that a few components may capture most of the information. Without labels, judging results is harder. Use inertia, the elbow method, and above all look at the clusters and ask whether they make sense.
keyPoints: KMeans(n_clusters=3).fit(X).
Assign, update, repeat until stable.
Scale features first.
PCA(n_components=2).fit_transform(X).
Elbow: plot inertia against k.

outline.title: Neural networks and Keras
outline.summary: A neuron computes a weighted sum of its inputs plus a bias and passes it through an activation function. A layer is many neurons side by side, and a network stacks layers. Without non-linear activations such as ReLU, a stack of layers would collapse into one linear model. Training adjusts the weights to reduce a loss, using gradient descent. Backpropagation applies the chain rule to find how the loss changes with every weight. One full pass over the training data is an epoch. Keras lets you describe a network in a few lines: a Sequential model of Dense layers, compile with a loss and optimiser, then fit. The key risk is overfitting, so watch validation loss.
keyPoints: Dense(16, activation='relu').
model.compile(optimizer='adam', loss='...').
model.fit(X, y, epochs=20, validation_split=0.2).
ReLU(z) = max(0, z).
Softmax turns scores into probabilities.

outline.title: Putting it together: projects, ethics and next steps
outline.summary: A good project starts with a clear question and a baseline, builds a simple model, adds complexity only when validation shows it helps, and reports results with honest uncertainty. Keep random seeds and package versions so others can repeat the work. Models learn from the data they are given, including its biases. Check performance for different groups, ask who might be harmed by errors, and be open about limits. From here: practise on real datasets, learn more statistics, try gradient boosting, deep learning for images and text, and deploy a small model.
keyPoints: Question, baseline, simple model, validate, improve.
Split before anything else.
Check subgroups, not only the average.
Set random_state; record versions.
Explain results to non-experts.

courses.title: Data Structures and Algorithms
courses.subtitle: Complexity, arrays, lists, hashing, trees, heaps, graphs, sorting, searching, recursion, dynamic programming and greedy methods, with Python labs
courses.author: Lilith Learning Lab
courses.description: The core data structures and algorithms every programmer needs, explained intuitively and practised in Python: Big-O, arrays and two pointers, linked lists, stacks and queues, hash tables, trees, heaps, graph traversal, sorting, binary search, recursion and divide and conquer, dynamic programming, and greedy algorithms with shortest paths and spanning trees. Every chapter has an ELI5 block.

outline.title: Complexity and Big-O
outline.summary: An algorithm is a step-by-step method that solves a problem. We compare algorithms not by seconds on one machine but by how the work grows as the input grows. Big-O notation describes that growth, keeping only the dominant term. Common classes, from fast to slow, are constant, logarithmic, linear, n log n, quadratic and exponential. Space complexity counts memory in the same way. Amortised analysis averages occasional expensive steps over many cheap ones. The labs count operations, compare growth rates and find the Big-O class of simple loops.
keyPoints: Order: O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n^2) < O(2^n) < O(n!).
Drop constants and lower terms: 3n^2 + 5n + 2 is O(n^2).
A single loop over n items is O(n); nested loops are O(n^2).
Halving the problem each step gives O(log n).
Appending to a growing array is O(1) amortised.
Big-O is an upper bound; Omega is a lower bound; Theta is both.

outline.title: Arrays, strings and two pointers
outline.summary: An array stores items side by side in memory, so any item is reached by its index in constant time. Inserting or deleting in the middle shifts later items and costs linear time. Dynamic arrays grow by doubling. Strings are arrays of characters. Many problems on arrays fall to simple patterns: two pointers moving from both ends, a sliding window over a range, and prefix sums that answer range-sum questions in constant time after one pass. The labs reverse in place, check palindromes, find pairs with a target sum, maximise a window and build prefix sums.
keyPoints: Access O(1); search O(n); insert or delete in the middle O(n); append O(1) amortised.
Two pointers on a sorted array finds a pair in O(n).
Sliding window turns an O(n k) scan into O(n).
Prefix sums answer sum(i..j) in O(1) after O(n) setup.
Strings are immutable in many languages: building by repeated joining costs O(n^2).
Check the empty array and one-element cases.

outline.title: Linked lists
outline.summary: A linked list is a chain of nodes; each node holds a value and a pointer to the next node. Unlike arrays there is no jump-by-index, but inserting or deleting at a known node needs only pointer changes. Classic tasks are reversing a list, finding the middle with a fast and a slow pointer, detecting a cycle and merging sorted lists. Doubly linked lists keep a pointer back as well, which makes deletion from both ends easy. The labs use arrays to simulate nodes: a list of values and a list of next-indices.
keyPoints: Insert or delete at the head: O(1).
Access or search by position: O(n).
Reverse in O(n) time and O(1) extra space.
Fast and slow pointers find the middle and detect cycles.
Linked lists use extra memory for pointers and are cache-unfriendly.
Arrays win for random access; lists win for frequent splicing.

outline.title: Stacks, queues and deques
outline.summary: A stack allows adding and removing only at one end: last in, first out, like a pile of plates. A queue adds at the back and removes from the front: first in, first out, like a line at a shop. A deque works at both ends. Stacks power undo, expression evaluation, bracket matching and the call stack of recursion. Queues power scheduling and breadth-first search. A monotonic stack solves next-greater-element problems in linear time. The labs match brackets, evaluate postfix expressions, simulate a queue and find the next greater elements.
keyPoints: All basic stack and queue operations are O(1).
A stack implemented on an array pushes and pops at the end.
A queue on an array uses head and tail indices or a deque.
Balanced brackets: push openers, pop on closers and match.
Postfix evaluation: push numbers, apply operators to the top two.
Next greater element: pop smaller items as larger ones arrive.

outline.title: Hash tables
outline.summary: A hash table stores key-value pairs and finds a key in constant time on average. A hash function turns the key into a number, which picks a bucket. Different keys can land in the same bucket, a collision, handled by chaining or probing. When the table fills up, the load factor grows and collisions rise, so the table is resized. Python dictionaries and sets are hash tables. They are the first tool for counting, grouping and finding duplicates. The labs implement a hash function, a chained table, two-sum with a dictionary and frequency counts.
keyPoints: Average insert, lookup and delete: O(1); worst case O(n).
A good hash spreads keys evenly over buckets.
Resize (double the buckets) when the load factor passes about 0.7.
