Keys must be hashable: immutable and with stable hashes.
Use a dictionary for counting, grouping and caching.
Hash tables do not keep sorted order.

outline.title: Trees and binary search trees
outline.summary: A tree is a hierarchy: a root with children, each a root of its own subtree. A binary tree allows at most two children. A binary search tree keeps smaller keys on the left and larger on the right, so search, insertion and deletion follow one path. Traversals visit every node: preorder, inorder, postorder and level order. Inorder on a BST gives sorted order. Cost depends on height; balanced trees such as AVL and red-black trees keep the height logarithmic. The labs build a BST from an array of nodes, search it, compute heights and traverse.
keyPoints: BST search, insert, delete: O(h), with h the height.
Balanced: h = O(log n); degenerate (sorted inserts): h = n.
Inorder (left, node, right) of a BST lists keys sorted.
Preorder copies a tree; postorder deletes it bottom-up.
Level order uses a queue.
AVL and red-black trees rebalance with rotations.

outline.title: Heaps and priority queues
outline.summary: A priority queue always serves the item with the highest priority next, like an emergency room. A binary heap implements it as a complete binary tree stored in an array where each parent is no larger than its children (a min-heap). Push adds at the end and sifts up; pop removes the top, moves the last item to the root and sifts down. Both take logarithmic time. Heapify builds a heap from n items in linear time, and heap sort uses it. Heaps power Dijkstra's algorithm and top-k queries. The labs implement push and pop, heapify, heap sort and a top-k selector.
keyPoints: Array layout: parent of i is (i-1)//2; children are 2i+1 and 2i+2.
Push and pop are O(log n); peek is O(1).
Heapify is O(n); heap sort is O(n log n) and in place.
A min-heap gives the smallest quickly, not full sorted order.
Top-k of n items: O(n log k) with a size-k heap.
Dijkstra and Huffman coding use heaps.

outline.title: Graphs and traversal
outline.summary: Graphs model networks of things and links. Stored as adjacency lists, they use memory proportional to vertices plus edges. Two traversals underlie almost every graph algorithm: breadth-first search with a queue and depth-first search with a stack or recursion. A visited set keeps traversals from looping. BFS finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs, DFS finds connected components, detects cycles and gives topological orders of dependency graphs. The labs build adjacency lists, run BFS and DFS, count components and sort tasks topologically.
keyPoints: BFS and DFS both run in O(V + E).
BFS gives fewest-edge paths in unweighted graphs.
DFS timestamps help find cycles and components.
Adjacency lists suit sparse graphs; matrices suit dense ones.
Topological order exists only for DAGs.
Always mark a vertex visited when you first reach it.

outline.title: Sorting
outline.summary: Sorting puts items in order and makes many other tasks easier, such as searching and finding duplicates. Simple methods like bubble and insertion sort take quadratic time. Merge sort and quick sort take n log n. Merge sort splits, sorts each half and merges, and it is stable. Quick sort partitions around a pivot and is fast on average. Comparison sorting cannot beat n log n, but counting sort uses the key values to reach linear time for small integer keys. The labs implement insertion sort, merge, quick sort partition and counting sort.
keyPoints: Insertion sort: O(n^2) worst, O(n) on nearly sorted data.
Merge sort: O(n log n), O(n) extra space, stable.
Quick sort: O(n log n) average, in place, not stable.
Heap sort: O(n log n), in place.
Counting and radix sort: linear for bounded keys.
Library sorts (Timsort) combine merge and insertion sort.

outline.title: Searching and binary search
outline.summary: Linear search checks every item, taking linear time. If the data is sorted, binary search compares with the middle item and discards half the range each step, taking logarithmic time. Binary search is easy to describe and easy to get wrong. A clear invariant, the answer lies within the current range, prevents off-by-one errors. Variants find the first or last position of a value. You can also binary search over an answer, such as the smallest speed that finishes in time. The labs write binary search, find insertion points, count occurrences and search on an answer.
keyPoints: Binary search needs sorted data and random access.
Time O(log n): 1000 items need at most 10 steps; a billion need 30.
Use mid = lo + (hi - lo) // 2 in languages with fixed-width integers.
Decide the invariant first, then write the loop.
Lower bound gives insertion points and counts via two searches.
Search on answer works whenever a yes/no test is monotonic.

outline.title: Recursion and divide and conquer
outline.summary: Recursion solves a problem by solving smaller versions of the same problem. Every recursive function needs a base case that stops it and a step that makes progress toward it. The call stack remembers pending work. Divide and conquer splits a problem into parts, solves them recursively and combines the answers. Merge sort and binary search are examples. The cost is written as a recurrence, and the master theorem gives its solution. Backtracking explores choices and undoes them to enumerate subsets, permutations and puzzles. The labs write recursive functions, count recurrence cost and enumerate subsets and permutations.
keyPoints: Always write the base case first.
T(n) = a T(n/b) + O(n^d): compare a with b^d (master theorem).
Binary search: T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1) = O(log n).
Merge sort: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) = O(n log n).
Naive Fibonacci is exponential; caching makes it linear.
Subsets: 2^n; permutations: n!.

outline.title: Dynamic programming
outline.summary: Dynamic programming solves problems whose recursive solution repeats the same subproblems. By storing each answer once, either top-down with a cache or bottom-up with a table, exponential work becomes polynomial. The recipe is to define the state, write the transition that builds a state from smaller ones, set the base cases and read off the answer. Classic problems include Fibonacci, coin change, the knapsack, the longest common subsequence and edit distance. The labs solve Fibonacci, coin change, 0/1 knapsack, longest common subsequence and edit distance.
keyPoints: Cost is (number of states) x (cost per transition).
Fibonacci: F(n) = F(n-1) + F(n-2); O(n) with a cache.
Coin change: ways[a] sums ways[a - coin] over coins.
Knapsack: best[i][w] = max(skip item, take item).
LCS: match extends the diagonal; else take the max of two neighbours.
Space can often be reduced to one or two rows.

outline.title: Greedy algorithms, shortest paths and spanning trees
outline.summary: A greedy algorithm makes the best-looking choice at each step and never looks back. It is fast and simple, and for the right problems it is provably optimal. The proof usually shows that an optimal solution can be changed to include the greedy choice. Classic greedy results: choosing the most intervals by earliest finish time, Huffman coding, Dijkstra's shortest paths with non-negative weights, and Kruskal's and Prim's minimum spanning trees. Union-find is the data structure that makes Kruskal fast. The labs schedule intervals, run Dijkstra, build a minimum spanning tree with union-find and compute Huffman code cost.
keyPoints: Interval scheduling: sort by finish time, take every compatible interval.
Dijkstra with a heap: O((V + E) log V); needs non-negative weights.
Kruskal: sort edges, add if they join different components; O(E log E).
Prim: grow a tree from a vertex by the cheapest edge out.
Union-find with path compression is almost O(1) per operation.
Greedy fails for coin change with odd coin sets and for knapsack.

courses.title: Decision Models and Generalised Classifiers
courses.subtitle: From BERT-style classifiers to the new System One decision models: typed questions, calibration, evaluation and routing, with Python labs
courses.author: Lilith Learning Lab
courses.description: A hands-on introduction to generalised classifiers and the new category of decision models, also called System One models. Learn how classifiers, encoders and ModernBERT work; zero-shot and embedding classification; the typed-question interface of boolean, choice and score answers; the masked-option encoder design reported for Laya; the prefill-only decoder design reported for Clef, with joint and pointer heads and KV-cache reuse; calibration with temperature scaling, ECE, Brier score and log loss; evaluation on your own data; and routing, cascades, guardrails and escalation in real systems. The field is only weeks old, so vendor figures are marked as reported and the course stresses durable concepts. Every chapter has Python labs verified in the built-in interpreter, plus a decision playground and a calibration lab.

outline.title: From classifiers to decision models
outline.summary: A classifier reads input and picks a label. A decision model is the newer idea of a small model that answers a typed question about some input, such as yes or no, one of these options, or a score from 0 to 1, in a single forward pass and with calibrated probabilities. The pitch is a split of labour. Fast System One models make the many routine decisions cheaply, and slow System Two models, the large reasoning LLMs, handle what is hard or uncertain. The idea is new, so products and numbers change quickly and vendor claims need checking. This course starts with the durable concepts: encoders, calibration, evaluation and routing. Vendor details are marked as reported as of late 2026.
keyPoints: Typed answer: yes/no, choice, score.
One forward pass, no chain of thought.
Probabilities must be calibrated.
Route easy cases here, hard cases to an LLM.
Treat vendor numbers as claims to verify.

outline.title: Encoders and generalised classifiers: from BERT to ModernBERT
outline.summary: Encoders turn text into contextual vectors. A small head on top turns a vector into a label. Fine-tuned on a few thousand examples, this is the classic classifier and still the efficient choice for many tasks. Generalised classifiers avoid retraining per label set: zero-shot natural language inference frames each label as a hypothesis to test, embedding models match text to label descriptions, and cross-encoders score a text and a candidate together. ModernBERT, released at the end of 2024, updates the BERT encoder with rotary positions, alternating local and global attention, unpadding, FlashAttention and an eight-thousand-token context. It is the base on which Laya is reported to be built.
keyPoints: Encoder + head = classifier.
NLI zero-shot: premise = text, hypothesis = 'This is about X'.
Bi-encoder is fast, cross-encoder is accurate.
ModernBERT: long context, RoPE, FlashAttention.
Fine-tuning needs hundreds to thousands of labels.

outline.title: The typed-question interface
outline.summary: A decision model is queried with a structured request: the input, a context or state, optional criteria, and a typed question. The type fixes the output: a probability for yes or no, a distribution over options for a choice, or a bounded score. Because the answer comes from a head rather than generated text, it is always well formed. The caller sets the policy: thresholds, how to treat low confidence and when to escalate. Good questions are specific, mutually exclusive and checkable. Designing the question and options is the main job of the person using a decision model.
keyPoints: Boolean: P(yes).
Choice: probabilities sum to 1.
Score: a value in a range, such as 0 to 1.
Put hard rules in criteria, not in hope.
Options should not overlap.

outline.title: Masked-option encoder designs (the Laya pattern)
outline.summary: One design for a decision model puts the input and the options into a single encoder prompt, each option followed by a mask token. After one pass, the vector at each mask is scored by a small head, and a softmax across the masks gives the option probabilities. Laya is reported to follow this pattern on a ModernBERT base of about 421 million parameters, offered openly. Details come from vendor material and may change; the pattern is what matters. Such a design is fast and small but limited by the encoder's context, its pretraining and the amount of adaptation. Specialised domains usually need fine-tuning.
keyPoints: [input] option A [MASK] option B [MASK] ...
score_i = head(vector at mask i).
p = softmax(scores / T).
Reported: ModernBERT base, 421M parameters.
Fine-tune for domain-specific decisions.

outline.title: Decoder-based decision models (the Clef pattern)
outline.summary: The other route builds a decision model on a decoder language model but never generates text. It runs only the prefill pass over the prompt, then reads the final hidden state with small heads. That keeps the language model's knowledge and instruction following while skipping slow token-by-token generation. Clef, from Cloudflare, is reported to use Qwen-based models of roughly 9 and 27 billion parameters with a joint schema head that fills several typed answers at once, and a pointer head that selects a span or item from the input. A related Kev design is described as a pointer head. Reported benefits are speed, typed outputs and shared computation through KV-cache reuse. Reports differ between sources, so verify specifics before relying on them.
keyPoints: Decoder + heads, no generation.
Cost = one prefill.
Pointer: choose among input items.
Shared prefix: reuse the KV cache.
Reported sizes: 9B and 27B (Clef).

outline.title: Calibration: making probabilities trustworthy
outline.summary: A decision model is only useful if its probabilities mean something: of the cases where it says 90 percent, about 90 percent should be right. Neural networks are often overconfident, so we measure and repair calibration. Expected calibration error bins predictions by confidence and averages the gap between confidence and accuracy. Brier score and log loss are proper scoring rules that reward honest probabilities. Temperature scaling fixes much overconfidence with a single parameter fitted on held-out data. Some vendors train for calibration directly, with reinforcement learning on calibration objectives; reports describe this as a selling point, which you should test yourself.
keyPoints: ECE = sum over bins of (n_bin / n) |acc - conf|.
Brier = mean (p - y)^2.
Log loss = -mean log p(true).
Fit T on a validation set, not the test set.
Calibrate after fine-tuning.

outline.title: Evaluating decision models
outline.summary: Do not rely on a vendor's headline numbers. Reports in this field include a Decision Index and results on public tasks such as BANKING77 intent classification, but they are self-reported and may not match your data. Build a labelled test set from your own traffic, measure accuracy, calibration, per-class errors, cost-weighted loss and latency at your batch size, and compare against a simple baseline and against a large LLM. Check the effect of fine-tuning: a few hundred of your own examples often add the most. Keep a separate untouched test set and watch for leakage.
keyPoints: Own data first.
Report accuracy, calibration, latency and cost.
Compare with a baseline and with an LLM.
Per-class precision and recall.
Re-test on every model update.

outline.title: Decision models in real systems
outline.summary: The usual home for a decision model is a cascade: the fast model decides most cases, the uncertain ones escalate to a large LLM or a human, and the outcomes feed back into the evaluation data. Cost and latency fall while quality is kept by the thresholds. Typical uses are routing support tickets and agent tool calls, content and policy guardrails, verifying that an answer matches its sources, relevance filtering, and workflow gates. Open models can be run locally for privacy. Plan for failure: distribution shift, adversarial inputs, over-trust in confidence and silent changes in vendor models. Humans stay responsible for high-stakes decisions.
keyPoints: Fast model first, escalate when unsure.
Log every decision and outcome.
Re-calibrate when inputs drift.
Local serving for private data.
Humans own high-stakes calls.

courses.title: DevOps from Scratch: Git, CI, Containers, Kubernetes and Reliability
courses.subtitle: From commit to production, with a working simulator of git, docker, kubectl and a pipeline in every lab
courses.author: Lilith Learning Lab
courses.description: A condensed, original course on DevOps. It covers the culture and the DORA metrics, Git and branching, continuous integration, build artifacts and semantic versioning, containers and Dockerfiles, Kubernetes, infrastructure as code, configuration and secrets, release strategies, monitoring, SLOs and incidents, DevSecOps, and a capstone that takes a change from bug to production. Every shell lab runs a Linux-like simulator inside the app, with simplified git, docker, kubectl, make, a CI runner and an infrastructure tool. These are teaching simulators, not the real programs, so they behave like the real tools in the common cases only. Credits: BusyBox (GPL-2.0) and the Jade Agent Kit (MIT).

outline.title: What DevOps is
outline.summary: DevOps is a way of working in which the people who build software and the people who run it share responsibility and tools. The goal is to deliver changes to users quickly, safely and repeatedly. It rests on a few habits: keep everything in version control, automate builds, tests and deployment, ship small changes often, and watch what happens in production so you can learn fast. Four measures from the DORA research show how a team is doing: how often it deploys, how long a change takes to reach users, how often changes fail, and how fast it recovers.
keyPoints: Share responsibility between building and running.
Automate everything you do more than twice.
Small, frequent changes are safer than big rare ones.
Measure: frequency, lead time, failure rate, recovery time.

outline.title: Git: tracking every change
outline.summary: Git is a distributed version control system. It records every change as a commit, a snapshot of your files with a message, and links the commits into a history. The everyday cycle is: edit files, git add to stage them, git commit to record them. git status tells you where things stand and git log shows the history. A commit has an id, an author, a message and a pointer to its parent. That chain of parents is the history, and it is what makes undo, review and collaboration possible.
keyPoints: Edit, add, commit.
git status first, always.
Write commit messages that say why.
Commits are cheap; commit often.

outline.title: Branches, merges and conflicts
outline.summary: A branch is a lightweight pointer to a commit. You create one to work on a feature without disturbing the main line, then merge it back when it is ready. If main has not moved since you branched, merging just slides the pointer forward, which is a fast-forward. If both sides changed, git makes a merge commit with two parents. When both sides changed the same lines, git cannot decide and marks a conflict. You edit the file, choose the right result, add it and commit.
keyPoints: Branch for every piece of work.
Keep branches short-lived.
A conflict is normal, not an error.
Test before and after merging.

outline.title: Continuous integration
outline.summary: Continuous integration means merging small changes into the shared branch often, and letting an automated pipeline build and test every one of them. A pipeline is a list of stages that run in order, such as build, test and package. If any stage fails, the pipeline stops and tells you which one, so a broken change never reaches the main line. Good pipelines are fast, reliable and the single source of truth about whether the code works.
keyPoints: Run the pipeline on every commit.
Fail fast: cheap checks first.
A red pipeline blocks the merge.
Fix flaky tests, do not ignore them.

outline.title: Build, test and release artifacts
outline.summary: A build turns source code into an artifact: a package, a binary or a container image. The same artifact should travel unchanged through every environment, so what you tested is what you ship. Version numbers follow semantic versioning: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. Increase PATCH for fixes, MINOR for compatible features and MAJOR for breaking changes. Tests come in layers: many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests and a handful of end-to-end checks. The pipeline runs them from fastest to slowest.
keyPoints: Build once, deploy many times.
Never rebuild for production.
PATCH fixes, MINOR features, MAJOR breaks.
Many unit tests, few end-to-end tests.

outline.title: Containers and Docker
outline.summary: A container packages an application with everything it needs to run, and runs it isolated from other processes using features of the Linux kernel. It starts in a fraction of a second and behaves the same on any machine. An image is the read-only template, a container is a running instance of it. You pull images from a registry, run them, stop them and remove them. Ports are mapped from the host to the container, so a web server inside can be reached from outside.
keyPoints: Image is the recipe, container is the dish.
docker run image starts a container.
-p host:container publishes a port.
Containers are disposable: keep data outside.

outline.title: Dockerfiles and image layers
outline.summary: A Dockerfile is a recipe for an image. Each instruction adds a layer: FROM chooses the base, COPY adds files, RUN executes a command during the build, and CMD says what runs when the container starts. Docker caches layers. If an instruction and everything before it are unchanged, the cached layer is reused. Once one step changes, every step after it is rebuilt. So order matters: put things that change rarely, such as installing dependencies, before things that change often, such as your own code.
keyPoints: Order from least to most frequently changing.
Copy requirements before code.
Keep images small.
Do not run as root in the container.

outline.title: Kubernetes
outline.summary: Kubernetes runs containers across many machines. You do not start containers by hand. You describe the state you want, for example three copies of this image, and Kubernetes works constantly to make reality match. A pod is the smallest unit and holds one or more containers. A deployment keeps a set number of identical pods running and rolls out new versions. A service gives them one stable address. Because Kubernetes compares desired and actual state in a loop, it heals itself: if a pod dies, a new one appears.
keyPoints: Declare the desired state; Kubernetes converges.
Deployments own pods; services find pods.
Scale with replicas.
Roll back with rollout undo.

outline.title: Infrastructure as code
outline.summary: Infrastructure as code means servers, networks and databases are described in files and created by tools, not by clicking in a console. The files live in version control and are reviewed like any other code. A good tool works in two steps. Plan compares the files with what exists and shows the difference. Apply makes the world match the files. Running apply twice changes nothing the second time. That property, idempotence, is what makes automation safe to run again and again.
keyPoints: Describe, plan, review, apply.
Never hand-edit what code manages.
Plans are reviewed like code.
Apply twice must change nothing.

outline.title: Configuration and secrets
outline.summary: The same build runs in development, staging and production, so what differs between them must be configuration kept outside the code: addresses, feature flags and credentials. Environment variables are the simplest way to pass configuration into a program. Settings are layered: defaults in code, then a config file, then environment variables, with later layers winning. Secrets such as passwords and API keys need extra care: never commit them, store them in a secrets manager, give them the least access needed and rotate them.
keyPoints: Code is the same everywhere; config differs.
Never commit secrets.
Layer settings: defaults, file, environment.
Rotate and limit every secret.

outline.title: Continuous delivery and release strategies
outline.summary: Continuous delivery means every change that passes the pipeline could be released at any moment. Continuous deployment goes one step further and releases automatically. Release safely by exposing a change gradually. A canary sends a small share of traffic to the new version and watches the errors. Blue-green keeps two full environments and switches between them. Feature flags separate deploying code from turning a feature on. Whatever the method, you need a fast, rehearsed way back: a rollback must be one command, not a project.
keyPoints: Deploy is not release: flags separate them.
Start with a few percent, then widen.
Watch error rate and latency during rollout.
Practise the rollback.

outline.title: Monitoring and observability
outline.summary: You cannot run what you cannot see. Observability rests on three kinds of data: metrics, which are numbers over time; logs, which are records of events; and traces, which follow a single request through many services. For averages, use percentiles. The 99th percentile latency says how slow the slowest one in a hundred requests is, and that is what unhappy users feel. Alert on symptoms that users notice, such as errors and slowness, not on every internal number, or people will learn to ignore the pager.
keyPoints: Metrics, logs and traces answer different questions.
Average hides pain; look at p95 and p99.
Alert on user-facing symptoms.
Every alert needs an action.

outline.title: SLOs, error budgets and incidents
outline.summary: A service level indicator, SLI, is a measurement of how well a service works, for instance the share of requests that succeed. A service level objective, SLO, is the target for it, such as 99.9 percent over 30 days. The gap between perfect and the SLO is the error budget. While budget remains you can ship quickly; when it runs out you slow down and fix reliability. When something breaks, handle it as an incident: one person leads, you communicate, you restore service first and investigate afterwards, then write a blameless postmortem.
keyPoints: 100% is the wrong target.
Budget = 100% minus the SLO.
Spend budget on change; protect it when low.
Restore first, find the cause second.

outline.title: DevSecOps and the software supply chain
outline.summary: DevSecOps builds security into the pipeline instead of adding it at the end. Scanning for secrets, vulnerable dependencies and risky configuration runs on every change, where fixes are cheap. Modern software is mostly other people's code. A software bill of materials lists every component so that when a flaw is announced you can find out at once whether you use it. Protect the pipeline itself: sign artifacts, use short-lived credentials, run containers as non-root users and give each job the least access it needs.
keyPoints: Scan every commit for secrets and known vulnerable dependencies.
Pin and update dependencies.
Run containers as non-root.
Sign what you build.

outline.title: Capstone: ship a change end to end
outline.summary: Put the whole path together. A small project has a bug, a pipeline, a Dockerfile and a Kubernetes manifest. You will fix the bug, make the pipeline pass, build a versioned image and roll it out. Work like a DevOps engineer: change one thing at a time, check the result of each step, and keep everything in version control. When the checklist is complete you will have touched version control, CI, containers and orchestration on one change.
keyPoints: Commit, test, package, deploy.
Tag images with a version, not latest.
Verify after rollout.
Keep the previous version ready.

courses.title: discord.py: Building Discord Bots
courses.subtitle: Clients, intents, commands, cogs, slash commands, views, modals, tasks and deployment, with Python labs
courses.author: Lilith Learning Lab
courses.description: A hands-on course based on the open-source discord.py library (github.com/Rapptz/discord.py, MIT), documented here as of its 2.8.0a development version. Learn how a bot connects, which intents it needs, how prefix and slash commands work, how to organise code with cogs and extensions, build buttons, selects and modals, run background tasks, log and handle errors, and keep tokens and permissions safe. Labs run offline and simulate the library's rules in Python, so no Discord account is needed.

outline.title: The client, events and the gateway
outline.summary: discord.py is an asynchronous Python library for the Discord API. You create a Client, give it intents, register event handlers, and call run with your bot token. The client keeps a websocket connection, called the gateway, open to Discord. Discord pushes events down it, such as a message being sent, and the library calls your matching coroutine. The repository at github.com/Rapptz/discord.py was at version 2.8.0a in its development branch when this course was written. The quickstart says to avoid naming your own file discord.py.
keyPoints: Create intents, then Client(intents=intents), then client.run(token).
Handlers are coroutines named on_ready, on_message and so on.
Always ignore your own messages so the bot does not reply to itself.
Never name your script discord.py.
Snowflake time = (id >> 22) + 1420070400000 milliseconds.

outline.title: Intents and the developer portal
outline.summary: Intents tell Discord which groups of events your bot wants. Fewer intents mean less data, less memory, and fewer events to process. Three intents are privileged: presences, members and message_content. You must switch each on in the Bot tab of the developer portal and also enable it in code. Enabling only one side fails. Bots in more than 100 guilds need verification and approval before they can use privileged intents. Intents.default() turns on everything except the privileged three.
keyPoints: Intents.default() leaves out presences, members and message_content.
Privileged intents need the portal toggle and the code flag.
Without message_content, message.content is empty for most messages.
Intents.none() plus the ones you need is the leanest start.
Over 100 guilds: apply for verification.

outline.title: commands.Bot and prefix commands
outline.summary: The commands extension adds a Bot class that extends Client with a command system. Messages that start with a prefix are parsed into a command name and arguments. Each command is a coroutine whose first parameter is a Context. Annotations such as int or discord.Member convert the text arguments for you, and checks decide who may run the command. Errors raised by conversion or checks arrive in an error handler as subclasses of CommandError, so you can answer with a friendly message instead of a traceback.
keyPoints: commands.Bot(command_prefix='!', intents=intents).
A command is async def name(ctx, ...) with @bot.command().
Quote arguments with spaces: !say "hello world".
Annotations convert: int, float, discord.Member, discord.TextChannel.
Handle on_command_error for BadArgument and MissingPermissions.

outline.title: Cogs, extensions and setup_hook
outline.summary: As a bot grows, one file becomes unmanageable. Cogs are classes that group related commands and listeners, and extensions are modules that can be loaded, unloaded and reloaded while the bot runs. An extension defines an async setup function that receives the bot and adds cogs. You load it with bot.load_extension('cogs.fun'), usually inside setup_hook, which runs once before the bot connects. Reloading an extension picks up new code without a restart, which makes development fast. A cog may also define cog-wide checks and an error handler.
keyPoints: class Fun(commands.Cog) holds commands; add it with await bot.add_cog(Fun(bot)).
Extension file defines async def setup(bot).
Load in setup_hook: await self.load_extension('cogs.fun').
Use @commands.Cog.listener() for events inside cogs.
load, unload and reload raise errors if already or not loaded.

outline.title: Slash commands and the command tree
outline.summary: Slash commands are registered with Discord, so users see them in a menu with descriptions and typed options. They arrive as interactions, not as messages, so they need no message content intent. You keep them in an app_commands.CommandTree, decorate functions with tree.command, and call tree.sync to publish them. Syncing to one test guild is instant, while global commands can take up to an hour to appear. Your handler receives an Interaction. You must respond within three seconds, either with response.send_message, or by deferring first if the work takes longer.
keyPoints: Create self.tree = app_commands.CommandTree(self) in your Client.
Sync in setup_hook: copy_global_to(guild=...), then sync(guild=...).
Respond to an interaction within 3 seconds.
Use describe and rename for friendly options.
Use ephemeral=True for private replies.

outline.title: Views, buttons and select menus
outline.summary: A View is a container for interactive components such as buttons and select menus. You attach it to a message, and each component calls one of your coroutines when a user presses it. Views time out after 180 seconds by default, after which the buttons stop working. A persistent view sets timeout to None, gives every item a custom_id and is registered at startup so it survives restarts. Discord limits a message to five rows with five buttons each, so at most 25 buttons, and a select menu takes a whole row.
keyPoints: Subclass discord.ui.View and decorate methods with discord.ui.button.
Handler signature: (self, interaction, button).
Respond with interaction.response.edit_message(view=self).
Default timeout is 180 seconds; use None plus custom_id for persistence.
Maximum 25 buttons: five rows of five.

outline.title: Modals, embeds and message limits
outline.summary: A Modal is a popup form. You declare TextInput fields on a class, show the modal in response to an interaction, and receive the typed answers in on_submit. An Embed is a formatted card with a title, description, fields, colour and footer. Discord limits sizes: a description up to 4096 characters, field values up to 1024, a footer up to 2048, at most 25 fields, and 6000 characters across the whole embed. Ordinary message text is limited to 2000 characters, so long output must be split.
keyPoints: Modal subclass with title and TextInput attributes.
Show it with interaction.response.send_modal(Feedback()).
Embed limits: 4096 description, 1024 field value, 25 fields, 6000 total.
Message text limit is 2000 characters.
A modal can only be opened from an interaction, not from a plain message.

outline.title: Background tasks, logging and error handling
outline.summary: The tasks extension runs a coroutine on a fixed schedule, such as every 60 seconds. You start it in setup_hook and make it wait until the bot is ready before it touches channels. discord.py uses the standard logging module. By default client.run sets up a handler and a level for you; you can pass your own log_handler and log_level, or pass log_handler=None to configure logging yourself. Network calls fail in predictable ways. Forbidden means the bot lacks access, NotFound means the object is gone, and HTTPException covers other API errors. Retrying should back off instead of hammering Discord.
keyPoints: @tasks.loop(seconds=60) repeats; start with .start() in setup_hook.
@loop.before_loop: await self.wait_until_ready().
client.run(token, log_handler=handler, log_level=logging.DEBUG).
log_handler=None disables the default setup.
Catch Forbidden, NotFound and HTTPException around API calls.

outline.title: Permissions, tokens and deployment
outline.summary: Your bot token is a password. Anyone who has it can act as your bot. Keep it out of source control and out of screenshots, and read it from an environment variable or a secrets file. Discord permissions are bit flags combined in one integer. Administrator overrides all of the others. Ask for the minimum your bot needs when you generate the invite link, and check the bot's own permissions before you act. If a token leaks, regenerate it in the developer portal at once. A deployed bot needs a process manager or container that restarts it after a crash and keeps logs.
keyPoints: Never hardcode or commit the token; read it from the environment.
If it leaks, reset it in the developer portal immediately.
Permissions are bits: administrator is 1 << 3, send_messages 1 << 11.
Administrator overrides every other permission.
Run under a supervisor with logs and a restart policy.

courses.title: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO)
courses.subtitle: From RLHF to a simple preference loss, with Python labs
courses.author: Lilith Learning Lab
courses.description: DPO (Rafailov et al., NeurIPS 2023) derived step by step: preference data and Bradley-Terry, the KL-regularised objective and its optimal policy, the loss, its gradient, implementation with sequence log-probabilities, choosing beta, and later variants (background). Theory plus Python labs.

outline.title: From RLHF to DPO
outline.summary: Direct Preference Optimization, DPO, is a way to align a language model with human preferences using a simple loss on pairs of responses, one preferred and one rejected. It was introduced by Rafael Rafailov and colleagues at Stanford, NeurIPS 2023. The usual route, RLHF, trains a reward model and then uses reinforcement learning such as PPO. DPO shows that, under the standard assumptions, the same goal can be reached by training the language model directly with a binary cross-entropy loss. No separate reward model and no sampling loop are needed. This course derives the loss step by step and builds each part in small Python labs.
keyPoints: DPO: Rafailov, Sharma, Mitchell, Ermon, Manning and Finn, NeurIPS 2023.
Input: triples (x, y_w, y_l) with a winner and a loser.
Loss: -log sigmoid(beta (log pi/pi_ref (y_w) - log pi/pi_ref (y_l))).
No reward model, no RL sampling during training.
It assumes the Bradley-Terry model of preferences.
It needs log-probabilities from the policy and the frozen reference.

outline.title: Preference data and the Bradley-Terry model
outline.summary: Human feedback usually comes as comparisons: given two responses, which is better? The Bradley-Terry model turns this into probability. If response A has reward r_A and B has r_B, the chance that A is preferred is the sigmoid of the reward gap. A reward model is trained by maximising the log-likelihood of the observed choices. RLHF does this as a separate stage. DPO reuses the same likelihood but with the reward expressed through the policy. The labs compute sigmoid, preference probabilities and the log-likelihood of a dataset.
keyPoints: p(y_w beats y_l) = sigmoid(r(y_w) - r(y_l)).
sigmoid(0) = 0.5; large positive gap gives probability near 1.
Training a reward model: minimise -log sigmoid(r_w - r_l).
Only reward differences matter, not absolute values.
Real labels are noisy; Bradley-Terry treats them as probabilistic.
The model assumes preferences come from a single underlying score.

outline.title: The KL-regularised objective and its optimal policy
outline.summary: The RL stage of RLHF maximises expected reward while keeping the policy near the reference model: a reward term minus beta times the KL divergence from the reference. This problem has a closed-form solution. The optimal policy is the reference policy reweighted by the exponential of reward over beta, then normalised. Responses with high reward get more probability, with beta controlling how strongly. The normaliser, called the partition function, is expensive to compute for language models. DPO's trick, in the next chapter, is that it will cancel.
keyPoints: max over pi of E_{y~pi}[r(x,y)] - beta KL(pi(.|x) || pi_ref(.|x)).
Solution: pi*(y|x) = pi_ref(y|x) exp(r(x,y)/beta) / Z(x).
beta -> infinity: pi* approaches pi_ref; beta -> 0: pi* concentrates on the highest-reward response.
Z(x) sums over all possible responses, which is intractable for language models.
The same form appears in maximum-entropy RL and in statistical physics (Boltzmann).
The paper derives this as a known result in the appendix.

outline.title: Deriving the DPO loss
outline.summary: Take the optimal policy formula and solve it for the reward: r equals beta times the log of the policy over the reference, plus beta times log Z of x. The reward is expressed through the policy. Substitute into the Bradley-Terry model. The reward gap between the winner and the loser contains log Z of x twice, with opposite signs, so it cancels. The preference probability depends only on the policy and reference. Maximum likelihood on the observed preferences then gives the DPO loss.
keyPoints: From pi*: r(x,y) = beta log(pi*(y|x)/pi_ref(y|x)) + beta log Z(x).
Gap: r(x,y_w) - r(x,y_l) = beta log(pi*(y_w)/pi_ref(y_w)) - beta log(pi*(y_l)/pi_ref(y_l)).
Z(x) cancels because both responses answer the same prompt.
Replace pi* by the trainable pi_theta and maximise the Bradley-Terry likelihood.
The result is the DPO loss; the policy network is the reward model.
The paper states the language model is secretly a reward model.

outline.title: The gradient: who gets updated and how much
outline.summary: Differentiating the DPO loss gives a clean result. For each pair, increase the log-probability of the winner and decrease that of the loser, and scale the step by a weight. The weight is the sigmoid of the negative margin: large when the implicit reward model ranks the pair wrongly, small when it is already right. This dynamic weighting is important. The paper reports that a naive version without it, which simply pushes winners up and losers down, can cause the model to degenerate. The labs compute the weight, the gradient with respect to log-probabilities and one update step on a small table-based policy.
keyPoints: grad L = -beta * w * (grad log pi(y_w) - grad log pi(y_l)), averaged over pairs.
w = sigmoid(r_hat(y_l) - r_hat(y_w)) = 1 - sigmoid(margin).
When the margin is large and positive, w is near 0: the pair is already satisfied.
When the margin is negative, w approaches 1: a strong update.
Scaling by beta means larger beta takes larger steps in log-probability, for the same learning rate.
The paper notes the importance of the weight in avoiding degeneration.

outline.title: Implementing DPO: sequences, batches and practicalities
outline.summary: A response is a sequence of tokens. Its log-probability is the sum of the log-probabilities of its tokens given the prompt and the earlier tokens. DPO needs this sum for the chosen and the rejected response under both the policy and the reference. Prompt tokens must be masked, so that only response tokens contribute. Reference log-probabilities do not change, so they can be computed once and stored. In the paper's experiments beta of 0.1 was a typical value. Learning rates are small, since the policy starts near the reference. A supervised fine-tuning stage usually comes first.
keyPoints: log pi(y|x) = sum over response tokens of log pi(y_t | x, y_<t).
Only response tokens count; prompt and padding are masked.
Reference log-probabilities can be precomputed once.
Common beta about 0.1 (the paper explores 0.1 to 0.5 in places); tuned per task.
DPO usually starts from a supervised fine-tuned model that also serves as the reference.
Longer responses have lower total log-probability, which can interact with the loss.

outline.title: Choosing beta and understanding behaviour
outline.summary: Beta is the most important knob. Small beta lets the policy move far from the reference, which can give larger gains and more risk. Large beta keeps it close. The right value depends on the data and the model. DPO is trained offline on a fixed set of pairs. If the responses came from another model, the reference may give them very low probability. Many practitioners therefore fine-tune on the preferred responses first. A reported effect, sometimes called likelihood displacement, is that DPO can lower the probability of both the chosen and the rejected response, so long as the gap grows. This is background knowledge from later analyses.
keyPoints: Larger beta keeps the policy closer to the reference.
Training on pairs not generated by the reference can cause distribution shift.
Margins can grow without bound; with noisy labels this overfits.
Both chosen and rejected log-probs may decline (later analyses; background).
Track: loss, reward accuracy, margin, chosen/rejected rewards, KL to reference.
Final evaluation uses held-out prompts and win rates against a baseline.

outline.title: Variants, relatives and where DPO fits
outline.summary: DPO started a family. IPO modifies the loss to avoid overfitting. KTO works with thumbs-up or thumbs-down labels on single responses. ORPO combines supervised fine-tuning and preference learning without a reference model. SimPO uses length-normalised log-probabilities. Online versions sample fresh responses during training. GRPO keeps the reinforcement learning loop but replaces the value model by group statistics. All of these are later work and are background knowledge in this course. Details differ and evidence about which is best is mixed; treat comparisons with some care. The labs implement small versions of three of these ideas.
keyPoints: IPO: loss = (margin_in_logratio - 1/(2 tau))^2 style regression to a target gap.
SimPO: reward = beta / |y| * log pi(y|x), with a target margin gamma.
KTO: needs only 'good' or 'bad' labels per response.
ORPO: adds an odds-ratio penalty to the SFT loss; no reference model.
Online methods reduce distribution shift by sampling from the current policy.
These variants are later than the DPO paper; evidence on which is best is mixed.

courses.title: Electronics from Scratch: Components, Circuits and Logic
courses.subtitle: From electric charge to op-amps and logic gates, with small Python models of each idea
courses.author: Lilith Learning Lab
courses.description: An original beginner course in electronics, covering the same ground as a classic introductory handbook. You will learn electricity and Ohm's law, resistors, capacitors, coils and transformers, diodes and LEDs, transistors, thyristors and light detectors, waves and signals, digital logic and memory, linear ICs such as the op-amp and the 555 timer, and how to build, solder and measure real circuits safely. Each chapter has an ELI5 block, a quiz and Python labs that calculate the circuits.

outline.title: Charge, current and voltage
outline.summary: Everything is made of atoms, and atoms hold electrons that carry negative charge. Electricity is what happens when charge moves or builds up. Current is the flow of charge, measured in amperes. Voltage is the push behind it, measured in volts. Direct current flows one way, like from a battery. Alternating current keeps reversing, like from a wall outlet.
keyPoints: One ampere is one coulomb of charge per second.
Voltage is measured between two points.
Metals conduct; glass, plastic and dry air insulate.
Static electricity is charge that sits still until it jumps.
DC has a fixed direction; AC reverses many times a second.
Current needs a complete loop to flow.

outline.title: The lumped circuit abstraction
outline.summary: Engineers do not model every electron. They squeeze a real part into a simple box with two ends and one rule. That box is a lumped element. Its rule links the voltage across it to the current through it. If the parts are small enough, two laws follow for free: currents at a node sum to zero, and voltages round a loop sum to zero.
keyPoints: A bulb can be replaced by a resistor if only V and I matter.
Inside a lumped element, charge does not pile up.
Outside, wires carry no changing magnetic flux.
KCL and KVL come from those two rules.
The model fails when a circuit is as big as the signal wavelength.

outline.title: Ohm's law, power and simple circuits
outline.summary: Ohm's law says voltage equals current times resistance. If you know two, you can find the third. Electrical power is voltage times current, measured in watts. A part that gets too much power gets hot. Resistors in series add up. In parallel, the total is smaller than the smallest one.
keyPoints: V = I x R, so I = V / R and R = V / I.
P = V x I = I squared x R = V squared / R.
Series resistors add: R = R1 + R2 + ...
Parallel: 1 / R = 1 / R1 + 1 / R2 + ...
In series, voltages add up to the supply.
In parallel, currents add up.

outline.title: Resistors
outline.summary: A resistor limits current. Small ones carry colored bands that give their value, and a final band gives tolerance. Two resistors in series form a voltage divider, which outputs a fraction of the input voltage. A potentiometer is a resistor with a sliding contact, so you can adjust it.
keyPoints: Bands: digit, digit, multiplier, tolerance.
Colors: black 0, brown 1, red 2, orange 3, yellow 4, green 5, blue 6, violet 7, gray 8, white 9.
Gold tolerance is 5 percent, silver 10 percent.
Vout = Vin x R2 / (R1 + R2).
A divider only holds when the load draws little current.
Common ratings are 1/8, 1/4 and 1/2 watt.

outline.title: Visual circuit simulator
outline.summary: A simulator turns your drawing into equations and solves them. It does what you would do with KCL and Ohm's law, only faster. You choose a ground, and every other point gets a voltage. Each part then gives a current from the voltage across it. The lab lets you place parts on a grid and press Solve. Build a divider that gives 3 V from 9 V.
keyPoints: Pick one ground node; all voltages are measured from it.
Wires merge nodes.
Each node gives one KCL equation.
Solving the equations gives every voltage and current.
An ideal battery across a wire is an error, not a circuit.

outline.title: Capacitors and timing
outline.summary: A capacitor stores charge on two plates separated by an insulator. Capacitance is measured in farads, though real parts are microfarads and smaller. With a resistor, a capacitor makes a timer. The time constant is R times C, in seconds. A capacitor blocks steady DC but lets changing signals through, which makes it useful for filtering and coupling.
keyPoints: Q = C x V.
Energy stored is one half C V squared.
Parallel capacitors add; series capacitors combine like parallel resistors.
Charging: V(t) = Vs x (1 - e to the minus t over RC).
After 5 time constants it is about 99 percent charged.
Electrolytic capacitors have a plus and a minus side.

outline.title: Coils, transformers, switches and relays
outline.summary: Current through a coil makes a magnetic field. A coil resists changes in current, and that property is called inductance. Capacitors and coils oppose AC in a way that depends on frequency, called reactance. A coil and capacitor together resonate at one frequency. A transformer changes AC voltage using two coils, and a relay lets a small current switch a bigger one.
keyPoints: Coil reactance X_L = 2 pi f L; it grows with frequency.
Capacitor reactance X_C = 1 / (2 pi f C); it shrinks with frequency.
Resonance: f = 1 / (2 pi sqrt(L C)).
Transformer: Vs / Vp = Ns / Np.
A transformer works only with changing current, not DC.
Put a diode across a relay coil to absorb the voltage spike.

outline.title: Diodes and LEDs
outline.summary: A diode lets current go one way and blocks it the other. A silicon diode drops about 0.6 to 0.7 volts when it conducts. Rectifiers use diodes to change AC into pulsing DC. A Zener diode is used backwards to hold a steady voltage. An LED is a diode that gives off light, and it always needs a resistor to limit its current.
keyPoints: Silicon diode forward drop is about 0.7 V; a red LED is about 2 V.
The stripe on a diode marks the cathode.
A half-wave rectifier uses one diode, a full-wave one uses four in a bridge.
A bridge loses about 1.4 V (two drops).
LED resistor: R = (Vsupply - Vled) / I.
Add a capacitor after the rectifier to smooth the ripple.

outline.title: Transistors
outline.summary: A transistor lets a small signal control a larger current. It can act as an amplifier or as an electronic switch. In a bipolar transistor, a small base current controls a collector current that is hundreds of times bigger. A field-effect transistor, or FET, is controlled by voltage on its gate and takes almost no current to do it.
keyPoints: NPN: current flows from collector to emitter when the base is driven above about 0.7 V.
Ic = beta x Ib while not saturated.
As a switch, drive the base hard: Ib about Ic / (beta / 10).
Vbe is about 0.7 V for silicon.
Use a resistor in series with the base.
A MOSFET gate draws almost no current; mind static.

outline.title: Thyristors and light
outline.summary: A thyristor, such as an SCR or a triac, is a switch that a small pulse turns on and that then stays on until the current drops. Triacs work with AC in both directions. Light is a wave, and LEDs, photoresistors, photodiodes and solar cells all turn electricity into light or light into electricity. A lens bends light; a convex lens can focus it onto a detector.
keyPoints: An SCR turns on with a gate pulse and off when its current falls to zero.
Triacs control AC power, for example in light dimmers.
Mains circuits are dangerous: only experiment with low voltage.
Light's frequency is the speed of light divided by wavelength.
A photoresistor in a divider gives a voltage that follows the light.
A convex lens brings parallel rays to a focus.

outline.title: Waves, signals and noise
outline.summary: A signal is a voltage that changes with time. A wave repeats: frequency counts how many cycles each second, and the period is the time of one cycle. The effective value of an AC wave is its RMS value. A sine wave's RMS is its peak divided by the square root of two. Noise is unwanted signal, and engineers compare size with decibels.
keyPoints: RMS of a sine = peak / 1.414.
Mains 120 V RMS has a peak of about 170 V.
Duty cycle = on time / period.
Pulses and square waves carry digital information.
dB = 20 log10 of a voltage ratio.

outline.title: Digital logic: gates
outline.summary: Digital circuits use only two voltage levels, called low and high, written 0 and 1. A bit is one such digit. Logic gates combine bits: AND is 1 only if all inputs are 1, OR is 1 if any input is 1, and NOT flips a bit. With NAND gates alone you can build every other gate, so digital chips can be made from one repeating cell.
keyPoints: AND: 1 only if both are 1.
OR: 1 if either is 1.
NOT: 1 becomes 0 and 0 becomes 1.
NAND is AND then NOT; NOR is OR then NOT.
XOR is 1 when the inputs differ.
A half adder is XOR for the sum and AND for the carry.

outline.title: Sequential logic: memory and counting
outline.summary: Combinational logic only reacts to its current inputs. Sequential logic also remembers the past, because its outputs feed back into its inputs. A flip-flop stores one bit, and changes only on the edge of a clock. Several flip-flops make a counter, a register or a shift register. A clock is a steady stream of pulses that keeps a digital system in step.
keyPoints: A D flip-flop copies D to Q on the rising clock edge.
A toggle flip-flop flips on each clock edge, so it halves the frequency.
An n-bit counter counts from 0 to 2 to the n minus 1.
A shift register turns serial data to parallel and back.
Cross-coupled NOR or NAND gates form an SR latch.
Count the bits: 4 flip-flops give 16 states.

outline.title: Linear ICs: op-amps, timers and regulators
outline.summary: An integrated circuit, or IC, packs many transistors and resistors onto one chip. Linear ICs handle continuous signals, while digital ones handle bits. An operational amplifier has huge gain, and feedback resistors set the exact gain. A 555 timer makes pulses and delays with two resistors and a capacitor. A voltage regulator holds a steady output voltage, whatever the input or load does.
keyPoints: Inverting gain = minus Rf / Rin.
Non-inverting gain = 1 + Rf / Rg.
A comparator's output swings to one supply rail or the other.
Linear regulator waste: (Vin - Vout) x I as heat.
Add capacitors near the chip's supply pins.

outline.title: Building real circuits
outline.summary: Start on a solderless breadboard, which lets you build, test and change circuits without tools. Move to soldering once a design works. A multimeter measures voltage, current and resistance. Check your supply and wiring before power goes on. Always respect limits: part ratings, battery capacity and especially mains voltage.
keyPoints: Test circuits on a breadboard before soldering.
Measure voltage in parallel, current in series, resistance with power off.
Heat both the pad and the lead, then add solder.
A good joint is shiny and shaped like a small cone.
Read the datasheet for pinouts and maximum ratings.
Never experiment with wall power. Use batteries or low-voltage supplies.

outline.title: Arduino: pins and sketches
outline.summary: An Arduino is a small computer board with pins you can set high or low or read. It is the bridge between code and the circuits you have learned. A program, called a sketch, has two parts. Setup runs once. Loop runs again and again. The lab below is a virtual Uno, so you can try each idea without any wiring.
keyPoints: Uno: 5 V logic, 14 digital pins, 6 analog inputs, 16 MHz.
setup() runs once; loop() repeats.
pinMode chooses input or output.
An LED pin needs about 220 ohms in series.
INPUT_PULLUP reads low when a button joins the pin to ground.

outline.title: Arduino: sensors, PWM and loads
outline.summary: Analog input turns a voltage into a number. PWM turns a number into an average voltage. A light sensor and a fixed resistor make a divider, and the Arduino reads the middle point. Pins are weak, so motors and relays need a transistor and a flyback diode.
keyPoints: Volts = reading / 1023 x 5.
Average PWM voltage = duty / 255 x 5.
A pin gives about 20 mA; use a transistor for more.
Put a diode across any coil.
Use millis() instead of delay() to do two things at once.

courses.title: Emulator Programming: From Fetch-Decode-Execute to JIT
courses.subtitle: Build the ideas of a computer emulator step by step, with a tiny CPU, a memory map, timing, interrupts, video, sound and testing
courses.author: Lilith Learning Lab
courses.description: Learn how to write a computer emulator. Starting from what an emulator is and how it differs from a simulator or a compatibility layer, you build a tiny 8-bit CPU and study the fetch-decode-execute loop, instruction decoding, bit tricks, flags and endianness, memory maps, mirroring, banking and memory-mapped devices, cycle timing, interrupts and event schedulers, video and sound, input and DMA, caches and just-in-time compilation, accuracy and hardware-derived test suites, and debuggers. The course updates the classic 1990s how-to advice for modern compilers, languages, tools and test suites. Each chapter has an ELI5 block, a quiz and Python labs that run on the built-in interpreter.

outline.title: What an emulator is
outline.summary: An emulator is a program, or a device, that lets one system, the host, behave like another, the guest. The goal is to run the guest's software unchanged. A simulator models behavior in the abstract, while an emulator reproduces the machine well enough to run its real binaries. In everyday use the two words blur. Emulators exist for consoles, computers, terminals, printers and chips, and are used for play, preservation, homebrew and development.
keyPoints: IBM engineers coined the term emulator in the 1960s for hardware-assisted imitation.
Types: console and arcade emulators, terminal emulators, in-circuit emulators, floating-point emulators and instruction-set simulators.
A compatibility layer is lighter than an emulator but needs the same kind of programs.
Interpreters are simple; recompilers are faster.
Accuracy needs depend on the guest: some software relies on exact timing.
You can write a small emulator in an afternoon and learn a great deal from it.

outline.title: Anatomy of an emulator
outline.summary: Split an emulator into modules that mirror the real machine: CPU, memory, video, sound, input and other chips. Each can be built and tested alone. A real bus connects the chips; emulators often skip it and give each device a direct link, or a central routing function. A frontend turns the emulated video and sound into a window and speakers on the host.
keyPoints: Keep the CPU core free of video and window code.
A memory function routes each address to RAM, ROM or a device.
Reads from nowhere return an open-bus value, often a leftover or 0xFF.
Writing to ROM is usually ignored.
Reusing a chip's module across machines saves work.
Separating core from frontend lets one core run in many places.

outline.title: Bits, numbers and flags
outline.summary: Real CPUs work with fixed-size numbers that wrap around. An emulator must reproduce that exactly, using masks. After most operations the CPU sets flags, such as carry, zero, negative and overflow, that later instructions test. Multi-byte numbers can be stored low byte first, called little-endian, or high byte first, big-endian. Combine bytes with shifts, never by peeking at memory layout.
keyPoints: Mask with & 0xFF to keep 8 bits and & 0xFFFF for 16.
Carry: the full sum is above 255.
Overflow (signed): two numbers of the same sign give a result of the other sign.
To read a signed byte: if it is 128 or more, subtract 256.
Little-endian word = low + (high << 8).
Use shifts and masks, not type punning; modern compilers and fixed-width types make that safe and portable.

outline.title: The fetch-decode-execute loop
outline.summary: The heart of every CPU emulator is a loop: fetch the opcode at the program counter, decode it, execute it, and add its cycles to a counter. The CPU's state is just a few variables: registers, flags and the program counter. Each instruction changes them. We use TOY8, a tiny accumulator CPU with nine opcodes, as the running example.
keyPoints: Loop: opcode = mem[pc]; advance pc; decode; execute; cycles += cost.
Jumps simply overwrite pc.
Conditional jumps read a flag.
Different opcodes take different numbers of cycles.
Stop on a halt instruction or after a step limit.
TOY8 opcodes: 0 HLT, 1 LDI, 2 ADD, 3 SUB, 4 STA, 5 LDA, 6 JMP, 7 JNZ, 8 OUT.

outline.title: Decoding instructions
outline.summary: Opcodes are numbers with structure: some bits pick the operation, others pick registers or addressing modes. Decoding by bit fields is often shorter than listing every opcode. Common ways to dispatch are a big switch, a table of handlers, or code generated from a table. Modern compilers turn a dense switch into a fast jump table. Real CPUs have undocumented opcodes, and some software uses them.
keyPoints: Split opcodes with shifts and masks: (op >> 5) & 7.
A switch on a dense range compiles to a jump table in modern compilers.
A table of function pointers is clear, but each call has some cost.
Generating decoder code from a table avoids typing mistakes.
Write instruction handlers once and reuse them across addressing modes.
Test undocumented opcodes against hardware-derived test suites.

outline.title: Memory maps
outline.summary: The simplest memory is an array of bytes, but real machines add mirroring, bank switching, ROM and memory-mapped I/O. Wrap every access in read and write functions that apply those rules in one place. Some addresses are devices: reading or writing them does something, such as clearing a flag or advancing a counter.
keyPoints: Mirroring: addr & (size - 1) when size is a power of two.
Bank window: physical = bank x window_size + (addr - window_start).
Reads happen far more often than writes, so keep the read path short.
ROM writes may be ignored, or used to switch banks.
A device read may change state, so never read a device just to look at it in a debugger.
Fast emulators use a table of page pointers for the common case.

outline.title: Timing and cycles
outline.summary: Every chip in a machine runs from clocks, so an emulator needs a notion of time. The CPU's cycle count is the usual yardstick. A frame lasts clock rate divided by frame rate cycles, and a scanline is a fraction of that. Video, sound and timer events fire at those intervals. Add the period to the counter instead of resetting it, so leftover cycles are not lost.
keyPoints: Cycles per frame = clock / fps.
Cycles per scanline = cycles per frame / lines.
Use the greatest common divisor of all periods as the tick.
When the counter reaches zero, handle events and add the period back.
Run no more than a few frames at once to avoid a spiral of death.
Use the host's monotonic clock to pace; never sleep in the middle of a frame.

outline.title: Interrupts and event schedulers
outline.summary: An interrupt makes the CPU stop what it is doing and run a handler. Maskable interrupts (IRQ) can be disabled; non-maskable ones (NMI) cannot. Rather than checking every device after every instruction, an event scheduler finds when the next thing happens and runs the CPU exactly that long. Video and timers usually raise interrupts at set cycle counts, such as the start of the vertical blank.
keyPoints: Check interrupt lines between instructions, not in the middle.
An IRQ is level-sensitive: it fires while the line is high and the mask allows it.
An NMI is edge-sensitive: it fires when the line goes from low to high.
A scheduler runs the CPU until the earliest event, then handles it.
Keep events in time order; use insertion order for ties.
A timer that wakes at cycle N is just an event.

outline.title: Video and sound
outline.summary: Many old machines draw the picture from tiles, sprites and palettes rather than a full bitmap. An emulator reads those tables and writes pixels into a framebuffer. Rendering a whole frame at once is simple; rendering line by line is needed when games change settings between lines. Sound is a stream of samples, often square waves mixed together. The emulator must make samples at the audio rate, in step with the cycles.
keyPoints: Tile maps store which tile goes where; the tiles store the pixels.
A scanline renderer draws one line at a time using the settings in force at that moment.
RGB565 packs a color in 16 bits: 5 red, 6 green, 5 blue.
A square wave toggles between high and low at a fixed frequency.
Mix by adding samples and clamping to the valid range.
Accuracy matters: games change registers mid-frame to get effects.

outline.title: Input, timers and devices
outline.summary: Input devices appear to the guest as registers. A joypad is often a byte where each bit is a button; a keyboard may be a matrix that the program scans row by row. Timers count down at a fixed rate, and fire an interrupt at zero. DMA lets a device copy memory without the CPU, and the CPU may have to wait while it does. Treat every device as a small state machine with registers, and update it by cycles, not by wall-clock time.
keyPoints: Map host keys to guest buttons in the frontend; the core just sees bits.
Timers must count in cycles, keeping the leftover cycles between updates.
DMA often steals cycles from the CPU: charge them.
A read of the key matrix returns the OR of the selected rows.
Fewer surprises: update devices only when their registers are accessed or their event fires.
Record inputs per frame to make runs repeatable.

outline.title: Speed: caches, JITs and what has changed since the 1990s
outline.summary: An interpreter is simple and portable but slow. A dynamic recompiler, or JIT, translates blocks of guest code into host code the first time they run and caches the result. Static recompilation translates a whole program ahead of time, but struggles with code that changes itself and with telling code from data. Much advice from the 1990s, written for assembly and early compilers, is out of date. Measure first, and let the compiler and the profiler help.
keyPoints: Interpret first; optimize only the hot paths found by a profiler.
A JIT translates basic blocks and caches them by guest address.
Self-modifying code means the cache must be invalidated when guest memory is written.
Modern systems often forbid memory that is both writable and executable; JITs write first, then switch to executable.
If the guest and host share an instruction set, virtualization can run guest code almost natively.
Prefer clear code in a modern compiled language; the compiler outperforms hand tuning for most uses.

outline.title: Accuracy and testing
outline.summary: How accurate an emulator must be depends on the guest. Some software works with approximate timing, while some relies on exact cycles and undocumented behavior. Test your CPU with test ROMs and with hardware-derived single-instruction test suites, which give the exact registers, memory and sometimes bus activity before and after each instruction. A deterministic core lets you save state, replay input, and compare runs, which makes bugs reproducible.
keyPoints: Pick the level of accuracy the software needs.
High-level emulation can be faster but can break software that depends on details.
Hardware-generated JSON suites exist for many CPUs, including the 6502 family, Z80, 8088 and 68000.
Test ROMs exist for many machines and run inside the emulator.
Keep the core deterministic: no clocks, no random numbers without a seed.
A checksum on save states catches corrupted files.

outline.title: Debuggers, preservation and next steps
outline.summary: A debugger and a disassembler are the emulator author's best tools: they let you stop at an address, look at registers and memory, and read the program as text. Emulation is also how old software and documents stay usable, and how new software for old systems gets made. Legal and ethical rules differ by country. Emulators themselves are widely treated as lawful, but sharing copyrighted ROMs or system software without permission is not; this course is not legal advice.
keyPoints: Build the debugger and disassembler early.
Peeking at memory must not trigger device side effects.
Trace logs let you compare your emulator against a known-good one line by line.
Dump your own cartridges and discs; do not distribute copyrighted system software.
The old HOWTO's links are mostly gone; use present-day wikis, test suites, forums and open-source cores instead.
Good places to learn: platform wikis such as the NESdev Wiki, Pan Docs for the Game Boy, public test ROMs and open emulator source code.

courses.title: Game Theory
courses.subtitle: Strategy, equilibrium, cooperation and auctions, with runnable Python labs and live simulations
courses.author: Lilith Learning Lab
courses.description: A hands-on introduction to game theory: players, strategies and payoffs; dominance and Nash equilibrium; mixed strategies and the minimax theorem; the classic games of dilemma, trust, chicken and coordination; sequential games with backward induction and credible threats; repeated games and the evolution of cooperation; evolutionary game theory with replicator dynamics; auctions, bargaining and mechanism design; and cooperative games with the Shapley value and social choice with Arrow's theorem. Every chapter has Python labs verified in the built-in interpreter, a tournament of repeated-game strategies and a replicator dynamics lab.

outline.title: Games, players and payoffs
outline.summary: Game theory studies strategic situations where each person's best choice depends on what the others choose. A game lists the players, the strategies each can pick, and the payoff each gets for every combination. A two-player game with few strategies is shown as a payoff matrix: rows for one player, columns for the other, and each cell holds a pair of payoffs. Players are assumed rational: they pick strategies to maximise their own utility, and they know the others do the same. Games can be simultaneous or sequential, one-shot or repeated, competitive or cooperative.
keyPoints: Players, strategies, payoffs.
Cell (row, column) = (payoff of row, payoff of column).
Rationality: maximise your own payoff.
Payoff numbers express preference, not money alone.
Zero-sum: payoffs add to a constant.

outline.title: Dominance and Nash equilibrium
outline.summary: A strategy strictly dominates another if it gives a higher payoff whatever the opponent does. A rational player never plays a dominated strategy, and removing dominated strategies can simplify a game, sometimes solving it. A best response is the strategy that maximises your payoff given what the others do. A Nash equilibrium is a combination of strategies where each player's strategy is a best response to the others, so no one gains by changing alone. To find pure Nash equilibria in a matrix, check every cell: is the row payoff the best in its column, and the column payoff the best in its row?
keyPoints: Nash: no one can gain by switching alone.
Check each cell: row best in column and column best in row.
Dominated strategies are never Nash strategies.
A game may have none, one or several pure equilibria.
Nash proved mixed equilibria always exist.

outline.title: Mixed strategies and zero-sum games
outline.summary: In matching pennies there is no pure equilibrium: whichever side you pick, the opponent wants to switch. The solution is to randomise, a mixed strategy, so the opponent cannot exploit a pattern. In a mixed equilibrium each player chooses probabilities that make the other player indifferent between their strategies. For a 2x2 game this gives a simple formula. In a zero-sum game, von Neumann's minimax theorem says the maximin value (the best guaranteed payoff) equals the minimax value (what the opponent can hold you to). This common number is the value of the game.
keyPoints: 2x2 mixing: choose p to make the opponent indifferent.
Matching pennies: 50-50.
Zero-sum: maximin = minimax.
Saddle point: pure equilibrium exists.
Mixed Nash always exists in finite games.

outline.title: Classic games: dilemmas, coordination and conflict
outline.summary: A handful of small games capture whole families of social situations. The prisoner's dilemma: defecting is dominant yet mutual cooperation is better for both. The stag hunt: two equilibria, one safe, one rewarding. Chicken (or hawk-dove) rewards the one who does not swerve but ruins both if neither swerves. The battle of the sexes: two people prefer to be together but disagree on where. The tension between individual incentive and group benefit appears in arms races, climate, overfishing, vaccination and team projects.
keyPoints: PD: T > R > P > S.
Stag hunt: trust gives R, safe gives P.
Chicken: two asymmetric equilibria.
Coordination games: several equilibria.
Nash does not imply Pareto optimal.

outline.title: Sequential games and backward induction
outline.summary: When players move in turn and see earlier moves, the game is drawn as a tree. Backward induction solves it by starting at the last decisions and working back to the root. A subgame perfect equilibrium is a Nash equilibrium that is also an equilibrium in every subgame. It rules out empty threats, plans nobody would carry out when the time came. Moving first can be an advantage when it commits you, as in Stackelberg competition, but can be a disadvantage when it reveals information.
keyPoints: Solve from the leaves upward.
At each node, the mover picks the best payoff for themselves.
Subgame perfect = backward induction in finite perfect-information games.
Commitment can create value.
Ultimatum game: theory vs people.

outline.title: Repeated games and the evolution of cooperation
outline.summary: If the prisoner's dilemma is played once, defection wins. If it is played repeatedly with no known end, the future can discipline the present: cooperating may be worth it to keep the other cooperating. Robert Axelrod's tournaments found that a simple strategy, tit for tat (cooperate first, then copy the opponent's last move), outscored far more elaborate ones. It is nice, retaliatory, forgiving and clear. The folk theorem says that when players value the future enough, almost any feasible outcome better than the minimum can be sustained as an equilibrium of the repeated game.
keyPoints: Grim trigger sustains cooperation if delta >= (T - R) / (T - P).
Sum of delta^t = 1 / (1 - delta).
Last-round unravelling: known end means defect.
Tit for tat: nice, retaliating, forgiving, clear.
Reputation and repeat business support cooperation.

outline.title: Evolutionary game theory
outline.summary: Evolutionary game theory replaces rational thought by selection: strategies that earn more payoff spread in the population, those that earn less shrink. No one needs to be clever. An evolutionarily stable strategy (ESS) is one that, once common, cannot be invaded by a small group using a different strategy. Every strict Nash equilibrium is an ESS. Replicator dynamics describe how the share of each strategy changes: x' = x (f - average fitness). In hawk-dove the population settles at a mix of hawks and doves.
keyPoints: x' = x (f(x) - average).
Hawk-dove ESS: share of hawks = V / C when C > V.
ESS: resists a small invasion.
Stable fixed point of the dynamics.
Payoffs become offspring.

outline.title: Auctions, bargaining and mechanism design
outline.summary: Auctions are games with money. In a sealed-bid second-price (Vickrey) auction the highest bidder wins but pays the second-highest bid, and bidding your true value is a dominant strategy. In a first-price auction you pay what you bid, so you shade your bid below your value. Under standard assumptions both formats give the seller the same expected revenue, the revenue equivalence theorem. Mechanism design runs game theory backward: choose the rules so that selfish play produces the outcome you want. Vickrey, Clarke and Groves showed how truthful reporting can be made optimal.
keyPoints: Vickrey: bid your value.
First price, 2 bidders uniform: bid v / 2.
Revenue equivalence: same expected revenue.
Nash bargaining: maximise (u1 - d1)(u2 - d2).
Incentive compatible: truth-telling is optimal.

outline.title: Cooperative games and social choice
outline.summary: Cooperative game theory asks how a group that can bind its members should split the gains. A characteristic function says what each coalition can achieve alone. The Shapley value gives each player their average marginal contribution over all orders in which the coalition could form. It is the unique allocation satisfying fairness axioms. The core is the set of allocations no coalition could improve on by leaving. Social choice asks how to combine individual rankings into a group decision. Condorcet's paradox shows majorities can cycle, and Arrow's impossibility theorem shows that no ranking method satisfies a short list of fairness conditions.
keyPoints: phi_i = average of v(S + i) - v(S) over orders.
Efficient: Shapley values add to v(all).
Core: no coalition gets less than v(S).
Condorcet winner beats every other option.
Arrow: no perfect ranking rule.

courses.title: Gödel Machine
courses.subtitle: Self-referential, provably optimal self-improvement
courses.author: Lilith Learning Lab
courses.description: A 12-chapter course on the Gödel machine, Jürgen Schmidhuber's 2003 design for a self-referential, self-improving problem solver that rewrites its own code only after proving the rewrite helps. Based on the Wikipedia article, Schmidhuber's technical report, the Steunebrink and Schmidhuber paper on implementation and the Yudkowsky and Herreshoff work on the Löbian obstacle.
