Covers Gödel's ideas, the machine model, the axioms, the proof searcher, the target theorem, global optimality, bias-optimal proof search, examples, related work and limits, with Python labs on the built-in MicroPython engine. It is a theoretical design with no full implementation; speculative claims are marked as the author's own.

outline.title: What is a Gödel machine?
outline.summary: A Gödel machine is a hypothetical self-improving computer program that aims to solve problems optimally. It rewrites its own code, but only when it can prove that the new code gives a better strategy. Jürgen Schmidhuber proposed it in 2003, and it is named after Kurt Gödel, whose work inspired its mathematical foundations. It belongs to meta-learning, or learning to learn. The motivation is that an ordinary program has one hardwired algorithm and does not account for a changing environment, whereas a Gödel machine can change its own algorithm, including the part that does the changing. No full implementation has been created. The course treats it as a theory: you learn the machine step by step and build toy versions of its parts in Python.
keyPoints: A Gödel machine rewrites its own code only after proving the rewrite helps.
It was proposed by Jürgen Schmidhuber in 2003 and named after Kurt Gödel.
It can rewrite any part of itself, including its proof searcher.
It is a theoretical design; no full implementation exists.
It is a form of meta-learning and is often compared with Hutter's AIXI.

outline.title: Gödel's ideas and the limits of proof
outline.summary: Gödel showed in 1931 that any consistent formal system strong enough to express arithmetic contains true statements it cannot prove. His proof encodes formulas as numbers, which lets a system talk about its own proofs and build a sentence that says it is not provable. Related limits: a consistent system cannot prove its own consistency, and Rice's theorem says every non-trivial question about what a program computes is undecidable in general. A Gödel machine reasons inside a formal system, so it inherits these limits. The paper accepts this: the machine ignores self-improvements whose usefulness it cannot prove.
keyPoints: Gödel's incompleteness theorem: powerful consistent systems have unprovable truths.
Gödel numbering lets a system reason about its own formulas.
The Gödel machine uses self-reference, so it is bound by the same limits.
Rice's theorem: no general procedure decides non-trivial program properties.
The machine simply ignores improvements it cannot prove.

outline.title: The machine model and utility
outline.summary: The machine's hardware has a single life made of discrete cycles t = 1, 2, ..., T. The state s(t) changes by a hardwired transition function that depends on the previous state and the environment. Four variables matter: time holds the binary encoding of t; x holds the environment's input; y holds the machine's output; and p is the software, which at the start contains an initial policy and an initial proof searcher. The goal is to maximize expected utility: the conditional expectation of the sum of future rewards from now until the end of life, under an unknown environment distribution drawn from a set of possible ones.
keyPoints: The machine lives for T cycles; T may or may not be known.
time, x, y and p are the main variables.
u(s, Env) is the expected sum of future rewards given the current state.
Variants: worst-case performance, or reward per time interval.
Utility is defined in terms of the current state, so it changes if the machine rewrites u.

outline.title: The axioms
outline.summary: The machine's initial software includes an axiomatic description of itself and its world. The proof searcher derives theorems from these axioms by inference rules. The axiom groups are hardware axioms, reward axioms, environment axioms, uncertainty and string-manipulation axioms, initial-state axioms and utility axioms. Together they let the machine prove statements about its own future states and rewards. Because the axiom system is part of the software, it can itself be rewritten, but only by a proven-useful rewrite. Optimality claims hold relative to a consistent axiom system.
keyPoints: Six axiom groups: hardware, reward, environment, uncertainty, initial state, utility.
The axioms are part of the software and can be improved by proven rewrites.
The environment axioms can be as weak as 'any computable distribution' or as strong as 'deterministic'.
Optimality holds if the axiom system is consistent.
Standard mathematics lets the machine reason about expected rewards.

outline.title: The proof searcher
outline.summary: The proof searcher does not enumerate proofs by brute force, which would take time exponential in the proof size. It tests proof techniques: programs, written in a universal language, whose output is a proof. A proof technique can modify the proof only through six instructions: get-axiom, apply-rule, delete-theorem, set-switchprog, check and state2theorem. Since there is no other way to change the proof, an incorrect theorem can never be inserted, which makes verifying a proof trivial. A proof is a list of theorems. Each theorem is either an axiom or follows from earlier theorems by an inference rule, such as modus ponens.
keyPoints: Proofs are built only by six instructions, so a wrong theorem cannot appear.
Verification is therefore trivial.
Proof techniques are programs that produce proofs; they are faster than brute-force enumeration.
delete-theorem saves space but deleted theorems cannot be reused.
state2theorem lets the machine use observations about its own current state.
check ends the search when the last theorem is a target theorem.

outline.title: The target theorem and the switch
outline.summary: A switchprog is a candidate program that can rewrite any part of the machine's software. The machine runs it only if it has proved a target theorem: the utility with the switch bit set to 1 is higher than with the bit set to 0. Setting the bit to 0 means continuing as before, with the searcher still looking for other rewrites. Setting it to 1 means running the switchprog at time t1. The time t1 accounts for the delay between finding the proof and acting on it. A relaxed version replaces the strict inequality with at least as high, so the machine rewrites itself as soon as the change is provably not harmful.
keyPoints: Target theorem: u(switch) > u(continue), at time t1.
The switch is executed only after the proof.
The comparison need not compute exact utilities, only which is higher.
A relaxed version uses at-least-as-high.
The switchprog can rewrite anything, even the axioms and the proof searcher.

outline.title: Global optimality
outline.summary: Theorem 4.1 in the paper says that once the machine has proved a target theorem and switched, the resulting change is globally optimal: no other self-rewrite, now or later, could have done better, given the axioms. The reason is that the continue option already includes every future rewrite the searcher might find. So the machine is not greedy. It does not take the first improvement; it takes a switch only when the proof says that switching now beats everything it could do by waiting. The paper also argues that all meta-levels collapse into one, because the same proof searcher improves itself. The guarantee is relative to the axioms and requires them to be consistent. It is not a guarantee about the real world beyond what the axioms say.
keyPoints: The continue branch of the target theorem contains all later rewrites.
Therefore a proved target theorem means switching now is at least as good as any alternative.
The machine is not greedy: it can leave a worse-looking but later-better path alone.
All meta-levels collapse into one level.
Guarantees hold only if the axioms are consistent.
A bogus utility change cannot be proved better under the present utility.

outline.title: Bias-optimal proof search (BIOPS)
outline.summary: Bias-optimal proof search, or BIOPS, is the paper's search scheme for the proof searcher. It tests proof techniques in phases: in phase i, each technique w with probability P(w) of at least 2 to the minus i receives a budget of 2 to the i times P(w) steps. Theorem 5.1 says that if a proof technique exists that proves the target theorem in time t, BIOPS finds it in time of order t divided by P(w), up to a constant factor. Bias-optimal means optimal given the bias, which is the probability distribution P over techniques. BIOPS is an online search. When a technique fails, the effects on the scratch memory are undone, and the next one runs. A successful technique may be reused: the Optimal Ordered Problem Solver shares this idea.
keyPoints: BIOPS runs in phases i = 1, 2, 3, ...
In phase i a technique w with P(w) >= 2^-i gets 2^i * P(w) steps.
Total time per phase is at most 2^i.
If a technique proves the theorem in t steps, BIOPS finds it in O(t / P(w)).
It is optimal only given the bias P.
The O() hides a constant factor, which may be large.

outline.title: Examples and kinds of self-improvement
outline.summary: The paper lists several kinds of self-improvement the machine could prove useful, from small speed-ups of a subroutine to replacing the utility function or the axioms themselves. Each kind needs a proof inside the axiom system. Three illustrative scenarios appear in the paper: a program that speeds up a graph or travelling-salesman solver, a search for a counterexample to Goldbach's conjecture, and a robot with limited fuel that must plan around depots under a weak environment assumption, the Speed Prior. These are thought experiments, not experimental results. They show how a target theorem could be stated and what must be proved.
keyPoints: The paper lists eight kinds of self-improvement.
A Gödel machine may improve its policy, its searcher, its axioms and even its utility function, always with a proof.
Speed-ups are the most direct example: a faster subroutine raises expected reward.
The Goldbach example shows search under a time limit.
The robot example shows planning under uncertainty about the environment.
No example has been demonstrated experimentally.

outline.title: Relations to other work
outline.summary: The Gödel machine is compared with several earlier ideas. Hutter's AIXI is a theoretically optimal agent that combines Solomonoff's universal prediction with expectimax planning, but it is incomputable. A resource-bounded variant, AIXI(t,l), is computable but still has a huge constant. Hutter's HSEARCH is a hardwired proof searcher whose search is bias-optimal but cannot be rewritten. The Gödel machine differs in that its proof searcher can rewrite itself. Related Schmidhuber methods include OOPS, the Success-Story Algorithm for evaluating self-modifications, and Universal Search. The differences are about what is fixed and what can change, so a table of what is hardwired in each approach is a good way to remember them.
keyPoints: AIXI is optimal but incomputable; AIXI(t,l) is computable but impractical.
HSEARCH uses a fixed bias-optimal proof search; the Gödel machine can rewrite its search.
OOPS is Schmidhuber's earlier solver that reuses solutions.
The Success-Story Algorithm checks self-modifications empirically, not by proof.
Levin's Kt measures length plus the log of running time.
Each approach differs in what is fixed.

outline.title: Limits, criticism and open problems
outline.summary: The Gödel machine remains a theoretical design. Resource limits mean it can prove only improvements whose proofs fit in time and space; by Rice's theorem it must ignore many useful changes; and by Blum's speed-up theorem some problems have no optimal program at all. Löb's theorem, a relative of Gödel's second incompleteness theorem, creates the Löbian obstacle: an agent that trusts its own proofs seems to run into a barrier when it tries to prove that a successor which uses the same reasoning is safe. Yudkowsky and Herreshoff studied this in the context of self-modifying systems. Steunebrink and Schmidhuber explored what an implementation would need, such as a solver and searcher pair and meta-circular evaluators. Claims about consciousness or about humans being Gödel machines are speculation by the author and are not results.
keyPoints: No complete implementation of the Gödel machine exists.
Unprovable improvements are ignored; Rice's theorem makes many properties undecidable.
Blum: some problems have no fastest program.
Löb's theorem limits an agent's trust in its own proofs.
Implementation studies define Solver and Searcher parts and use meta-circular evaluators.
Philosophical claims such as that humans are Gödel machines are speculation.

outline.title: Build a toy Gödel machine
outline.summary: The capstone is a toy model that keeps the essential logic: the machine earns reward at a rate, searches for proofs about candidate rewrites, and switches only when the proved total reward is strictly higher than staying. Each candidate has a new rate, a switching cost and a proof time. Searching takes part of the machine's effort, modelled by a share. The toy leaves out real logic: the proofs are replaced by arithmetic. Building it ties the earlier chapters together: the target theorem is the comparison, the proof time is the delay, and the order of candidates is the search order.
keyPoints: Process candidates in order.
Searching for the proof of a candidate takes its proof time, during which reward is earned at a reduced rate.
Switch only if switching is strictly better than staying for the remaining time.
Skip candidates whose proof would not finish before the end.
Integer arithmetic keeps results exact.
This is a model, not an implementation.

courses.title: GOFAI: Symbolic AI
courses.subtitle: Logic, search, rules and planning: how Good Old-Fashioned AI reasons, with runnable Python labs and a search visualiser
courses.author: Lilith Learning Lab
courses.description: A hands-on course in symbolic AI, also called Good Old-Fashioned AI: its history, knowledge representation with networks and frames, propositional and predicate logic with resolution and unification, uninformed and heuristic search, game playing with minimax and alpha-beta, rule-based and expert systems, STRIPS planning and the frame problem, constraint satisfaction and Prolog, and the limits and legacy of the approach including neuro-symbolic AI. Every chapter has Python labs, and an interactive grid shows breadth-first, depth-first and A* search side by side.

outline.title: What GOFAI is: symbols, rules and the dream of reasoning machines
outline.summary: GOFAI, Good Old-Fashioned Artificial Intelligence, is the approach that builds intelligence from explicit symbols and rules: facts written down, logic applied to them, and search through possible answers. The name was coined by the philosopher John Haugeland in 1985. It dominated AI from the 1950s to the 1980s and produced theorem provers, game players, planners and expert systems. Its rival, connectionism, learns patterns in numbers, as neural networks do. This course teaches the core ideas with small programs you can run: representation, logic, search, rules, planning, constraints and what GOFAI could not do.
keyPoints: GOFAI = symbols + rules + search.
Dartmouth workshop, 1956, named the field.
Logic Theorist (1956) and GPS (1957) were early programs.
Expert systems peaked in the 1980s.
AI winters followed over-promising.

outline.title: Knowledge representation: networks, frames and ontologies
outline.summary: How you write knowledge down decides what a program can do with it. A semantic network draws concepts as nodes and relations as labelled links, such as canary IS-A bird. A frame bundles slots and values for a concept, such as a bird with wings and a way of moving. IS-A links allow inheritance: a canary inherits what is true of birds unless told otherwise. Defaults can be overridden, so a penguin IS-A bird but cannot fly. An ontology is a shared list of categories and relations, and a knowledge graph stores facts as subject, relation, object triples.
keyPoints: IS-A links build a hierarchy.
Members inherit properties from categories.
Defaults: birds fly, unless exceptions say otherwise.
Frames: slots with values and defaults.
Knowledge graph: facts as triples.

outline.title: Propositional logic and resolution
outline.summary: Propositional logic works with statements that are true or false and connectives such as not, and, or and implies. A truth table lists the value of a formula for every assignment of truth values to its variables. A formula is a tautology if it is true in every row, satisfiable if true in some row, and a contradiction if true in none. A set of premises entails a conclusion if the conclusion is true in every row that makes all premises true. Resolution is a single rule that is complete for refutation: to show that premises entail a goal, add the negation of the goal and derive the empty clause.
keyPoints: n variables give 2^n rows.
Tautology: always true. Contradiction: never.
P implies Q is the same as not P or Q.
Resolution: cancel a literal and its negation.
Empty clause means contradiction.

outline.title: Predicate logic and unification
outline.summary: Predicate logic adds objects, predicates and quantifiers to propositional logic. It lets you say all humans are mortal and Socrates is human, so Socrates is mortal. To apply a general rule to a particular fact, a program must match patterns. Unification finds a substitution of variables that makes two terms identical, such as turning Human(x) and Human(Socrates) into the same term by setting x to Socrates. Unification is the core operation of resolution theorem provers and of Prolog.
keyPoints: All humans are mortal: for all x, Human(x) implies Mortal(x).
Variables begin with a lowercase letter; constants are capitalised, in this course.
Unify Human(x) with Human(Socrates): x = Socrates.
A variable can unify with any term not containing itself.
Different constants never unify.

outline.title: Search: finding answers by exploring
outline.summary: Many AI problems are search problems: a start state, operators that move from one state to another, and a goal test. Finding a route, solving a puzzle or planning a move are all ways of exploring a graph of states. Breadth-first search expands states level by level, and finds a shortest path when every step costs the same. Depth-first search goes deep along one branch first, using little memory but possibly missing short answers. The enemy of search is the exponential growth of states with depth, called the combinatorial explosion.
keyPoints: BFS uses a queue; DFS uses a stack.
BFS is complete and finds fewest steps.
DFS uses less memory but is not optimal.
Branching b and depth d give about b^d states.
Keep a visited set to avoid loops.

outline.title: Heuristic search and A*
outline.summary: A heuristic is a rule of thumb that estimates how far a state is from the goal. Using it to choose which state to expand next makes search much faster than blind search. A* orders states by f = g + h, where g is the cost so far and h is the heuristic estimate to go. If h never overestimates the true cost (it is admissible), A* finds a cheapest path. On a grid the Manhattan distance, the sum of horizontal and vertical steps, is a common admissible heuristic.
keyPoints: f(n) = g(n) + h(n).
Admissible: h(n) never exceeds the true cost.
Admissible h gives optimal A*.
Greedy search uses only h and is not optimal.
Manhattan distance for 4-way grids.

outline.title: Game playing: minimax and alpha-beta
outline.summary: For two-player games with perfect information, GOFAI builds a game tree of moves and counter-moves. Minimax assumes both sides play the best they can: MAX picks the move with the highest value and MIN picks the lowest. Real games are too big to search completely, so programs search to a depth limit and score positions with an evaluation function that counts material, mobility and similar features. Alpha-beta pruning gives the same result as minimax while skipping branches that cannot affect the answer, which roughly doubles the reachable depth.
keyPoints: MAX picks the largest child value; MIN the smallest.
Leaves hold scores; internal nodes get backed-up values.
Alpha-beta never changes the minimax value.
Good move ordering prunes more.
Deep Blue beat Kasparov in 1997 using search.

outline.title: Rule-based systems and expert systems
outline.summary: A production system has a set of if-then rules, a working memory of facts, and an inference engine that matches rules against facts and fires them. Expert systems apply this to specialised fields such as medicine and chemistry. Forward chaining starts with known facts and fires rules to derive new ones until nothing changes. Backward chaining starts with a goal and works back to see which facts would prove it. Expert systems like MYCIN also attach certainty factors and can explain their reasoning by showing the rules used.
keyPoints: IF conditions THEN conclusion.
Forward chaining is data-driven.
Backward chaining is goal-driven.
Explanation: show the rules that fired.
The knowledge acquisition bottleneck: rules are hard to collect.

outline.title: Planning: STRIPS and the frame problem
outline.summary: Planning finds a sequence of actions that turns an initial state into a goal state. In STRIPS, a state is a set of facts, and each action has preconditions that must hold, an add list of facts it makes true, and a delete list of facts it makes false. Applying an action to a state removes the delete list and adds the add list, leaving everything else unchanged. Planning is then a search over states, where good heuristics and clever representations matter. The frame problem is the difficulty of stating, in a general logic, everything that an action does not change.
keyPoints: State = set of facts.
Apply: new = (state minus delete) plus add.
Applicable if preconditions are a subset of state.
Plan = sequence of applicable actions reaching the goal.
STRIPS assumption solves the frame problem for simple domains.

outline.title: Constraints and logic programming
outline.summary: A constraint satisfaction problem (CSP) has variables, each with a domain of possible values, and constraints on combinations of values. Map colouring, scheduling and Sudoku are classic examples. Backtracking search assigns variables one at a time and undoes a choice when a constraint is violated. Constraint propagation prunes domains early, such as removing values that conflict with a neighbour's only remaining value. Logic programming, as in Prolog, states facts and rules as Horn clauses and answers queries by backward chaining with unification and backtracking.
keyPoints: CSP = variables + domains + constraints.
Backtracking: assign, check, undo.
Choose the most constrained variable first.
Prolog: facts, rules and queries.
Prolog searches depth-first with backtracking.

outline.title: Limits, legacy and the road to neuro-symbolic AI
outline.summary: GOFAI ran into walls. Everyday common sense turned out to need millions of facts and exceptions. Rule systems were brittle at the edges of their knowledge, and the frame, qualification and ramification problems made precise logical descriptions of the world endless. Projects like Cyc, started by Douglas Lenat in 1984, tried to write down common sense by hand, and are still running. Meanwhile, learning from data overtook hand-written rules in vision, speech and language. The symbolic legacy remains in search, planning, verification, databases and knowledge graphs. Neuro-symbolic AI tries to give learned systems the ability to reason, and symbolic systems the ability to learn.
keyPoints: Common sense needs huge amounts of knowledge.
Rule systems are brittle at their edges.
Searle's Chinese Room argued against pure symbol manipulation.
Symbolic ideas survive in search, planning and verification.
Neuro-symbolic AI mixes learning and reasoning.

courses.title: Harness Engineering for AI Agents
courses.subtitle: The loop, tools, context, memory, guardrails, orchestration and evals, with Python labs
courses.author: Lilith Learning Lab
courses.description: Agent = model + harness. Build the pieces of an agent harness in small deterministic Python labs: the agent loop, tool schemas, context management, memory and checkpoints, guardrails and permissions, sub-agents, retries and limits, traces and evals. Based on recent practitioner write-ups, which are secondary sources.

outline.title: What is a harness?
outline.summary: A language model on its own only turns text into text. To act in the world, it needs a harness: the code and configuration around the model that gives it tools, memory, instructions, permissions and a loop to run in. A common way to put it: an agent is a model plus a harness. Harness engineering is the craft of designing that wrapper so the agent is useful, safe and reliable. It sits above prompt engineering, which tunes one instruction, and context engineering, which tunes what the model sees at each step. This course is practical. The labs build small, deterministic pieces of a harness in plain Python with a scripted fake model, so every result can be checked.
keyPoints: Agent = model + harness.
The model is stateless: it sees only what the harness puts in its context.
A harness provides: instructions, tools, memory, context management, permissions, orchestration, observability and evaluation.
Prompt, context and harness engineering are nested layers.
A good harness lets a fixed model do more and fail more safely.
This course draws on recent practitioner write-ups, which are secondary sources and are still changing.

outline.title: The agent loop
outline.summary: The core of every agent harness is a loop. Build the prompt from the task and the history, ask the model, and look at the reply. If the reply asks for a tool, run it, append the result to the history and go round again. If the reply is a final answer, stop. Real models reply in free text or in structured tool calls. Either way, the harness must parse the reply, handle replies that do not parse and stop after a maximum number of steps. The labs use a scripted model, a list of canned replies, so the loop's behaviour is exactly repeatable.
keyPoints: Loop: build prompt, call model, parse, act or finish.
A reply is either 'CALL tool arg' or 'FINAL text' in the labs.
Tool results go back into the history as observations.
Always bound the loop with a step limit.
Handle malformed replies without crashing: tell the model and continue.
The loop is simple; most engineering effort goes around it.

outline.title: Tools and schemas
outline.summary: Tools are how the model touches the world. Each tool has a name, a description the model reads, and a schema for its arguments. The harness validates the arguments before running anything. Good tool design is a large part of harness engineering: clear names, a description that says when to use the tool, few overlapping tools, helpful error messages and compact outputs. The Model Context Protocol, MCP, is an open standard for exposing tools and data to models in a uniform way.
keyPoints: A tool = name + description + argument schema + function.
Validate arguments: required fields, types and ranges.
Return errors as text the model can act on.
Prefer a few well-named tools over many overlapping ones.
Keep outputs short; truncate and say so.
MCP gives a common way to publish tools across harnesses.

outline.title: Context management
outline.summary: The model can only attend to a limited number of tokens: its context window. An agent's history grows with every step and soon would not fit. Managing what stays in view is context engineering. Basic tools: keep the instructions and the task pinned; drop or summarise the oldest observations; truncate large tool outputs; fetch documents on demand instead of loading them up front. The labs approximate token counts by words, then implement a budgeted history that keeps the newest messages and pins the first.
keyPoints: Every model call must fit the window; the harness enforces a budget below it.
Pin the system prompt and the task; drop oldest observations first.
Summarise before you drop, if the old content may matter.
Truncate large tool outputs.
Retrieve on demand rather than preloading.
Long contexts can degrade quality even when they fit; practitioners call this context rot.

outline.title: Memory and state
outline.summary: The model forgets everything between calls except what is in its context. Anything that must survive a long task, a restart or a handoff has to be saved by the harness: notes, a todo list, a progress file. Two kinds of memory are often distinguished: working memory, the current context, and long-term memory, stored outside the model and read back when needed. Memory is usually exposed as tools the model can call to write and read. Checkpoints save the whole state of a run so that a crash or a pause need not lose the work. The labs build a key-value memory and a checkpoint.
keyPoints: The model is stateless; state belongs to the harness.
Long-term memory is exposed as tools: remember(key, value), recall(key).
Progress notes help an agent continue after the context is reset.
Checkpoint after each step so crashes lose at most one step.
Keep memory small and curated; stale entries can mislead.
State should be serialisable, for example to JSON.

outline.title: Guardrails and permissions
outline.summary: A model that can run commands can also run harmful ones, by mistake or because text it read told it to. The harness is where limits are enforced, in code, not by asking the model nicely. Common controls: an allowlist of tools, approval for risky actions, a sandbox that confines files and network, path checks, and logs. The principle is least privilege: give the agent only what the task needs. Instructions hidden in web pages or files, called prompt injection, are a standing risk. Treat tool results as data, not as commands.
keyPoints: Enforce rules in the harness, not only in the prompt.
Default deny: unknown tools and paths are refused.
Ask a human before irreversible actions such as deleting or sending.
Confine file access to a workspace folder; reject paths that escape it.
Tool results are untrusted data and may contain injected instructions.
Log every action for review.

outline.title: Orchestration and sub-agents
outline.summary: Big tasks can be split. An orchestrator agent plans, hands subtasks to sub-agents, and combines their results. Each sub-agent works in its own fresh context and returns only a short summary. That separation is called a context firewall: the long, noisy trail of a sub-agent's work stays out of the parent's context. It keeps the parent focused and the budget small. Independent subtasks can run in parallel. The labs implement a splitter, a result merger and a simple scheduler.
keyPoints: Split by independence: pieces that do not depend on each other can run in parallel.
Give each sub-agent a precise brief; it cannot see the parent's history.
Return summaries, not transcripts.
More agents cost more tokens; use them when the gain is clear.
Dependencies between subtasks form a graph; run in topological order.
Keep the orchestration logic in code where you can test it.

outline.title: Reliability: retries, loops and limits
outline.summary: Real systems fail. Networks drop, tools time out, models return junk and agents get stuck repeating themselves. A harness must retry what is worth retrying, give up on what is not, and stop runs that go nowhere. Standard tools: retries with exponential backoff, timeouts, loop detection, step and cost limits, and fallbacks. These are ordinary reliability engineering applied to a new kind of component. The labs implement backoff delays, a retry runner over scripted outcomes, a repeat detector and a budget guard.
keyPoints: Retry transient errors; do not retry permanent ones such as invalid arguments.
Backoff: delay = base * 2^attempt, usually with a cap.
Set timeouts on every tool and model call.
Detect loops: the same action repeated several times with the same result.
Cap steps, tokens and money per run.
Make actions idempotent so retries are safe.

outline.title: Observability and evaluation
outline.summary: You cannot improve what you cannot see. A trace records every model call, tool call, result, time and cost, so you can replay a run and find where it went wrong. Evals are tests for agents: a set of tasks with a way to grade the outcome. Run them whenever you change the model, the prompts, the tools or the harness. Capability evals measure what the agent can do; regression evals make sure that what worked still works. Because models are random, one run proves little. The labs compute success rates, pass at k and a regression check.
keyPoints: Log every model call and tool call with inputs, outputs, latency and cost.
Grade outcomes (did the tests pass?) rather than exact wording.
Run each task several times; report the success rate.
Use isolated environments so runs do not contaminate each other.
Keep a regression suite from past failures.
pass@k = 1 - (1 - p)^k for independent attempts with success rate p.

outline.title: Putting it together: a design checklist
outline.summary: A good harness is built up, not designed in one go. Start with the simplest loop that works, add tools one at a time, write evals early, and let the traces tell you what to fix next. A checklist: clear instructions, a few well-described tools, bounded loops and budgets, managed context, saved state, enforced permissions, retries and loop detection, traces and evals. Remember that harnesses age. As models improve, workarounds you added may become unnecessary; re-test and remove them.
keyPoints: Start simple; add a component only when a trace shows a need.
Bound everything: steps, tokens, time, money, retries.
Enforce permissions in code; ask for approval on irreversible actions.
Evals before optimisation; regressions after every change.
Revisit scaffolding when the model changes.
Prefer clear tools and short, current context over clever tricks.

courses.title: Hermetic Qabalah: A Historical and Symbolic Study
courses.subtitle: The Tree of Life, the Hebrew letters, Tarot correspondences and where they came from, taught as history and symbolism
courses.author: Lilith Learning Lab
courses.description: A beginner-friendly study of Hermetic Qabalah as a historical and symbolic tradition: how Jewish Kabbalah, Renaissance Hermeticism and the Golden Dawn fed into it, the ten sephiroth and 22 paths of the Tree of Life, the four worlds, the Hebrew letters with real script and number values, Tarot and planetary correspondences, the methods of gematria, notarikon and temurah, and how to read the whole thing critically. Python labs encode the tables; an interactive Tree of Life lets you explore the spheres. No claims of supernatural effect are made.

outline.title: What Hermetic Qabalah is: a historical map
outline.summary: The word Qabalah means 'received tradition'. Three spellings mark three streams. Kabbalah is the Jewish mystical tradition. Cabala is the Christian reading of the Renaissance. Qabalah is the Hermetic system of Western esotericism. Hermetic Qabalah blends Jewish Kabbalah, Renaissance Hermetism, astrology, alchemy and Tarot, and was systematised in the 19th century by groups such as the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn. This course treats it as a historical and symbolic study: where the ideas come from, how the Tree of Life is organised, and how people have used it as a map of symbols.
keyPoints: Kabbalah, Cabala, Qabalah: three streams.
Hermetic Qabalah is a 19th-century synthesis.
Its Tree has 10 sephiroth and 22 paths.
Study it as history and symbolism.
Claims of results are beliefs, not tested facts.

outline.title: Sources: Hermes, Sefer Yetzirah and the Zohar
outline.summary: The Hebrew letters and the ten sephiroth first appear together in the Sefer Yetzirah, the Book of Formation, a short text of uncertain date, probably between the second and sixth centuries. The Bahir (12th century) and the Zohar (13th) developed the sephiroth into a map of the divine. In the 16th century, Isaac Luria added the ideas of the breaking of vessels and the repair of the world. The Hermetic side comes from the Corpus Hermeticum, Greek texts of the early centuries CE attributed to Hermes Trismegistus, and from a short Arabic text called the Emerald Tablet.
keyPoints: Sefer Yetzirah: 10 sephiroth + 22 letters = 32 paths.
Zohar: 13th century, Moses de Leon.
Luria: 16th century, shattering and repair.
Hermetica: Greek, early centuries CE.
Emerald Tablet: 'as above, so below'.

outline.title: The Tree of Life: ten sephiroth
outline.summary: The Tree of Life is a diagram of ten spheres, the sephiroth, joined by twenty-two paths. Read from the top, it shows how the unity of Kether, the Crown, unfolds step by step into the world of Malkuth, the Kingdom. The sephiroth sit on three pillars. The right pillar is Mercy, the left is Severity, and the middle pillar balances them. Each sephirah has a name, a number, a Divine Name, an archangel and, in the Hermetic system, a planet. Names with Hebrew spelling: Kether כתר, Chokmah חכמה, Binah בינה, Chesed חסד, Geburah גבורה, Tiphareth תפארת, Netzach נצח, Hod הוד, Yesod יסוד, Malkuth מלכות.
keyPoints: 10 sephiroth, 22 paths, 3 pillars.
Mercy (right): Chokmah, Chesed, Netzach.
Severity (left): Binah, Geburah, Hod.
Balance (middle): Kether, Tiphareth, Yesod, Malkuth.
Order: Kether 1 to Malkuth 10.

outline.title: Four Worlds, divine names and the planes of the Tree
outline.summary: Kabbalah describes four worlds, or levels: Atziluth (emanation), Briah (creation), Yetzirah (formation) and Assiah (action). In the Hermetic system each has its own Tree, and each links to an element, a card suit and a letter of the Divine Name. The four-letter Name of God, the Tetragrammaton, Yod Heh Vav Heh (יהוה), is traditionally not pronounced. The letters map to the four worlds and the four elements: fire, water, air and earth. Each sephirah also has a Divine Name, an archangel, and an angelic order in Hermetic tables.
keyPoints: Atziluth (Yod, fire, wands).
Briah (Heh, water, cups).
Yetzirah (Vav, air, swords).
Assiah (final Heh, earth, pentacles).
Ain Soph lies beyond Kether.

outline.title: The Hebrew letters and the 22 paths
outline.summary: The 22 letters of the Hebrew alphabet correspond to the 22 paths linking the sephiroth. The Sefer Yetzirah divides the letters into three mothers (Aleph א, Mem מ, Shin ש), seven doubles (Beth ב, Gimel ג, Daleth ד, Kaph כ, Peh פ, Resh ר, Tav ת) and twelve simples. The Golden Dawn linked the mothers with the elements air, water and fire, the doubles with the seven classical planets, and the twelve simples with the signs of the zodiac. Each letter also has a numerical value, which is the basis of gematria.
keyPoints: Mothers: Aleph (air), Mem (water), Shin (fire).
Doubles: Beth Mercury, Gimel Moon, Daleth Venus, Kaph Jupiter, Peh Mars, Resh Sun, Tav Saturn.
Simples: Heh Aries to Qoph Pisces.
Values run 1 to 10, then 20 to 90, then 100 to 400.
Paths are numbered 11 to 32.

outline.title: The 22 paths and the Tarot
outline.summary: The Hermetic Qabalah pairs each of the 22 paths with a letter and with one of the 22 trumps of the Tarot, the Major Arcana. The most common table is from the Golden Dawn. This pairing is a 19th-century invention. Tarot cards first appeared in the 15th century as a card game, and the link to Kabbalah was proposed by French occultists such as Eliphas Levi and refined by the Golden Dawn. As a symbolic system it works as a memory aid: each path becomes an image with associated letters, planets and meanings.
keyPoints: 22 letters = 22 paths = 22 Major Arcana.
Aleph = The Fool; Beth = The Magician; Gimel = The High Priestess.
Tav = The World; Shin = Judgement; Resh = The Sun.
Crowley swapped Heh (Star) and Tzaddi (Emperor).
The pairing dates from the 19th century.

outline.title: Correspondences: planets, elements and the zodiac
outline.summary: The Hermetic system builds big tables of correspondence. Every sephirah and path gets a planet, element or zodiac sign, a colour, a metal, a stone, a god or angel, and a number. The planets on the Tree are Saturn (Binah), Jupiter (Chesed), Mars (Geburah), the Sun (Tiphareth), Venus (Netzach), Mercury (Hod) and the Moon (Yesod). Kether is the Primum Mobile, Chokmah the zodiac, and Malkuth the Earth. These come from medieval and Renaissance sources such as Agrippa, and were tabulated by Crowley in 777 (1909).
keyPoints: Saturn: Binah. Jupiter: Chesed. Mars: Geburah.
Sun: Tiphareth. Venus: Netzach. Mercury: Hod. Moon: Yesod.
Kether: Primum Mobile. Chokmah: zodiac. Malkuth: earth.
Path doubles: planets. Simples: zodiac. Mothers: elements.
Tables are tools for memory.

outline.title: Methods: gematria, notarikon and temurah
outline.summary: Kabbalists developed three classic methods of reading hidden links in words. Gematria adds the numerical values of letters. Notarikon treats each letter of a word as the start of another word, or builds one word from the first letters of many. Temurah swaps letters by a rule. Atbash is the best-known temurah: it swaps the first letter with the last, the second with the second last, and so on. The word Sheshach in the Book of Jeremiah has been read as an Atbash form of Babel. Used as a game, these methods reveal wordplay and links between ideas. As evidence, they prove nothing, because with enough words you can find a match for any number.
keyPoints: Gematria: add letter values.
Notarikon: initials make a phrase.
Temurah: swap letters by a rule; Atbash reverses the alphabet.
Equal sums are links in play, not proof.
Shalom שלום = 376.

outline.title: Golden Dawn and after: a short history
outline.summary: The Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn was founded in London in 1888 by three Freemasons: William Wynn Westcott, William Robert Woodman and Samuel Liddell MacGregor Mathers. It taught Qabalah, astrology, Tarot and ritual in graded degrees. Its members included W. B. Yeats, A. E. Waite and Aleister Crowley. After it split in the early 1900s, Waite produced the Rider-Waite Tarot (1909), and Crowley, the Thoth Tarot (1944) and the tables of 777. Dion Fortune's The Mystical Qabalah (1935) gave a popular, psychological reading, and Carl Jung's work encouraged reading such symbols as maps of the psyche.
keyPoints: Levi: 1850s. Golden Dawn: 1888.
Rider-Waite Tarot: 1909. 777: 1909.
Fortune: 1935. Thoth Tarot: 1944.
The Golden Dawn was a secret society with degrees.
Jung gave a psychological reading of symbols.
glossary: Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn

outline.title: Reading critically and using the Tree as a symbol map
outline.summary: Hermetic Qabalah is best studied with a historian's care. Many claims of ancient origin, such as that the Tarot is Egyptian or that the Golden Dawn tables are millennia old, do not survive checking. The system is a creative modern synthesis built from older parts. It is also wise to respect the living Jewish tradition of Kabbalah, which is a different thing: a scholarly and devotional discipline within Judaism, with a long, rigorous history. The Hermetic system borrows its vocabulary, often loosely. As a personal tool, the Tree can serve as a map of symbols for memory, reflection and creative work, without needing to believe in any hidden powers.
keyPoints: Check the date of every claim of ancient origin.
Hermetic Qabalah is a 19th-century synthesis.
Jewish Kabbalah is a living tradition; credit it.
Equal sums and matching tables are not proofs.
Use the Tree as a memory and reflection tool.

courses.title: Homotopy Type Theory
courses.subtitle: Types as spaces, proofs as programs, equality as paths: a first course with Python labs and a circle explorer
courses.author: Lilith Learning Lab
courses.description: A beginner-friendly introduction to homotopy type theory: types and terms, dependent Pi and Sigma types, propositions as types, identity types and paths, higher paths and groupoids, homotopy levels, equivalences and univalence, higher inductive types such as the circle, the fundamental group of the circle, and cubical type theory with proof assistants. Python labs recompute counts, reduce path words and compute winding numbers; two small interactive apps let you explore loops on the circle and propositions as types.

outline.title: Why types? The big idea of HoTT
outline.summary: Homotopy type theory, or HoTT, reads types as spaces, terms as points, and equalities as paths between points. A proof that two things are equal becomes a path you can walk, bend and compose. It combines two old ideas: Martin-Lof type theory, a foundation for mathematics and programming, and homotopy theory, the study of shapes up to continuous deformation. The result is a foundation where equal things really are interchangeable, which is exactly what mathematicians always wanted equality to mean.
keyPoints: a : A means the term a has type A, like 3 : Nat.
Statements are types; proofs are terms.
Equal means connected by a path.
Paths can be reversed and composed, like loops on a map.
Univalence: equivalent types are equal.
HoTT gives a foundation that proof assistants can check.

outline.title: Functions, pairs and dependent types
outline.summary: A dependent type is a family of types B(x) indexed by x : A. For each x you get a type, called the fibre over x. A dependent function type, Pi over x : A of B(x), has functions that send each x to a term in its own fibre B(x). A dependent pair type, Sigma over x : A of B(x), holds pairs of a point x and a term in the fibre over x. When B does not depend on x, Pi becomes the function type A -> B and Sigma becomes the product A x B. Counting terms of finite types shows the names: Pi multiplies, Sigma adds.
keyPoints: Pi: for all. Sigma: there exists.
|Pi x:A. B(x)| = product of |B(x)|.
|Sigma x:A. B(x)| = sum of |B(x)|.
Non-dependent Pi is A -> B; non-dependent Sigma is A x B.
A universe U holds small types as terms.

outline.title: Propositions as types: Curry-Howard
outline.summary: Under the Curry-Howard correspondence, a logical formula is a type and a proof of it is a program of that type. Proving a theorem and writing a program are the same activity. Implication is a function type, and is proved by a function. And is a pair type. Or is a sum type, with a left and a right case. False is the empty type, and not-A means A -> False. Excluded middle and double negation elimination have no general proof in pure type theory. Statements that need them are not provable constructively.
keyPoints: A -> B is both implication and function.
A x B is both 'and' and pair.
A + B is both 'or' and sum.
Empty type: false. Not A is A -> Empty.
Excluded middle is not provable in pure type theory.

outline.title: Identity types and paths
outline.summary: For terms a, b : A, the identity type a = b holds the proofs that a and b are equal. In HoTT we call a term p : a = b a path from a to b. The basic path is refl : a = a. The induction principle for paths, written J, says that to prove something about all paths it is enough to prove it for refl. From this one rule come symmetry (reverse a path), transitivity (compose paths), ap (apply a function to a path) and transport (move a term along a path).
keyPoints: refl : a = a.
Reverse: p : a = b gives inverse p : b = a.
Compose: p : a = b and q : b = c give p . q : a = c.
ap f p : f a = f b.
transport B p : B(a) -> B(b).

outline.title: Higher paths and the groupoid structure
outline.summary: Paths are terms of the identity type, so two paths p, q : a = b can themselves be compared by the type p = q. A term of that is a 2-path, a path between paths. Composition of paths is associative, has refl as a unit, and has inverses, but only up to a higher path. A type with this structure is an infinity-groupoid. A loop at a is a path a = a. The loops at a form the loop space, and its structure is where homotopy groups come from.
keyPoints: p = q is a type; its terms are 2-paths.
Associativity: (p . q) . r = p . (q . r) by a path.
p . inverse p = refl by a path.
Loops at a form the loop space Omega(A, a).
Each type is a tower of paths: an infinity-groupoid.

outline.title: Homotopy levels: propositions and sets
outline.summary: Types come in levels by how complicated their paths are. A contractible type is a single point up to paths. A proposition has at most one term up to paths. A set has no interesting paths between paths. Level n + 1 means that all path types a = b have level n. The levels start at -2 for contractible, -1 for propositions, 0 for sets and 1 for groupoid-like types. Truncation squeezes a type into a lower level. For example, a set truncation keeps only which component you are in, forgetting the paths.
keyPoints: Level -2: contractible. Level -1: proposition. Level 0: set.
A proposition has at most one proof.
A set has paths that are all unique.
Nat and Bool are sets.
Truncation forgets higher paths.

outline.title: Equivalences and univalence
outline.summary: An equivalence between types A and B is a function with an inverse up to paths, written A ~ B. For sets it is exactly a bijection. Every path A = B in the universe gives an equivalence, by transport. The univalence axiom says that this map is itself an equivalence, so equivalences are the same as paths in the universe. Therefore equivalent types are interchangeable: any property proved for A can be transported to B.
keyPoints: A ~ B: a function with an inverse up to paths.
For finite sets, equivalence = bijection.
Univalence: (A = B) is equivalent to (A ~ B).
Isomorphic things are equal; use either.
n points have n! self-equivalences.

outline.title: Higher inductive types: the circle
outline.summary: An ordinary inductive type lists point constructors. A higher inductive type, or HIT, may also list path constructors: new equalities that must hold. The circle S1 has one point base and one path loop : base = base. The interval has two points and a path joining them. Spheres and other shapes are built the same way. These are the types that let HoTT reason about real shapes directly.
keyPoints: S1: base : S1 and loop : base = base.
Interval: two ends joined by a path; it is contractible.
Suspension of S^n is S^(n+1).
To map out of S1, give a point and a loop in the target.
HITs add shape, not just data.

outline.title: Homotopy groups and the fundamental group of the circle
outline.summary: The n-th homotopy group of a pointed type is the set of n-fold loops, with 'same up to a path' as equality. For n = 1 this is the fundamental group. The fundamental group of the circle is the integers. In HoTT the proof uses a type family over the circle, whose fibre over every point is the integers and where transport along loop adds one. The homotopy groups of spheres are a famous hard table. Some entries are easy, and some are still being computed.
keyPoints: pi1(S1) = Z: loops are counted by integers.
Encode: send a loop to its winding number.
Decode: send n to loop to the n.
pi_k(S^n) = 0 for k < n; pi_n(S^n) = Z.
Stable groups appear by Freudenthal.

outline.title: Cubical type theory and proof assistants
outline.summary: Plain HoTT assumes univalence as an axiom, so programs using it can get stuck. Cubical type theory builds paths from an interval, so univalence computes. Cubical Agda is a proof assistant with these features. Rocq (formerly Coq) has HoTT libraries, and Lean has a large library of ordinary mathematics. The HoTT book, free online, is the standard introduction. This course is a gentle path to it.
keyPoints: Cubical: a path is a function from the interval.
Univalence computes in cubical type theory.
Agda, Rocq and Lean can all check proofs.
The HoTT book is free and written by a large group.
Types you write in Haskell show the idea in small.

courses.title: Jade Agent Kit: A Workspace for AI Agents
courses.subtitle: Files, shell, code, search, tools, agents and safe automation in the browser, with Python labs
courses.author: Lilith Learning Lab
courses.description: Learn the Jade Agent Kit (version 3), a lean browser workspace for AI agents: the virtual file system, shell, Python, JavaScript and SQLite runtimes, BM25 and vector search, tools for language models, the agent loop and brain, decisions, scheduling, Sentry, notes and safe automation with approvals and secrets. Each chapter has an ELI5 block and Python labs that rebuild the ideas.

outline.title: Meet the kit and lean loading
outline.summary: The Jade Agent Kit is a workspace that lives inside a web page and gives an AI agent a place to get things done. It has a virtual file system, a shell, Python, JavaScript, SQLite, search, decisions, scheduling and an agent, and every piece is optional. Its main idea is lean loading. The first call, createKit, sets up only the file system. Each other feature is its own module that downloads the first time a page uses it. A page that needs only files stays tiny. This course follows the kit's documentation, version 3, and builds small working models of each idea in Python so you understand how the real thing behaves.
keyPoints: You import createKit from a CDN, pinned to a version such as v3.0.0.
createKit alone loads just the file system (about 6.6 KB gzipped).
kit.use('python') loads Python; kit.use('sqlite', 'bm25') loads several.
Helpers such as kit.run, kit.tool, kit.decide, kit.embed and kit.agent load what they need by themselves.
kit.has('python') tells whether a feature is loaded.
createKit({ use: [...] }) preloads; use: 'all' loads everything.

outline.title: The virtual file system
outline.summary: kit.vfs is a small file system in the browser. Paths look like /notes/a.md. Writing a file creates any missing folders. Because the shell, Python, JavaScript, SQLite, the agent's tools and the brain all use the same file system, a file written by one is seen by all. By default it lives in memory. With persist set to a name, changes are saved to IndexedDB shortly after each change, and flush saves immediately. The lab builds a tiny file system to see how paths and folders work.
keyPoints: write(path, data) takes a string or bytes and creates missing folders.
read gives a string; readBytes gives a Uint8Array.
list(dir) returns the names in a folder.
exists, isDir and stat inspect a path.
move, copy and rm change the tree.
Data persists only if you set persist; otherwise it is memory only.

outline.title: The shell: kit.run and sessions
outline.summary: kit.run executes a shell command string against the virtual file system. It understands pipes, redirects, and, or, variables, command substitution and globs. The commands come from BusyBox 1.37 compiled to WebAssembly, with JavaScript versions of common ones as a fallback. A session gives you your own working directory and environment variables, with options for streaming output, a timeout and cancellation. You can also register your own commands as functions. There are no if or for blocks in the shell. For real scripting, call node or python.
keyPoints: kit.run returns an object with stdout (and the exit status).
A && B runs B only if A succeeds; A || B runs B only if A fails.
kit.shell.session({ cwd, env }) creates a separate shell.
session.run(cmd, { onOutput, timeoutMs, signal }) streams, limits time and can be cancelled.
kit.shell.commands.name = fn registers a custom command.
Built-in extras: node, js, python, python3, sqlite3, sh, xargs, cd, export, which, help.

outline.title: Python, JavaScript and SQLite
outline.summary: The kit can run code. kit.python runs MicroPython 1.27 in a Web Worker; its open and os see the same virtual file system. kit.js runs JavaScript in another worker with require, fs, path, node:sqlite and fetch, but no npm packages. kit.sqlite opens database files stored in the VFS and runs SQLite 3.53 in WebAssembly. With sqlite-vec it can store and search vectors, and FTS5 gives full-text search. In the lab you will build a safe parameterised query.
keyPoints: kit.python.run(code, { cwd }) runs Python; open() and os use the VFS.
kit.js.run(code, { cwd, timeoutMs, globals, network }) returns the script's return value as r.result.
Inside JavaScript, kit.tool(name, args) calls any kit tool.
kit.sqlite.open(path) takes a VFS path or ':memory:'.
db.exec for schema, db.run for writes with params, db.query for rows as objects.
Always pass values as parameters, never glue them into SQL.

outline.title: BM25 keyword search
outline.summary: BM25 is a ranking formula for keyword search: documents that contain the query words more often, especially rare words, and that are not too long, score higher. It needs no downloads and is only 2.1 KB in the kit. kit.bm25.search ranks an array of texts for one query. The BM25 class builds an index once for many queries. searchFiles ranks files under a folder, which is how an agent finds the right note. The lab implements the scoring yourself.
keyPoints: search(docs, query) returns objects with id, text and score.
new kit.bm25.BM25(docs) builds a reusable index; index.search(query, { limit }).
searchFiles(query, { root }) returns path, score, line and snippet.
Scores are relative: compare them within one search, not across searches.
BM25 matches words, not meaning; embeddings come next.
The page says its scoring follows Python's rank_bm25.

outline.title: Embeddings and vector search
outline.summary: An embedding turns text into a list of numbers so that texts with similar meaning have nearby vectors. kit.embed makes them using a model running locally through Ollama, such as embeddinggemma or nomic-embed-text. Ollama Cloud has no embedding models. kit.vectors keeps embeddings in a SQLite file using sqlite-vec. A search embeds your question and returns the nearest records. Hybrid search also uses BM25 and merges the two rankings. The labs compute similarity and merge rankings.
keyPoints: kit.embed(text) gives one vector; kit.embed(array, { model }) gives many.
store = await kit.vectors.open(path); store.add(items); store.search(query, { limit }).
Results have id, text, meta, distance and score.
{ hybrid: true } merges meaning search with BM25.
A store remembers its model and rejects vectors from another.
Pull an embedding model in Ollama first.

outline.title: Tools for language models
outline.summary: A language model cannot touch files or run code by itself. It can only ask for a tool call. kit.tools gives the model a description of each tool, and kit.tool(name, args) runs the call and returns the result as text. The kit generates definitions in two shapes: the OpenAI shape, which Ollama also uses, and the Anthropic shape. You can add your own tools with a description, a JSON Schema for the inputs and a run function. The labs build a dispatcher and a schema generator.
keyPoints: kit.tools.openai() returns { type: 'function', function: { name, description, parameters } } entries.
kit.tools.anthropic(['read', 'bash']) returns { name, description, input_schema } entries.
kit.tool(name, args) always returns a string; errors begin with 'Error:'.
Built in: read, write, edit, bash, python, javascript, sqlite, search_files, decide, tasks, schedule, sentry, search, fetch.
kit.tools.add(name, { description, parameters, run }) registers a tool.
edit needs oldText to be unique unless replaceAll is set.

outline.title: The agent loop
outline.summary: kit.agent() builds a small coding agent in the style of the pi agent. It pairs a model running on Ollama with a loop and a fixed set of tools: read, write, edit, bash, search and fetch. Ask it to write a file, run it and report, and it does so. The loop is simple. Send the conversation to the model. If the reply asks for tools, run them and add the results to the conversation, then ask again. When the reply is plain text, the turn is over. maxSteps stops runaway loops. The lab simulates the loop with a scripted model.
keyPoints: Pass ollamaKey to createKit for Ollama Cloud; omit it for Ollama on your machine.
Defaults: gpt-oss:120b on cloud, qwen3:8b locally; maxSteps defaults to 40.
Methods: prompt(text), abort(), reset(), and the messages list.
Events: text, thinking, tool_call, tool_result, turn_end, done, error (and route, context, compaction with a brain).
search and fetch always use Ollama Cloud, so they need a cloud key.
Give extra tools with tools: [...DEFAULT_TOOLS, 'tasks', 'schedule'].

outline.title: The agent brain
outline.summary: The brain is a set of optional parts you switch on with kit.agent({ brain }). Each part downloads on first use, adds its own tool and hooks into the loop. Their files live as plain text under /.kit/ in the file system, so people can read and edit them. Memory remembers facts and finds the right ones for each prompt. Skills are instructions the agent loads when needed. The guard keeps long chats inside the model's context window. The router sends only the tools a message seems to need. Other parts add a knowledge graph with proofs, tree-of-thoughts thinking, sub-agents and chat history. The labs build a compactor, a secret filter and a tool router.
keyPoints: brain: ['memory', 'skills', 'history', 'guard'] picks parts; brain: true turns on memory, skills, history and guard; 'all' loads everything.
memory keeps /.kit/memory/Memory.md, retrieves by BM25 (or embeddings) and filters out anything that looks like a password or key.
skills reads /.kit/SOUL.md, /AGENTS.md and /.kit/SYSTEM.md, and skills in /.kit/skills/<name>/SKILL.md.
guard estimates request size and compacts older turns near the limit.
router sends core tools and exposes the rest through more_tools.
delegate spawns a read-only sub-agent unless write: true; knowledge proves or contradicts claims; think runs a verified search.

outline.title: Decisions: fast calibrated choices
outline.summary: Not every question needs a long conversation. kit.decide sends a state, such as a log line or a message, and a question to a small decision model that answers with calibrated probabilities. It is meant for quick, cheap jobs like triage, routing and checks. There are three kinds. choice picks one of your options. score rates the state on a scale you define. yesno answers a question with a boolean. The result always includes how confident the model is. The labs reshape probabilities into the kit's result form.
keyPoints: type: 'choice' (default) needs options; the result has result, choice, confidence and probabilities.
type: 'score' rates against your options such as low, medium, high.
type: 'yesno' returns a boolean answer.
kit.decisions picks the server: 'ollaya' (default), 'ollama' (0.35 or later) or 'cloud'.
The kit translates between server formats so answers look the same.
Give an agent the decide tool by adding it to tools.

outline.title: Scheduling and tasks
outline.summary: kit.schedule runs jobs at times you describe in plain English, like every monday at 6pm, or in five-field cron form. A job can run a shell command, a JavaScript or Python snippet, an agent prompt, or a function. kit.tasks keeps a simple task list that people and agents share. Jobs run only while a page with the kit is open. A job missed while the page was closed runs once when it reopens. Jobs are saved to /.kit/schedule.json, except function jobs, which you re-add on each load. The labs write a cron matcher and a small task list.
keyPoints: kit.schedule.add({ name, when, command | prompt | js | python | run }).
when understands 'every day at 2am', 'in 20 minutes', '@hourly' or 5-field cron, in local time.
list(), runNow(name), disable(name), remove(name); on emits run, error, change.
scheduler: false in createKit keeps it stopped until kit.schedule.start().
kit.cron has fromText, parse, next, upcoming and describe.
kit.tasks: add, start, done, update, list, text, on, clear.

outline.title: Sentry, notes and senses
outline.summary: Sentry is a rule engine that watches the page and the device and acts when a condition occurs. It can watch things like battery, network, idle time, keys, motion, light, location, sound level, camera changes, and your own states and events. Sensitive sources must be allowed by the app. The kit also includes a notes vault in the style of Obsidian, stored on the file system, with wiki links, backlinks, tags, search, renames that update links, daily notes and templates. Senses let an agent reach the world: HTTP with secrets, MCP servers, camera, microphone, location, other sensors, and a look tool that lets the agent see an image.
keyPoints: Sentry watches battery, network, idle, keys, motion, light, location, sound level, camera change and custom events.
createKit({ sentry: { allow: ['location'] } }) lets the app permit sensitive systems.
Agents manage rules through the sentry tool.
Notes support [[wiki links]], backlinks, #tags, search, daily notes and templates.
Renaming a note updates every link to it.
look lets the agent see an image; backups can be gzip, optionally encrypted.

outline.title: Automation and staying safe
outline.summary: The kit can automate. Flows are n8n-style workflows of steps with triggers. Playbooks are Ansible-style task lists that run without a model. Autonomy keeps a work queue within budgets, a heartbeat checks a list every few minutes, and curiosity makes the agent explore on its own. Automation needs guard rails. A playbook runs unattended only after your app approves it, and any change needs approval again. Agents can save playbooks but cannot approve them. Secrets such as API keys are passed in by the app, kept out of the file system, and referred to by name only. This final chapter ties the kit together and ends with a design checklist.
keyPoints: Flows: step types include tool, js, shell, decide, llm, agent, file, set, if, switch, each, wait, notify, playbook, flow and stop; triggers are manual, schedule or file change.
Playbooks support when, loop, register, retries, block/rescue/always, assert, tags and secrets redacted from logs.
playbooks.approve(name) or an approve callback in createKit; changes require re-approval.
Autonomy: queue with priorities that age, deadlines, budgets, quiet hours; it pauses while the user is active.
Heartbeat: a reply of HEARTBEAT_OK stays silent; anything else raises an alert.
createKit({ secrets: { NAME: value } }); agents see names and use {{ NAME }}.

courses.title: Jade Agent Stack
courses.subtitle: Driving Jade Vault and Agent Base safely: harness, approvals, playbooks, sites, surfaces and security, with Python labs
courses.author: Lilith Learning Lab
courses.description: A hands-on course based on the open Jade Agent Stack toolkit (github.com/lucky-edgelord/jade-agent-stack, MIT). Learn how the Jade parts fit together (Vault asks, Base answers, Base logs, Base can say no); configuration, the OS keyring and header-only authentication; the harness with approval patterns where deny wins, idempotency keys and short-lived task credentials; stable error codes, exit codes and version compatibility; portable YAML playbooks with check, plan, approve, run, rollback and resume; the site compiler from a YAML spec to pages and a Base backend; the CLI, REPL, JSON lines, MCP, HTTP and Python surfaces and how agents work through them; and the threat model with defences against prompt injection. Based on version 0.1.0 of the documentation; check the repository for later changes. Every chapter has Python labs verified in the built-in interpreter, plus an approvals tester and a playbook run simulator.

outline.title: The stack: five parts and one contract
outline.summary: Jade Agent Stack is one Python package that drives four other Jade repositories: Vault, Agent Base, Agent Kit and Agent UI/UX. It is a client, not a fork, and it speaks to them only through documented interfaces. The division of labour is summed up in one line: Vault asks, Base answers, Base logs, Base can say no. Vault owns the agent loop and the person's transcript; Base owns identity, the database, the model gateway, billing and the authoritative audit log. The rules between them are short: tool calls over MCP or REST, one short-lived credential per task, an idempotency key on every mutation, and a refusal means stop and tell the person.
keyPoints: Vault asks. Base answers. Base logs. Base can say no.
Seam: MCP at /api/agent/mcp, same tools over REST.
Vault owns the transcript; Base owns the audit.
One credential per task, at most 24 h.
403 credential_refused: stop, do not retry.

outline.title: Install, configuration and secrets
outline.summary: Install with pip (Python 3.11 or later, needing only PyYAML). The setup wizard jade init writes jade.config.yaml, and jade doctor checks that every target is reachable, authenticated, compatible and free of tokens in URLs. The config is found by walking up from the working directory, or from the JADE_CONFIG variable. Unknown keys are errors, and the file never holds secrets. Secrets are looked up in an order: JADE_SECRET environment variables first (good for CI), then the OS keyring, then an opt-in 0600 file. Tokens travel only in the Authorization header.
keyPoints: pip install jade-agent-stack.
jade init, then jade doctor.
Config: $JADE_CONFIG, else walk up.
Secrets: env, keyring, 0600 file.
A URL with a token is refused.

outline.title: The harness: approvals, idempotency and task credentials
outline.summary: Every SDK call and command passes through the harness before it leaves, in the same process. It applies approvals, attaches idempotency keys and mints short-lived credentials. Approvals are patterns by capability and target, such as base.write: record_*:bookings. Deny rules win over allow rules. A call that no rule covers needs a person to confirm, and destructive tools need confirmation even when allowed. Mutations always carry an idempotency key, so a retry cannot run twice. Task credentials last minutes and carry only the scopes the task needs; a refusal stops the run.
keyPoints: base.write: ["record_*:bookings"].
Deny wins.
Uncovered call: confirm or --yolo.
Reads retry; mutations do not.
Credential TTL 15 minutes by default.

outline.title: Errors, exit codes and version compatibility
outline.summary: Every failure has a stable code of the form JADE and three digits, a message and a remediation. The first digit groups them: 1xx auth and secrets, 2xx remote, 3xx safety, 4xx user input, 5xx doctor. Exit codes tell scripts what kind of failure it was: 0 ok, 1 user error, 2 remote error, 3 refused for safety. A script should treat 3 as a stop, not something to retry. Version checks keep the parts compatible: a different major version is refused (JADE203), an older minor is a warning. A Vault that accepts tokens in URLs is refused (JADE102).
keyPoints: JADE1xx auth, 2xx remote, 3xx safety, 4xx input.
0 ok, 1 user, 2 remote, 3 safety.
Never retry exit 3.
Major mismatch refused, older minor warns.
str(error) never shows a secret.

outline.title: Playbooks: portable automation
outline.summary: A playbook is a YAML file of tasks that compile to the targets' existing primitives: Base tools, Vault's HTTP API, a Kit page and local commands. You check it, plan it, approve it and run it. Each task can register its result, run only when a condition holds, retry, and declare an undo. Three failure modes decide what a failed task does: stop, continue, or roll back by running undos in reverse. Runs are resumable and idempotent. Approval is bound to the SHA-256 of the file, so any edit needs a new approval, and unattended runs require it.
keyPoints: check, plan, approve, run.
Fail modes: stop, continue, rollback.
Rollback needs undo on mutating tasks.
Key = hash of playbook, task and vars.
Edit the file, lose the approval.

outline.title: Sites: one YAML file to a website and its backend
outline.summary: A site is one file, jade.site.yaml, compiled to static HTML that loads the Agent UI/UX components. A name, a tagline and a template make a whole site; the same spec can also configure the Base backend with collections, sign-in, models, plans and billing. Eight templates, twelve themes and nineteen sections give the building blocks. Pages in the spec replace the template's page at the same path, and backend lists merge by name. A settled design can be saved as a reusable template. Deploying is a generated playbook, so approvals, idempotency keys, task credentials and resumption all apply. Plan first: it lists every Base call and makes none.
keyPoints: name + tagline + template = a site.
Merge by name, replace by path.
Field: name:type!  (! = required).
Rules: anyone, users, owner, admin.
plan before deploy.

outline.title: Every surface: CLI, REPL, MCP, HTTP and Python, and working with agents
outline.summary: Every capability is a command in one registry, reachable the same way everywhere: the command line, an interactive REPL (or JSON lines for programs), an MCP server over stdio, a local HTTP server and the Python SDK. Results are the same JSON values. A command named site.build is jade site build on the CLI, site.build in JSON lines, site_build over MCP and POST /v1/commands/site.build over HTTP. jade commands lists them all with parameters as data. Agents can do nearly everything except widen their own permissions: approvals, secrets, playbook approval and deploy confirmation need a person at a terminal.
keyPoints: site.build = jade site build = site_build.
Exit 0 ok, 1 user, 2 remote, 3 safety.
JSON: {schema: jade.v1, ok, command, data}.
Agents cannot widen permissions.

outline.title: Security: threats, defences and responsible use
outline.summary: The threat model assumes agents can be fooled. A malicious note, web page or MCP server can carry instructions that steer an agent. The defence is not hoping the agent resists; it is limiting what a steered agent can do: approvals, narrow scopes, short credentials and an audit log it cannot edit. The toolkit adds header-only auth, keyring secrets, redaction of output, hashed playbook approvals, a sandboxed expression language and escaped page output. Treat data from targets as data, never as instructions. Some Base scopes, schema, hooks and settings, are close to root and should be granted sparingly. Report vulnerabilities privately through GitHub security advisories.
keyPoints: Assume the agent can be steered.
Bound the blast radius: scopes, TTL, approvals.
Results are data, not instructions.
schema, hooks, settings are root-equivalent.
Report privately via security advisories.

courses.title: Jade Vault: A Markdown Vault with an AI Agent
courses.subtitle: Notes, memory, tools, flows, playbooks and a knowledge graph, explained with small Python models
courses.author: Lilith Learning Lab
courses.description: Learn how Jade Vault works: an Obsidian-style markdown vault with an AI agent called Jade, as one HTML page and an Android app. You will follow a turn step by step, then study tools and safety, memory and hybrid search, skills, the heartbeat, schedules and curiosity, flows, playbooks, the knowledge graph with Datalog rules, autonomous mode and Gantt plans, the think tool, delegation, Jade Lisp, the HTTP API, backups and the patch-based build. The course follows version 2.28.1. Each chapter has an ELI5 block and Python labs.

outline.title: What Jade Vault is
outline.summary: Jade Vault is a markdown vault in the style of Obsidian with an AI agent called Jade built in. It runs as one page in a browser and as an Android app. The vault is a virtual file system. Jade is a loop: your message plus a prompt built from her steering files, memory and skills goes to a model, she may call tools, and she answers. The model is not part of the app. You point it at Ollama, Ollama Cloud, Groq, OpenRouter, llama.cpp or any OpenAI compatible server.
keyPoints: Jade Vault is a markdown vault with a built-in agent, as one browser page or an Android app.
The vault is the shared ground; Jade is a model driven loop around it.
You choose the model: local Ollama, Ollama Cloud, Groq, OpenRouter, llama.cpp or any OpenAI style endpoint.
Around the loop sit memory, autonomy, world tools, integrations and safety.
Anything that runs on its own is off until you switch it on.
Her settings and work products are ordinary files in the vault.

outline.title: Notes and the vault
outline.summary: Notes are markdown files. A link to another note is written in double square brackets, and an embed, such as an image, puts an exclamation mark in front. Tags start with a hash sign. The notes screen shows backlinks, a graph, a reader and a split editor. Obsidian style scripts and Templater templates are supported inside a sandbox. Her own files live under /Jade. The labs classify files, find links and build backlinks.
keyPoints: Links are [[Note]]; an alias is [[Note|text]]; a heading link is [[Note#Heading]].
Images and notes embed with ![[photo.png|300]].
Backlinks list the notes that point at the current note.
Templates use <% tp.date.now() %> style code from Templater.
Note scripts (dataviewjs) run in a sandbox: they read the vault, with no network and no file changes.
Jade's files, such as /Jade/SOUL.md and /Jade/Memory.md, are ordinary notes.

outline.title: A turn, step by step
outline.summary: A turn begins when a message arrives. The harness builds a prompt, calls the model, runs any tools the model asks for, feeds the results back, and repeats until the model answers without a tool call. The system prompt is built in a fixed order from the base text, SOUL.md, AGENTS.md, memory and the skill list. Before each call the context guard checks the whole request fits in the model's window. A limit on tool rounds stops a runaway loop. She tells you when it stopped, and you can send continue.
keyPoints: send(text) records the message with a timestamp, runs any slash command, then runs the agent loop.
The system prompt joins base or SYSTEM.md, SOUL.md, AGENTS.md files, the memory block, the skill list and tool text.
Before each call, the harness may prefetch memory hits and matching skills.
A tool error becomes an Error result that the model can react to.
The loop ends on a reply with no tool calls, a user abort, or maxTurns rounds.
Messages you type while she works are queued and added before her next model call.

outline.title: Tools, gating and safety
outline.summary: Jade has about thirty tools: notes, shell, node, Python, SQLite, web, MCP, flows, schedules and more. On Android there are packs for senses, phone, screen, a second browser and SSH. A tool exists for the model only if the pack switch allows it and any special condition holds. Each pack shows its context cost, because tool descriptions take room in the prompt. Secrets are written as {{NAME}} and filled in outside the model, and risky actions ask you first.
keyPoints: Tools are listed to the model only when their switch and conditions allow.
Each pack in Settings → World shows how much context it costs.
Secrets are placeholders like {{NAME}}; the real value is added outside the model and echoes are redacted.
Calls, texts, SSH commands, new playbooks and restore ask you first.
Web pages, SSH output and screen text are labelled as data, not instructions.
During a curiosity wake her tools are filtered, so she cannot reach phone or Sentry unless you widen it.

outline.title: Memory, search and context
outline.summary: Jade remembers in layers: a Memory file of durable facts that goes into every prompt, a journal entry per chat, your notes, the raw chats, and a vector index that makes all of it searchable. Search is hybrid. It runs keywords and meaning at the same time and merges the two ranked lists with reciprocal rank fusion. If the embedder is missing, it falls back to keywords and then BM25.
