When a chat grows too long, old turns are compacted into a summary so the request fits the model's window.
keyPoints: Memory layers: Memory.md, journal, notes, raw chats and a vector index.
The index is /Jade/.index/vectors.db, an ordinary SQLite file that is a cache you can delete.
A search runs FTS5 keywords and vector nearest neighbours, then fuses them with RRF.
BM25 rewards rare query words that appear often, and normalises for document length.
Auto-compaction runs after a number of turns or when the last answer filled too much of the window.
The /context command shows where the window goes.

outline.title: Skills and the skill router
outline.summary: A skill is a folder under /Jade/skills with a SKILL.md file. The file starts with frontmatter that has a name and a description, then the instructions. Jade loads a skill on demand with the skill tool. Listing every skill costs context. With fifteen or fewer, all are listed. With more, only the six best for the current message are listed, chosen by meaning and whole word overlap, and a search tool finds the others. The description is all the router sees, so write it as when to use the skill, in the words a user would say.
keyPoints: A skill folder is /Jade/skills/kebab-name/ with SKILL.md and optional files.
Run one with the skill tool or /skill:name.
Up to 15 skills are all listed; with more, the best 6 are listed.
Ranking fuses vector meaning with whole word overlap.
Strict mode drops a match with a vector distance over 0.6 and no word overlap.
Write a description that says when to use the skill; put the procedure in the body.

outline.title: Running on her own: heartbeat, schedules and curiosity
outline.summary: Everything that runs without you is off until you switch it on, runs only while the app is alive, and is logged. The heartbeat reads a checklist file every N minutes and answers HEARTBEAT_OK when nothing needs attention. Schedules run a prompt, a shell command or a flow, written in plain English or as cron. Command and flow schedules run without the model. Curiosity wakes her at random times to explore, reflect, connect notes, practice, anticipate, ask a question or rest. It scores activities by learning progress, so noise earns no bonus.
keyPoints: Heartbeat: every N minutes (default 30) inside active hours; an empty checklist skips the model call.
Schedules accept plain English like every weekday at 9am, cron, or @daily.
Command and flow schedules log to /Jade/Logs/cron.log and notify on failure.
Curiosity: a window (default 08:00 to 22:00), a daily cap (default 5) and a steering file CURIOSITY.md.
Learning progress is the slow error average minus the fast one, never below zero.
Reward is measured by diffing the vault; her self-score cannot exceed the measured value by more than 0.2.

outline.title: Flows: automations in steps
outline.summary: A flow is an n8n style automation kept as JSON in /Jade/Flows. It is a list of steps that run in order, and each step's output becomes $json for the next step. Step types include Tool, JavaScript, Shell, Decide, Ask AI, Jade agent, Note, Set fields, If, Switch, For each, Wait, Notify, Run flow and Stop. Text fields may hold double-brace expressions. A flow starts by hand, on a schedule, or when a note changes, and each run is logged step by step.
keyPoints: Flows are JSON files /Jade/Flows/NAME.flow.json.
Each step's output is $json for the next; other names are $input, $node["Step"], $vars, $item, $index, $now and $today.
Steps can retry 0 to 3 times or continue on error.
Triggers: by hand, a schedule (every weekday at 9am, cron, @daily), or a note or folder change.
Flows also run from the shell (flow run), scripts (jade.flow), the API and Jade's flow tool.
Every run is logged with each step's input, output and time.

outline.title: Playbooks: deterministic automation
outline.summary: A playbook is Jade's version of Ansible: a saved JSON list of tasks that call any tool, the browser or built-in actions, in the same order each time, with no model in the loop. Tasks have a do action and keywords such as when, loop, register, retries, until, failed_when, ignore_errors, block, rescue and always. Strings may hold double-brace expressions in a small safe language. You approve a playbook when it is saved, and again whenever its content changes, so a schedule or flow can run it unattended.
keyPoints: Chat is for exploring and deciding; a playbook is for repeating.
Playbooks live in /Jade/Playbooks/NAME.json and are edited in the Playbooks tab.
The expression language has no JavaScript: only variables, literals, operators and listed functions.
An undefined name is an error, not an empty string.
At most 1000 tasks and 300 seconds per run (maximum 900).
Only an approved, unchanged playbook runs from a flow or a schedule.

outline.title: The knowledge graph
outline.summary: The knowledge graph holds facts such as works_at(alice, acme), rules that derive new facts, and constraints that must never be broken. A Datalog reasoner, written in Rust and run as WebAssembly, checks claims against them. Every answer is one of three: proven with its proof, contradicted, or unknown. The graph is open-world: something missing is not false. Facts Jade adds are proposed until you confirm them, so you decide what counts.
keyPoints: Facts live in /Jade/Knowledge/facts.jsonl and rules in /Jade/Knowledge/rules.dl.
Rules use variables that start with a capital letter: above(X, Z) :- reports_to(X, Y), above(Y, Z).
A constraint such as ! one_employer: works_at(P, A), works_at(P, B), A != B. flags any match.
Verdicts are proven, contradicted (the opposite holds or a constraint would break) or unknown.
Confirmed facts are yours; proposed ones wait for you; rejected ones can never be added again.
A graph of 180,000 derived facts took about 0.15 s in the browser's tests.

outline.title: Autonomous mode and plans
outline.summary: In autonomous mode Jade works through a queue on her own, the way an operating system schedules programs: interrupts first, then a priority queue with aging, then round robin with feedback for long goals. You set the limits: steps per hour, a daily cap, quiet hours, a pause while you use the app, and approval for tools that reach outside the vault. Everything is logged. Plans are Gantt charts for projects with dependencies, milestones and a critical path.
keyPoints: Tier 1 interrupts go first in arrival order; Jade may hold at most 3 of her own.
Tier 2 orders by priority 0 to 100, plus up to 40 for waiting, plus 10, 30 or 50 for a deadline within a day, an hour or already passed.
Tier 3 gets slices of 2, 4 or 8 steps; a goal that uses its slice drops a level, one that waits 30 minutes rises one.
Tier 3 gets every 4th turn when tier 2 also has work.
Each slice ends with STATUS: done, continue or blocked.
Defaults: 60 steps an hour, 600 a day, quiet hours 11pm to 7am.

outline.title: Think, delegate and the model router
outline.summary: The think tool searches a tree of reasoning lines and checks each with something that can say no, such as running code or checking a file. The best verified line is the answer. A failed check from a real verifier is a veto, not an average, so a confident judge cannot rescue a solution that fails its test. The delegate tool runs a sub-agent with a clean context and returns one report. The model router chooses a quick or strong model for each message.
keyPoints: think verifiers: code (read-only JavaScript), file, rubric and an independent judge.
Search modes are beam (default), best_first and puct, with budgets in nodes, seconds and tokens.
Trees are saved after each step and episodes are logged.
delegate is read-only by default, with 8 steps (max 15) and 120 s (max 300), and its report is capped at 6000 characters.
A delegate cannot nest or run twice at once.
The router uses the decision model to send everyday chat to a quick model and hard questions to a strong one.

outline.title: Jade Lisp and scripting
outline.summary: Jade Lisp is a small Lisp in the style of Scheme and Clojure, part of the base system. It builds small languages for rules and workflows, and scripts that call Jade's tools. Programs can run in a sandbox with only the verbs you give them and a step limit called fuel, so a program written by someone else cannot read files, call tools or loop forever. Scripts in node can also use a jade object: jade.tool, jade.ask, jade.decide, jade.flow, jade.shell, jade.notify and a key value store.
keyPoints: Data: numbers, strings, symbols, :keywords, lists, maps, nil, #t and #f.
Forms include define, lambda, let, if, cond, while and defmacro; tail calls run in constant space.
(tool/NAME :arg value) runs any tool; jade/ask, jade/flow, jade/shell and jade/notify are also available.
pure=yes runs a whole program without tools, files or JavaScript; fuel=N limits steps.
Three ways to build a DSL: macros, a sandbox, or parsing the text as data.
In node: await jade.tool(name, args), jade.ask(prompt), jade.decide({...}), jade.flow(name, input), jade.kv.

outline.title: Connect, back up, secure and build
outline.summary: Jade Vault connects outward in several ways: an HTTP API on the phone, MCP servers, the Vector and Discord messengers, webxdc mini apps, and a fleet broker that shares one vault between devices. A scheduled backup uploads a compressed, optionally encrypted file to your own server. Jade can start one but she cannot restore. The app is built by applying ordered exact-match patches to a base page; if a patch does not match, the build fails loudly.
keyPoints: The API is off by default; every call except /v1/health needs the token.
/v1/chat?message=TEXT sends a message that also appears in the app; errors are JSON with HTTP 400, 401, 404, 409, 502 or 504.
A backup is JSON, gzip, then optionally AES-GCM with a PBKDF2 key of 210,000 rounds; the server checks a SHA-256 header.
Backup names use only letters, digits, dot, dash and underscore and end in .json or .json.gz.
Webxdc apps are sandboxed with no vault access and no network.
npm run build makes dist/jade-vault.html; npm test runs dozens of Playwright suites; the APK needs a JDK, not the Android SDK.

courses.title: NVIDIA Jetson AGX Xavier
courses.subtitle: Hardware and software, from the chip to a multi-engine pipeline
courses.author: Lilith Learning Lab
courses.description: Learn the NVIDIA Jetson AGX Xavier: every processor, the memory, power, JetPack, CUDA, TensorRT, the DLA, VPI, cameras, containers and troubleshooting. Each chapter has a concept map, summary, glossary, key points, a lesson, a quiz and practice labs.

outline.title: Read me first
outline.summary: The Jetson AGX Xavier is a small computer built around one chip (the Xavier SoC) that contains several different processors, each good at a different kind of work, all sharing one pool of memory. This tutorial explains each processor, how to power and flash the board, which software drives which processor, and how to design models that make good use of all of them. Every chapter has the same four parts: Summary, Key points, Examples, and Check yourself. A glossary and a command cheat sheet are near the end.
keyPoints: Read chapters 1 to 4 for the hardware, 5 to 7 to get the board running, 8 to 10 for compute, 11 to 15 for design and pipelines.
Commands are shown for a Jetson running Linux (JetPack). Lines starting with `$` are typed at the Jetson's shell; `#` lines are comments.
Numbers are given as ranges or "about" where they depend on your exact module, power mode or software version.
Where a statement is not verified against NVIDIA documentation, it is marked (from memory) and listed in chapter 21.
The companion interactive tutorial (a webxdc app and an Android APK) is generated from this file, so they always agree. Teacher, the avatar in the app, reads any chapter aloud.
Chapter 22 holds four concept maps: relationship diagrams that show how the ideas connect. Tap a node in the app to jump to its chapter.

outline.title: The big picture
outline.summary: The AGX Xavier is NVIDIA's 2018-generation edge-AI module. It is a system-on-module (SoM): the Xavier SoC, memory, flash storage and power management on a small board that plugs into a carrier board through a 699-pin connector. It targets robots, drones, cameras and vehicles that must run several neural networks at low power. It was sold as 16 GB, 32 GB and 64 GB modules and an Industrial version, with a developer kit (module plus carrier board, fan heatsink and power supply) for development.
keyPoints: Module: the Xavier SoC plus memory, eMMC storage and power circuitry, about 100 mm by 87 mm.
Carrier board: breaks out the connectors (USB, Ethernet, display, camera, PCIe, M.2, GPIO header). The developer kit includes one; products use custom ones.
Headline figure: up to 32 TOPS INT8 combined across GPU and the two DLAs, in 10 to 30 W modes.
Variants: AGX Xavier (16/32 GB), 64 GB, and Industrial (lower clocks, ECC memory, wider temperature range).
It is end-of-life as a new purchase (chapter 18), but it remains widely deployed and well documented.
It is not a PC: there is no BIOS setup menu for boot order; you flash images onto it from a host PC.

outline.title: Hardware tour: the processors
outline.summary: Inside the Xavier SoC are a CPU cluster, a GPU, two deep-learning accelerators (DLAs), two programmable vision accelerators (PVAs), fixed-function image and video blocks, and several small helper cores. You choose which block runs each part of your application; the operating system does not do this automatically for neural networks.
keyPoints: CPU: 8 NVIDIA Carmel cores (Arm v8.2, 64-bit), arranged as four dual-core clusters, with about 8 MB of L2 and 4 MB of L3 cache in total. Runs Linux, your Python, networking and orchestration.

GPU: NVIDIA Volta with 8 streaming multiprocessors (512 CUDA cores) and 64 Tensor Cores. Compute capability 7.2 (`sm_72`). General CUDA, plus fast FP16/INT8 deep learning. Maximum clock about 1377 MHz (Industrial: about 1211 MHz).

DLA (NVDLA): two fixed-function inference engines. They run supported neural-network layers (convolution, pooling, activation, and so on) in FP16 or INT8 with low power, leaving the GPU free. They are driven through TensorRT (or cuDLA), not CUDA.

PVA: two Programmable Vision Accelerators, vector (VLIW) processors for classic computer vision such as filtering, optical flow and feature tracking. They are not for neural networks. Used through VPI.
ISP: image signal processor that turns raw camera sensor data into usable images (debayer, denoise, white balance), reached through Argus.
Video: hardware H.264/H.265/VP9 encoder (NVENC) and decoder (NVDEC), reached through GStreamer or the Multimedia API.
VIC: video image compositor for fast scaling, color conversion and cropping with no GPU cost.
Helper cores (from memory): Arm Cortex-R5 cores for boot and power management (BPMP), a safety cluster running in lockstep, and an audio processing engine. You rarely touch these directly.

outline.title: Memory, I/O and the carrier board
outline.summary: All the processors share one pool of LPDDR4x memory. This unified memory removes copies between CPU and GPU (zero-copy is possible) but means every block competes for the same bandwidth. The module exposes cameras, PCIe, USB, display and general I/O through its connector; a carrier board turns these into physical ports.
keyPoints: Memory: 256-bit LPDDR4x at about 136.5 GB/s, shared by CPU, GPU, DLAs, PVAs and media blocks. There is no separate "GPU memory"; `nvidia-smi` memory figures do not apply the way they do on a desktop.
Memory bandwidth, not compute, is usually the bottleneck when you run everything at once.
Storage: 32 GB eMMC on the module (64 GB Industrial). The developer kit also has an M.2 NVMe slot; for real work, boot or store models on NVMe.
Camera: up to 6 cameras directly (36 through virtual channels) on 16 MIPI CSI-2 lanes.
PCIe: up to 8 lanes of Gen 4 (on the dev kit, a PCIe slot plus M.2 slots, from memory).
USB 3.1, gigabit Ethernet, three display outputs (DP 1.2 or HDMI 2.0), UART, SPI, I2C, I2S, CAN, GPIO.
Dev kit extras (from memory; confirm in the Developer Kit User Guide): 40-pin expansion header, 19 V power input, a USB-C port used for flashing, Wi-Fi/Bluetooth card.

outline.title: Power, clocks and thermals
outline.summary: The module is designed for 10 W, 15 W and 30 W budgets. A power mode (set with `nvpmodel`) chooses how many CPU cores are online and the maximum CPU, GPU, DLA and memory clocks. `jetson_clocks` pins clocks at their maximum within the mode. Heat is managed by a heatsink and fan; if temperatures rise, the system throttles clocks.
keyPoints: `sudo nvpmodel -q` shows the current mode; `sudo nvpmodel -m <id>` sets it. Mode ids and names vary by board and release: list yours with `sudo nvpmodel -q --verbose` and read `/etc/nvpmodel.conf`.
Typical AGX Xavier modes (from memory): MAXN (unrestricted), 10 W, 15 W, several 30 W variants with different numbers of enabled CPU cores, and a 15 W desktop mode.
`sudo jetson_clocks` locks clocks high for stable benchmarks; `sudo jetson_clocks --show` prints the state; `--store` and `--restore` save and restore settings.
`sudo jetson_clocks --fan` forces the fan to maximum.
Always benchmark in a fixed power mode with clocks locked, or your numbers will move around.
The dev kit power input is about 19 V; a weak supply causes brownouts and throttling under load.

outline.title: The software stack and JetPack versions
outline.summary: NVIDIA ships Jetson software as JetPack, a bundle that contains Jetson Linux (L4T: an Ubuntu-based OS, kernel and drivers) plus CUDA, cuDNN, TensorRT, VPI and multimedia libraries. Your JetPack version is fixed by your hardware generation. The AGX Xavier works with JetPack 4.6.x and JetPack 5.x; it does not work with JetPack 6.
keyPoints: JetPack 4.6.x (from memory): L4T 32.7.x, Ubuntu 18.04, CUDA 10.2, TensorRT 8.2. This line has reached end of life.

JetPack 5.1 (checked in NVIDIA release notes): Jetson Linux 35.2.1, Linux kernel 5.10, Ubuntu 20.04 root filesystem, UEFI bootloader, CUDA 11.4, TensorRT 8.5.2, cuDNN 8.6.0, VPI 2.2. It supports the AGX Xavier series.

NVIDIA staff say JetPack 6 does not support the Xavier series (forum thread, cited in chapter 21). JetPack 5.1.x is the latest software for AGX Xavier; one NVIDIA forum table lists 5.1.4 as the latest sustaining release.
Consequence: you cannot update TensorRT or CUDA freely. Newer library versions require building from source or using containers built for JetPack 5.
The layers, bottom to top: hardware, bootloader and firmware, Linux kernel and drivers (L4T), CUDA/cuDNN/TensorRT/VPI/multimedia libraries, frameworks and your application.

Which library reaches which processor: CPU (Linux), GPU (CUDA, cuDNN, TensorRT), DLA (TensorRT, cuDLA), PVA and VIC (VPI), ISP (Argus), NVENC/NVDEC (GStreamer, Multimedia API), Tensor Cores (cuDNN, TensorRT, cuBLAS).

outline.title: Setup: flashing and first boot
outline.summary: You do not install an OS from a USB stick. You connect the Jetson to a Linux host PC over USB in recovery mode and flash JetPack with NVIDIA SDK Manager. After the first boot you complete the Ubuntu setup and install the optional JetPack components.
keyPoints: Host: an x86-64 Ubuntu PC (the version must be supported by your SDK Manager release; check the SDK Manager download page). A virtual machine is possible but less reliable for USB.
Connect the host to the Jetson's flashing USB-C port (the dev kit port next to the buttons; confirm in the user guide) with the cable that came in the box.

Recovery mode (dev kit, from memory): power off; hold the Force Recovery button; press and release Power; release Force Recovery after a couple of seconds. On the host, `lsusb` should list an NVIDIA device.
In SDK Manager choose the product (Jetson AGX Xavier), the JetPack version (5.1.x recommended unless a project needs 4.6), the target storage (eMMC or NVMe), and let it flash and install components.
First boot: accept the license, create a user, set the network. Then install any components that were skipped (`sudo apt install nvidia-jetpack`).
Keep a spare copy of any images you customize; re-flashing wipes the device storage.
Booting from NVMe is much faster and larger than eMMC; many people flash the OS to NVMe and keep eMMC as a backup.

outline.title: Monitoring and system tools
outline.summary: Because so many blocks share the chip, you need to see what is busy. `tegrastats` prints a line of CPU, GPU, memory and temperature data; `jtop` shows the same in a friendly full-screen view; `nvpmodel` and `jetson_clocks` control power; `htop` and `top` show processes.
keyPoints: `tegrastats` reports RAM and swap, per-core CPU load and frequency, `GR3D_FREQ` (GPU load and clock), `EMC_FREQ` (memory controller load, a proxy for bandwidth pressure), and temperatures and power rails. On some releases it also lists the DLA, NVENC and NVDEC clocks.
`jtop` (from the `jetson-stats` package) gives pages for CPU, GPU, memory, engines (DLA/NVENC/NVDEC), power and controls.
`sudo tegrastats --interval 500` samples every 500 ms; `--logfile out.txt` writes to a file.
`nvidia-smi` is limited on Jetson; use `tegrastats` or `jtop` instead.
Check the GPU is really being used: watch `GR3D_FREQ` rise while your model runs.
To see DLA use, watch the engine view in `jtop` (if available) or time your engine with `trtexec`.

outline.title: GPU programming with CUDA
outline.summary: The Xavier GPU runs ordinary CUDA code. You write kernels executed by thousands of threads, organized into blocks and a grid, and compile with `nvcc` for compute capability 7.2. Because memory is unified, `cudaMallocManaged` or mapped pinned memory avoid copies.
keyPoints: Thread hierarchy: a kernel launches a grid of blocks; each block has threads (commonly 128 to 256); each thread computes its global index `blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x`.
Grid size for `n` elements and block size `b`: `(n + b - 1) / b` (ceiling division).
Compile with `nvcc -arch=sm_72 -O2 file.cu -o file`.
Always check errors: `cudaGetLastError()` after a launch and `cudaDeviceSynchronize()` before reading results on the CPU.
8 SMs is a small GPU; keep launches large enough to fill it and avoid many tiny kernels.
Tensor Cores are used automatically by cuDNN, cuBLAS and TensorRT in FP16 (and INT8); you rarely program them by hand.
CUDA is at 11.4 on JetPack 5 (10.2 on JetPack 4.6), so some new CUDA features are not available.

outline.title: TensorRT: from model to fast engine
outline.summary: TensorRT converts a trained network (usually exported to ONNX) into an optimized engine for your exact device: it fuses layers, picks fast kernels, and can use FP16 or INT8. Engines are specific to the GPU, the TensorRT version and the settings, so you build them on the Jetson itself. `trtexec` is the command-line tool for building, benchmarking and inspecting engines.
keyPoints: Workflow: train in PyTorch/TensorFlow, export to ONNX with fixed input shapes, build an engine on the Jetson, run it.
`trtexec` lives at `/usr/src/tensorrt/bin/trtexec`.
Precision: FP32 (default), `--fp16` (usually the best first choice on Xavier), `--int8` (needs calibration for accuracy; running it without calibration data is only useful for timing).
Building an engine can take minutes, so save it with `--saveEngine` and load it at run time with `--loadEngine`.
Engines are not portable across devices, TensorRT versions or (usually) JetPack versions.
Use `--verbose` to see which layers were fused and which tactics were chosen.
In Python, TensorRT is installed system-wide with JetPack (`import tensorrt`); virtual environments need `--system-site-packages` to see it.

outline.title: The DLA in depth
outline.summary: The Xavier has two Deep Learning Accelerators. Each can run a supported subset of neural-network layers in FP16 or INT8 using little power and without using GPU compute. You enable the DLA in TensorRT; layers the DLA cannot run fall back to the GPU only if you allow it. Every switch between DLA and GPU adds copy and synchronization cost, so good DLA models keep as many consecutive layers on the DLA as possible.
keyPoints: Two cores (`--useDLACore=0` and `1`); you can run separate engines on each, plus the GPU, at the same time.
Precision: FP16 or INT8 only (no FP32). Xavier is the first-generation DLA; Orin's second-generation DLA supports more. For example, DLA Softmax is documented as Orin only.

Supported (broadly, from NVIDIA's DLA restrictions page): convolution, fully connected, deconvolution (with restrictions), pooling (max/average, small windows), activations (ReLU, sigmoid, tanh, clipped ReLU, leaky ReLU), batch norm and scale, element-wise ops, concatenation along channels, resize (integer scale factors only), some reshape/transpose forms, local response normalization.

Common limits: 2D (4D tensor) layers only, static shapes only, channels commonly capped at 8192, small kernel/stride limits, and for deconvolution a zero padding requirement in recent docs. Read the restrictions page that matches your TensorRT version (8.5 on JetPack 5.1); limits differ between versions.

Not supported (typically fall back): ArgMax/TopK, general matrix multiply that is not expressed as a convolution or fully connected layer, Reduce other than MAX, recurrent layers (LSTM/GRU), attention, dynamic shapes, 3D convolution. (RNN and attention items are from memory; check the docs.)
`--allowGPUFallback` lets TensorRT run unsupported layers on the GPU. Without it, the build fails when a layer is unsupported.
INT8 needs calibration or quantization-aware training to keep accuracy.
Each DLA/GPU partition boundary adds overhead. A model that falls back in many places may be slower than all-GPU.
For best DLA I/O speed you can set formats such as `--inputIOFormats=fp16:chw16` and `--outputIOFormats=fp16:chw16` (INT8 uses `chw32`) to avoid reformat layers.

outline.title: Designing DLA-friendly models (VAE, VQ-VAE, PPO)
outline.summary: The rule is to turn logic (sampling, searching, branching) into tensors (convolution, addition, scaling) and push the unavoidable non-tensor step to the very end of the network, where the CPU or GPU can do it cheaply. This chapter applies the rule to a VAE, a VQ-VAE and a PPO policy, and notes what was checked and what is only approximate.
keyPoints: VAE: at deployment ignore the variance and the noise; pass the mean `mu` straight to the decoder. This makes it a plain autoencoder and removes the sampling step. Drop the log-variance head from the exported model. Caveat: if your anomaly score needs the KL term or ELBO, you still need sigma; with `mu` only you can use reconstruction error.

Decoder: transposed convolutions are supported on DLA with restrictions (for example, zero padding in recent docs), so they sometimes fall back. Replacing them with nearest-neighbor `Upsample` (integer factor) followed by a convolution is a reliable alternative.

VQ-VAE: the nearest-codebook search uses `||a-b||^2 = ||a||^2 + ||b||^2 - 2 a.b`. For the argmin, `||a||^2` is the same for every codebook entry, so drop it. Then the score for each entry is `||b||^2 - 2 a.b`: a 1x1 convolution with weights `-2 * codebook` and bias `||b||^2`. The DLA computes all scores; the argmin runs on CPU or GPU.

After the argmin you need the chosen codebook vectors for the decoder (an embedding lookup). That is another non-DLA step, or can be done with a one-hot 1x1 convolution. So the pipeline may cross DLA to CPU and back twice.
Large score tensors (for example 32 x 32 positions by 512 codes, about 524,000 values) are cheap for the CPU to argmin, but the memory transfer is not free. Measure.
FP16 precision: keep codebook and activations in a modest range (for example, normalize them) so distance scores do not lose resolution.

PPO: training (rollouts, advantage estimation, clipped loss) never runs on the DLA. At deployment export only the actor. For continuous actions use the Gaussian mean (ignore `log_std` and noise); for discrete actions take the argmax of the logits on the CPU (tiny). Fold observation normalization into the first layer. Recurrent policies (LSTM/GRU) fall back; use frame stacking or unroll the recurrence.
Quantizing to INT8 can hurt RL policies because small action errors compound; start with FP16 and verify closed-loop behavior.

outline.title: The PVA and VPI
outline.summary: The PVA is a pair of vector processors for classic vision algorithms. You use them through VPI (Vision Programming Interface), a library that offers the same algorithm on several backends (CPU, CUDA GPU, PVA, VIC) so you can choose where each step runs.
keyPoints: VPI versions: 1.x on JetPack 4.6, 2.x on JetPack 5 (2.2 in JetPack 5.1).
Backends on Xavier: CPU, CUDA, PVA, VIC (and NVENC for encode). The OFA backend belongs to Orin.
Not every algorithm runs on every backend. PVA supports a subset (filters, some conversions, features); check the VPI algorithm table for your version.
Moving frames between backends can cost conversions; keep a stage on one backend where possible.
The PVA is a good home for always-on preprocessing when the GPU should stay idle.
Python bindings are available (`import vpi`); C++ is also supported.

outline.title: Cameras, video and GStreamer
outline.summary: Camera frames flow through the ISP (Argus), can be resized and converted by the VIC (`nvvidconv`), and encoded or decoded by NVENC/NVDEC (`nvv4l2` elements), all without touching the GPU or CPU much. GStreamer pipelines connect these blocks; frames stay in special NVMM (device) memory between hardware stages to avoid copies.
keyPoints: `nvarguscamerasrc` reads MIPI cameras through the ISP; USB cameras use `v4l2src` instead.
`nvvidconv` converts format and scales using the VIC. Use caps with `(memory:NVMM)` to keep frames in hardware memory.
`nvv4l2h264enc` / `nvv4l2h265enc` encode; `nvv4l2decoder` decodes.
Getting frames into Python/OpenCV: end the pipeline with `appsink` after converting to a CPU format (BGR). That copy is the costly step; keep it small by scaling first.
OpenCV on JetPack may lack GStreamer support if you install it from pip; the system OpenCV package from JetPack includes it.
DeepStream builds on these pieces for multi-stream video analytics (batching, tracking, inference).
Capture to model: camera, ISP, VIC (resize), then DLA/GPU inference, so the CPU only handles control and small tensors.

outline.title: Containers and Python machine learning
outline.summary: Python machine learning on Jetson is easiest through NVIDIA's JetPack-matched wheels and containers. A generic `pip install torch` gives you a CPU-only or wrong-architecture build. Containers also give you a way around the old Ubuntu release by shipping their own libraries.
keyPoints: PyTorch for Jetson comes from NVIDIA-provided wheels built for each JetPack version (found in NVIDIA's Jetson forum and docs), or from community builds such as the `jetson-containers` project.
Container tags must match your L4T release; check with `cat /etc/nv_tegra_release`.
Run containers with the NVIDIA runtime: `--runtime nvidia`.
Prefer exporting models to ONNX and running them with TensorRT for production; keep PyTorch for development.
ONNX Runtime has Jetson-specific builds with TensorRT and CUDA execution providers.
Use swap (zram or a swap file on NVMe) when compiling large packages.

outline.title: Putting it together: a multi-engine pipeline
outline.summary: A well-designed Xavier application assigns each stage to the cheapest capable block and keeps frames in shared memory. This chapter sketches an "always-on" pipeline (the Sentry idea): the DLA reconstructs the scene continuously at low power, and the GPU wakes only when the reconstruction disagrees with reality.
keyPoints: Stage plan: camera (ISP) -> VIC resize -> DLA0 encoder/decoder (VAE mean path, or VQ-VAE score path) -> CPU computes error (and argmin for VQ-VAE) -> GPU detector wakes only on a high error.
Use one process or thread per engine, each with its own CUDA stream, so DLA0, DLA1 and the GPU overlap.
Keep the CPU free for orchestration: it should handle small tensors only.
Budget memory bandwidth: add up bytes per frame times frames per second times the number of times each tensor moves.
Add a watchdog: if the DLA engine stalls or errors, fall back to a simple CPU/GPU check rather than silently failing.
Log `tegrastats` while testing so you can see the GPU idle during quiet scenes and wake during events.
Design for degradation: if temperatures climb and clocks drop, the always-on path should still meet its deadline.

outline.title: Performance tuning
outline.summary: Performance on Xavier comes from choosing the right processor, the right precision, and avoiding wasteful transfers. Measure first, change one thing at a time, and always compare at a fixed power mode with locked clocks.
keyPoints: Use FP16 everywhere you can; use INT8 with proper calibration where accuracy allows.
Fuse operations in the model (conv + batchnorm + ReLU) so TensorRT and the DLA can run them as one unit.
Keep shapes static and sizes divisible by small powers of two when possible.
Minimize DLA/GPU partitions; look at the build log.
Avoid CPU-GPU ping-pong: do pre- and post-processing on the same device as the model (VIC, PVA or CUDA).
Use pinned or managed memory for transfers; avoid Python-level per-pixel loops.
Batch size 1 is typical for latency; DLA batch handling differs from the GPU, so test.
Warm up engines before timing; first iterations include initialization.
Watch thermals: sustained load at 30 W in a warm enclosure will throttle.

outline.title: Troubleshooting
outline.summary: Most Jetson problems fall into a few families: software version mismatches, power or thermal limits, memory exhaustion, unsupported DLA layers, and USB/flash issues. A systematic check usually finds the cause quickly.
keyPoints: Always record versions first: L4T, JetPack, CUDA, TensorRT, power mode.
Out-of-memory kills happen when CPU and GPU together exceed the shared RAM; add swap, reduce batch/workspace, or close processes.
Engines built on one version will not load on another: rebuild.
If `import tensorrt` fails in a virtual environment, create it with `--system-site-packages`.
If the board will not enter recovery mode, retry the button sequence with the power fully off and try another USB cable or port.
Unexpected slowness: check power mode, `jetson_clocks`, thermal throttling and fallbacks.
Brownouts or random reboots under load point to a weak power supply.

outline.title: Lifecycle, support and what comes next
outline.summary: The AGX Xavier is a mature, discontinued platform. Its software reached the end of the line at JetPack 5.x, so plan around that. Newer Jetson modules (Orin family) use JetPack 6 and have a more capable second-generation DLA.
keyPoints: Distributors have published end-of-life notices for the AGX Xavier module with last-time-buy dates.
Software support ends at JetPack 5.x (sustaining updates only); JetPack 6 does not support Xavier.
Orin modules have newer DLAs and Ampere GPUs; much Xavier knowledge carries over (TensorRT, DLA workflow).
Jetson Thor has no DLA (per NVIDIA's TensorRT documentation); recent TensorRT release notes also limit DLA support on newer releases, so check before choosing a platform for a new DLA-heavy design.
If you start a new product today, plan for an Orin-class module; use Xavier for learning, existing designs and cost-sensitive reuse.
Keep your flashed image, engine build scripts and a record of exact versions to make the system reproducible.

outline.title: Cheat sheet
outline.summary: The commands and flags you will use most, in one place.
keyPoints: Identify: `cat /etc/nv_tegra_release`, `sudo apt-cache show nvidia-jetpack`.
Power: `sudo nvpmodel -q`, `sudo nvpmodel -m <id>`, `sudo jetson_clocks`.
Monitor: `tegrastats`, `jtop`.
Build engines: `trtexec --onnx=... --fp16 --saveEngine=...`, add `--useDLACore=N --allowGPUFallback` for DLA.
Compile CUDA: `nvcc -arch=sm_72`.
Camera: `nvarguscamerasrc`, `nvvidconv`, `nvv4l2h265enc`, `nvv4l2decoder`.

outline.title: Glossary
outline.summary: Short definitions of the terms used in this tutorial.
keyPoints: Every term used in the course is here, with a one-line meaning.
Slash terms such as DLA / NVDLA name two spellings of the same idea.
Use the flashcards and the glossary search in the Practice tab to review them.

outline.title: Verification notes and sources
outline.summary: This chapter lists what was checked and what was not, so you know which claims to double-check before relying on them.
keyPoints: Checked on 2026-11-06 against vendor and NVIDIA pages: GPU (Volta, 512 CUDA cores, 64 Tensor Cores), CPU (8-core Carmel, Arm v8.2), 2 DLAs, 2 PVAs, 256-bit LPDDR4x about 136.5 GB/s, 10/15/30 W modes, 22 TOPS GPU + about 10 TOPS DLA = 32 TOPS INT8, camera and video capability, 8 SMs.

Checked: JetPack 5.1 contents (L4T 35.2.1, kernel 5.10, Ubuntu 20.04, CUDA 11.4, TensorRT 8.5.2, cuDNN 8.6.0, VPI 2.2) and that it supports AGX Xavier; forum statements that JetPack 6 does not support Xavier and that JetPack 5.1.x is its latest software.

Checked (current NVIDIA DLA restrictions page; versions differ): Deconvolution limits including zero padding, Resize limits (nearest up to 32, bilinear up to 4, integer scales), Reduce MAX only, Softmax Orin only, static shapes only, 4D inputs, channel limit 8192.

Not re-checked (from memory): JetPack 4.6 component versions; the exact `nvpmodel` mode list for your release; dev kit port locations and button procedures; helper cores (BPMP, safety cluster, APE); RNN and attention not being supported on DLA; the exact VPI algorithm table for PVA; the `tegrastats` fields on each release; container tag names.
Where this tutorial disagrees with the documentation for your exact JetPack/TensorRT release, trust the documentation.

outline.title: Concept maps
outline.summary: A concept map shows how ideas connect, using labeled links such as "has", "runs" or "causes". Use the four maps below as a revision tool: first try to explain each link in your own words, then check the chapter named on the node. The same maps are drawn as tappable diagrams in the app.
keyPoints: Map 1 shows what the Xavier is made of and why shared memory matters.
Map 2 shows which software reaches which processor.
Map 3 shows the path from a trained model to the DLA, and what causes fallbacks.
Map 4 shows how power modes, clocks, heat and memory bandwidth affect speed.
Each node can carry a chapter tag such as `[ch10]`, which the app turns into a link.
A good habit: cover the link words, then say the sentence "A <link> B" aloud for every line.

courses.title: Welcome to Lilith University
courses.subtitle: A very short guide to finding, getting, studying and making courses
courses.author: Lilith Learning Lab
courses.description: A four-chapter orientation to Lilith University and the Lilith Learning Lab app: what a course is, how to find and download one, how to study a chapter with quizzes, flashcards and labs, and how to build and share your own course.

outline.title: What Lilith University is
outline.summary: Lilith University is a free library of self-study courses. Each course is one file that you download once and then use offline in the Lilith Learning Lab app. The website lets you search and read each course outline before you download it. The app holds your courses, shows lessons, reads them aloud with the Teacher, and runs the labs on your own device. There are no accounts, no tracking and no payments. Your progress stays on your device.
keyPoints: A course is one file; the app is the reader.
Browse online in the app, or use the website, to find courses.
Get downloads and imports a course in one tap.
Everything runs on your device, offline.
Categories group courses; levels tell you where to start.

outline.title: Finding and getting a course
outline.summary: Open Library, then Browse online in the app. Search by name or tag, filter by category, and read the chapter outline. Tap Get to download a course into your library. You can also import a course file that someone sent you. Courses are plain JSON files, so they can be shared like any other file. Start with the level that fits you, and look at the outline first: a good course shows its chapters in a sensible order, from basics up.
keyPoints: Search, filter, read the outline, tap Get.
Level tells you where to start.
Import adds a file you already have.
Your library holds every course on your device.

outline.title: How to study a chapter
outline.summary: Each chapter has the same shape: a short lesson, a quiz, flashcards and labs. Read or listen to the lesson, answer the quiz, then do the labs, which turn ideas into skill. Flashcards work best in short daily sessions. Seeing a card again after a day, then three days, then a week, makes it stick. Do not skip the labs. Typing a line of code or putting steps in order shows you what you really understand.
keyPoints: Lesson, quiz, cards, labs: the same loop every chapter.
Short daily sessions beat one long one.
Labs turn knowing into doing.
Listen with the Teacher when your eyes are busy.

outline.title: Make your own course
outline.summary: Anyone can write a course. A course is a JSON file in the lilith-course format, and the web editor lets you build one without writing JSON by hand. Each chapter needs a title, a lesson, a few quiz questions and cards. Labs can be fill-in-the-blank, matching, ordering, Python code, a terminal, or a small web app. Export your file and import it in the app to try it. If it is good, share it so others can learn from it.
keyPoints: A course is a plain JSON file.
The editor means no hand-written JSON.
Each chapter: lesson, quiz, cards, labs.
Test by importing into the app, then share.

courses.title: Linux from Scratch: The Shell, Files, Permissions and Servers
courses.subtitle: A hands-on tour of the Linux command line, with a working Linux-like shell in every lab
courses.author: Lilith Learning Lab
courses.description: A condensed, original course on using and administering Linux. It covers the filesystem tree, the shell and its commands, files and directories, redirection and pipes, text tools, permissions and ownership, users and sudo, processes and signals, packages and services, shell scripting, networking basics, disks, logs and cron, security basics, and a capstone where you fix a broken server. Every shell lab runs a Linux-like simulator inside the app, built on the Jade Agent Kit virtual filesystem, with real BusyBox WebAssembly tools for grep, sed, awk and sort. It is a teaching sandbox, not a full Linux: some commands are simulated. Credits: BusyBox (GPL-2.0) and the Jade Agent Kit (MIT).

outline.title: What Linux is
outline.summary: Linux is a kernel, the core program that talks to the hardware and shares it between programs. Around it sits a set of tools, and the bundle is called a distribution, such as Debian, Ubuntu or Fedora. Everything is organised as one tree of files starting at a single root called slash. Devices, settings and even running processes appear as files in that tree. You will work in a terminal and a shell, because that is how servers, containers and cloud machines are run.
keyPoints: Linux is the kernel; a distribution is the complete system.
One tree of files starts at /.
Almost everything is a file or behaves like one.
Servers, phones, routers and clouds mostly run Linux.

outline.title: The shell and your first commands
outline.summary: The shell shows a prompt and waits. You type a command, possibly with options and arguments, and press Enter. The shell finds the program, runs it and prints the result. Start with five commands: pwd says where you are, ls lists what is here, cd moves, cat shows a file, and man or --help explains anything. Tab completes names and the up arrow recalls earlier lines, which saves a lot of typing.
keyPoints: A command line is command, options, arguments.
Absolute paths start with /; relative paths do not.
. is here, .. is the parent, ~ is your home.
Tab completes and history recalls.

outline.title: Files and directories
outline.summary: You create, copy, move and delete with a small set of commands. mkdir makes directories, touch makes an empty file, cp copies, mv moves or renames, and rm removes. Deleting is permanent: there is no recycle bin on the command line. Use rm -r for directories and think before you press Enter. Wildcards let one pattern name many files, and find searches by name, type and more.
keyPoints: mkdir -p makes parent directories too.
mv is also rename.
rm is permanent; rm -r removes directories.
* matches any characters, ? matches one.

outline.title: Viewing, searching and redirecting
outline.summary: Every program has three streams: standard input, standard output and standard error. By default they connect to the terminal, but you can redirect them. > sends output to a file and replaces it, >> appends, < feeds a file in, and 2> catches errors. This turns commands into building blocks. To look at files, use cat for short ones, head and tail for the ends, less to page, and grep to find lines.
keyPoints: > replaces, >> appends.
2> redirects errors; 2>&1 merges them.
head and tail show the ends of a file.
grep prints lines that match.

outline.title: Pipes and text tools
outline.summary: A pipe, written |, sends the output of one command into the input of the next. Small tools that each do one thing combine into powerful one-line programs. The core toolbox: grep to filter, sort to order, uniq -c to count repeats, wc to count, cut and awk to pick columns, sed to edit streams and tr to translate characters. A classic pipeline counts something in a log: filter with grep, take a column, sort, count with uniq -c, sort again.
keyPoints: cmd1 | cmd2 feeds output to input.
sort | uniq -c counts repeats; uniq needs sorted input.
awk '{print $1}' prints the first column.
sed 's/old/new/' replaces text.

outline.title: Permissions and ownership
outline.summary: Every file has an owner, a group and three sets of permission bits: for the owner, for the group and for everyone else. Each set can allow read, write and execute. ls -l shows them as ten characters like -rwxr-xr--. chmod changes them with numbers, such as 755, or letters, such as u+x. Permissions on a directory mean something different: read lists names, write adds or removes entries, execute lets you enter.
keyPoints: r=4, w=2, x=1; add them per set.
755 is rwxr-xr-x, 644 is rw-r--r--.
Directories need x to be entered.
umask 022 gives files 644 and directories 755.

outline.title: Users, groups and sudo
outline.summary: Every process and file belongs to a user and a group. A user is a number, the UID, with a name; root is UID 0 and may do anything. Day to day you work as a normal user and borrow root's power only when needed, with sudo, which asks for your password and logs what you ran. Users and groups live in plain text files under /etc, and a handful of commands manage them: useradd, usermod, groupadd, passwd, id and groups.
keyPoints: id shows your uid, gid and groups.
Work as a normal user; use sudo only when needed.
usermod -aG adds a user to a group; forget -a and you replace the groups.
/etc/passwd has seven colon-separated fields.

outline.title: Processes, jobs and signals
outline.summary: A process is a running program with its own number, the PID, an owner and its own memory. The first process, init or systemd, is PID 1 and starts the rest. ps shows a snapshot, top shows it live. kill does not just kill: it sends a signal. SIGTERM, the default, asks politely; SIGKILL cannot be ignored. Add & to run a command in the background so you keep your prompt.
keyPoints: ps aux lists all processes.
kill sends TERM (15) by default; kill -9 sends KILL.
A trailing & runs a command in the background.
Exit code 0 means success.

outline.title: Packages and services
outline.summary: A package manager installs software, resolves what it depends on, and keeps it updated from trusted repositories. On Debian and Ubuntu that is apt. A service is a program that runs in the background, such as a web server. systemd starts services at boot and systemctl controls them. The pattern is always the same: install the package, start the service, enable it for boot, check its status and read its logs.
keyPoints: sudo apt update refreshes the list; apt install adds a package.
systemctl start, stop, restart, status control a service.
enable makes it start at boot; start runs it now.
journalctl -u name reads its log.

outline.title: Shell scripting I: variables, arguments and tests
outline.summary: A shell script is a text file of commands. Start it with a shebang line like #!/bin/bash, make it executable with chmod +x, and run it with ./script.sh. Variables hold text. Assign with name=value, no spaces, and read with $name. Arguments arrive as $1, $2 and so on, and $# is how many there are. if tests a condition, usually with [ ] and operators such as -f for file exists, -eq for equal numbers and = for equal text.
keyPoints: No spaces around = in an assignment.
Quote variables: "$name".
[ -f file ] tests that a file exists.
$? holds the last exit code.

outline.title: Shell scripting II: loops, functions and robustness
outline.summary: for repeats a block for each item in a list, while repeats as long as a test succeeds. Functions give a name to a group of commands. Scripts should fail loudly. set -e stops the script at the first failing command, and checking exit codes lets you react to problems. Small, tested scripts are the glue of system administration: backups, deployments, reports and clean-up jobs.
keyPoints: for x in list; do ...; done.
while test; do ...; done.
set -e stops at the first error.
Write idempotent scripts: mkdir -p, not mkdir.

outline.title: Networking basics
outline.summary: Every machine on a network has an IP address. A port number picks the program on that machine, so a web server listens on 80 or 443 and SSH on 22. DNS turns names such as example.com into addresses. A subnet like 192.168.1.0/24 describes a block of addresses that share a prefix. Learn four tools: ip addr to see your address, ping to test reachability, curl to talk to web services, and ss to see what is listening.
keyPoints: 22 is SSH, 80 HTTP, 443 HTTPS, 53 DNS.
/24 means the first 24 bits are the network.
ping tests reachability; curl tests a service.
ss -tln shows listening TCP ports.

outline.title: Disks, logs and scheduled jobs
outline.summary: Disks are split into partitions, each with a filesystem, and each mounted at a directory. df shows free space for every mount and du shows how much a directory uses. Logs under /var/log and in the journal are where machines explain themselves. The first question when something breaks is: what does the log say? cron runs commands on a schedule written as five time fields.
keyPoints: df -h shows free space; du -sh shows a directory's size.
Full disks are a very common failure.
crontab fields: minute hour day month weekday.
*/5 means every five.

outline.title: Security basics
outline.summary: Security is a habit of small controls: give every user and program only the access it needs, keep software updated, use keys instead of passwords, and close ports you do not use. On a server, the usual first steps are to disable root login over SSH, disable password logins, turn on a firewall and set up automatic security updates. Assume something will fail anyway. Logs help you notice and backups help you recover.
keyPoints: Disable root and password SSH logins.
Open only the ports you need.
Apply security updates promptly.
Test your backups by restoring one.

outline.title: Capstone: look after a small server
outline.summary: Put everything together. You are handed a small server with a few problems. Look around, install and start the web service, fix risky permissions, add a teammate and check your work. Work like a system administrator: inspect first, change one thing at a time and verify each change before moving on. When the checklist is complete you will have used navigation, files, permissions, users, packages, services and scripting on one machine.
keyPoints: Look before you change.
Change one thing and verify it.
Keep scripts and notes of what you did.
Prefer reversible changes.

courses.title: The LMFDB: L-functions, Modular Forms and Elliptic Curves
courses.subtitle: A guided tour of the L-functions and Modular Forms Database: number fields, characters, elliptic curves, modular forms and L-functions, with Python labs that recompute the data
courses.author: Lilith Learning Lab
courses.description: Learn the mathematics behind the LMFDB, the free online atlas of number theory. Start with primes and quadratic residues, meet number fields and Dirichlet characters, count points on elliptic curves, compute modular forms such as Delta, and see how the modularity theorem ties curves, forms and L-functions together. Every chapter has labs that recompute what the database lists, plus an elliptic curve explorer.

outline.title: What the LMFDB is
outline.summary: The L-functions and Modular Forms Database (LMFDB) is a free online atlas of objects from number theory: elliptic curves, modular forms, number fields, Dirichlet characters, L-functions, genus 2 curves, Galois groups and more. Each object has a unique label, a page of properties, and links to related objects. The links are the real point: the same L-function can arise from an elliptic curve and from a modular form. This course teaches the mathematics behind the main collections and how to read their pages, with Python labs that recompute what the database lists.
keyPoints: An LMFDB page lists invariants you can recompute and cross-check.
Elliptic curves, modular forms and L-functions are tied by the modularity theorem.
Labels follow patterns: number fields d.r.D.i, newforms N.k.a.x, curves N.a.n.
The database holds computed data, so the data is checkable but not a proof.
Always check the live site: collections grow and pages change.

outline.title: Arithmetic toolkit: primes, congruences and squares
outline.summary: Almost everything in the LMFDB is detected one prime at a time. We need quick tools: primes, congruences modulo n, quadratic residues and the Legendre symbol. The Legendre symbol (a/p) is 1 if a is a nonzero square mod p, -1 if not, and 0 if p divides a. It is the key to counting points on a curve mod p. The labs sieve primes and compute the Legendre symbol by Euler's criterion.
keyPoints: Sieve of Eratosthenes finds all primes up to n.
Modular arithmetic: add and multiply, then reduce mod n.
Half of the nonzero residues mod an odd prime p are squares.
(a/p) = a^((p-1)/2) mod p, read as 1 or -1 (p - 1).
Counting solutions mod p is how a_p is defined.

outline.title: Number fields
outline.summary: A number field is a finite extension of the rationals, such as Q(sqrt(-3)). The LMFDB lists them by degree, signature and discriminant, with the ring of integers, the class number and the Galois group. The discriminant tells which primes ramify. The class number measures how far unique factorisation fails. The Galois group records the symmetries of the roots. The labs compute class numbers of imaginary quadratic fields by counting reduced quadratic forms.
keyPoints: Q(sqrt d) has degree 2 and discriminant d (or 4d).
The label d.r.D.i gives degree, real places, |discriminant| and an index.
Class number 1 means unique factorisation of ideals into primes is also element-wise.
Heegner: the imaginary quadratic fields with class number 1 have discriminants -3, -4, -7, -8, -11, -19, -43, -67, -163.
A prime p ramifies in K if it divides the discriminant.
The Galois group of a quadratic field is Z/2.

outline.title: Dirichlet characters and their L-functions
outline.summary: A Dirichlet character is a function chi on the integers that is periodic mod N, multiplicative and zero when n shares a factor with N. Each gives an L-function, the sum of chi(n)/n^s. The Riemann zeta function is the case chi = 1. The Dirichlet L-functions prove that arithmetic progressions contain infinitely many primes. The LMFDB lists characters by modulus and Conrey label. The labs compute a quadratic character and an Euler product.
keyPoints: chi(mn) = chi(m) chi(n); chi(n + N) = chi(n).
The quadratic character mod p is the Legendre symbol.
L(s, chi) = sum chi(n) n^(-s) = product over p of 1/(1 - chi(p) p^(-s)).
Zeta(s) = sum n^(-s) = product of 1/(1 - p^(-s)).
Dirichlet's theorem: infinitely many primes in a + Nk when gcd(a, N) = 1.
The LMFDB label N.k names the character with modulus N and Conrey number k.

outline.title: Elliptic curves over the rationals
outline.summary: An elliptic curve is a smooth cubic curve with a chosen point. Its rational points form a group, described by a rank (how many independent infinite-order points) and a finite torsion part. A model y squared = x cubed + ax + b has discriminant -16(4a cubed + 27b squared). The curve is smooth when this is nonzero. The conductor packages the primes where the curve has bad reduction, and appears in the LMFDB label. The labs compute the discriminant and the j-invariant.
keyPoints: Short Weierstrass form: y^2 = x^3 + ax + b over Q.
Discriminant: -16(4a^3 + 27b^2); nonzero means smooth.
Mordell's theorem: the rational points form a finitely generated group.
Torsion subgroups over Q: Mazur lists the 15 possibilities.
The LMFDB label 11.a2 is conductor 11, class a, number 2.

outline.title: Counting points and the numbers a_p
outline.summary: Reduce an elliptic curve mod a prime p and count the points N_p. The number a_p = p + 1 - N_p is the trace of Frobenius, and Hasse proved |a_p| is at most 2 times the square root of p. The sequence a_2, a_3, a_5 ... is a fingerprint of the curve. It is the data the LMFDB shows under 'Frobenius traces' and the input to the curve's L-function. The labs count points by brute force and check the Hasse bound.
keyPoints: N_p = 1 + number of solutions (x, y) in F_p x F_p.
a_p = p + 1 - N_p.
Hasse: |a_p| <= 2 sqrt p, or a_p^2 <= 4p.
For short form, N_p = 1 + sum over x of (1 + (f(x)/p)).
Bad primes divide the conductor; there a_p is 0 or plus or minus 1.
For the conductor 11 curve: a_2 = -2, a_3 = -1, a_5 = 1, a_7 = -2, a_13 = 4.

outline.title: Modular forms
outline.summary: A modular form is a complex function on the upper half-plane with a rigid symmetry under a group of matrices. Its Fourier expansion in q = e^(2 pi i z) carries arithmetic information in the coefficients. Weight k and level N classify the space of forms. Eisenstein series give simple examples with divisor sums as coefficients; cusp forms, such as Delta, have arithmetic coefficients like Ramanujan's tau. The labs compute Eisenstein series and the first coefficients of Delta.
keyPoints: f((az+b)/(cz+d)) = (cz+d)^k f(z) for matrices in the group.
q = e^(2 pi i z) and f = sum a_n q^n.
E_4 = 1 + 240 sum sigma_3(n) q^n; E_6 = 1 - 504 sum sigma_5(n) q^n.
Delta = q prod (1 - q^n)^24 is a weight 12 cusp form of level 1.
Dimensions of spaces are finite and known by formulas.
The LMFDB labels spaces as N.k.chi.

outline.title: Hecke operators and newforms
outline.summary: Hecke operators T_p act on spaces of modular forms. A form that is an eigenvector of all of them has multiplicative coefficients and a nice Euler product. The new part of the space is spanned by newforms, which the LMFDB labels N.k.a.x. For a newform the q-expansion coefficient a_p is the Hecke eigenvalue at p. The a_p sometimes lie in a larger number field, and Galois conjugate newforms are grouped into an orbit. The labs test multiplicativity and compute the Hecke relation for tau.
keyPoints: T_p on weight k, level N, prime p not dividing N, takes a_n to a_{pn} + p^(k-1) a_{n/p}.
For a newform, a_1 = 1 and a_{mn} = a_m a_n for coprime m, n.
a_{p^(r+1)} = a_p a_{p^r} - p^(k-1) a_{p^(r-1)} for good p.
Tau satisfies tau(p^2) = tau(p)^2 - p^11.
The LMFDB label N.k.a.x = level, weight, character orbit, newform orbit.

outline.title: L-functions
outline.summary: An L-function packages the local data at every prime into one analytic function. It has a Dirichlet series, an Euler product, an analytic continuation and a functional equation. The LMFDB lists many of them with plots, zeros and special values. The Riemann zeta function is the simplest. A newform f gives L(f, s) = sum a_n n^(-s), and an elliptic curve gives L(E, s) built from its a_p. The generalised Riemann hypothesis says the nontrivial zeros all lie on the critical line. The labs form Euler factors and partial products.
keyPoints: Zeta: sum n^-s = product 1/(1 - p^-s).
Newform: L(f, s) = sum a_n n^-s = product 1/(1 - a_p p^-s + p^(k-1-2s)).
Elliptic curve (weight 2): factor 1/(1 - a_p p^-s + p^(1-2s)).
Functional equation relates s and k - s (weight k) with a root number.
GRH: nontrivial zeros of L-functions have real part (k/2) on the critical line.
The LMFDB lists zeros, plots, and degree and conductor for each L-function.

outline.title: Modularity: curves meet forms
outline.summary: The modularity theorem says that every elliptic curve over Q corresponds to a weight 2 newform whose level equals the curve's conductor, with matching coefficients: a_p(E) = a_p(f) for all good primes. The conductor 11 curve and the newform 11.2.a.a have the same a_p. Wiles proved a large part of this, enough to prove Fermat's Last Theorem, and the full theorem followed. The labs compare a curve's a_p with the q-expansion of a newform.
keyPoints: Conductor of E = level of the newform f.
a_p(E) = a_p(f) for p not dividing the conductor.
Isogenous curves correspond to the same newform.
Wiles (1995) and Taylor-Wiles for semistable curves; Breuil-Conrad-Diamond-Taylor (2001) for all.
Ribet showed that a Frey curve would not be modular; Wiles proved it must be, so no solutions.
In the LMFDB, a curve page links to its modular form, with the same L-function.

outline.title: Galois representations, Sato-Tate and BSD
outline.summary: A Galois representation records how the Galois group of Q acts on the points of a curve or the roots of a polynomial. At each prime, Frobenius has a trace a_p, and the representation is determined by these traces. The Sato-Tate theorem says that a_p divided by 2 sqrt p is distributed like cos of an angle with a sine squared density. The Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture ties the rank to the order of vanishing of L(E, s) at s = 1. The labs normalise a_p and test a Hasse-style bound.
keyPoints: Normalised trace: a_p / (2 sqrt p) lies in [-1, 1].
Sato-Tate: the angle theta with a_p = 2 sqrt p cos(theta) has density (2/pi) sin^2(theta).
BSD: rank = ord_{s=1} L(E, s), plus a formula for the leading coefficient.
Artin representations match Galois representations of finite image to L-functions.
The Langlands program: automorphic representations correspond to Galois representations.
The LMFDB lists Sato-Tate groups for curves and abelian varieties.

outline.title: Using the LMFDB and what lies beyond
outline.summary: The LMFDB has collections beyond those in this course: genus 2 curves, abelian varieties over finite fields, Siegel and Hilbert modular forms, Maass forms, Artin representations and local fields. Each follows the same plan: invariants, labels, links. You can search by invariants (conductor, rank, torsion, degree, discriminant), open a page by label, or query the data through an API. Pages show proven and computed data; read the notes on what is proven. The labs read a label and compute simple statistics, and the last exam checks the whole course.
keyPoints: Each LMFDB collection has search forms, label pages and downloadable data.
Labels encode invariants: conductor, class, and index.
Genus 2 curves have L-functions of degree 4.
Pages distinguish proven from computed data; look for notes.
You can reproduce an a_p or a class number yourself, as in the labs.
Cross-links between collections show the Langlands correspondences.

courses.title: Mathematics for Computer Science and AI
courses.subtitle: Discrete maths, linear algebra, calculus, probability, information theory, category and type theory, with Python labs
courses.author: Lilith Learning Lab
courses.description: The mathematics behind modern computer science and machine learning, built from the ground up and explained intuitively: logic and proof, sets, counting, graphs, number theory, linear algebra, calculus and multivariate calculus, optimization, probability and statistics, information theory, Markov chains, abstract algebra and category theory, type theory and the lambda calculus. Every chapter has an ELI5 block, quizzes and Python labs.

outline.title: Logic and proof
outline.summary: Logic is the grammar of mathematics and of programs. A proposition is a statement that is true or false. Connectives such as and, or, not and implies build new propositions from old ones, and truth tables say exactly when they hold. Quantifiers say for all and there exists. Proofs are arguments that a statement must hold: direct proof, proof by contradiction, and mathematical induction, which proves a statement for every natural number. Every later chapter relies on these tools. The labs evaluate formulas, check tautologies and prove a sum formula by testing it.
keyPoints: Connectives: not, and, or, implies, if and only if.
p implies q is equivalent to (not p) or q, and to its contrapositive.
De Morgan: not (p and q) = (not p) or (not q); not (p or q) = (not p) and (not q).
Negating for all gives there exists not; negating there exists gives for all not.
Induction: P(0) and (P(n) implies P(n+1)) give P(n) for all n.
Strong induction assumes P(k) for all k below n.

outline.title: Sets, relations and functions
outline.summary: A set is a collection of distinct things. Sets have union, intersection and complement; the Cartesian product forms pairs. A relation is a set of pairs, and a function is a relation that gives exactly one output for each input. Injective functions never merge inputs, surjective ones hit every output, and bijective ones are both and so can be inverted. Equivalence relations split a set into disjoint classes, which is how we define things like integers modulo n. The labs implement set operations, compose functions and test properties of relations.
keyPoints: |A union B| = |A| + |B| - |A intersect B|.
|A x B| = |A| |B|; a set of n elements has 2^n subsets.
A function f: A -> B has one output per input.
f is invertible exactly when it is a bijection.
Equivalence: reflexive, symmetric, transitive; its classes partition the set.
Composition: (g o f)(x) = g(f(x)).

outline.title: Counting and combinatorics
outline.summary: Counting is the maths behind complexity, probability and hashing. The product rule multiplies independent choices; the sum rule adds disjoint cases. A permutation orders items; a combination picks a subset. The number of ways to choose k of n items is the binomial coefficient n choose k. The pigeonhole principle says that more items than boxes forces a box with two, and inclusion-exclusion corrects for overlaps. The labs compute factorials, binomials, derangement-style counts and the birthday collision probability.
keyPoints: C(n, k) = C(n-1, k-1) + C(n-1, k) (Pascal).
Sum of C(n, k) over k equals 2^n.
Pigeonhole: if more than n items go into n boxes, some box holds at least two.
Birthday problem: collisions appear after about sqrt(n) draws from n values.
Stars and bars: ways to split n identical items into k groups is C(n+k-1, k-1).

outline.title: Graphs, trees and relations as graphs
outline.summary: A graph is a set of vertices joined by edges. Graphs model networks, dependencies, states and relations. Degree counts the edges at a vertex, and the handshake lemma says the degrees add up to twice the number of edges. A tree is a connected graph without cycles; a tree on n vertices has n minus 1 edges. Graphs are stored as adjacency lists or matrices and explored with breadth-first or depth-first search. The labs build adjacency structures, count degrees, test for trees and run a breadth-first search.
keyPoints: Sum of degrees = 2 |E| (handshake lemma).
A tree on n vertices has n - 1 edges and a unique path between any two vertices.
A connected graph on n vertices has at least n - 1 edges.
Powers of the adjacency matrix count walks: (A^k)[i][j] is the number of walks of length k.
BFS finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs.
A directed acyclic graph can be topologically ordered.

outline.title: Number theory and modular arithmetic
outline.summary: Number theory studies integers. Divisibility, primes and the greatest common divisor underlie hashing, random number generators and cryptography. Modular arithmetic, which wraps numbers around a modulus, is arithmetic on a clock. Euclid's algorithm computes the greatest common divisor quickly. Fast exponentiation computes large powers modulo n, and Fermat's little theorem gives modular inverses for a prime modulus. These tools make public-key cryptography possible. The labs implement gcd, modular exponentiation, the sieve of Eratosthenes and modular inverses.
keyPoints: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b); gcd(a, 0) = a.
Modular arithmetic respects + and x: (a + b) mod n = ((a mod n) + (b mod n)) mod n.
Square-and-multiply computes a^e mod n in O(log e) steps.
Fermat: a^(p-1) = 1 mod p, so a^(-1) = a^(p-2) mod p.
Every integer above 1 factors uniquely into primes.
RSA's security rests on the difficulty of factoring large products of primes.

outline.title: Linear algebra I: vectors and matrices
outline.summary: Linear algebra is the language of data and of neural networks. A vector is a list of numbers, a point or an arrow in space. The dot product measures how aligned two vectors are, and the norm measures length. A matrix is a table of numbers and also a linear map: it turns vectors into vectors. Multiplying matrices composes maps. Almost every layer of a neural network is a matrix multiplication followed by a simple nonlinear function. The labs implement dot products, norms, cosine similarity, matrix-vector and matrix-matrix products and the transpose.
keyPoints: Dot product: x . y = |x||y| cos(theta); zero for orthogonal vectors.
Cauchy-Schwarz: |x . y| <= |x||y|.
Matrix product is associative but not commutative.
(AB)^T = B^T A^T.
A linear map satisfies f(ax + by) = a f(x) + b f(y).
Cosine similarity = (x . y)/(|x||y|), used to compare embeddings.

outline.title: Linear algebra II: systems, determinants, eigenvalues and SVD
outline.summary: A linear system A x = b asks which input x the matrix A maps to b. Gaussian elimination solves it by row operations. The determinant tells how a matrix scales volume and whether it can be inverted. An eigenvector of A is a direction the matrix only stretches; the stretch factor is its eigenvalue. The singular value decomposition factors any matrix into rotations and a stretch, and powers principal component analysis and low-rank compression. The labs solve systems, compute determinants, find a dominant eigenvalue by power iteration and project data onto a direction.
keyPoints: Gaussian elimination solves A x = b in O(n^3) operations.
det(AB) = det(A) det(B); det of a triangular matrix is the product of its diagonal.
A v = lambda v; det(A - lambda I) = 0 gives the eigenvalues.
Symmetric matrices have real eigenvalues and orthogonal eigenvectors.
SVD: A = U S V^T; truncating small singular values gives the best low-rank approximation.
PCA keeps the top eigenvectors of the covariance matrix.

outline.title: Calculus: limits, derivatives and the chain rule
outline.summary: Calculus is the mathematics of change. The derivative of a function measures how fast its output changes as its input changes: the slope of the curve at a point. The integral adds up small pieces to find total change or area. The chain rule differentiates a function of a function. It is the single most important rule for AI, because a neural network is a long composition of simple functions and backpropagation is the chain rule applied to it. The labs estimate derivatives numerically, apply the rules, integrate by the trapezoid rule and build a Taylor approximation.
keyPoints: d/dx x^n = n x^(n-1); d/dx e^x = e^x; d/dx ln x = 1/x.
Sum rule, product rule, quotient rule, chain rule.
Derivative of sigmoid: s'(x) = s(x)(1 - s(x)).
Fundamental theorem: the integral of f' from a to b equals f(b) - f(a).
Taylor: f(x+h) ~ f(x) + f'(x) h + f''(x) h^2/2.
At a minimum or maximum the derivative is zero.

outline.title: Multivariate calculus: gradients, Jacobians and backpropagation
outline.summary: Functions in AI take many inputs, so we need derivatives in many dimensions. A partial derivative changes one variable and holds the others still. The gradient collects all partials into a vector pointing in the direction of steepest increase. The Jacobian is the matrix of partials of a vector-valued function, and the Hessian is the matrix of second derivatives, describing curvature. The multivariate chain rule multiplies Jacobians, and backpropagation does it efficiently from the loss backwards. The labs compute gradients, check them numerically, and run backpropagation through a tiny network.
keyPoints: grad f = (df/dx1, ..., df/dxn); it is orthogonal to level sets.
Directional derivative = grad f . u for a unit vector u.
Chain rule: J of (f o g) = J_f J_g.
For a linear layer y = W x: dL/dW = (dL/dy) x^T and dL/dx = W^T (dL/dy).
Hessian positive definite means a local minimum at a critical point.
Reverse mode costs about the same as one forward pass for a scalar loss.

outline.title: Optimization: gradient descent, convexity and Lagrange multipliers
outline.summary: Training a model means minimising a loss. Gradient descent repeats a simple step: move a little against the gradient. The learning rate is the step size, and too large a step overshoots while too small a step crawls. A convex function has a single valley, so descent finds the global minimum. Deep networks are not convex, yet descent works well in practice. Momentum, stochastic mini-batches and adaptive methods improve it. Lagrange multipliers handle constraints. The labs run gradient descent, show how the step size matters, implement momentum and solve a constrained problem.
keyPoints: Update: x_{t+1} = x_t - eta * grad f(x_t).
For f = a x^2, descent converges when 0 < eta < 1/a.
Convex: f(tx + (1-t)y) <= t f(x) + (1-t) f(y).
Momentum: v <- beta v + grad; x <- x - eta v.
Constrained optimum: grad f = lambda grad g with g(x) = 0.
SGD uses a random mini-batch to estimate the gradient.

outline.title: Probability: axioms, conditional probability and Bayes' rule
outline.summary: Probability measures uncertainty. A sample space lists all outcomes, an event is a set of them, and probability assigns a number between zero and one. The axioms make these numbers behave consistently. Conditional probability asks: given that this happened, how likely is that? Independence means one event tells you nothing about the other. Bayes' rule reverses a conditional and is the engine of learning from evidence. The labs compute conditional probabilities, apply Bayes to a medical test, check independence and simulate with a counting argument.
keyPoints: Axioms: P(event) >= 0; P(whole space) = 1; probabilities of disjoint events add.
P(not A) = 1 - P(A); P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B).
Law of total probability: P(B) = sum over i of P(B | A_i) P(A_i).
Bayes: posterior is proportional to likelihood times prior.
Independent events: P(A | B) = P(A).
Base-rate neglect: ignoring P(A) when reading a test result.

outline.title: Random variables, distributions and expectation
outline.summary: A random variable has a distribution: how likely each value is. The expectation is the average value, the variance measures spread and the standard deviation is its square root. Common distributions include Bernoulli, binomial, uniform and Gaussian. Two theorems explain why statistics works. The law of large numbers says averages settle on the expectation. The central limit theorem says sums of many small independent effects look Gaussian. The labs compute expectations and variances, evaluate the Gaussian density, compute binomial probabilities and simulate averages.
keyPoints: E[a X + b Y] = a E[X] + b E[Y] always (linearity).
Var(X) = E[X^2] - (E[X])^2; Var(aX) = a^2 Var(X).
Binomial: P(k) = C(n, k) p^k (1-p)^(n-k); mean np, variance np(1-p).
Gaussian density: exp(-(x-mu)^2/(2 sigma^2)) / (sigma sqrt(2 pi)).
Law of large numbers: the sample mean tends to E[X].
CLT: the mean of n samples has standard deviation sigma/sqrt(n).

outline.title: Statistics: estimation, likelihood and hypothesis tests
outline.summary: Statistics goes from data back to the world. We draw a sample and estimate properties of the population. The likelihood scores how well a parameter explains the data, and maximum likelihood picks the best parameter. A prior adds earlier belief, giving the MAP estimate. A confidence interval says how precise an estimate is. A hypothesis test asks whether the data would be surprising if nothing were going on. The bias-variance trade-off explains overfitting and underfitting in machine learning. The labs compute estimates, a maximum-likelihood coin bias, a confidence interval, a z statistic and a bias-variance example.
keyPoints: Sample mean estimates the mean; sample variance divides by n - 1.
For a coin with k heads in n flips, the MLE of p is k/n.
95 percent interval for a mean: mean +/- 1.96 s/sqrt(n).
z = (mean - mu0) / (s / sqrt(n)).
MSE = bias^2 + variance (+ noise).
Least squares is the MLE under Gaussian noise.

outline.title: Information theory: entropy, cross-entropy and KL divergence
outline.summary: Information theory measures uncertainty and information in bits. A rare event is more surprising than a common one, so surprise is minus the log of the probability. Entropy is the average surprise of a distribution: how unpredictable it is. Cross-entropy measures the cost of coding data from one distribution with a model of another, and is the standard loss for classifiers and language models. The KL divergence is the extra cost, a measure of how far a model is from the truth. Mutual information measures what two variables share. The labs compute entropy, cross-entropy, KL divergence and mutual information.
keyPoints: A fair coin has entropy 1 bit; a certain event has 0.
Entropy is maximal for the uniform distribution: log2 n.
KL divergence is never negative and zero only when p = q.
KL is not symmetric: D(p||q) differs from D(q||p).
Minimising cross-entropy over q equals minimising KL to p.
Shannon: no lossless code beats the entropy on average.

outline.title: Markov chains and stochastic processes
outline.summary: A Markov chain moves between states with fixed probabilities where the next state depends only on the current one. A transition matrix lists the probabilities, and multiplying a distribution by it advances one step. Under mild conditions the chain forgets its start and settles into a stationary distribution. This idea gives PageRank, sampling methods such as MCMC, hidden Markov models and the Markov decision processes of reinforcement learning. The labs step a chain, compute its stationary distribution by iteration, simulate a random walk exactly by enumeration and evaluate a small MDP value.
keyPoints: A distribution evolves by pi_{t+1} = pi_t P.
The stationary pi satisfies pi = pi P and sums to 1.
n-step probabilities are entries of P^n.
PageRank adds random jumps to guarantee a unique answer.
MDP value: V(s) = max_a [R + gamma sum P V(s')].
MCMC builds a chain whose stationary distribution is the target.

outline.title: Algebra and category theory
