outline.summary: Algebra studies structures with operations. A monoid has an associative operation and a do-nothing element; a group also has inverses. These abstract patterns appear all over computing: strings under concatenation, numbers under addition, permutations and symmetries. Category theory goes one level up and studies structure by arrows alone. A category has objects and composable arrows. A functor maps one category to another preserving structure, which is exactly what a map over a list does. Monads package effects such as state and failure. The labs check monoid and group laws, implement a functor on lists and options, compose arrows and build a tiny monad.
keyPoints: Monoid laws: (a b) c = a (b c); e a = a e = a.
Group: every a has an inverse with a a^-1 = e.
Category: composition is associative; id composes neutrally.
Functor laws: F(id) = id; F(g o f) = F(g) o F(f).
Monad laws: left identity, right identity, associativity of bind.
Product and sum types are universal constructions.

outline.title: Type theory and the lambda calculus
outline.summary: The lambda calculus is the smallest programming language: just functions and application. A function is written with lambda, and applying it substitutes the argument. Everything computable can be expressed in it. Types classify terms and rule out nonsense, like adding a string to a number. The Curry-Howard correspondence says types are propositions and programs are proofs. Dependent types let types mention values, and proof assistants use them to check mathematics by computer. The labs evaluate lambda terms with Church numerals, type-check tiny expressions and implement a Boolean type.
keyPoints: Syntax: x | lambda x. t | t u.
Beta: (lambda x. t) u -> t[x := u].
Typing: if x : A and t : B then lambda x. t : A -> B.
Church numerals: n = lambda f. lambda x. f^n x.
A -> B reads as 'A implies B'; a pair type reads as 'and'; a sum type as 'or'.
Simply typed terms always terminate.

courses.title: Monte Carlo Tree Search
courses.subtitle: Playouts, bandits, UCT and enhancements, with Python labs on Nim
courses.author: Lilith Learning Lab
courses.description: Monte Carlo tree search from first principles (Coulom 2006; Kocsis and Szepesvari 2006; Browne et al. 2012): game trees and minimax, random playouts, multi-armed bandits and UCB1, the four steps, a complete UCT search on Nim, choosing the final move, RAVE and other enhancements, two-player perspective, and the road to AlphaGo's PUCT. Theory plus Python labs.

outline.title: What is Monte Carlo tree search?
outline.summary: Monte Carlo tree search, MCTS, is a way to choose good actions in a decision problem by growing a search tree guided by random simulations. It needs little domain knowledge beyond the rules. It was developed around 2006. Remi Coulom described the idea and gave it the name. Levente Kocsis and Csaba Szepesvari proposed UCT, which uses a bandit rule to decide which branch to explore. It then transformed computer Go. MCTS repeats four steps: selection, expansion, simulation and backpropagation. This course builds each step in small Python labs on the game of Nim.
keyPoints: MCTS needs only a model of the rules: legal moves, transitions and terminal results.
Four steps per iteration: selection, expansion, simulation, backpropagation.
The tree grows towards promising moves, so it is asymmetric.
UCT (Kocsis and Szepesvari, 2006) applies the UCB1 bandit rule at every node.
Coulom (2006) used the term Monte Carlo tree search.
Browne and colleagues (2012) surveyed the method and its many variants.

outline.title: Games, trees and the need for search
outline.summary: A game can be drawn as a tree. The root is the current position, each edge is a legal move, and the leaves are finished games. Solving a small game means labelling every node as a win or a loss for the player to move. Minimax does this exactly, working up from the leaves. A position is a win if some move leads to a position that is a loss for the opponent. Minimax is perfect but needs the whole tree, which grows exponentially: with b moves per state and depth d there are about b to the d leaves. Go has about 250 moves per position and games of 150 moves, so exact search is hopeless. That is the gap MCTS fills.
keyPoints: Nim: take 1 to 3 stones; the player who takes the last stone wins.
A position with 0 stones is lost for the player to move: the opponent just took the last.
Minimax: win if any move leads to a loss for the opponent.
The tree has about b^d leaves; Go's b is about 250.
In Nim with a take limit of 3, positions that are multiples of 4 are lost for the player to move.
MCTS estimates what minimax computes, using samples.
glossary: Win or loss for the player to move

outline.title: Random playouts and Monte Carlo estimation
outline.summary: A playout (also called a rollout or simulation) plays a game to the end with random moves. Its result, win or loss, is a noisy estimate of the position's value. Averaging many playouts reduces the noise. The standard error of an average of n samples shrinks like one over the square root of n. Ten times more playouts make the estimate about three times more accurate. The labs use a tiny linear congruential generator for pseudo-random numbers, so that every result is exactly repeatable.
keyPoints: The playout result for the player to move is 1 for a win and 0 for a loss.
Win rate = wins / playouts.
Standard error is about sqrt(p (1 - p) / n).
A random playout policy picks uniformly among legal moves.
Estimates from random play are noisy and may be biased as a measure of perfect-play value.
In the labs: x -> (75 x + 74) mod 65537, a small LCG, picks the move index as x mod number of moves.

outline.title: Bandits and the UCB1 rule
outline.summary: A multi-armed bandit is the simplest setting where exploration and exploitation clash. There are several arms, each paying a random reward with an unknown mean. You pull one arm per round and want the highest total reward. UCB1, by Auer, Cesa-Bianchi and Fischer in 2002, picks the arm with the highest upper confidence bound: its average reward plus a bonus that is large for rarely pulled arms. Its regret grows only logarithmically with the number of pulls. In MCTS, each move at each node is an arm and each playout is a pull.
keyPoints: UCB1 value of arm i: mean_i + c * sqrt(2 ln N / n_i).
N is the total number of pulls and n_i the pulls of arm i; untried arms are pulled first.
The bonus shrinks as n_i grows and grows slowly as N grows, so every arm is revisited eventually.
UCB1 has logarithmic regret in the number of pulls (Auer et al., 2002).
In UCT the constant is written C_p; the survey notes 1/sqrt(2) for rewards in [0, 1].
In MCTS the arm is a child move; the reward is a playout result.

outline.title: The four steps: selection, expansion, simulation, backpropagation
outline.summary: Each iteration starts at the root. Selection walks down through nodes already in the tree, following a tree policy. When it reaches a node with an untried move, expansion adds a child for one. Simulation plays from the new node to the end with a default policy. Backpropagation then updates every node on the path with the result. Each node stores two numbers: its visit count N and its total reward W. The mean reward is W over N. Because the players alternate, the result must be flipped as it travels up: a win for one player is a loss for the other.
keyPoints: Selection: from the root, follow the tree policy to a node that is not fully expanded or is terminal.
Expansion: add one child for an untried move.
Simulation: play the default policy from the new child to a terminal state.
Backpropagation: add 1 to N on every node of the path, and add the result to W from that node's perspective.
Rewards from a node's parent's perspective alternate with depth.
After the iterations, the move is chosen from the root's children.

outline.title: UCT and a complete search
outline.summary: UCT is MCTS with UCB1 as the tree policy: at each node, descend to the child maximising its mean reward plus an exploration bonus. This treats every node as a bandit problem. With the pieces from earlier chapters we can write a full search. Run a fixed number of iterations from the current position, then play the root move with the most visits. The labs do exactly that on Nim, with a small deterministic random generator, so the whole search is repeatable.
keyPoints: UCT picks the child maximising mean + C * sqrt(ln(N_parent) / n_child).
Browne et al. write the bonus as 2 C_p sqrt(2 ln n / n_j); the constants differ only by scaling C.
Kocsis and Szepesvari proved that UCT converges to the minimax value for finite games.
Choose the final move by visits.
More iterations give better play.
The labs fix C = 1 and a deterministic generator.

outline.title: Choosing the final move
outline.summary: After the iterations, the program must pick a move from the root's children. The survey lists several criteria. The max child has the highest mean reward. The robust child has the highest visit count. The max-robust child is the one with both, and if none exists the search continues. The secure child maximises a lower confidence bound. The mean of a barely visited child is unreliable: a single lucky playout can make it look perfect. Visit counts are steadier, so the robust child is the usual choice. The labs implement each criterion and show where they disagree.
keyPoints: Robust child: argmax visits.
Max child: argmax mean.
Secure child: argmax of mean - A / sqrt(n) for a constant A.
A child with 1 visit and mean 1.0 is not trustworthy.
UCT concentrates visits on good moves, so max and robust usually agree after many iterations.
Disagreement signals that more iterations are needed.

outline.title: Enhancements: RAVE, priors, widening and more
outline.summary: Plain UCT is slow to learn in big games. The survey describes many enhancements. All-moves-as-first, AMAF, and its tree version RAVE share information between positions: a move that did well when played later in a playout is probably good now. Other ideas: give unvisited children a first-play urgency value; widen the set of considered moves gradually as the node gets more visits; use domain knowledge or a policy to bias playouts; merge identical positions in a transposition table; and run many threads using virtual loss. These are from the survey and later work; the labs implement three of the simplest.
keyPoints: AMAF/RAVE: from Gelly and Silver's work on Go, described in the survey.
RAVE blends: beta * AMAF mean + (1 - beta) * ordinary mean, with beta falling as visits grow.
First-play urgency: unvisited children get a fixed score instead of infinity.
Progressive widening: allowed children = ceil(k * visits^alpha).
Heuristic or learned playout policies play better than uniform random.
Parallelisation: tree parallelism with virtual loss, leaf or root parallelism.

outline.title: Two players, perspective and heuristics
outline.summary: Two-player games need care with perspective. A node should store results from the viewpoint of the player who moved into it, and the reward flips at every level. Draws score one half. MCTS is often seen as a selective, sampled version of minimax: the mean values in the tree approach minimax values, while the tree grows deeper along strong lines. Compared with alpha-beta, MCTS shines when evaluation functions are hard to write and branching is large; alpha-beta shines when a good evaluation function exists and tactics are narrow.
keyPoints: Win = 1, draw = 0.5, loss = 0 from the perspective of the player who moved into the node.
Backup: r for the leaf's mover; 1 - r for the other player, alternating.
MCTS needs no evaluation function; alpha-beta usually does.
Alpha-beta prunes exactly; MCTS focuses statistically.
MCTS can be weak in narrow tactical lines with traps.
Hybrid systems exist; AlphaGo-style systems mix MCTS with learned networks.

outline.title: Applications, limits and where it leads
outline.summary: MCTS was the breakthrough behind the strong Go programs of 2006 to 2015 and then became a general tool: in video games, general game playing, planning, scheduling and optimisation problems. The survey lists applications across games and non-game domains. It has weak spots. Traps can fool it; very long games with sparse rewards give little signal; the cost per iteration limits depth. Remedies include better playouts, learned priors and learned values. The modern line of work, AlphaGo, AlphaZero and MuZero, keeps the tree search and replaces random playouts by learned networks.
keyPoints: Go programs using MCTS reached strong amateur level before 2015.
The survey covers games and non-game domains such as planning and scheduling.
Weaknesses: traps, long sparse-reward horizons, memory growth.
PUCT adds a policy prior to the selection rule.
AlphaGo (2016) and AlphaZero (2017) combine MCTS with deep networks.
MCTS needs a model of the environment, or a learned one as in MuZero.

courses.title: Meta-Learning for Compositionality
courses.subtitle: An intuitive walk through Lake and Baroni's Nature paper on how a plain neural network can learn to combine known parts in new ways
courses.author: Lilith Learning Lab
courses.description: An intuitive, step-by-step retelling of the open-access Nature paper Human-like systematic generalization through a meta-learning neural network by Brenden Lake and Marco Baroni (Nature 623, 115-121, 2023, CC BY 4.0). Learn what systematic generalization is, play a made-up colour language, meet the three human habits the paper measures, see why ordinary networks stumble, and follow the meta-learning for compositionality (MLC) recipe, its results and its limits, with numbered figures, recaps, memory tricks, concept maps and short Python labs. The examples and words in this course are our own illustrations in the spirit of the paper, and this course is not affiliated with or endorsed by the authors or the journal.

outline.title: Why systematicity matters
outline.summary: People understand new combinations of words they already know. If you know what skip means and what twice means, you understand skip twice the first time you hear it. This skill is called systematic generalization, or compositionality. In 1988 the scientists Jerry Fodor and Zenon Pylyshyn argued that neural networks could not do this. For decades the argument has been debated, and even today's big networks often stumble on tests of it. In 2023 Brenden Lake and Marco Baroni published a paper in the journal Nature that trains a plain neural network in a new way, called meta-learning for compositionality or MLC. This course walks through that paper step by step.
keyPoints: Systematic means new combinations of known parts.
Humans do it easily, even from a few examples.
Fodor and Pylyshyn (1988) said networks cannot.
MLC is a training method, not a new kind of network.
The paper is Lake and Baroni, Nature 2023.

outline.title: A tiny language and its rules
outline.summary: To study systematic generalization, the researchers invented a small made-up language. A handful of nonsense words stand for coloured circles, and a few function words act on them. Each sentence has an exact answer, a row of coloured circles, that you can work out by following rules. The rules are called an interpretation grammar. The words and rules in this course are our own simple illustration in the same spirit as the paper's task. The meanings of the words are different for every person, so nobody can have memorised them.
keyPoints: Primitive words stand for colours.
Function words act on other words.
Our three: fep repeats, blicket sandwiches, kiki swaps.
A grammar gives every sentence one exact answer.
Word meanings are re-shuffled for each person.

outline.title: How people learn it: the few-shot experiment
outline.summary: In the paper's first experiment, 25 people learned such a language from only 14 study examples and then answered 10 new questions. This is few-shot learning: very few examples. People matched the exact rule 80.7 percent of the time, and 72.5 percent of their answers were right even when the answer was longer than any study example. Their mistakes were not random. The mistakes followed habits that you will meet in the next chapter. These habits are the clue that the researchers wanted their network to copy.
keyPoints: 14 study examples, then 10 queries.
People matched the rule 80.7 percent of the time.
72.5 percent right on answers longer than any studied.
Mistakes were patterned, not random.
Meanings were re-shuffled for each person.

outline.title: Three habits of the human mind
outline.summary: When examples do not settle an answer, people lean on built-in habits called inductive biases. The paper finds three that matter in this task: one-to-one mapping, iconic concatenation and mutual exclusivity. In a second experiment, 29 people guessed answers to seven instructions with no examples at all. That reveals their habits in the open. Most people used all of the habits at once. The goal of the paper is a network that is systematic like an algebra and also has these human habits, without having them written in by hand.
keyPoints: Inductive biases guide guesses when data runs out.
One-to-one: one piece per word.
Iconic concatenation: pieces in the order heard.
Mutual exclusivity: different words, different answers.
58.6 percent of people used all three together.

outline.title: Why standard networks stumble
outline.summary: A standard neural network learns from many examples of one fixed task. It can memorise the training phrases very well, but memorising is not understanding. In the paper, a basic sequence-to-sequence network with no study examples and no meta-learning scored zero percent exact match on the few-shot task, because it never sees the new meanings. The network MLC uses is just as ordinary: a transformer with an encoder and a decoder. The difference is what it has been trained to do, not how it is built.
keyPoints: Standard training teaches one fixed task.
Memorising fails on new meanings.
A basic seq2seq model scored 0 percent on the few-shot task.
MLC uses a plain transformer encoder-decoder.
The change is in the training, not the architecture.

outline.title: Meta-learning: learning how to learn
outline.summary: Meta-learning means practising the skill of learning itself. Instead of learning one task, a network sees a long stream of small tasks, each with its own examples. Because the meanings of the words change in every task, the network cannot memorise them. The only thing that helps across tasks is the skill of reading the examples and working out the rule. That skill is what we want: look at a few examples, work out the pattern, apply it to a new question.
keyPoints: An episode is a tiny task with its own examples.
Meta-learning practises a stream of episodes.
Word meanings change each episode.
So the network cannot memorise; it must infer.
At test time the weights are frozen.

outline.title: The MLC recipe
outline.summary: MLC stands for meta-learning for compositionality. It is a recipe for training a standard transformer on a stream of episodes made from randomly generated grammars. Each episode has study examples and a query. The target answer is the exact rule answer 80 percent of the time and a human-like guess 20 percent of the time, so the network learns both rules and habits. Because the guessing habits are written into the targets, the network learns them from data. The network itself has no built-in rules.
keyPoints: Episodes come from random grammars.
Study examples plus a query go in as one input.
80 percent of targets are exact algebraic answers.
20 percent follow human-like habits.
No rule machinery is added to the network.

outline.title: Results: does MLC act like people?
outline.summary: MLC can be compared with people on the very same tasks. On the few-shot task its best run reached perfect exact-match accuracy, and its sampled answers matched human behaviour closely. Sampled answers followed the rule 82.4 percent of the time, against 80.7 for people, and handled longer outputs 77.8 percent of the time against 72.5. Its types of mistakes also looked human. A basic network scored zero, and a purely symbolic model with built-in biases needed much more hand-built structure to come close.
keyPoints: Best MLC run: perfect exact match on rule answers.
Sampled MLC: 82.4 percent systematic, people 80.7.
Longer outputs: MLC 77.8, people 72.5.
MLC predicted which items were hard for people.
Basic seq2seq scored 0 percent.

outline.title: Benchmarks: SCAN and COGS
outline.summary: Besides the human tasks, the paper tests MLC on two machine-learning benchmarks: SCAN, which turns commands into actions, and COGS, which turns sentences into logical forms. On the lexical generalization tests MLC slashed error rates. For example on SCAN add jump the error fell from 99.27 percent for a basic network to 0.22 percent. But MLC still fails some tests, such as the SCAN length split and three COGS structural splits, where the error stays at 100 percent.
keyPoints: SCAN turns commands into actions.
COGS turns sentences into logical forms.
MLC cut lexical errors sharply.
Add jump: 99.27 percent down to 0.22 percent.
Length and some structure splits still fail.

outline.title: Limits, lessons and where to go next
outline.summary: MLC shows that a plain neural network can acquire human-like systematic generalization from a smart training stream. It is a big step but not a finished story. The authors list honest limits: entirely new structures, new symbols that were never seen, and full natural language are all outside what has been shown. Future work may add this kind of specialised training to large language models and vision models, and may draw lessons from how children learn.
keyPoints: MLC works inside its meta-training distribution.
It cannot yet handle entirely new structures.
It cannot emit brand new symbols without extra machinery.
It is not yet shown on full natural language.
Children's word learning may offer further clues.

courses.title: Music Theory
courses.subtitle: Notes, scales, chords and harmony from the ground up, with Python labs, an ear trainer and a circle of fifths
courses.author: Lilith Learning Lab
courses.description: A beginner-friendly course in Western music theory: pitch and notes, reading the staff and rhythm, intervals, major and minor scales and modes, key signatures, triads and seventh chords, inversions, Roman numeral harmony and cadences, melody, form, transposition and writing a simple song. Python labs build scales and chords from numbers; an interactive ear trainer and a circle of fifths let you hear and see the ideas.

outline.title: Sound, pitch and the notes
outline.summary: Sound is vibration. How fast something vibrates, its frequency in hertz (Hz), sets the pitch. A faster vibration sounds higher. Western music divides the octave, a doubling of frequency, into twelve equal steps called semitones. The seven white keys on a piano are the notes A to G, and the black keys are sharps or flats. Each note has a letter name and an octave number, such as C4 for middle C. Concert A, A4, is 440 Hz.
keyPoints: Pitch goes up with frequency.
An octave doubles the frequency: A4 = 440 Hz, A5 = 880 Hz.
12 semitones make an octave.
Letter names A B C D E F G, then repeat.
Sharp (♯) raises by one semitone; flat (♭) lowers by one.

outline.title: Reading music: staff, clefs and rhythm
outline.summary: Music is written on a staff of five lines and four spaces. A clef at the start says which pitches the lines stand for. The treble clef fixes the second line as G4, and the bass clef fixes the fourth line as F3. The shape of a note shows how long it lasts. A whole note lasts four beats in 4/4 time, a half note two, a quarter one, an eighth half a beat. Each next shape halves the value before it. The time signature at the start tells how many beats are in each measure and which note gets the beat. In 3/4 there are three quarter-note beats per measure.
keyPoints: Treble clef: lines E G B D F; spaces F A C E.
Bass clef: lines G B D F A; spaces A C E G.
Whole = 4 beats, half = 2, quarter = 1, eighth = 1/2 (in 4/4).
A dot adds half the note's value.
Time signature 4/4: four quarter beats per measure.

outline.title: Intervals
outline.summary: An interval is the distance between two notes. It has a number, counted in letter names (C up to E is a third), and a quality, found from the semitones (major, minor, perfect, augmented or diminished). Unisons, fourths, fifths and octaves come in a perfect quality. Seconds, thirds, sixths and sevenths come in major and minor. Learn the intervals by their semitone count and by a familiar song to hear them.
keyPoints: 0 unison, 1 minor 2nd, 2 major 2nd, 3 minor 3rd, 4 major 3rd.
5 perfect 4th, 6 tritone, 7 perfect 5th.
8 minor 6th, 9 major 6th, 10 minor 7th, 11 major 7th, 12 octave.
Invert: 2nd and 7th, 3rd and 6th, 4th and 5th swap.
Perfect inverts to perfect; major to minor.

outline.title: Major scales and key signatures
outline.summary: A scale is a ladder of notes. The major scale follows the step pattern whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half. Starting on C and playing only white keys gives C major. The first note of a scale is the tonic, the home note that gives the key its name. Each scale degree has a name: tonic, supertonic, mediant, subdominant, dominant, submediant and leading tone. To play a major scale from any note, apply the same pattern. This forces some notes to be sharp or flat, and these are listed in the key signature.
keyPoints: Major scale pattern: W W H W W W H.
Sharps in order: F C G D A E B.
Flats in order: B E A D G C F.
Up a fifth: add one sharp; down a fifth: add one flat.
Relative minor starts on the sixth degree.

outline.title: Minor scales and modes
outline.summary: The natural minor scale follows the step pattern whole, half, whole, whole, half, whole, whole. It sounds darker than major because of its lowered third, sixth and seventh. The harmonic minor raises the seventh degree to make a stronger pull to the tonic. The melodic minor raises the sixth and seventh going up and uses natural minor coming down. A mode is a scale built by starting the major scale on a different degree. The seven modes are Ionian, Dorian, Phrygian, Lydian, Mixolydian, Aeolian and Locrian.
keyPoints: Natural minor: W H W W H W W.
Harmonic minor: raise the 7th.
Modes start on degrees 1 to 7 of the major scale: Ionian Dorian Phrygian Lydian Mixolydian Aeolian Locrian.
Major pentatonic: 1 2 3 5 6.
Minor pentatonic: 1 b3 4 5 b7.

outline.title: Chords: triads
outline.summary: A chord is three or more notes sounded together. The simplest is the triad, made by stacking two thirds on a root: the root, the third and the fifth. The quality depends on the thirds. A major triad is a major third then a minor third, 4 + 3 semitones. A minor triad is 3 + 4. A diminished triad is 3 + 3, and an augmented triad is 4 + 4. Building a triad on each degree of a major scale gives three major, three minor and one diminished triad.
keyPoints: Major triad: 0 4 7. Minor: 0 3 7.
Diminished: 0 3 6. Augmented: 0 4 8.
In a major key: I ii iii IV V vi vii-dim.
Major chords sound bright; minor chords sound sad.
Chord symbols: C, Cm, Cdim, Caug.

outline.title: Seventh chords and inversions
outline.summary: A seventh chord adds a note a third above the fifth. Stack three thirds on a root and you have four notes: root, third, fifth and seventh. The main types are major seventh (0 4 7 11), dominant seventh (0 4 7 10), minor seventh (0 3 7 10) and half-diminished (0 3 6 10). The dominant seventh is the engine of classical and jazz harmony. An inversion puts a note other than the root in the bass. The chord is the same, only the lowest note changes.
keyPoints: V7 is a dominant seventh built on the 5th degree.
Root position, first inversion (6), second inversion (6/4).
A triad has 3 positions; a seventh chord has 4.
C/E means a C chord with E in the bass.

outline.title: Harmony: progressions and cadences
outline.summary: Roman numerals name chords by the scale degree of their root: I, ii, iii, IV, V, vi and vii-dim in a major key. Big numerals are major chords and small ones are minor, so the same pattern works in every key. Chords have jobs. The tonic (I) is home. The subdominant (IV, ii) moves away. The dominant (V, vii-dim) creates tension that wants to return home. Common progressions combine these jobs. A cadence is a chord pair that ends a phrase, like a full stop or a comma. The authentic cadence V to I is a full stop, and the half cadence ending on V is a comma.
keyPoints: I ii iii IV V vi vii-dim.
Tonic: I vi. Subdominant: IV ii. Dominant: V vii.
Authentic cadence V-I, plagal IV-I, half cadence ends on V, deceptive V-vi.
Pop loop: I-V-vi-IV.
Jazz turnaround: ii-V-I.

outline.title: Melody, rhythm and form
outline.summary: A melody is a line of notes that makes sense as a tune. It is built from motifs, short ideas that are repeated, varied and developed into phrases. Rhythm gives melody its shape in time. Syncopation puts stress on weak beats, and a groove repeats a pattern. Form is the large-scale plan. Common forms use letters for sections: AB, ABA, verse and chorus, rondo, theme and variations.
keyPoints: Motif, phrase, period, section.
A period = antecedent (question) + consequent (answer).
Forms: AB, ABA, rondo ABACA, verse-chorus.
Syncopation: accents off the beat.
Counterpoint: independent lines that make good harmony.

outline.title: Transposition, ear training and putting it together
outline.summary: To transpose a piece, shift every note by the same interval. The pattern of intervals, and therefore the tune, is unchanged, only the pitch level moves. Ear training links sounds to names. Learn the intervals from songs, sing scale degrees with solfege (do re mi), and hear chord qualities as colours. Writing a short song uses everything you have learned: pick a key, choose a progression, write a melody that uses chord tones on strong beats, and shape the form.
keyPoints: Transpose: add the same number of semitones to each note.
Solfege: do re mi fa sol la ti do.
Hear intervals through songs.
Strong beats: chord tones; weak beats: passing notes.
A lead sheet = melody + chords.

courses.title: Natural Language Processing
courses.subtitle: From tokens and TF-IDF to n-grams, taggers, embeddings, transformers and large language models, classical and modern, with Python labs
courses.author: Lilith Learning Lab
courses.description: A hands-on course in natural language processing covering classical and modern techniques: tokens, normalisation, stemming and Zipf's law; bag of words, TF-IDF, cosine similarity and edit distance; n-gram language models and perplexity; Naive Bayes text classification and evaluation; part-of-speech tagging with Viterbi, CKY parsing and entity extraction; word embeddings; recurrent networks, LSTMs, sequence-to-sequence models and attention; the transformer, positional encoding and subword tokenisers; BERT, GPT, prompting and sampling; and search with BM25, retrieval-augmented generation, evaluation metrics and responsible NLP. Every chapter has Python labs verified in the built-in interpreter, plus an n-gram text generator and a self-attention explorer.

outline.title: Text as data: tokens, normalisation and patterns
outline.summary: Natural language processing (NLP) lets computers work with human language. Text is first split into tokens (words, pieces of words or characters) and normalised: lower-cased, stripped of punctuation, perhaps reduced to stems or lemmas. Counting words already reveals a lot, and Zipf's law says a few words are extremely common while most are rare. Classical NLP is a pipeline of such steps; modern NLP learns many of them end to end, but tokenisation and data hygiene still matter.
keyPoints: Tokenise, lower-case, remove noise.
Stem is a chopped root; lemma is a real word.
Zipf: frequency is about 1 / rank.
Out-of-vocabulary words are a problem for word-level models.
Subword tokens fix that.

outline.title: Bag of words, TF-IDF and similarity
outline.summary: The bag-of-words model describes a document by how often each word occurs, ignoring order. TF-IDF multiplies term frequency by inverse document frequency, so words that are common everywhere count for little and distinctive words count for a lot. Cosine similarity compares two document vectors by the angle between them, regardless of document length. Ranking documents by similarity to a query is the basis of classic search. Edit distance (Levenshtein) measures how many insertions, deletions and substitutions turn one string into another, useful for spelling correction.
keyPoints: tfidf = tf x log(N / df).
cos = a.b / (|a||b|).
Sparse vectors: store only non-zeros.
Query and documents in the same space.
Edit distance by dynamic programming.

outline.title: N-gram language models
outline.summary: A language model assigns a probability to a sequence of words, or equivalently predicts the next word. An n-gram model assumes that the next word depends only on the previous n-1 words, and estimates probabilities by counting in a corpus. Unseen word pairs would get probability zero, so we smooth: add-one (Laplace) smoothing, or back off to shorter contexts. Quality is measured by perplexity, the model's average surprise on held-out text; lower is better. Language modelling is the idea behind autocomplete, speech recognition and, at a much larger scale, today's large language models.
keyPoints: P(w | prev) = count(prev w) / count(prev).
Add-k: (count + k) / (total + k V).
log P(sentence) = sum of log P(w | prev).
Perplexity = exp(-mean log P).
Larger n: more context, more sparsity.

outline.title: Text classification: Naive Bayes and sentiment
outline.summary: Text classification assigns a label to a document: spam or not, topic, sentiment, language. A strong classical baseline is Naive Bayes, which combines the class prior with the likelihood of each word given the class, assuming words are independent. Logistic regression or linear SVMs on TF-IDF features are usually stronger. Sentiment analysis can also use lexicons of positive and negative words, with care over negation. Evaluate with held-out data and per-class precision, recall and F1, especially when classes are imbalanced.
keyPoints: class = argmax log P(c) + sum log P(w | c).
P(w | c) = (count + 1) / (total + V).
Work in logs to avoid underflow.
Negation flips polarity: 'not good'.
Macro F1 treats classes equally.

outline.title: Linguistic structure: tagging, parsing and entities
outline.summary: Language has structure. Part-of-speech tagging labels each word as noun, verb and so on; context matters, since 'duck' can be either. A hidden Markov model with the Viterbi algorithm finds the most probable tag sequence. A context-free grammar describes how phrases build sentences, and a parser recovers the tree, for example with the CKY algorithm. Dependency parsing links each word to its head. Named entity recognition finds names of people, places and organisations, usually by tagging tokens with B-I-O labels.
keyPoints: Viterbi: best[t][s] = max over p of best[t-1][p] T[p][s] E[s][w].
CKY fills a chart for spans.
BIO tags: B-PER begins, I-PER continues, O outside.
Dependency: each word has one head.
Neural taggers now give the best accuracy.

outline.title: Word embeddings: meaning as geometry
outline.summary: You shall know a word by the company it keeps. Words that appear in similar contexts have similar meanings. Counting co-occurrences and reducing the table to dense vectors gives word embeddings, in which similar words are close together. Word2vec and GloVe learn vectors of a few hundred numbers. Cosine similarity finds neighbours, and directions encode relations: king minus man plus woman lands near queen. Embeddings reflect the text they were trained on, including its social biases, which must be audited.
keyPoints: PMI = log P(w, c) / (P(w) P(c)).
Similar words, similar contexts.
Skip-gram pairs (centre, context) in a window.
king - man + woman is about queen.
Contextual embeddings replaced static ones.

outline.title: Neural sequence models: RNNs, LSTMs and attention
outline.summary: A recurrent neural network reads text one token at a time, updating a hidden state that summarises everything so far. It can predict the next word, tag every word or encode a whole sentence. Plain RNNs forget over long distances because gradients shrink; LSTMs and GRUs add gates that control what to keep. Sequence-to-sequence models use an encoder RNN and a decoder RNN for translation and summarisation. Attention lets the decoder look back at every encoder state and focus on the relevant ones. It removed the bottleneck of squeezing a sentence into one vector and led directly to the transformer.
keyPoints: h_t = tanh(W x_t + U h_{t-1} + b).
LSTM: forget, input and output gates.
Teacher forcing: feed the true previous token in training.
Beam search keeps top-k hypotheses.
Attention weights = softmax(scores).

outline.title: Transformers: self-attention, positions and tokenisers
outline.summary: The transformer replaces recurrence with self-attention: every token compares its query with every token's key and takes a weighted average of their values. All positions are processed in parallel, which makes training fast on GPUs. Because attention ignores order, positional information is added. Several attention heads run in parallel, followed by feed-forward layers, residual connections and layer normalisation, repeated in a stack of blocks. Text enters as subword tokens, built by algorithms such as byte-pair encoding, which merges the most frequent adjacent pairs to make a vocabulary of tens of thousands of pieces.
keyPoints: Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d)) V.
Block = attention + MLP, each with residual and norm.
Causal mask: position i sees positions up to i.
Sinusoidal positions: sin and cos at many frequencies.
BPE: merge most frequent pair, repeat.

outline.title: Pretrained language models: BERT, GPT and beyond
outline.summary: Modern NLP follows pretrain then adapt. A transformer is first trained on huge text with a self-supervised goal, then fine-tuned or prompted for tasks. Encoder models like BERT read the whole text both ways and produce contextual embeddings, suited to classification and tagging. Decoder models like GPT, Llama and Claude generate text left to right, one token at a time. Scaling model size, data and compute improved quality predictably and revealed abilities such as in-context learning, where the model follows examples in its prompt. Large models are further aligned with instruction tuning and human feedback so they follow requests helpfully and safely.
keyPoints: Encoder: BERT, bidirectional, masked LM.
Decoder: GPT, Llama, Claude, causal LM.
Fine-tune with a small labelled set.
Prompt: instructions plus examples.
Temperature, top-k and top-p control sampling.

outline.title: Applications: search, QA, translation and responsible NLP
outline.summary: Search engines use an inverted index to find documents containing query words and rank them with BM25, a refined TF-IDF. Modern systems add embedding-based dense retrieval and neural rerankers. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) retrieves relevant passages and puts them in the prompt of a language model so its answer is grounded in sources. Machine translation, summarisation and question answering are evaluated with overlap metrics such as BLEU and ROUGE, and increasingly by human or model judges. Responsible NLP means checking for hallucination, bias, privacy leaks and misuse, and testing on the people the system will serve.
keyPoints: Inverted index: word -> document ids.
BM25 saturates term frequency.
RAG: retrieve, then generate.
Chunk long documents with overlap.
Check facts, bias and privacy.

courses.title: Operating Systems
courses.subtitle: Theory and practice, with Python labs
courses.author: Lilith Learning Lab
courses.description: A 15-chapter course based on the Tutorialspoint Operating System tutorial: processes, scheduling, threads, memory, virtual memory, I/O, file systems, security and Linux. Each chapter has theory, then Python labs that run on the built-in MicroPython engine. The scheduling data set is the course's own consistent example.

outline.title: Operating system overview
outline.summary: An operating system is a program that sits between the user and the computer hardware. It controls how every other program runs and performs the basic tasks: memory, processor, device and file management, plus security and error handling. Popular examples are Linux, Windows, VMS, OS/400, AIX and z/OS. Each function follows the same pattern: keep track of a resource, decide who gets it and for how long, allocate it, and take it back when it is no longer needed. Once you see that pattern, the rest of the course is variations on it.
keyPoints: The OS is the interface between users and hardware.
Main functions: memory, processor, device and file management, security, performance control, job accounting and error detection.
Memory management tracks what is in use, allocates on request and frees on exit.
Processor management is process scheduling.
Device management works through drivers and an I/O controller.
Every resource follows the same cycle: track, decide, allocate, de-allocate.

outline.title: Types of operating systems
outline.summary: Operating systems have evolved with each computer generation. The tutorial describes five types: batch, time-sharing, distributed, network and real-time systems. In a batch system the user does not interact with the computer. Similar jobs are grouped and run together, so the CPU is often idle waiting for slow mechanical I/O. Time-sharing lets many users share one machine, switching so fast that each gets quick responses. Distributed systems spread work over several loosely coupled processors. Network operating systems run on a server and share files and printers. Real-time systems must respond within fixed time limits, hard or soft.
keyPoints: Batch: no interaction, similar jobs grouped, CPU often idle, hard to set priorities.
Time-sharing minimizes response time. Multiprogrammed batch maximizes processor use.
Distributed systems: several processors, sites can fail independently, resources are shared.
Network OS: runs on a server, centralizes security and shared files and printers.
Real-time: fixed deadlines. Hard guarantees them, soft gives priority.
Real-time examples: industrial control, medical imaging, air traffic control, robots.

outline.title: Operating system services
outline.summary: An operating system provides services both to the programs that run on it and to the users who run them. The tutorial lists seven: program execution, I/O operations, file system manipulation, communication, error detection, resource allocation and protection. Program execution means loading a program, running it, and offering process synchronization, communication and deadlock handling. File services decide which program may read or write which file. Communication between processes uses shared memory or message passing. Errors are detected and handled so computing stays correct. Resources are allocated by schedulers. Protection controls access to resources, authenticating users by passwords.
keyPoints: Seven services: program execution, I/O, file system, communication, error detection, resource allocation, protection.
A process includes the code, data, registers and OS resources in use.
File permissions vary from read-only to read-write to denied.
Communication is by shared memory or message passing.
The OS constantly checks for errors in CPU, I/O devices and memory.
Protection means all access to resources is controlled.

outline.title: Properties of operating systems
outline.summary: This chapter covers the properties an operating system can have: batch processing, multitasking, multiprogramming, interactivity, real-time operation, a distributed environment and spooling. Multiprogramming keeps several jobs in memory so the CPU always has one to run, which raises CPU utilization but requires CPU scheduling and memory management. Multitasking adds rapid switching so users interact with each program while it runs. Spooling, short for simultaneous peripheral operations on line, puts the data of I/O jobs in a buffer so slow devices can catch up while the CPU keeps computing.
keyPoints: Batch: jobs run in submission order; when one finishes its memory is released and output goes to a spool.
Multitasking is time-sharing: each user feels they have their own CPU.
Multiprogramming increases CPU utilization; it needs scheduling and memory management.
Interactivity demands a short response time.
Real-time systems read sensors and must respond in fixed time.
Spooling uses a disk as a very large buffer and overlaps I/O of one job with computation of another.

outline.title: Processes
outline.summary: A process is a program in execution: the basic unit of work in the system. A program is passive code; a process is its dynamic instance. In memory a process has four sections: stack for function parameters, return addresses and local variables, heap for memory allocated at run time, text for the code and current activity, and data for global and static variables. A process passes through five states: start, ready, running, waiting and terminated. The OS tracks each process in a process control block, identified by an integer process ID.
keyPoints: A program is code; a process is a program in execution.
A process has stack, heap, text and data sections.
Five states: start, ready, running, waiting, terminated.
Ready: waiting for the CPU. Running: executing. Waiting: needs a resource such as input or a file.
A PCB holds state, privileges, ID, parent pointer, program counter, registers, scheduling, memory, accounting and I/O information.
The PCB exists for the lifetime of the process and is deleted when it terminates.

outline.title: Process scheduling
outline.summary: Process scheduling is the activity of the process manager that removes the running process from the CPU and selects another by some strategy. It is essential in a multiprogramming system. The OS keeps PCBs in queues: a job queue of all processes, a ready queue of processes in memory waiting for the CPU, and device queues of processes blocked on I/O. A process moves between queues as its state changes. Three schedulers act at different speeds: the long-term job scheduler admits jobs, the short-term CPU scheduler picks the next process to run, and the medium-term scheduler swaps processes out and back in. A context switch saves one process's state in its PCB and loads another's.
keyPoints: A separate queue exists for each process state; a PCB is moved when the state changes.
Job queue: all processes. Ready queue: in memory, waiting for the CPU. Device queues: blocked on I/O.
Long-term: slowest, controls the degree of multiprogramming. Short-term: fastest. Medium-term: swapping.
Time-sharing systems have little or no long-term scheduler.
Swapping removes a suspended process from memory to make room.
Context switches cost time because register and memory state must be saved and restored.

outline.title: Scheduling algorithms
outline.summary: A process scheduler picks processes for the CPU with a scheduling algorithm. The tutorial covers six: first come first served, shortest job next, priority, shortest remaining time, round robin and multiple-level queues. Non-preemptive algorithms let a process run until it finishes its allotted time; preemptive ones may take the CPU away, for example when a higher-priority or shorter job arrives, or when a quantum expires. Shortest job next gives the lowest average waiting time but needs to know run times in advance. First come first served is simple but can make short jobs wait behind long ones. Round robin is fair and responsive but costs context switches.
keyPoints: FCFS: simple, non-preemptive, average wait often high.
SJN: best average wait, non-preemptive, needs known run times, impossible for interactive use.
Priority: highest priority first, ties first come first served, non-preemptive in the tutorial.
SRT: preemptive SJN; a shorter newcomer takes the CPU.
Round robin: preemptive, quantum-based, uses context switches.
Multiple-level queues group processes, for example CPU-bound and I/O-bound, each queue with its own algorithm.

outline.title: Multithreading
outline.summary: A thread is a flow of execution through the process code with its own program counter, registers and stack. Threads of one process share the code segment, data segment and open files, so one thread's change to shared memory is seen by all. Threads are lightweight: cheaper to create and switch than processes, and they let one process do several things at once. The price is that threads can read and write each other's data, so they must coordinate. Threads are implemented at user level, by a library, or at kernel level, by the OS. Models map user threads to kernel threads many-to-one, one-to-one or many-to-many, trading concurrency against cost.
keyPoints: A thread has its own program counter, registers and stack, and shares code, data and open files with its peers.
Each thread belongs to exactly one process.
Thread switching needs less OS interaction than process switching.
User threads: fast to create, but a blocking call can block the whole process and they cannot use multiple processors.
Kernel threads: can run in parallel and one can block without blocking others, but are slower to create.
Many-to-one, one-to-one and many-to-many are the three mapping models.

outline.title: Memory management
outline.summary: Memory management handles primary memory and moves processes between main memory and disk. It tracks every memory location, decides which process gets memory and when, and updates the status when memory is freed. Programs use logical addresses; the memory management unit translates them to physical addresses at run time. Memory can be allocated in single or multiple partitions, which leads to fragmentation: external, when free space is split into unusable pieces, and internal, when a block is larger than needed. Paging splits a process into fixed-size pages loaded into fixed-size frames, avoiding external fragmentation. Segmentation splits a process into variable-size segments that match program modules.
keyPoints: Symbolic addresses become relative at compile time and physical at load time.
Compile-time and load-time binding give identical virtual and physical addresses; execution-time binding does not.
The MMU translates logical to physical addresses at run time.
Static linking combines modules into one program; dynamic linking keeps a reference resolved at run time.
Fragmentation: external (enough space, not contiguous) and internal (block bigger than needed).
Paging: pages and frames same size, page table, offset stays the same. Segmentation: variable-size segments with base and length.

outline.title: Virtual memory
outline.summary: Virtual memory lets a computer address more memory than is physically installed by using disk to emulate RAM. Programs can be larger than physical memory, and each virtual address is translated, which also gives memory protection. It is usually implemented by demand paging: pages are loaded only when referenced. Referencing a page that is not in memory causes a page fault, and the OS brings the page in, possibly replacing another page. A page replacement algorithm decides which page to evict. FIFO evicts the oldest, optimal evicts the one used furthest in the future, LRU evicts the least recently used, and LFU and MFU use counts. Algorithms are compared by their page faults on a reference string.
keyPoints: Virtual memory extends physical memory using disk and provides protection.
Not all of a program is needed at once: error routines, rare features, tables with unused space.
Demand paging loads on reference; a page fault transfers control to the OS.
Quality of a replacement algorithm: less time waiting for page-ins is better.
OPT has the lowest fault rate; LRU is a good practical approximation.
Evaluate with a reference string and count page faults.

outline.title: I/O hardware
outline.summary: One of the OS's jobs is to manage devices. I/O devices are block devices, character devices or network-like devices, and each is attached to the computer through a controller. The CPU talks to a device by memory-mapped I/O, special I/O instructions or direct memory access. Polling keeps the CPU busy checking a status bit; interrupts let the device signal when it is done. With DMA, a controller moves a whole block between the device and memory and interrupts the CPU once, which saves one interrupt per word.
keyPoints: Block devices: fixed blocks, random access. Character devices: streams, no addressing.
Controllers hide device details from the OS.
Polling is simple but wastes CPU time.
Interrupts let the CPU do other work while the device operates.
DMA: one interrupt per block rather than per word.
Memory-mapped I/O avoids special instructions.

outline.title: I/O software
outline.summary: I/O software is organized in layers: interrupt handlers at the bottom, then device drivers, then device-independent OS software, then user-level libraries. Each layer hides details from the one above. Device drivers contain the device-specific code. The device-independent layer gives uniform naming, buffering, error reporting, allocation and protection. Three ideas smooth device speed differences: buffering holds data in memory during a transfer, caching keeps copies in faster memory, and spooling queues jobs for a device like a printer that cannot share.
keyPoints: Layers: user-level, device-independent, driver, interrupt handler, hardware.
Drivers are device specific; the layer above is not.
Uniform interface: all devices look like files.
Buffering deals with speed mismatch and block size mismatch.
Spooling lets many processes share a non-shareable device in turn.
Caching keeps a copy; a buffer may hold the only copy.

outline.title: File system
outline.summary: A file is a named collection of related information on secondary storage. The file system gives users a way to name, organize, store, retrieve and protect files, and maps files onto disk blocks. Files have attributes such as name, type, location, size, protection and time. Directories organize files, and access is sequential or direct. Three ways to allocate disk blocks: contiguous, linked and indexed. Each trades speed, fragmentation and random access differently.
keyPoints: File attributes: name, type, location, size, protection, time and date.
File types: ordinary, directory and special files.
Contiguous: fast direct access, external fragmentation, files hard to grow.
Linked: no external fragmentation, slow direct access, pointers lost if damaged.
Indexed: supports direct access, needs an index block.
Free space can be tracked with a bit map or a linked list.

outline.title: Security
outline.summary: Security means protecting the system's resources from unauthorized access. Operating system security measures include authentication, one-time passwords, and monitoring against program and system threats. Authentication proves the user's identity by something they know, have or are. One-time passwords protect against replay of captured passwords. Threats include trojan horses, trap doors, worms, viruses and denial of service. Defences include least privilege, monitoring, and a trusted computing base, rated in classes from D (minimal) up to A (verified design).
keyPoints: Security covers authentication, one-time passwords, and defence against program and system threats.
Authentication factors: what you know, have or are.
Program threats: trojan horse, trap door, logic bomb, buffer overflow.
System threats: worms, viruses, denial of service.
Computer security classes: D, C1, C2, B1, B2, B3, A.
Least privilege limits damage.

outline.title: Linux
outline.summary: Linux is a popular open source Unix-like operating system whose kernel was written by Linus Torvalds. Its main parts are the kernel, system libraries and system utilities. The kernel runs in kernel mode with full access to hardware; utilities and applications run in user mode. System libraries are standard functions applications use to reach the kernel. Key features are portability, open source, multiuser and multiprogramming support, a hierarchical file system, a shell and security. The architecture has four layers: hardware, kernel, shell and utilities.
keyPoints: Linux has a kernel, system libraries and system utilities.
The kernel runs in kernel mode; applications and utilities run in user mode.
Features: portable, open source, multiuser, multiprogramming, hierarchical file system, shell, security.
Layers: hardware, kernel, shell, utilities.
The shell turns commands into kernel requests.
Everything is a file: devices are files in the file system.

courses.title: PocketBase: A Backend in One File
courses.subtitle: Collections, rules, auth, realtime, files, hooks and production, with Python labs that rebuild the ideas
courses.author: Lilith Learning Lab
courses.description: Learn PocketBase, the open source Go backend with an embedded SQLite database. You will design collections and fields, use the records API and the JavaScript SDK, write API rules and filters, sign users in with passwords, OAuth2 and one-time codes, expand relations, subscribe to realtime events, handle files, extend the server with JavaScript hooks and Go, manage migrations, and run it in production with backups and rate limits. Each chapter has an ELI5 block and Python labs.

outline.title: What PocketBase is
outline.summary: PocketBase is an open source backend in a single file. It is written in Go and uses an embedded SQLite database. One program gives you a database, a REST style API, realtime updates, user accounts, file storage and an admin dashboard. You start it with serve. It is still before version 1.0, so details can change between releases.
keyPoints: PocketBase is open source, written in Go and MIT licensed.
It bundles SQLite, a REST style API, realtime subscriptions, auth, files and a dashboard.
Run it with ./pocketbase serve; the default address is 127.0.0.1:8090.
The dashboard is at /_/ and the API is under /api/.
Folders next to the program: pb_data, pb_public, pb_hooks and pb_migrations.
It is pre-1.0, so read the release notes before upgrading.

outline.title: Collections and fields
outline.summary: A collection is a table of records, and each record has fields. There are three types of collection: base for ordinary data, auth for accounts that can sign in, and view for a read-only result of a SQL query. Every record has an id, created and updated. Fields have types such as text, number, bool, email, url, date, select, file, relation, json and password. The lab checks records against a field list.
keyPoints: Collections are backed by plain SQLite tables.
Base, auth and view are the three collection types.
Every record has id, created and updated.
The default id is a 15 character string of lowercase letters and digits.
Auth collections add email, password, verified and token fields.
View collections never get create, update or delete, and send no realtime events.

outline.title: The records API
outline.summary: Every collection gets a REST style API automatically. You list, view, create, update and delete records under /api/collections/NAME/records. A list call returns a page: page, perPage, totalItems, totalPages and items. You can pass sort, filter, expand and fields to shape the result. The labs compute page counts and parse sort strings.
keyPoints: List is GET /api/collections/NAME/records; view adds /ID.
Create is POST, update is PATCH, delete is DELETE.
A page response has page, perPage, totalItems, totalPages and items.
sort=-created,title sorts newest first, then by title.
filter takes an expression like title ~ 'abc' && created > '2022-01-01'.
Which records you may touch depends on the collection's API rules.

outline.title: The JavaScript SDK
outline.summary: The official JavaScript SDK works in browsers, Node.js and React Native. You create a client with new PocketBase(url) and then work through pb.collection(name). The common calls are getList, getFullList, getOne, getFirstListItem, create, update and delete. Never paste user input into a filter string. Use pb.filter with placeholders so values are escaped.
keyPoints: Install with npm install pocketbase, or import it as an ES module in a browser.
pb.collection('posts').getList(1, 20, { filter, sort, expand }) returns one page.
getFullList loops through pages for you, so use it only for small collections.
getFirstListItem fetches one record and errors if none matches.
pb.filter('title = {:t}', { t }) escapes and binds values.
The authStore saves the token and updates after sign-in.

outline.title: API rules: who can do what
outline.summary: API rules are access control and a record filter at once. Each collection has five: listRule, viewRule, createRule, updateRule and deleteRule. Auth collections also have a manage rule. A rule can be null, which locks the action to superusers, an empty string, which lets anyone in, or an expression that must be true. Superusers always bypass rules. The labs check rule outcomes and run a small rule evaluator.
keyPoints: null means locked, an empty string means open, and an expression means conditional.
A failed list rule returns an empty list with status 200; a failed create rule returns 400.
A failed view, update or delete rule returns 404; a locked rule for a non-superuser returns 403.
@request.auth.id != "" means a signed-in user.
@request.body.role:isset = false blocks sending a role field.
Rules also act as filters: a list rule of status = 'active' returns only active records.

outline.title: Authentication
outline.summary: Any auth collection can sign users in. The classic way is a password: the server checks it and returns a signed token, a JWT, plus the record. The client sends the token in the Authorization header on later requests. The SDK keeps it in the authStore. PocketBase also supports OAuth2 providers, one-time passwords by email, and multi-factor authentication. Superusers sign in the same way, but cannot use OAuth2.
keyPoints: pb.collection('users').authWithPassword(email, password) returns the token and record.
A JWT has header, payload and signature, joined by dots; the payload carries the id and the expiry.
The token goes in the Authorization header.
OAuth2 uses the redirect address /api/oauth2-redirect; _superusers do not support OAuth2.
requestOTP returns an otpId, even if the email is unknown, so attackers cannot probe for accounts.
Record creation does not sign the user in; you sign in after creating.

outline.title: Relations, expand and view collections
outline.summary: A relation field stores the id of a record in another collection, or several ids for a multiple relation. Rules can follow relations too, for example author.verified = true. The expand option loads the related records in the same response, under record.expand. Nested paths like author.team work too, and a back-relation can be expanded in the other direction. The labs join records and find back-relations.
keyPoints: A relation stores ids, so a plain read shows only an id like author: 'abc123'.
expand: 'author' adds record.expand.author with the full record.
Nested paths use dots: expand: 'author.team'.
Related records you may not view are left out of expand, because their view rule applies.
A back-relation expand uses the form COLLECTION_via_FIELD.
cascadeDelete true removes dependent records; false blocks deleting the parent.

outline.title: Realtime subscriptions
outline.summary: Realtime uses Server-Sent Events, a one-way stream from server to browser. The client opens a connection, the server answers with a client id, and then the client says what it wants to follow. You subscribe to a whole collection with the star topic or to one record by id. Each event says whether a record was created, updated or deleted. The same rules apply: you only receive events for records you may view.
keyPoints: The realtime API is SSE with two steps: connect, then submit subscriptions.
SSE events are sent for create, update and delete.
pb.collection('posts').subscribe('*', cb) follows the collection; subscribe(id, cb) follows one record.
Events respect the list and view rules, and a subscribe can take filter and fields options.
View collections send no realtime events.
The SDK reconnects by itself and resubscribes.

outline.title: Files and storage
outline.summary: A file field stores uploads in the record. You send them as multipart form data, and PocketBase saves them on disk under pb_data, or in an S3 compatible store if you configure one. Each file is served at /api/files/COLLECTION/RECORD/FILENAME. For images you can ask for a thumbnail with the thumb query parameter. A protected file needs a short-lived file token and obeys the view rule.
keyPoints: File fields set maxSelect, maxSize and allowed MIME types.
The record keeps the file name; the file lives under pb_data/storage/COLLECTION_ID/RECORD_ID/.
PocketBase adds a random suffix to uploaded names so they do not collide.
The URL is /api/files/COLLECTION/RECORD_ID/FILENAME, and ?thumb=100x100 returns a thumbnail.
Thumb sizes must be listed in the field options.
Protected files are fetched with ?token= from a file token request.

outline.title: Extending with JavaScript
outline.summary: The prebuilt PocketBase runs JavaScript files that end in .pb.js from the pb_hooks folder. With them you add routes, react to events, and schedule jobs, without compiling anything. An event hook is a function that receives an event e. Code before e.next runs before the action, code after it runs after. Not calling e.next, or throwing, stops the chain. The engine is goja, a JavaScript interpreter written in Go, so it supports ES5 and a good part of newer syntax, but no ES modules.
keyPoints: Put hooks in pb_hooks/*.pb.js next to the executable.
routerAdd('GET', '/hello/{name}', (e) => e.json(200, {...})) adds a route.
onRecordCreate runs before the insert; onRecordAfterCreateSuccess runs after it commits.
A hook must call e.next() to continue; throwing an error stops the chain.
You can add collection names after the handler to run it only for those collections.
cronAdd('name', '*/30 * * * *', fn) runs a job on a five field cron schedule.

outline.title: Go framework, migrations and the CLI
outline.summary: Instead of the prebuilt program you can import PocketBase into your own Go program. You call pocketbase.New, register routes and hooks, and build one static executable. Schema changes are stored as migration files in pb_migrations, named with a timestamp. When you change collections in the dashboard in development, PocketBase writes a migration for you. Everyday commands are serve, superuser create, migrate and update.
keyPoints: Create main.go with pocketbase.New() and register routes inside app.OnServe().
Build a static executable with CGO_ENABLED=0 go build, then run ./myapp serve.
Migration files live in pb_migrations and are named TIMESTAMP_description.js (or .go).
Applied migrations are recorded in the database so each runs once.
./pocketbase superuser create EMAIL PASSWORD makes an admin.
./pocketbase update updates the prebuilt executable.

outline.title: Going to production
outline.summary: Running PocketBase for real takes a few steps. Put it on a small server with a persistent pb_data folder, serve it over HTTPS, back it up, and turn on rate limiting. Built-in backups make a ZIP snapshot of pb_data and can run on a cron schedule, keeping the newest few. For a very large pb_data, use a different strategy such as an SQLite backup copy. The labs rotate backups and simulate a rate limiter.
keyPoints: Persist the pb_data folder; in Docker mount it as a volume.
serve with a domain name can handle HTTPS with an automatic Let's Encrypt certificate, or put Nginx or Caddy in front.
Backups are ZIP snapshots of pb_data and can be scheduled by cron, with cronMaxKeep controlling how many remain.
Large data folders, about 2 GB or more, need a different backup plan.
The built-in rate limiter takes rules with a label, max requests and duration.
--encryptionEnv=NAME encrypts the settings with a key from an environment variable; never lose that key.

outline.title: Designing an app and knowing the limits
outline.summary: A good PocketBase app is mostly collections and rules. Take a notes app: a notes collection with an owner relation to users, and rules that let each person see and change only their own notes. PocketBase fits small and medium apps, prototypes, internal tools and mobile backends well. It is less suited to apps that need many servers writing at once. The last labs audit rules and tie the course together.
keyPoints: Start with all rules locked and open each action as narrowly as possible.
Ownership pattern: author = @request.auth.id for list, view, update and delete.
Create rule: @request.auth.id != "" && @request.body.author = @request.auth.id.
Block ownership changes with @request.body.author:changed = false.
SQLite handles many readers and one writer at a time; scale up one server first.
Before upgrading, read the release notes and test a copy of pb_data.

courses.title: Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO)
courses.subtitle: Policy gradients, GAE, clipping and RLHF, with Python labs
courses.author: Lilith Learning Lab
courses.description: PPO (Schulman et al., 2017) built piece by piece: policy gradient recap, advantages and GAE, the probability ratio and trust regions, the clipped surrogate objective, the full loss, the training loop and its practical details, PPO for language models (background), and diagnostics. Theory plus Python labs.

outline.title: From policy gradients to PPO
outline.summary: Proximal Policy Optimization, PPO, is a reinforcement learning algorithm from John Schulman and colleagues at OpenAI, 2017. It improves a policy by gradient ascent, but with a trick that stops each update from changing the policy too much. Plain policy gradient methods can ruin a policy with one oversized step. TRPO prevented this with a constraint but was complicated. PPO gets much of the benefit with a simple clipped objective that works with ordinary first-order optimizers. This course builds PPO piece by piece in small Python labs: returns, advantages, the ratio, clipping, the loss, the update loop and its use for language models.
keyPoints: PPO: Schulman, Wolski, Dhariwal, Radford and Klimov, 2017.
It keeps the new policy close to the old one by clipping the probability ratio.
It is simpler than TRPO: no second-order optimisation, no explicit constraint.
It reuses each batch for several epochs of minibatch updates.
It is on-policy: after updating, fresh data is collected.
It became a default choice for many RL problems and for RLHF fine-tuning of language models (background knowledge).

outline.title: Policy gradient recap
outline.summary: A policy gradient step increases the log-probability of actions in proportion to how good they turned out to be. The measure of goodness is the return, or better, the return minus a baseline. For a softmax policy over discrete actions the gradient of the log-probability with respect to the logits has a simple form: the one-hot vector of the chosen action minus the probability vector. The labs compute discounted returns, the softmax, the log-probability gradient and a policy gradient update on a small bandit.
keyPoints: G_t = r_t + gamma r_{t+1} + gamma^2 r_{t+2} + ...
Policy gradient: grad J = E[ grad log pi(a|s) * (G - b) ].
For a softmax policy: d log pi(a) / d theta = onehot(a) - pi.
A baseline that depends only on the state leaves the gradient unbiased.
A learned value function V(s) is the usual baseline.
Common gamma in practice: 0.99.

outline.title: Advantages and generalized advantage estimation
outline.summary: The advantage of an action is how much better it is than the policy's average action in that state: A(s, a) = Q(s, a) - V(s). Weighting the policy gradient by the advantage is the standard way to reduce variance. Generalized advantage estimation, GAE, by Schulman and colleagues in 2015, builds advantage estimates from a learned value function. A parameter lambda interpolates between a low-variance, biased one-step estimate and a high-variance, unbiased Monte Carlo estimate. PPO typically uses GAE, with gamma of 0.99 and lambda of 0.95 as common defaults.
keyPoints: delta_t = r_t + gamma V(s_{t+1}) - V(s_t).
GAE: A_t = delta_t + gamma lambda A_{t+1}.
lambda = 0 gives the one-step estimate (low variance, more bias).
lambda = 1 gives return minus value (higher variance, low bias).
Common defaults: gamma 0.99, lambda 0.95 (practice, not the only choice).
Normalising advantages per minibatch is common in implementations.

outline.title: Trust regions, KL divergence and the ratio
outline.summary: The data comes from the old policy, but we want to evaluate a new one. The probability ratio r = pi_new(a|s) / pi_old(a|s) corrects for this: it is importance sampling. The surrogate objective weights each advantage by r. The surrogate is a good approximation only near the old policy. TRPO keeps the policy there by bounding the average KL divergence between old and new. PPO will keep the ratio near one instead. The labs compute ratios from log-probabilities, KL divergence for categorical policies and a KL-penalised surrogate.
keyPoints: r = exp(log pi_new - log pi_old).
Surrogate: L(theta) = E[ r * A ]. At theta = theta_old, r = 1.
KL(p || q) = sum p log(p / q), zero only when p = q.
TRPO: maximise the surrogate subject to mean KL <= delta.
PPO-penalty variant: maximise L - beta * KL, adapting beta.
PPO-clip: remove the incentive to push r outside [1 - eps, 1 + eps].

outline.title: The clipped surrogate objective
outline.summary: The PPO objective is L = E[ min( r A, clip(r, 1 - eps, 1 + eps) A ) ]. The clip cuts the ratio to the band from 1 - eps to 1 + eps, where eps is about 0.2. The min then picks the more pessimistic of the clipped and unclipped terms. If an action had positive advantage, increasing its probability helps only until the ratio reaches 1 + eps; beyond that the gradient is zero. If the advantage is negative, decreasing helps only until 1 - eps. This removes the incentive for large policy changes without a hard constraint. The labs compute the objective and its gradient in each region.
keyPoints: L_clip = min(r A, clip(r, 1 - eps, 1 + eps) A).
A > 0: gradient is zero once r > 1 + eps.
A < 0: gradient is zero once r < 1 - eps.
Otherwise the gradient is that of r A: r * A with respect to log pi.
The min makes the objective a lower bound on the unclipped surrogate.
eps = 0.2 was a good value in the paper's experiments (the paper compared several).

outline.title: The full loss: value, entropy and the update
outline.summary: When the policy and value function share a network, PPO combines three terms: the clipped policy objective, a value function loss and an entropy bonus. L = L_clip - c1 L_value + c2 Entropy, maximised (or its negative minimised). The value loss is the squared error between the predicted value and the target return. The entropy bonus rewards a spread-out policy, which prevents it from becoming deterministic too early. Common defaults for the coefficients are c1 = 0.5 and c2 = 0.01; these are conventions in popular implementations, not requirements.
keyPoints: L = L_clip - c1 * L_value + c2 * H, maximised; minimise the negative.
L_value = (V(s) - R)^2 (sometimes clipped).
Entropy of a discrete policy: -sum p log p.
Typical coefficients: c1 about 0.5 and c2 about 0.01 (implementation defaults).
Without the entropy term the policy may collapse to a single action early.
The PPO paper presents this combined objective for shared architectures.

outline.title: The PPO algorithm and its practical details
outline.summary: The algorithm runs in rounds. Actors run the current policy for T steps and record states, actions, rewards, values and old log-probabilities. Advantages are computed. Then the batch is shuffled and split into minibatches, and for K epochs we take a gradient step on the combined loss for each minibatch. Implementations add practical touches: gradient norm clipping, learning rate annealing, advantage normalisation, observation normalisation and sometimes an early stop when the measured KL grows too large. Many of these are conventions found in popular code, which studies have shown can matter as much as the clip itself. The labs implement minibatch splitting, gradient clipping, learning rate annealing and the early-stop test.
keyPoints: Collect T steps from N parallel actors; batch size = N * T.
Run K epochs of minibatch gradient steps on that batch.
Compute advantages once, with the old value estimates.
Clip the global gradient norm (0.5 is a common value).
Anneal the learning rate linearly to zero (a common choice).
Results vary a lot between random seeds; report several.

outline.title: PPO for language models (RLHF)
outline.summary: Reinforcement learning from human feedback, RLHF, fine-tunes a language model with PPO. A reward model trained on human preferences scores whole responses. The language model is the policy, each token is an action, and the response is the episode. This chapter is background knowledge: it goes beyond the 2017 PPO paper. To stop the model drifting into gibberish that fools the reward model, the reward includes a penalty on the KL divergence between the tuned model and a frozen reference model. Often a value head is added to the language model to supply advantages. The labs compute a KL-penalised token reward and the per-token advantages.
keyPoints: Policy = language model; state = prompt plus tokens so far; action = next token.
Reward model gives a score at the end of the response.
Per-token KL penalty: -beta * (log pi(token) - log pi_ref(token)).
A value head predicts expected final reward for advantages (GAE).
PPO-clip stabilises the updates.
Alternatives skip the RL step: DPO trains directly on preferences (see the DPO course).

outline.title: Diagnostics, pitfalls and relatives
outline.summary: Training curves lie. To understand a PPO run, watch several diagnostics: the approximate KL, the clip fraction, the entropy, the explained variance of the value function and the return itself. A healthy run shows small KL and moderate clip fraction, entropy that falls slowly and a value function that explains much of the return. Common failure modes: entropy collapse, value function that lags, learning rate too high, advantage scale wrong, reward hacking. Many fixes are simple once the right plot is on screen. PPO has relatives: A2C, TRPO, off-policy methods such as SAC, and for language models GRPO and DPO. The labs compute the diagnostics.
keyPoints: Watch: approximate KL, clip fraction, entropy, explained variance, episode return.
Explained variance near 1 is good; near 0 or negative means a poor critic.
A clip fraction near 0 suggests tiny updates; near 1 suggests too large.
Entropy collapse: raise c2, check advantage scale, lower the learning rate.
Reward hacking: inspect behaviour, not just the reward number.
PPO is on-policy and sample-hungry; off-policy methods can be more data-efficient.

courses.title: Python Tutorial: From First Line to Small Projects
courses.subtitle: Learn Python by doing: values, loops, lists, functions, classes and more, with a lab in every chapter
courses.author: Lilith Learning Lab
