courses.description: A hands-on Python tutorial for beginners. You will learn variables and types, numbers and strings, decisions, loops, lists and tuples, dictionaries and sets, functions, comprehensions, errors, classes, modules and generators, then combine them in small projects. Every chapter has a short ELI5 block, a quiz and Python labs that run on the built-in interpreter, so you can practise without installing anything.

outline.title: Hello, Python
outline.summary: Python is a language for giving a computer instructions. You write lines, and the interpreter runs them top to bottom. A variable is a name for a value. The equals sign puts a value into a name. Every value has a type, such as int, float, str or bool.
keyPoints: Lines run from top to bottom.
name = value creates or changes a variable.
print(a, b) shows values separated by spaces.
type(x) tells you the type.
Names use letters, digits and underscores, and cannot start with a digit.
A # starts a comment.

outline.title: Numbers and strings
outline.summary: Python does arithmetic with + - * / and more: // for whole division, % for the remainder and ** for powers. A string is text. You can join strings, repeat them, pick characters by index and cut pieces with slices. Strings have methods such as upper, split, replace and strip.
keyPoints: Dividing with / always gives a float.
s[0] is the first character; s[-1] is the last.
s[1:4] gives characters 1, 2 and 3.
Strings never change; methods return new strings.
round(x, 2) rounds to 2 decimals.

outline.title: Making decisions
outline.summary: An if statement runs a block of code only when a condition is True. Add elif and else for other cases. Conditions come from comparisons like == != < > <= >=, joined with and, or and not. Indentation, four spaces, shows which lines belong to the block.
keyPoints: == compares; = assigns.
Python checks if, then each elif, then else, and runs the first match only.
and needs both True; or needs one; not flips.
Chained comparisons work: 0 < x < 10.
Empty values are falsy.
Indent with four spaces and stay consistent.

outline.title: Loops
outline.summary: A for loop repeats code for each item in a sequence. A while loop repeats as long as a condition is True. range(n) gives the numbers 0 to n minus 1. break leaves a loop early and continue skips to the next round. A common pattern is an accumulator: start with an empty total, then add to it in each round.
keyPoints: for x in items: runs once per item.
while cond: repeats; make sure something changes.
break exits; continue jumps to the next round.
enumerate(items) gives index and item.
Loops can sit inside loops.

outline.title: Lists and tuples
outline.summary: A list holds items in order and can change. Square brackets make one, and you reach items by index. Lists have methods: append, pop, insert, remove, sort and more. Slices copy parts. A tuple is like a list that cannot change. Use it for small fixed groups, like a point.
keyPoints: items = [3, 1, 2]; items[0] is 3.
append adds, pop removes the last, insert and remove work by place and value.
sorted(items) returns a new list; items.sort() changes in place.
len, sum, min and max work on lists.
b = a makes an alias; b = a[:] or list(a) makes a copy.
Tuples: (1, 2); unpack with x, y = point.

outline.title: Dictionaries and sets
outline.summary: A dictionary stores pairs: a key and its value. You look things up by key, and lookups are fast. Methods such as get, items, keys and values help you read a dict. Keys must be unchangeable, like text, numbers or tuples. A set holds unique items and supports union, intersection and difference.
keyPoints: d.get('z', 0) gives 0 if missing; d['z'] would raise KeyError.
for k, v in d.items() visits each pair.
'a' in d tests for a key.
Sets: {1, 2}; set(list) removes duplicates.
a | b union, a & b intersection, a - b difference.

outline.title: Functions
outline.summary: A function is a named block of code you can run again and again. def starts it, and return sends a value back. Parameters are names for the inputs. Default values make some inputs optional. Names made inside a function are local to it. A function can call itself, which is called recursion.
keyPoints: def name(params): then an indented body.
A function without return gives back None.
def f(x, y=10): y is optional.
Call with names: f(1, y=2).
Variables made inside are local.
A recursive function needs a base case that stops it.

outline.title: Comprehensions and functional tools
outline.summary: A list comprehension builds a list in one line: [x * 2 for x in nums if x > 0]. It reads like a sentence. lambda makes a tiny unnamed function. sorted, min and max accept a key function. zip pairs up sequences, and any and all test whole lists.
keyPoints: [expr for x in items if cond] makes a list.
{k: v for ...} makes a dict; {x for ...} makes a set.
lambda x: x * 2 is a function.
sorted(items, key=len) sorts by length.
zip(a, b) pairs items by position.
any(...) and all(...) test conditions.

outline.title: Errors and exceptions
outline.summary: When something goes wrong Python raises an exception. If nothing handles it, the program stops and prints a traceback. try and except let you handle an error and carry on. raise lets your own code signal a problem. Catch the specific error you expect, not everything.
keyPoints: Common errors: ValueError, TypeError, KeyError, IndexError, ZeroDivisionError.
try: ... except ValueError: ... handles one kind.
except Exception as e: gives you the error object.
raise ValueError('message') makes your own.
finally runs whether or not an error happened.
Read tracebacks from the bottom up.

outline.title: Classes and objects
outline.summary: A class is a blueprint, and an object is one thing built from it. Objects bundle data (attributes) and behaviour (methods). The __init__ method sets up a new object. Every method takes self, the object it works on. A class can inherit from another to reuse and change its behaviour.
keyPoints: class Name: starts a class.
def __init__(self, ...): runs when you create an object.
self.x = x stores an attribute.
obj.method() calls a method.
class Dog(Animal): inherits from Animal.
Methods can be overridden in the child class.

outline.title: Modules, iterators and generators
outline.summary: A module is a file of Python code you load with import. Python ships with a large standard library: math, random, json, datetime and more. An iterator hands out items one at a time. A generator is a function that uses yield to make one. Generators are lazy: they make each value only when asked, so they can be very long, even endless.
keyPoints: import math; math.sqrt(16) is 4.0.
from math import pi imports one name.
json.dumps and json.loads turn data to text and back.
A for loop works on anything iterable.
yield pauses a function and gives a value.
next(gen) asks a generator for its next value.

outline.title: Putting it together
outline.summary: Real programs split a problem into small functions, test each one, and combine them. Test normal inputs and edge cases such as empty input, one item or negative numbers. When something fails, print values or use a debugger to find out why. You now know enough Python to build small tools, and to keep learning from documentation.
keyPoints: Start with the smallest working version.
Write a function for each idea.
Test with simple, edge and large inputs.
Print or log values to see what the code does.
Read error messages carefully.
Improve names and remove repetition only after it works.

courses.title: Quantum Computing for Beginners
courses.subtitle: Qubits, gates, the Bloch sphere, interference and entanglement with hands-on circuit labs, for curious kids, teens and adults
courses.author: Lilith Learning Lab
courses.description: A friendly first course on quantum computing with no maths beyond squares and multiplication. Learn bits and qubits, amplitudes and measurement, the X, H, Z and T gates, interference, circuit text, CNOT, entanglement and Bell states, Deutsch and Grover's algorithms, noise and shots, and what quantum computers are really good for. Every chapter has a hands-on lab built on our own Quantum Web Lab (github.com/lucky-edgelord/quantum-web-lab): a mobile-friendly circuit composer with live chances, Inspect view, a friendly console, ASCII and Q text notation, MicroQiskit (a tiny Qiskit that runs offline) and micro OpenQASM. A few short Python labs build the maths in code. The circuit text notation is inspired by Q.js by Stewart Smith (github.com/stewdio/q.js, MIT) and the layout by the IBM Quantum Composer. Includes an intuitive intro to quantum mechanics, an interactive Bloch sphere chapter, a Qiskit chapter and an OpenQASM chapter.

outline.title: Quantum mechanics in plain words
outline.summary: Everything is made of tiny things, and tiny things do not behave like baseballs. Quantum mechanics is the rulebook for the small world of atoms, electrons and light. Three ideas carry the whole subject. Things come in packets. Before you look, a thing can be a blend of possibilities. And looking changes what you get. You do not need to believe it blindly. You will test it with a simulated experiment about light and sunglasses, which gives a surprise that normal thinking cannot explain.
keyPoints: Energy and light come in packets, called quanta.
Tiny things act like waves that can add or cancel.
Before you look, a thing can be a blend of possibilities.
Looking changes the result.
A photon's polarization is the easiest real qubit.

outline.title: Bits, chance and why quantum is different
outline.summary: A normal computer stores everything as bits. A bit is a tiny switch that is either 0 or 1. Photos, games and messages are all long rows of switches. A quantum computer uses qubits. A qubit can be 0, 1, or a special mix of both until you look at it. Looking at it is called measuring, and it always gives a plain 0 or 1. This is not magic and it is not faster at everything. It is a different way to compute, and for a few jobs it can be much faster. This course teaches the real ideas, and you will play with a real simulator all the way.
keyPoints: A bit is 0 or 1. A qubit can be a mix of both.
n bits hold one value. n qubits need 2 to the power n numbers to describe.
Measuring always gives a plain 0 or 1.
Quantum computers help with some jobs, not everything.
We use our own Quantum Web Lab, which runs right here.

outline.title: The qubit: states, amplitudes and measurement
outline.summary: A qubit state has two numbers called amplitudes, one for 0 and one for 1. Write the state as (a, b). The state |0> is (1, 0) and |1> is (0, 1). The chance of seeing 0 is a squared, and the chance of seeing 1 is b squared. This is the Born rule. The chances must add to 1, so the state is always scaled to fit. Measuring makes the qubit pick one answer using those chances, and afterwards it stays as that answer. The blend is gone. That is why you measure at the end of a circuit.
keyPoints: State (a, b): amplitude a for 0, b for 1.
Chance of 0 is a squared. Chance of 1 is b squared.
Chances add up to exactly 1.
Measuring picks one and the blend is gone.
Amplitudes can be negative. Chances never are.

outline.title: One-qubit gates: X, H, Z and T
outline.summary: A gate is a tiny step that changes a qubit. You build a quantum program by lining gates up on a wire, like beads on a string. Time moves left to right. X flips 0 and 1, like a NOT. H, the Hadamard, turns a plain 0 into a fair blend. Z flips the sign of the 1 amplitude, which you cannot see directly. T is a smaller sign turn, a quarter of a half-turn. Every gate can be undone, because it is reversible. Doing X twice is a no-op, and doing H twice gets you back where you started. That is one big difference from normal logic gates.
keyPoints: X swaps the two amplitudes.
Z negates the 1 amplitude. T turns the phase by a quarter step.
H twice is the same as nothing.
Gates are reversible, unlike measuring.

outline.title: Interference: the real power
outline.summary: Amplitudes are like waves. Two waves that line up make a bigger wave. Two waves that are opposite cancel out to nothing. Quantum computers use exactly this. When two paths lead to the same answer, you add their amplitudes first, and then square. Same sign gives a bigger chance, called constructive interference. Opposite signs cancel, called destructive. That is the whole trick behind quantum speedups: use phases so that wrong answers cancel and the right answer grows. A coin cannot do this, because ordinary chances only add.
keyPoints: Add amplitudes, then square.
Same sign grows. Opposite sign cancels.
H, then Z, then H turns 0 into 1.
H, then T, then H gives an in-between chance.
Quantum speedups come from steering interference.

outline.title: The Bloch sphere: a globe for one qubit
outline.summary: A single qubit can always be drawn as an arrow from the centre of a ball to its surface. This ball is called the Bloch sphere. It turns the two hidden numbers of a qubit into a picture you can hold in your head. The north pole is a plain 0 and the south pole is a plain 1. The equator holds the fair blends. How far east you are on the globe is the phase. Every gate is just a turn of the globe. The sphere only works for one qubit at a time. When a qubit is entangled, its arrow shrinks and sits inside the ball, and that shrinking is a way to see entanglement.
keyPoints: The north pole is 0 and the south pole is 1.
Height on the sphere sets the chance: chance of 1 = (1 minus z) / 2.
Longitude (turning around the vertical axis) is the phase.
X, Y and Z are half turns about the x, y and z axes.
H is a half turn about the line between x and z.
S and T are quarter and eighth turns about the vertical axis.
An entangled qubit has a shorter arrow, inside the ball.

outline.title: Reading circuits and the text syntax
outline.summary: A quantum circuit is a grid. Each row is one qubit and each column is one moment in time. A gate sits where a row and a column meet. An empty spot is the identity, written I, which does nothing. The Q text notation, borrowed from Q.js, writes a circuit as plain text. Gates in a row are joined with a dash, and rows are on separate lines. So H-X-I on one line means H, then X, then nothing. To link two qubits you tag gates with #. X#0 is the control and X#1 is its target, together a CNOT. Typing circuits as text is quick and easy to share.
keyPoints: Rows are qubits. Columns are moments.
I is a gate that does nothing.
Separate gates in a row with a dash.
X#0 and X#1 in one column form a CNOT.
The Q Console builds circuits with commands such as h 0.

outline.title: Two qubits: tensor products and CNOT
outline.summary: Two qubits have four possible answers: 00, 01, 10 and 11. So a two qubit state is four amplitudes. In our composer the left bit is qubit 0, the top wire. If the qubits are separate, you can build the four amplitudes by multiplying: the tensor product. A, B gives a0 b0, a0 b1, a1 b0 and a1 b1. A state you can build this way is called a product state. The CNOT gate links two qubits. If the control is 1, it flips the target. If the control is 0, nothing happens. With H plus CNOT you can make states that are not product states.
keyPoints: Two qubits have 4 amplitudes, one per answer.
Tensor product: multiply the amplitudes.
CNOT swaps the amplitudes of 10 and 11.
A state is a product if a0*d equals b*c for amplitudes a, b, c, d.
Not every two qubit state is a product.

outline.title: Entanglement and Bell states
outline.summary: Entanglement is when qubits are linked so tightly that you cannot describe one without the others. The famous recipe: put H on qubit 0, then a CNOT from 0 to 1. The result is the Bell state. It is half 00 and half 11. Measure it and you get 00 or 11, each 50 percent of the time, never 01 or 10. Each qubit alone is a fair coin, but the two coins always agree. Entanglement does not send messages faster than light. The results look random to each side. You only see the link when you compare them afterwards.
keyPoints: H on qubit 0, then CNOT 0 to 1, makes a Bell state.
Bell outcomes: 00 or 11, 50 percent each.
Each qubit alone looks like a fair coin.
The two coins always agree.
No message is sent: the results are random until compared.

outline.title: Small algorithms: Deutsch and Grover
outline.summary: An oracle is a black box that hides a secret function. Deutsch's problem: is the hidden rule constant (same answer for both inputs) or balanced (different answers)? A normal computer must ask twice. A quantum circuit can ask once. Grover's search finds a marked item in an unsorted list of N items. A normal computer needs about N over 2 tries on average. Grover needs about the square root of N steps. For a million items that is about a thousand steps instead of half a million. Both use the interference you learned: the oracle marks the answer with a phase, and the other gates make wrong answers cancel and the right one grow.
keyPoints: Deutsch: one oracle query tells constant from balanced.
Grover: about the square root of N steps for N items.
Both mark answers with a phase and interfere.
Grover's speedup is quadratic, not magic.
You can build 2 qubit Grover in the lab.

outline.title: Noise, shots and real hardware
outline.summary: Real quantum chips are fragile. Heat, vibration and stray signals disturb qubits and make mistakes. This is noise, and the loss of the quantum blend is called decoherence. Many chips work near absolute zero. Because one measurement gives one random answer, you run the circuit many times. Each run is a shot. A hundred shots show you the chances roughly, a thousand show more. The error shrinks with the square root of the shots. A normal computer can simulate a quantum one, but it needs 2 to the n numbers. Around 30 qubits fills a normal PC and around 50 fills a supercomputer. That is exactly why real hardware is interesting.
keyPoints: A shot is one run and one measurement.
Estimates improve with the square root of the shots.
Noise and decoherence cause errors.
Error correction needs many extra qubits.
Simulating n qubits needs 2^n numbers.

outline.title: OpenQASM: the shared language of circuits
outline.summary: OpenQASM stands for Open Quantum Assembly Language. It writes a circuit as plain lines of text, one gate per line. IBM Quantum Composer, Qiskit and many other tools can read and write it. A program has a header, a place to declare qubits, a list of gates and a measurement. Every line ends with a semicolon. Comments start with two slashes. Version 3 is the modern one and the composer shows it. Older files use version 2, with slightly different words, and you can convert them by hand.
keyPoints: Start with OPENQASM 3.0; and include stdgates.inc.
qubit[2] q; makes two qubits. bit[2] c; makes two result bits.
h q[0]; is an H on the first qubit. cx q[0], q[1]; is a CNOT.
c = measure q; reads all qubits into bits.
Version 2 used qreg, creg and measure q -> c.

outline.title: Qiskit: real quantum code in Python
outline.summary: You have seen a circuit as a picture, as Q text and as OpenQASM. Now meet Qiskit, an open source Python toolkit from IBM that people use to write real quantum programs. The Python tab in our lab shows the same circuit in Qiskit style. In Qiskit you make a QuantumCircuit and call methods like h, x and cx. A Statevector gives you the exact chances, and a Sampler runs shots on a simulator or a real chip. Watch one trap: Qiskit counts qubits from 0 and prints qubit 0 on the right, while our composer reads q[0] at the top and writes it on the left.
keyPoints: qc = QuantumCircuit(2) makes 2 qubits.
qc.h(0) is an H on qubit 0. qc.cx(0, 1) is a CNOT.
Statevector(qc).probabilities_dict() gives exact chances.
Qiskit prints qubit 0 on the right.
OpenQASM 3 is the shared text format.

outline.title: Uses, myths and where to go next
outline.summary: Quantum computers are expected to help with a few kinds of problems: simulating molecules and materials, searching, and breaking some codes. Shor's algorithm can factor large numbers much faster than known normal methods. That is why people are building new codes that resist quantum attacks. Everyday tasks like browsing, email, games and spreadsheets will not get faster. Quantum computers are co-processors for special jobs. To keep going: play with the Quantum Web Lab, try IBM Quantum and other free cloud services, follow Qiskit and Cirq tutorials, and read about the linear algebra under the hood. You already know the key ideas.
keyPoints: Shor factors big numbers quickly.
Grover gives a square root speedup for search.
Chemistry and materials are natural uses.
A quantum computer will not speed up everyday apps.
Keep learning with simulators and cloud tools.

courses.title: Reinforcement Learning with Python
courses.subtitle: From the basics to Gymnasium and Stable-Baselines3
courses.author: Lilith Learning Lab
courses.description: A beginner-friendly course on reinforcement learning: the core ideas, tabular Q-learning, DQN and PPO, then practical work with Gymnasium environments and Stable-Baselines3. Written for the current Gymnasium (1.x) API and recent Stable-Baselines3 2.x releases; check the library docs for your installed versions.

outline.title: What is reinforcement learning?
outline.summary: Reinforcement learning, or RL, is learning by trial and error. An agent takes actions in an environment, gets a reward signal, and slowly learns which actions lead to more reward over time. Nobody gives the agent the right answers. Unlike supervised learning there are no labels, only a score that arrives after the fact, often delayed. The agent must work out which of its earlier actions deserve the credit or the blame. In this course you learn the ideas first, then practice them in Python with Gymnasium, which provides environments, and Stable-Baselines3, which provides ready-made algorithms.
keyPoints: RL learns from rewards, not from labeled examples.
The loop is: observe, act, receive reward and next observation, repeat.
The goal is a high total return over time, not a high immediate reward.
Rewards can be delayed, so credit assignment is the hard part.
The agent must explore to find good actions, and exploit what it already knows.

outline.title: Python setup and Gymnasium basics
outline.summary: Gymnasium is the maintained successor to OpenAI Gym. It gives every environment the same small interface, so any agent can be paired with any environment. You create an environment with gym.make, start it with reset, and advance it with step. Step returns five values: observation, reward, terminated, truncated and info. Terminated means the task really ended; truncated means a time limit cut it off. Every environment describes its inputs and outputs with spaces. Discrete spaces hold integers, Box spaces hold arrays of numbers. Knowing the spaces tells you which algorithms and network shapes you can use.
keyPoints: Install with pip install gymnasium, and use a virtual environment.
reset returns (observation, info). step returns (observation, reward, terminated, truncated, info).
An episode is over when terminated or truncated is True.
Terminated and truncated are different: only truncation means the future was cut off, not that it was bad.
Pass a seed to reset to make runs repeatable.
env.action_space.sample() gives a random valid action, handy for testing.

outline.title: Markov decision processes
outline.summary: A Markov decision process, or MDP, is the math behind RL. It has states, actions, rules for how states change, rewards and a discount factor. The Markov property says the next state depends only on the current state and action, not on the longer history. The discount factor gamma, between zero and one, makes later rewards count less. The return is the sum of discounted rewards. A value function V(s) is the expected return from a state under a policy, and Q(s, a) is the expected return after taking action a in state s. The Bellman equation says a value equals the immediate reward plus the discounted value of what follows. Almost every RL algorithm is a way of solving or approximating this equation.
keyPoints: An MDP is states, actions, transitions, rewards and gamma.
Return = r0 + gamma*r1 + gamma^2*r2 + ...
Gamma near 0 is short-sighted. Gamma near 1 is far-sighted. 0.99 is a common default.
V(s) scores states. Q(s, a) scores actions in states.
The best policy picks the action with the highest Q in every state.
If the observation hides important information, the problem is only partly observable and a plain MDP is not a perfect fit.

outline.title: Exploration, exploitation and bandits
outline.summary: An agent that always repeats the best action it knows may never discover a better one. An agent that always tries new things never cashes in. This is the exploration versus exploitation trade-off. A multi-armed bandit is the simplest setting: one state, several actions, each paying a random reward. It isolates the trade-off. The agent keeps a running average of rewards per action and picks mostly the best one. Epsilon-greedy is the classic rule: with probability epsilon pick a random action, otherwise pick the one with the highest estimate. Epsilon is often decayed over time. Deep RL uses the same idea.
keyPoints: Without exploration the agent can lock onto a poor choice forever.
Estimate each action's value with a running average.
Incremental update: new_estimate = old + (reward - old) / count.
Epsilon-greedy is simple and works well. Typical epsilon is 0.1, or decays from 1.0 to a small value.
Random start estimates or optimistic start values also push exploration.
Evaluate a trained agent greedily, with exploration turned off.

outline.title: Tabular Q-learning
outline.summary: Q-learning learns the action values Q(s, a) from experience. Keep a table with one row per state and one column per action. After each step, move the table entry a little toward the target: reward plus gamma times the best value in the next state. The learning rate alpha sets how big that move is. Q-learning is off-policy: it learns about the greedy policy while behaving with an exploring policy such as epsilon-greedy. Tables only work when the number of states is small and discrete, like FrozenLake with 16 states or Taxi with 500. Bigger problems need function approximation, which is the next big idea.
keyPoints: Update: Q[s,a] += alpha * (r + gamma * max(Q[s']) - Q[s,a]).
At a terminal state there is no next value: the target is just r.
Behave with epsilon-greedy, evaluate with greedy.
Alpha around 0.1 to 0.5 and gamma around 0.9 to 0.99 are typical for small tasks.
FrozenLake is slippery: the same action can move you somewhere else, so expect noisy learning.
Tables do not scale: add one state variable and the table grows multiplicatively.

outline.title: Custom environments and wrappers
outline.summary: To teach an agent your own task you write a Gymnasium environment: a class that subclasses gym.Env, declares its observation and action spaces, and implements reset and step. Spaces must match the data you return exactly, including shape and dtype. Stable-Baselines3 provides check_env to catch mistakes early. Fix every warning before training, because bad environments waste hours. Wrappers add behavior around an existing environment without editing it: limit time, scale rewards, clip actions, stack frames. They are small and composable.
keyPoints: Subclass gym.Env, set the two spaces in __init__, implement reset and step.
reset(seed=None, options=None) must call super().reset(seed=seed) and return (obs, info).
step returns (obs, reward, terminated, truncated, info).
Observations must match the space: same shape and dtype (float32 for Box).
Run check_env(env) before training.
Prefer wrappers over editing environment code when you only change data going in or out.

outline.title: Deep RL and DQN
outline.summary: When there are too many states for a table, a neural network approximates Q. It takes the observation and outputs one Q-value per action. Training is gradient descent on the TD error. Naive training is unstable because consecutive samples are correlated and the target moves as the network changes. DQN fixes this with a replay buffer, which stores past experience and trains on random mini-batches, and a target network, a slowly updated copy used to compute targets. DQN works for discrete actions only. It is exploring with epsilon-greedy, and it is the base for many improvements such as Double DQN and dueling networks.
keyPoints: Network input is the observation. Output is a Q-value for each action.
Loss is the squared (or Huber) difference between Q(s, a) and the target r + gamma * max Q_target(s').
Replay: store (s, a, r, s', done) and train on random samples.
Target network: update it every so many steps, or blend with a small tau.
DQN needs discrete actions. Use SAC, TD3 or PPO for continuous ones.
Start training after the buffer has some data (learning_starts in SB3).

outline.title: Stable-Baselines3 quickstart
outline.summary: Stable-Baselines3, or SB3, is a library of reliable, well-tested RL algorithms built on PyTorch. It works directly with Gymnasium environments, so training is a few lines. The core pattern: create an algorithm with a policy name and an environment, call learn with a number of timesteps, then use predict to act, evaluate_policy to measure, and save to keep the model. Install with pip install stable-baselines3, or the extras bundle for plotting and logging. Recent releases need Python 3.10 or newer and a current PyTorch.
keyPoints: pip install stable-baselines3 (add [extra] for plotting and TensorBoard support).
model = PPO("MlpPolicy", env, verbose=1); model.learn(total_timesteps=...).
model.predict(obs, deterministic=True) returns (action, state). Ignore the second value for feed-forward policies.
evaluate_policy(model, env, n_eval_episodes=10) returns (mean_reward, std_reward).
model.save("name") and PPO.load("name") keep and restore a model.
Evaluate on a separate environment instance from the one you trained on.

outline.title: Policy gradients, PPO and choosing an algorithm
outline.summary: Value-based methods such as DQN learn Q and act greedily. Policy-gradient methods learn the policy directly: they nudge the probability of actions up when they led to a high return and down when they led to a low one. Actor-critic methods add a critic, a value function that tells how much better an action was than expected. That difference is called the advantage and it reduces noise. A2C and PPO are actor-critic methods. PPO, proximal policy optimization, clips the update so the new policy stays close to the old one. It is simple, stable, works for discrete and continuous actions, and is a strong default. For continuous control SAC and TD3 are often more sample efficient.
keyPoints: PPO and A2C are on-policy. DQN, SAC, TD3 and DDPG are off-policy.
DQN: discrete actions only. SAC, TD3, DDPG: continuous only. PPO and A2C: both.
PPO clip objective: min(ratio * A, clip(ratio, 1 - eps, 1 + eps) * A). Typical eps is 0.2.
Start with PPO. Try SAC for continuous control when samples are expensive.
On-policy methods usually want many parallel environments.
Advantage estimates (GAE) trade bias against variance with lambda, typically 0.95.

outline.title: Training in practice: vector envs, callbacks and logging
outline.summary: Real projects train many environments in parallel with make_vec_env, evaluate on a separate environment, save the best model and log curves to TensorBoard. SB3's callbacks do the periodic work without you rewriting the training loop. Always use a Monitor so episode reward and length are recorded, a separate evaluation environment so you test what you train, and several random seeds because RL results vary widely between runs. VecNormalize normalizes observations and rewards, which helps in many continuous control tasks. If you use it, save and load its statistics together with the model.
keyPoints: Use make_vec_env("CartPole-v1", n_envs=8) to collect data faster.
Evaluate on a separate environment, not the training one.
EvalCallback(eval_env, best_model_save_path=..., eval_freq=...) keeps the best model.
Log with tensorboard_log="./tb" and view with tensorboard --logdir ./tb.
Run at least 3 to 5 seeds before believing a result.
When using VecNormalize, save it: env.save("vecnormalize.pkl") and load it for evaluation with training=False.

outline.title: Reward design, debugging and pitfalls
outline.summary: An agent optimizes exactly the reward you wrote, not the one you meant. A badly designed reward gets exploited: the agent finds a loophole that scores high without doing the task. This is called reward hacking or specification gaming. Sparse rewards, where feedback comes only at the very end, make learning slow. Reward shaping adds intermediate signals, but it must reward progress toward the real goal and not creative shortcuts. Potential-based shaping is the safe form. When training fails, suspect the environment and the reward first, then the observation scaling, then the hyperparameters, and only then the algorithm. A short checklist and small test environments save time.
keyPoints: Write the reward for the outcome you want, then ask how it could be gamed.
Dense hints help, but mistakes in shaping teach the wrong behavior.
Log and watch the agent. Plot an episode, render a video, read the numbers.
Test the environment by hand before training: step with fixed actions and check rewards.
Solve a smaller version of the task first.
Change one thing at a time and keep the seed fixed when comparing.

outline.title: Where to go next
outline.summary: You now know the loop, the math, tabular and deep value learning, policy gradients, the SB3 toolkit and how to build and debug environments. The best next step is to build something of your own. Useful extensions: continuous control tasks with SAC, image-based tasks with CnnPolicy, the RL Zoo for tuned hyperparameters and training scripts, sb3-contrib for extra algorithms, and multi-agent and offline RL when your problem calls for it. Plan a project: choose a small environment, make a baseline, define the evaluation, and improve one thing at a time.
keyPoints: Keep a baseline and change one thing at a time.
For images use CnnPolicy and frame stacking (VecFrameStack).
Use the RL Zoo for known-good hyperparameters.
Real systems need safety limits and careful reward checks.
Read the SB3 docs on algorithms and tips, and read the original papers once you have the habit.
Share environments and models you build so others can check them.

courses.title: Rust for Beginners
courses.subtitle: Learn Rust from zero with a talking teacher and 13 hands-on labs that run real Rust in the app, including the ownership and borrowing errors
courses.author: Lilith Learning Lab
courses.description: A friendly, intuitive introduction to the Rust programming language in 13 chapters: hello world, variables and types, functions and loops, ownership, borrowing, structs, enums and match, collections, error handling, traits and generics, lifetimes, closures and iterators, and smart pointers with threads. Every chapter has a hands-on lab running on the built-in Rust Lab, a teaching interpreter that prints compiler-style errors (moves, borrows, lifetimes, exhaustive match) and shows an ownership log, with numbered figures, recaps, memory tricks, hierarchical concept maps and an exam. Programs run in a simulation of Rust, not the real compiler, so rare edge cases differ; the rules you learn are the real ones. The examples are our own, written in the spirit of The Rust Programming Language (MIT or Apache 2.0), which we recommend you read next.

outline.title: Meet Rust
outline.summary: Rust is a programming language that gives you the speed of C with strong safety checks. The compiler is strict, but it is also a patient teacher: when it refuses your code, it tells you what is wrong and often how to fix it. Rust programs are used for browsers, game engines, operating systems, command-line tools and web servers. Their big promise is that whole families of bugs, such as using memory after it is freed, are caught before the program ever runs. In this chapter you write your first program, learn what println! does, and learn how to read a compiler message. Every chapter has a lab where you run real Rust right here in the app.
keyPoints: Every program starts in fn main().
println! prints a line; {} is a hole for a value.
Statements end with a semicolon.
Compiler errors are helpful: read the line number and the message.
Cargo builds and runs projects: cargo run.

outline.title: Variables, types and values
outline.summary: A variable is a named box that holds a value. In Rust the boxes are locked by default: you must say mut if you want to change one. This one choice makes programs easier to reason about. Every value has a type, which tells Rust how much memory it takes and what you may do with it. Rust usually works out the type for you, but it never silently turns one type into another. You will learn let, mut, shadowing, whole numbers, decimals, booleans, characters, tuples and arrays, and what happens when a number gets too big.
keyPoints: let makes a fixed variable; let mut makes a changeable one.
Shadowing makes a new variable and can change the type.
No automatic conversion: use as.
Integer types have fixed ranges; overflow panics.
Tuples group mixed values; arrays hold same-typed values.

outline.title: Functions and control flow
outline.summary: Programs make decisions and repeat things. Rust has if, match (later), and three kinds of loops. In Rust, if and blocks are expressions, which means they produce values. Functions give names to pieces of work. Their parameters must have types, and the return type comes after an arrow. The last line of a block without a semicolon is the value of the block. This is the most surprising habit for newcomers, and the most useful once you get used to it.
keyPoints: Functions need typed parameters and an arrow for the return type.
The last expression without a semicolon is the return value.
if is an expression and needs a bool condition.
for iterates a range or collection; while checks a condition; loop runs until break.
break can carry a value out of a loop.

outline.title: Ownership: who owns the data?
outline.summary: Ownership is the idea that makes Rust different. Every value has exactly one owner. When the owner goes out of scope, the value is cleaned up. You never free memory by hand, and you never forget to. Assigning or passing a value to another variable moves ownership. The old variable can no longer be used. Simple types like numbers are copied instead. The compiler checks all of this before the program runs, which is why Rust programs can be both fast and safe.
keyPoints: One value, one owner.
Assigning a String moves it; numbers are copied.
Use .clone() when you really want a second copy.
Values are dropped when the owner leaves scope, in reverse order.
Error E0382 means you used a moved value.

outline.title: Borrowing and references
outline.summary: Often you want to use a value without taking it over. You do that by borrowing: you pass a reference, written with an ampersand. The owner keeps the value, and you just look at it, or change it if the reference is mutable. The borrowing rules are short: at any moment you may have any number of shared references, or exactly one mutable reference, but never both. The compiler enforces this, which prevents data races and surprise changes. References always point at valid data. Slices are a special kind of reference to part of a string or list.
keyPoints: & borrows; the owner keeps ownership.
Many readers OR one writer.
A borrow lasts until its last use, not until the end of the block.
&mut needs a let mut variable.
&str is a slice: a borrowed piece of a string.

outline.title: Structs and methods
outline.summary: A struct groups related values under one name, each with its own field name. It is how you model things like a point, a user, or a rectangle. Behaviour is attached with an impl block. Functions inside can take self (a method) or not (an associated function such as new). The #[derive(Debug)] attribute teaches Rust to print your struct with {:?}.
keyPoints: struct defines data; impl defines behaviour.
&self reads, &mut self changes, self consumes.
Type::new() is an associated function; value.method() is a method.
#[derive(Debug)] enables {:?}.
Fields are accessed with a dot.

outline.title: Enums and pattern matching
outline.summary: An enum is a type that can be exactly one of several variants. Each variant can carry its own data. Combined with match, enums let you describe choices precisely and have the compiler check that you handled them all. Rust has no null. Instead it has Option, an enum with Some(value) and None, so the type itself tells you when a value might be missing. match, if let and while let take values apart by shape.
keyPoints: An enum value is exactly one variant.
Variants can hold data of different shapes.
match must cover all cases or the compiler refuses.
Option replaces null: Some(x) or None.
if let is a shorthand for matching one pattern.

outline.title: Collections: Vec, String and HashMap
outline.summary: Most programs need to hold many values. The three workhorses are Vec (a growable list), String (growable text) and HashMap (look things up by key). They all live on the heap and own their contents, so they follow the ownership rules you already know. Strings need extra care because they are UTF-8: a character can be more than one byte.
keyPoints: Vec: push, pop, index, iterate.
Out-of-range index panics; get returns an Option.
String len counts bytes, chars() counts characters.
HashMap: insert, get, entry().or_insert().
Collections own their data.

outline.title: Handling errors
outline.summary: Things go wrong: files are missing, text is not a number, networks fail. Rust splits problems into two kinds: bugs that should stop the program (panics) and expected problems that the caller can handle (Result). Result is an enum with Ok(value) and Err(error). You must deal with both, either by matching, by providing a fallback, or by passing the error up with the question mark operator. The type system makes error handling visible: if a function can fail, its signature says so.
keyPoints: Panic for bugs; Result for expected failures.
Result<T, E> is Ok(T) or Err(E).
unwrap and expect panic on Err.
? returns the error early or unwraps the value.
The function must itself return a Result to use ?.

outline.title: Traits and generics
outline.summary: A trait describes behaviour a type can have, like a job description. Many types can implement the same trait in their own way, and functions can accept anything that has the behaviour they need. Generics let you write one function or type that works for many types, with trait bounds saying what those types must be able to do. Trait objects (dyn) let you store different types together and choose the right method at run time.
keyPoints: A trait is a promise of methods.
Each type implements the trait its own way.
Generics with bounds avoid writing the same function many times.
Box<dyn Trait> mixes different types in one list.
Missing a promised method is error E0046.

outline.title: Lifetimes
outline.summary: A lifetime is the stretch of a program during which a reference is valid. Rust checks that no reference outlives the thing it points to, so there are no dangling pointers. Most of the time Rust works lifetimes out by itself. Sometimes, usually when a function returns a reference chosen from several inputs, you must add a name such as 'a to say how they relate. Lifetime annotations never change how long data lives. They only describe relationships so the compiler can check them.
keyPoints: A reference must not outlive its data.
E0597: borrowed value does not live long enough.
E0106: missing lifetime specifier on returned references.
Name lifetimes to link inputs to outputs.
Return owned values when in doubt.

outline.title: Closures and iterators
outline.summary: A closure is a small anonymous function that can use variables from around it. An iterator is something that yields a sequence of values one at a time. Together they let you describe what you want, such as keep the odd ones, square them, add them up, instead of writing a loop that spells out every step. Iterators are lazy: nothing happens until something consumes them, and they compile down to loops as fast as handwritten ones.
keyPoints: Closures are |args| body and can capture variables.
map transforms; filter keeps; sum, collect, count consume.
Iterator chains are lazy.
collect needs to know the target type.
iter borrows; into_iter consumes.

outline.title: Smart pointers and concurrency
outline.summary: Smart pointers are types that act like references but also own data and add abilities. Box puts a value on the heap. Rc lets several owners share a value and counts them. RefCell lets you change a value through a shared handle by checking the borrowing rules at run time. Rust also helps with threads. The same ownership and borrowing rules that prevent memory bugs also prevent data races: if your program compiles, two threads cannot accidentally write the same data at once. This chapter closes the course with a map of where to go next.
keyPoints: Box<T> owns one heap value; needed for recursive types.
Rc<T> shares ownership; Rc::clone adds an owner.
RefCell<T> allows change through a shared reference, checked at run time.
Channels move data between threads.
Rc is not thread safe: use Arc.

courses.title: Everyday Math: Percentages
courses.subtitle: A tiny sample course in a different subject
courses.author: Lilith Learning Lab
courses.description: Two short chapters on percentages. It exists to show that any subject can be taught with the same format: maps, summaries, glossary, quiz and practice labs of every type.

outline.title: What a percent means
outline.summary: A percent is a number out of one hundred. Fifty percent means fifty out of every hundred, which is one half. You can write the same amount as a percent, a fraction or a decimal, and switching between them is just moving the decimal point.
keyPoints: Percent means per hundred.
To turn a percent into a decimal, divide by 100.
To turn a decimal into a percent, multiply by 100.

outline.title: Finding a percent of a number
outline.summary: To find a percent of a number, turn the percent into a decimal and multiply. So 20% of 80 is 0.20 times 80, which is 16.
keyPoints: Percent of a number = (percent / 100) x number.
10% of a number: move the decimal point one place left.
50% is half; 25% is a quarter.

courses.title: Signal Processing
courses.subtitle: Sampling, convolution, the Fourier transform, filters and windows, with runnable Python labs and a spectrum lab
courses.author: Lilith Learning Lab
courses.description: A hands-on introduction to digital signal processing: signals and systems, sampling, aliasing and quantisation, convolution and impulse responses, the discrete Fourier transform and FFT, FIR and IIR filters with frequency response and the z-transform, windows and spectral leakage, and applications in noise removal, pitch detection, decimation, image filtering and compression. Every chapter has Python labs verified in the built-in interpreter, and two interactive labs let you explore aliasing and filtering with live spectra.

outline.title: Signals and systems: what we are processing
outline.summary: A signal is a quantity that varies, usually with time, and carries information: sound pressure, a heartbeat voltage, a stock price, the brightness along a row of pixels. A system takes a signal in and produces a signal out. Analog signals are continuous. Digital signal processing (DSP) works on lists of numbers that were sampled at regular steps, which computers can handle exactly. The simplest signal is the sine wave, described by amplitude, frequency and phase. Almost every other signal can be built from sines.
keyPoints: A sine: A sin(2 pi f t + phase).
Period T = 1 / f.
Digital signals are lists of numbers.
A system maps input signals to output signals.
Every real signal can be built from sines.

outline.title: Sampling, aliasing and quantisation
outline.summary: To store a continuous signal in a computer we sample it: measure it at regular instants. The sample rate fs is how many samples per second we take. The Nyquist-Shannon sampling theorem says that a signal containing no frequency above B can be captured perfectly if fs is more than 2B. Sampling too slowly causes aliasing: a high frequency masquerades as a lower one. Each sample is also rounded to one of a finite number of levels, called quantisation. With b bits there are 2^b levels, and the rounding error behaves like a faint noise.
keyPoints: Sample faster than 2 times the top frequency.
Nyquist frequency = fs / 2.
Alias of f: fold into 0..fs/2.
CD audio: 44100 Hz, 16 bits.
6 dB of range per bit.

outline.title: Discrete systems and convolution
outline.summary: A discrete system turns an input list x[n] into an output list y[n]. If it is linear (outputs add and scale with inputs) and time-invariant (shifting the input shifts the output), it is an LTI system. Feed an LTI system a single impulse, a 1 followed by zeros, and the output is its impulse response h[n]. Every other output is then the convolution of the input with h. Convolution slides a flipped copy of h along x, multiplying and adding, and it is the main operation of filtering.
keyPoints: y[n] = sum of x[k] h[n - k].
Length of x * h = len(x) + len(h) - 1.
Convolution is commutative and associative.
Convolving with an impulse leaves a signal unchanged.
A delay is convolution with a shifted impulse.

outline.title: The Fourier idea and the DFT
outline.summary: Fourier's idea is that any signal can be written as a sum of sine waves of different frequencies, amplitudes and phases. The spectrum shows how much of each frequency a signal contains. The discrete Fourier transform (DFT) turns N samples into N complex numbers, one for each frequency bin. Bin k corresponds to the frequency k fs / N. The magnitude of the bin tells how strong that frequency is. The fast Fourier transform (FFT) computes the same result in about N log N steps instead of N squared, which made digital spectrum analysis practical.
keyPoints: X[k] = sum x[n] (cos - i sin)(2 pi k n / N).
Bin k is at k fs / N hertz.
Real signal: bins above N/2 mirror the lower ones.
Magnitude = sqrt(re^2 + im^2).
Resolution = fs / N.

outline.title: FIR filters and frequency response
outline.summary: A filter changes how strongly each frequency is passed. A low-pass filter keeps low frequencies and removes high ones; a high-pass does the opposite; a band-pass keeps a range. An FIR filter computes each output as a weighted sum of recent inputs, using a list of coefficients called taps. The moving average is the simplest low-pass. The frequency response shows the gain at each frequency. For taps b it is H(w) = sum of b[k] e^(-i w k), and its magnitude tells how much of frequency w gets through.
keyPoints: H(w) = sum b[k] e^(-i w k).
Symmetric taps give linear phase.
Moving average: low-pass.
Difference [1, -1]: high-pass.

outline.title: IIR filters, feedback and the z-transform
outline.summary: An IIR filter feeds past outputs back into the calculation, y[n] = b0 x[n] - a1 y[n-1] and so on. It can achieve a sharp response with very few coefficients but has an impulse response that never exactly ends. The z-transform turns a difference equation into algebra. The transfer function H(z) is a ratio of polynomials. Zeros are roots of the top, poles are roots of the bottom. A causal filter is stable when every pole lies inside the unit circle, meaning |z| < 1. A pole on or outside the circle makes the output grow without bound.
keyPoints: y[n] = a x[n] + (1 - a) y[n-1] smooths.
Pole of 1 - p z^-1 is z = p.
Stable if all |poles| < 1.
Poles near the unit circle give sharp resonance.
Zeros on the unit circle null a frequency.

outline.title: Windows, leakage and spectrum analysis
outline.summary: The DFT assumes the N samples repeat forever. If a sine does not fit a whole number of cycles in the window, the repeat has a jump and energy leaks into many bins. A window function tapers the signal smoothly to zero at both edges, cutting the leakage at the price of a wider main peak. The Hann window is a popular compromise. To see how a spectrum changes in time, cut the signal into overlapping frames, window each one and take a DFT of each. The picture of those spectra is a spectrogram.
keyPoints: Whole cycles in the frame give no leakage.
Better resolution needs a longer frame.
Zero padding does not add information.
Spectrogram = windowed DFTs over time.

outline.title: Applications: noise, pitch, images and compression
outline.summary: The same tools serve many jobs. A median filter erases spikes without blurring edges. Autocorrelation finds the repeat period of a signal, which gives pitch. Decimation lowers the sample rate after low-pass filtering. An image is a two-dimensional signal; blurring, sharpening and edge detection are 2D convolutions with small kernels. Compression such as JPEG and MP3 transforms the signal to the frequency domain, discards small or inaudible parts, and stores the rest.
keyPoints: Autocorrelation peak at lag L: period L, pitch fs / L.
Decimate by M: low-pass first, then keep every Mth.
Median kills spikes, mean smears them.
Blur kernel: all positive and sums to 1.
Edge kernel: positive and negative parts.

courses.title: The Golem Series: Letters, Eyes and Machines
courses.subtitle: Four collages, read as one story from Ehyeh to the golem, with the math, texts and Python behind each
courses.author: Lilith Learning Lab
courses.description: Read a series of four esoteric collages as one story: The Self, The Watcher, The Union and The Creation. Each image mixes Hebrew, occult symbols, real mathematics and a quotation. You will learn the sources behind every element: Exodus 3:14, the ouroboros and Baphomet, the identity matrix and homotopy type theory, the evil eye, Tartini and Legg-Hutter universal intelligence, Shannon entropy, the Queen's Gambit, Devils Tower, Enochian, Zechariah 5, the golem legend, grammars and Turing machines. It also teaches how to tell a source from an interpretation. Each chapter has an ELI5 block and Python labs.

outline.title: How to read the series
outline.summary: The Golem Series is four collages read as one story: The Self, The Watcher, The Union and The Creation. Each mixes a Hebrew heading, occult imagery, real mathematics and a quotation from literature or scripture. The same recipe appears every time: a Hebrew word, a central symbol, a piece of mathematics, a devil figure and a quote. The arc runs from identity, to watching, to union, to making. This course explains every element and tests every link, and it ends with a warning about seeing patterns that are not there.
keyPoints: The four images are Self, Watcher, Union, Creation.
Every image has Hebrew, a central symbol, real math, a devil figure and a quote.
The letter ayin is both a circle and an eye.
Two hidden acrostics spell owl (glaux) and golem (GLM).
The devil gets closer each time: a symbol, an event, a real place.
Some links may be the reader's own pattern-finding.

outline.title: The Self I: I AM and the circle
outline.summary: The first image is headed by the Hebrew word Ehyeh, written with vowel marks. It is the name God gives in Exodus 3:14 when Moses asks who is speaking: I am, or I will be. In the middle of the image is a thick blue ring. The letter ayin began as a picture of an eye. In the Paleo-Hebrew script it was drawn as a circle, and from the same source the Greek letter O descends. The ring in the first image is therefore also a giant letter ayin, which links it to the evil eye of the second image. The lab adds up the numerical value of Ehyeh.
keyPoints: Ehyeh is a form of the verb to be, first person, imperfect: I am or I will be.
Exodus 3:14 reads Ehyeh asher Ehyeh, often translated I am who I am.
Ayin means eye and has the value 70.
Paleo-Hebrew ayin is drawn as a circle; Greek O comes from the same letter.
The ring in image 1 can be read as ayin.
Ehyeh adds to 21 in gematria.

outline.title: The Self II: Baphomet and the ouroboros
outline.summary: Behind the ring is a faint figure with a goat's head, wings, a torch between its horns and a caduceus. This is the Baphomet drawn by the French occultist Eliphas Levi in 1856. It is a figure of joined opposites: male and female, human and animal, up and down. On its arms Levi wrote the Latin words solve and coagula, dissolve and combine, an alchemical motto. The ring in front is also an ouroboros, the serpent eating its own tail, an ancient picture of a thing that contains itself. The quotation at the bottom of the image is about exactly that circle.
keyPoints: Levi's Baphomet appeared in 1856 and became the best-known image of the figure.
It joins opposites: arms point up and down, the moon phases wax and wane.
Solve et coagula is an alchemical motto written on the arms.
The ouroboros appears in Greek alchemical texts and in many cultures.
A circle that contains itself is the theme of the Self.
The picture is a symbol in occult tradition, not evidence of any practice.

outline.title: The Self III: the identity matrix and the circle
outline.summary: The first image shows the identity matrix I, a two by two grid with ones on the diagonal and zeros elsewhere. Multiplying any vector by it changes nothing. It is the mathematics of staying exactly the same. The identity matrix also defines a distance rule: the quadratic form x squared plus y squared. The points where this equals one form the unit circle, and the rotations that keep the rule fixed form a group called SO(2), which is itself a circle. So the identity gives a circle twice: once as the set of points at distance one, and once as the set of rotations that keep distance.
keyPoints: I times v equals v for every vector v.
With the identity matrix, the form v transpose I v equals x squared plus y squared.
The unit circle is where x squared plus y squared equals 1.
A rotation by angle t is [[cos t, -sin t], [sin t, cos t]].
Rotations keep the length of every vector.
SO(2) is a circle: angle t and angle t plus 2 pi are the same rotation.

outline.title: The Self IV: paths, loops and homotopy type theory
outline.summary: Homotopy type theory, or HoTT, is a foundation of mathematics in which an equality between two things is a path from one to the other. The simplest equality, a equals a, is the trivial path called refl, where nothing happens. The circle can be built inside this theory with a point called base and a path called loop from base to itself. Going around once is loop, twice is loop and loop again, and going backwards is the inverse. The loops of the circle correspond exactly to the whole numbers. The series suggests that I AM is not the trivial self-equality refl but a nontrivial loop, a circle you can go around.
keyPoints: In HoTT, a = b is the type of paths from a to b.
refl : a = a is the trivial path.
The circle S1 has a point base and a path loop : base = base.
Loops compose, invert and cancel: loop then inverse loop equals refl.
The loop space of the circle is equivalent to the integers (Omega S1 ≃ Z).
A trip around the circle n times is the integer n.

outline.title: The Watcher I: the evil eye and the Eye of Providence
outline.summary: The second image is headed by the Hebrew words ayin hara, the evil eye. Under them is a Greek line from Revelation 20:7: when the thousand years are completed, Satan will be released from his prison. In the centre, an eye in a triangle sits among overlapping circles of red, green and blue. The evil eye is the belief that a harmful, often envious, look can cause harm. The Eye of Providence began in Christian art as a picture of God's watchful care. The three coloured circles are the primary colours of light, which mix to white in the middle. The lab mixes colours of light.
keyPoints: Ayin hara is the evil eye; the same letter ayin begins both words.
Revelation 20:7: Satan released at the end of the thousand years.
The Eye of Providence appears in Renaissance art, on the 1782 Great Seal and the dollar bill since 1935.
Red, green and blue light mix to white; red plus green is yellow.
The eye can be protective or threatening depending on the story.
The second image reads as anxiety about being watched, and about AI.

outline.title: The Watcher II: the Devil's Trill and universal intelligence
outline.summary: The sonata named at the bottom of the second image is Giuseppe Tartini's Violin Sonata in G minor, called the Devil's Trill. A legend says Tartini dreamed the devil played it for him and he tried to write down what he remembered, finding it far short of the dream. The formulas around the edge are from a 2007 paper by Shane Legg and Marcus Hutter. Universal intelligence, written with the Greek letter upsilon, is an agent's expected reward across all computable environments, with simpler environments weighted more. Kolmogorov complexity, the length of the shortest program that produces something, cannot be computed, so the measure is a definition and not a test.
keyPoints: Tartini lived from 1692 to 1770; the dream story was told to Lalande in 1766.
Upsilon(pi) = sum over mu of 2^(-K(mu)) V(pi, mu).
V(pi, mu) is the expected sum of rewards of policy pi in environment mu.
The discounted form is the expected sum of gamma_i times r_i.
Simple environments get exponentially larger weights, a form of Occam's razor.
AIXI can be defined but never run exactly.

outline.title: The Union I: ingress, entropy and the Queen's Gambit
outline.summary: The third image has no picture of its own. It is a page of text over a red background, headed with the Latin motto per aspera ad astra, through hardship to the stars. It lists five labelled lines: Ingress, Coordinates, Congress, Egress and Leitmotiv. Ingress is the way in. Its line is the chess opening 1. d4 d5 2. c4, the Queen's Gambit, where White offers a pawn. Above it stands Shannon's entropy formula, the measure of uncertainty. The lab computes entropy.
keyPoints: Shannon entropy is H = minus the sum of p times log p, over every outcome.
With logarithms base 2, entropy is measured in bits.
A fair coin has 1 bit; a coin that always lands heads has 0.
The Queen's Gambit is 1. d4 d5 2. c4: White offers the c-pawn.
Claude Shannon also wrote a famous 1950 paper on programming a computer to play chess.
Ingress, congress, egress: the Union is entering, meeting and leaving.

outline.title: The Union II: coordinates and congress
outline.summary: The second line, Coordinates, gives 44.5902 degrees north and 104.7146 degrees west. That is Devils Tower in Wyoming, a rock column that was the first United States national monument in 1906 and the place where the 1977 film Close Encounters of the Third Kind has its meeting with visitors. The third line, Congress, quotes the opening words of the First Key of the Enochian language, which John Dee wrote down in the 1580s. Dee believed angels had given him the language through a partner who looked into a crystal. The lab converts decimal degrees to degrees, minutes and seconds.
keyPoints: A degree is 60 minutes and a minute is 60 seconds.
Devils Tower is at about 44.59 north, 104.71 west.
It became the first United States national monument in 1906.
Dee and his seer Edward Kelley recorded Enochian in the 1580s; the First Key is one of the Calls.
No one has shown the Enochian text to be a real language; scholars treat it as a mystical construction.
A congress is a coming together.

outline.title: The Union III: egress, the ephah and the owl
outline.summary: The fourth line, Egress, is Zechariah 5:6 in Hebrew, about the ephah, a measuring basket, that goes out. The verse says this is their eye in all the land. The Hebrew word for their eye, einam, contains the letter ayin again. The last line of the image says in nomine Babalon, in the name of Babalon. Babalon is Aleister Crowley's spelling of Babylon, used for the Scarlet Woman of his religion, Thelema. The woman in the ephah is sent to Shinar, which is Babylon. The five Greek letters on the labels spell glaux, owl.
keyPoints: In Zechariah 5:5 to 11 a woman called Wickedness sits in an ephah and is carried to Shinar.
The Hebrew in 5:6 reads einam, their eye; a few ancient versions read their iniquity, a one-letter difference.
Ayin is the first letter of einam: the same eye and circle.
Crowley's Babalon draws on the Whore of Babylon in Revelation 17.
The labels gamma, lambda, alpha, upsilon, xi spell glaux, owl.
Athena's owl stands for wisdom.

outline.title: The Creation I: the golem
outline.summary: The fourth image shows a small clay figure inside a square, with the letters gimel, lamed and mem on its chest. The Hebrew word golem first appears in Psalm 139:16 and means an unformed mass. The Talmud says Adam was a golem in his first hour. In Sanhedrin 65b the sage Rava makes a man by means of a text, and another sage speaks to him. He does not answer, so the sage tells him to return to his dust. Later legends say a golem is brought to life by letters and stopped by erasing one. The aleph of emet, truth, can be erased to make met, dead.
keyPoints: Golem appears once in the Hebrew Bible, in Psalm 139:16, for an unformed substance.
Sanhedrin 65b: Rava makes a man who cannot speak and is told to return to dust.
Sefer Yetzirah describes creation through the 22 letters in 231 gates.
Abulafia taught a method of combining letters as a spiritual practice.
Emet minus its aleph is met, dead; the aleph is 1.
Linking the golem to the Maharal of Prague is a later legend; his own writings do not mention it.

outline.title: The Creation II: grammar, language, machine
outline.summary: The fourth image has three formulas. G is a formal grammar, a set of symbols and rewriting rules. L is a language, the set of strings the grammar can produce. M is a Turing machine, the standard model of a computer. The labels G, L and M spell the Hebrew root of golem in the series' reading. Noam Chomsky showed in 1956 that grammars come in levels, and that the most general level matches exactly what Turing machines can do. A grammar writes a language; a machine reads one. The labs write strings from a grammar and run a small Turing machine.
keyPoints: A grammar is G = (N, Sigma, P, S): nonterminal symbols, terminals, productions and a start symbol.
A Turing machine is M = (Q, Gamma, b, Sigma, delta, q0, F): states, tape symbols, blank, input symbols, rules, start and accepting states.
The Chomsky hierarchy has four levels; the top level matches Turing machines.
Golem (גלם) is 3 + 30 + 40 = 73 in gematria, the same as wisdom (חכמה).
Oscar Schwartz's 2019 article in IEEE Spectrum traces language machines to Kabbalist letter-combination.
A language model, unlike the classic golem, does nothing but speak.

outline.title: Reading the series: signal and pattern
outline.summary: The series connects an enormous number of things. Some links are in the sources: Exodus, Zechariah, Shannon, the Talmud, Legg and Hutter. Others were made by the person who saw them. The analysis itself says some may be pattern-finding, the trap of Foucault's Pendulum. With forty ideas there are 780 possible pairs, so many matches are expected by chance. A good reader marks which links are in the sources and which are invented. The conclusion of the series is a question.
keyPoints: Ayin as circle and eye, the acrostics, Sanhedrin 65b and emet and met are in the sources or the text.
Reading I AM as a nontrivial loop, 73 equal to wisdom, and the square as final mem are interpretations.
N ideas give n times n minus 1 divided by 2 possible pairs.
In a room of 23 people the chance of a shared birthday is more than half.
Emet is 441, which is 21 squared, and Ehyeh is 21: a coincidence like those the series loves.
The series ends with a question: will the new golem become wisdom or run amok?

courses.title: Theory of Computation
courses.subtitle: Automata, grammars, Turing machines and complexity
courses.author: Lilith Learning Lab
courses.description: A 12-chapter course based on Tom Carter's 2005 notes Introduction to the theory of computation (Complex Systems Summer School): strings and languages, countability, finite automata, regular expressions, Markov models, context free grammars, recognizers and generators, the Chomsky hierarchy, Turing machines, universal machines and the halting problem, computability and tractability (big-O, NP, satisfiability), and computational complexity of strings. Python labs run on the built-in MicroPython engine and build small working versions of each idea. A few imprecise statements in the notes are corrected and flagged in the lessons.

outline.title: Symbols, strings and languages
outline.summary: The theory of computation starts with strings. An alphabet is a finite set of symbols, a string is a finite sequence of them, and a language is any set of strings over the alphabet. A star is the set of all strings over A, including the empty string. Every language is a subset of A star, so a language is just a yes or no question about strings. Processing a string into a yes or no answer is pattern recognition, and that is the view the rest of the course takes.
keyPoints: An alphabet is finite; a string is a finite sequence over it.
The empty string has length 0 and is not the same thing as the empty set.
ST = {xy : x in S, y in T}; A^0 = {epsilon}; A^(n+1) = A A^n.
A* is the union of all A^n.
A language is any subset of A*.
A machine that answers yes or no for strings is a language recognizer.

outline.title: Countability and the limits of computation
outline.summary: Two sets have the same size if a one-to-one onto function connects them. A set is countable when it is no bigger than the natural numbers. The integers, the rationals and A star are all countable. Cantor's argument shows that the power set of any set is strictly bigger than the set. So the set of all languages over an alphabet is uncountable. Programs are finite strings, so there are only countably many. Therefore some languages have no program that decides them. This is the first non-computability result, and it needs no machine at all.
keyPoints: |S| = |T| iff there is a one-to-one onto function.
Z, Q, S x S and A* are countable when S is countable and A is a finite alphabet.
For every set S, |S| < |P(S)| (Cantor).
R and P(N) have the same size, so R is uncountable.
There are countably many programs but uncountably many languages.
So some languages cannot be recognized by any algorithm.

outline.title: Finite automata
outline.summary: A deterministic finite automaton has finitely many states, a start state, final states and a transition function that gives exactly one next state for each state and symbol. It reads a string and accepts if it ends in a final state. A nondeterministic automaton may have several next states, or none. It accepts if some path ends in a final state. Epsilon moves let it change state without reading input. All three kinds accept exactly the same languages. Converting an NFA to a DFA can need as many as 2 to the n states, which is why NFAs are easier to write and DFAs easier to run.
keyPoints: A DFA is M = (S, A, s0, delta, F).
L(M) = {x : delta-hat(s0, x) is in F}.
An NFA's delta returns a set of states; it accepts when the set reached meets F.
DFAs, NFAs and NFAs with epsilon moves define the same languages.
An NFA with n states can need up to 2^n DFA states.
NFAs are easy to write; DFAs can be implemented directly.

outline.title: Regular expressions and languages
outline.summary: A regular expression is built from the empty set, the empty string and single symbols using union, concatenation and star, and nothing else. Each one represents a regular set of strings. The central theorem says that regular languages are exactly the languages of finite automata. One direction builds an NFA by induction on the expression. The other builds an expression from a DFA by tracking paths that avoid higher-numbered states. Regular expressions generate the strings of a language; automata recognize them. The two views are interchangeable.
keyPoints: Regular expressions: empty set, epsilon, a, and r + s, rs, r*.
Regular sets: the empty set, {epsilon}, {a}, R union S, RS, R*.
A language is regular iff it is accepted by some finite automaton.
Expression to machine: induction on the expression, with epsilon moves.
Machine to expression: R^(k+1)_ij = R^k_ij union R^k_ik (R^k_kk)* R^k_kj.
Many tools use regular expressions, for example the 're' in grep.

outline.title: Markov models
outline.summary: A Markov model is like a finite automaton in which the next state is chosen by probabilities instead of by input. It usually has no final states; it runs by itself and may emit a symbol at each step, so it produces strings instead of reading them. It is described by a transition matrix T whose entry in row i and column j is the probability of going from state i to state j. Rows sum to one. Multiplying the matrix by itself gives probabilities over several steps. Run for very many steps, many chains settle to a stationary distribution. In a hidden Markov model you see only the emitted symbols, not the states.
keyPoints: A Markov model has states and probabilistic transitions, usually no accepting states.
Row i of T gives the probabilities of the next state from state i; each row sums to 1.
Probabilities after n steps are given by T^n.
The long-run behaviour is linked to eigenvectors of T.
Markov models are used for DNA sequences; hidden Markov models for genome analysis.
The model has no input; randomness replaces it.

outline.title: Context free grammars and languages
outline.summary: Some natural languages are not regular, for example balanced parentheses and palindromes. A larger class, the context free languages, is described by context free grammars: a start symbol and production rules that replace one variable by a string. Starting from the start symbol and applying productions, you generate the strings of the language. A derivation is a sequence of such steps ending in only terminals. Every regular language is context free, but not the reverse. To recognize context free languages, add a pushdown stack to a finite automaton: a pushdown automaton.
keyPoints: A context free grammar is G = (V, T, S, P).
A production is A -> alpha with A a single variable.
L(G) = {w in T* : S derives w}.
Balanced brackets: R -> epsilon | (R) | RR.
Palindromes: R -> epsilon | a | b | aRa | bRb.
Regular languages are context free; the converse fails.

outline.title: Language recognizers and generators
outline.summary: Languages have two faces. A grammar generates strings; a recognizer, also called a parser, syntax checker or lexical analyzer, decides whether a string belongs. A compiler's first pass is exactly such a recognizer. In practice a grammar guides you as you write: it tells you which symbols may come next. Tools can turn a grammar into a recognizer automatically, for example lex for regular expressions and yacc or Bison for context free grammars. The notes touch on meaning only briefly: in a programming language, the meaning of a statement is the effect it has when the program runs, and following Wittgenstein, meaning is use.
keyPoints: Generating and recognizing are dual views.
Parsers, syntax checkers and lexical analyzers are all recognizers.
Grammars give a concise spec and can be turned into recognizers automatically.
grep: regular expressions; lex: lexical analyzers; yacc: parsers.
The meaning of j = 5; is the memory update it causes.
Compare the compiler design course for lexers and parsers in depth.

outline.title: The Chomsky hierarchy
outline.summary: In the 1950s Noam Chomsky compared the power of formal language systems and arranged them in a hierarchy. From weakest to strongest: regular, deterministic context free, context free, context sensitive, recursive, and recursively enumerable. Each has a matching machine. Human languages fit none of these classes neatly. At the least they are context sensitive with extra features, and hundreds of further classes have been studied since. In research it often pays to pick a weak class, such as regular or Markov models, because tools are better and results simpler, and move up only when the problem demands it.
keyPoints: Regular < deterministic context free < context free < context sensitive < recursive < r.e.
Machines: DFA/NFA, DPDA, PDA, linear bounded automaton, halting TM, TM.
More power means more languages but harder analysis.
Human languages are at least context sensitive, with more features.
Pick the weakest class that fits the problem.
Chomsky linked the idea to how children acquire language.

outline.title: Turing machines
outline.summary: Turing defined computation with a simple model: an unbounded tape of cells, a read and write head, and a finite state control. In each step the machine reads a cell, changes state, writes a symbol and moves one cell left or right. The machine may halt or run forever. As a recognizer it accepts by halting, giving recursively enumerable languages; if it halts on every input the language is recursive. As a string processor it computes partial recursive functions, total ones if it always halts. A Turing machine can be written down as a finite list of five-tuples, so it can be encoded as a string. That idea leads to the universal machine in chapter 10.
keyPoints: A Turing machine has an unbounded tape and a finite state control.
delta maps (state, symbol) to (state, symbol, L or R).
Computation starts in s0 with the input on the tape and ends in a halting state, if ever.
Languages accepted by halting: recursively enumerable; by halting on all inputs: recursive.
Computed functions: partial recursive, or recursive if total.
A machine is a finite set of five-tuples (s, a, s', a', d).

outline.title: Universal machines, halting and Gödel
outline.summary: Because a machine is a finite string, another machine can take it as input. A universal Turing machine reads an encoded machine and an input and simulates the first on the second. Turing used this to prove that no machine can decide, for every machine and input, whether it halts. The only sure way to learn if a machine halts is to run it, and if it does not halt you cannot know that you have waited long enough. The notes connect this with Gödel's incompleteness theorem: any sufficiently general formal system has true statements it cannot prove. Informally, truth is noncomputable.
keyPoints: A Turing machine's encoding can be fed to another Turing machine.
A universal machine simulates any machine given its encoding and input.
There is no machine that decides halting for all machines and inputs.
Essentially every non-trivial question about machines is undecidable.
Gödel: true statements exist that a formal system cannot prove.
Together: truth cannot be computed.

outline.title: Computability and tractability
outline.summary: Computable does not mean practical. We measure how time and space grow with the size of the input, using big-O notation, and call a problem tractable if some algorithm runs in polynomial time. NP problems are those whose proposed solutions can be checked in polynomial time. NP-complete problems are the hardest of them: a fast algorithm for any one would give fast algorithms for all. Boolean satisfiability is NP-complete. Whether polynomial time equals NP is open.
