Factoring is in NP, and the security of RSA relies on its apparent difficulty; primality, by contrast, is decidable in polynomial time.
keyPoints: g in O(f) iff there are c > 0 and N with |g(n)| <= c |f(n)| for all n >= N.
Classes: logarithmic, linear, quadratic, polynomial, exponential, factorial.
Tractable: polynomial; intractable otherwise (as far as we know).
NP: verifying a solution is easy, finding one may not be.
NP-complete: if one is solved in polynomial time, all of NP is.
Satisfiability is NP-complete; factoring is in NP; whether P = NP is open.

outline.title: Computational complexity of strings
outline.summary: Given a long string of bits recording a system, how complex is the system? One answer is information entropy, but it depends on a probability model and has no model-free value: it ranges from zero to the length of the string. Another is computational complexity: the length of the shortest machine and input pair that makes a standard universal machine output the string. It is well defined but noncomputable, by the halting problem. We can improve upper bounds by trying many programs with time limits, and the two measures are in a precise sense essentially equal, so either can be useful. The measure is also called Kolmogorov or algorithmic complexity.
keyPoints: Entropy needs a probability model; there are many.
Under a fair-coin model the entropy of a string is its length; under a model that predicts it exactly it is zero.
Computational complexity: the shortest (machine, input) pair giving the string.
Its upper bound is about the length of the string; the lower bound is zero.
It is noncomputable because of the halting problem; better upper bounds come from trying machines.
The two measures are essentially equal.

courses.title: The Transformer: Encoder and Decoder
courses.subtitle: Attention, heads, masks, layers and training, with Python labs
courses.author: Lilith Learning Lab
courses.description: Attention Is All You Need (Vaswani et al., 2017): positional encoding, scaled dot-product and multi-head attention, masks, feed-forward layers with residuals and layer norm, the encoder stack, the decoder stack with cross-attention, training schedule and label smoothing, and beam search. Theory plus Python labs.

outline.title: Attention Is All You Need: the big picture
outline.summary: The Transformer is a sequence model built from attention alone. It was introduced in the 2017 paper Attention Is All You Need by Vaswani and colleagues at Google. Earlier translation models read words one at a time with recurrent networks. The Transformer lets every position look at every other position in one step, which is easier to run in parallel and easier to train. It has two stacks. The encoder reads the source sentence. The decoder writes the target sentence one word at a time, looking at the encoder's output.
keyPoints: Published at NeurIPS 2017: Attention Is All You Need.
The base model has 6 encoder layers, 6 decoder layers, model width 512 and 8 heads.
It achieved 28.4 BLEU on English to German with the big model, and 41.8 on English to French.
No recurrence and no convolution: only attention and feed-forward layers.
Training is parallel over positions, unlike a recurrent network.
The same blocks later became the basis of BERT, GPT and most large language models (background).

outline.title: Embeddings and positional encoding
outline.summary: Attention treats its input as a set: it does not know which word came first. So the model adds a positional encoding to each embedding. The paper uses fixed sine and cosine waves of different wavelengths. Each token id is first mapped to a vector of size d_model by an embedding table. The paper multiplies the embeddings by the square root of d_model, then adds the positional encoding. The labs compute the encoding and look at how neighbouring positions relate.
keyPoints: PE(pos, 2i) = sin(pos / 10000^(2i/d_model)); PE(pos, 2i+1) = cos(same).
Wavelengths run from 2 pi to 10000 times 2 pi.
The authors chose sinusoids because they might let the model extrapolate to longer sequences.
They also tried learned position embeddings and found nearly identical results.
Embedding weights are multiplied by the square root of d_model.
The encoding is added, not concatenated.

outline.title: Scaled dot-product attention
outline.summary: Attention takes three sets of vectors: queries Q, keys K and values V. Each query is compared with every key by a dot product. The scores are scaled, turned into weights by a softmax, and used to average the values. The scaling by the square root of d_k keeps the dot products from growing large with the dimension, which would push the softmax into regions with tiny gradients. Everything in this chapter is a few lines of arithmetic, and the labs write each of them.
keyPoints: Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(Q K^T / sqrt(d_k)) V.
Weights in each row are positive and sum to 1.
Without scaling, dot products grow with d_k and the softmax saturates.
Dot-product attention is much faster and more space-efficient than additive attention in practice.
Cost grows with the square of the sequence length.
Each output is a convex combination of the value vectors.

outline.title: Multi-head attention
outline.summary: Instead of one attention, the paper runs several in parallel, called heads. Each head applies its own learned projections to the queries, keys and values, shrinking them to a smaller size, and runs attention there. In the base model there are 8 heads, each with d_k = d_v = 64, so the total width is 8 times 64, or 512. The outputs of the heads are concatenated and mixed by a last projection. The reason is that a single attention averages over many things at once. Several heads can look at different relations at the same time.
keyPoints: head_i = Attention(Q W_i^Q, K W_i^K, V W_i^V).
MultiHead = Concat(head_1 ... head_h) W^O.
Base model: h = 8, d_k = d_v = d_model / h = 64.
Because each head is smaller, the cost is similar to one full-width head.
Heads can specialise; some look like they track syntax, per the paper's visualisations.
Projection matrices are learned, one set per head.

outline.title: Masks: padding and causal
outline.summary: Some positions must not be looked at. Padding tokens added to make a batch rectangular carry no meaning. In the decoder, the word at position t may not look at positions after t, otherwise it could copy the answer. A mask is applied to the scores before the softmax. Forbidden entries are set to a very negative number, minus infinity in the paper's description, so that their weights become zero. The causal mask is what lets the decoder train on a whole target sentence in one pass while still behaving as a left-to-right generator.
keyPoints: Masked scores are set to minus infinity before the softmax, giving zero weight.
The decoder's self-attention uses a causal mask: position t sees positions 0 to t.
The decoder's outputs are also shifted right by one position.
Padding masks keep real tokens from attending to pad tokens.
Training with teacher forcing and a mask computes all positions in parallel.
At generation time there is no future to mask, so tokens are produced one by one.

outline.title: Feed-forward layers, residuals and layer normalization
outline.summary: Each layer has attention and a position-wise feed-forward network. Around each sublayer sits a residual connection and layer normalization: output = LayerNorm(x + Sublayer(x)). The feed-forward network is two linear maps with a ReLU between them, applied to each position separately: max(0, xW1 + b1)W2 + b2. In the base model the inner width d_ff is 2048. Residual connections help gradients flow through deep stacks. Layer normalization keeps activations in a stable range.
keyPoints: FFN(x) = max(0, x W1 + b1) W2 + b2, d_model 512 to d_ff 2048 and back.
Sublayer wrapper: LayerNorm(x + Dropout(Sublayer(x))).
All sublayers and embeddings output vectors of size d_model so residuals can add.
Layer norm statistics are computed over the features of one position.
The big model uses d_model 1024, d_ff 4096, 16 heads.
Parameter counts: about 65 million for the base model and 213 million for the big model.

outline.title: The encoder stack
outline.summary: The encoder is a stack of N = 6 identical layers. Each layer applies multi-head self-attention, then a feed-forward network, each wrapped in a residual connection and layer norm. Encoder self-attention is bidirectional: every source position can look at every other, left and right. There is no causal mask, only a padding mask. The output of the last layer is the memory, one vector per source position, that the decoder will read.
keyPoints: Encoder layer: x1 = LN(x + SelfAttn(x)); x2 = LN(x1 + FFN(x1)).
Six layers, each with its own parameters.
Input and output have shape (source length, d_model).
Self-attention uses a padding mask but no causal mask.
BERT (background knowledge) is built from encoder-style layers.
The encoder runs once per sentence, not once per output word.

outline.title: The decoder stack
outline.summary: The decoder has the same kind of layers as the encoder with one extra sublayer. In order: masked self-attention over the target so far, cross-attention to the encoder memory, then the feed-forward network. Each is wrapped by a residual connection and layer norm. In cross-attention the queries come from the decoder and the keys and values come from the encoder's output. That is how the decoder reads the source sentence. After the last layer, a linear map and a softmax turn each position's vector into probabilities over the vocabulary, for the next token.
keyPoints: Decoder layer: masked self-attention, cross-attention, feed-forward; each with residual and layer norm.
Cross-attention: Q from the decoder, K and V from the encoder memory.
Output: softmax(linear(decoder output)) over the vocabulary.
The paper shares the weights of the two embedding layers and the pre-softmax linear map.
The decoder input is the target sequence shifted right, starting with a start symbol.
Six decoder layers in the base model.

outline.title: Training: loss, optimizer and schedule
outline.summary: Training minimizes cross-entropy between the model's next-token probabilities and the true tokens. The paper adds label smoothing of 0.1, which makes targets slightly less certain and improves BLEU even though perplexity gets worse. The optimizer is Adam with beta1 0.9, beta2 0.98 and epsilon 1e-9. The learning rate rises linearly for 4000 warmup steps then falls with the inverse square root of the step number. The base model trained for 100,000 steps, about 12 hours on 8 P100 GPUs; the big model for 300,000 steps, 3.5 days.
keyPoints: lrate = d_model^(-0.5) * min(step^(-0.5), step * warmup^(-1.5)); warmup = 4000.
Adam: beta1 = 0.9, beta2 = 0.98, epsilon = 1e-9.
Label smoothing 0.1 hurts perplexity but improves accuracy and BLEU.
Dropout 0.1 on sublayers and embeddings in the base model.
Base: 100k steps, 12 hours, 8 P100 GPUs; big: 300k steps, 3.5 days.
WMT 2014 English-German had about 4.5 million sentence pairs.

outline.title: Decoding, results and what came next
outline.summary: To translate, the decoder is run repeatedly: feed the tokens so far, take the next-token distribution, choose a token, append, repeat until an end symbol. Greedy decoding always picks the most probable token. Beam search keeps several partial translations and extends the best ones. The paper used beam search with beam size 4 and a length penalty of 0.6 for translation. The big model scored 28.4 BLEU on English to German and 41.8 on English to French. Later models showed that the same blocks scale. Encoder-only models such as BERT and decoder-only models such as GPT are background knowledge in this course.
keyPoints: Greedy decoding is fast but can miss better sequences.
Beam search scores a hypothesis by the sum of log probabilities (with a length correction).
The paper used beam size 4 and length penalty alpha = 0.6.
Results: big model 28.4 BLEU (EN-DE) and 41.8 BLEU (EN-FR).
Generation cost: each new token needs a decoder pass; caching keys and values avoids recomputation (background).
Encoder-only (BERT) and decoder-only (GPT) models are descendants (background).

courses.title: vector-sdk-py: discord.py-style Vector Bots
courses.subtitle: Write Vector messenger bots in Python with the discord.py API, on top of the Rust vector_sdk, with Python labs
courses.author: Lilith Learning Lab
courses.description: A hands-on course based on lucky-edgelord/vector-sdk-py (MIT, alpha), a discord.py-style Python library for Vector messenger bots built on the official Rust vector_sdk with PyO3. Learn the mapping from discord.py, installing and keys, events (including Vector's own), prefix and native slash commands with type hints, cogs, checks, cooldowns and tasks, embeds rendered as markdown, views built from reactions, community moderation, voice, Mini Apps and the development workflow. Labs run offline and simulate the library's rules in Python.

outline.title: What vector-sdk-py is and how it maps from discord.py
outline.summary: vector-sdk-py is a Python library for Vector messenger bots. It copies the discord.py style: the same decorators, cogs, ctx, checks, cooldowns, converters, wait_for, tasks.loop, embeds and views. Underneath, every network, crypto and storage call runs in the official Rust vector_sdk crate, compiled into the package with PyO3. You get its communities, private messages, Mini Apps and voice without writing Rust. The repository is github.com/lucky-edgelord/vector-sdk-py, MIT licensed, marked alpha, and needs Python 3.9 or newer. Most discord.py bots port by changing the imports.
keyPoints: import vector; from vector.ext import commands, tasks.
Layers: src/ is the PyO3 binding, python/vector/ is the discord.py style API.
Guild is an alias of Community; user.id is an alias of npub.
Intents are accepted and ignored: Vector sends every event.
Anything not wrapped is reachable through bot.native.

outline.title: Installing, keys and starting the bot
outline.summary: Install with pip install git+https://github.com/lucky-edgelord/vector-sdk-py. This compiles the Rust SDK, so you need a Rust toolchain and cmake for the Opus voice codec. Prebuilt wheels are produced by the GitHub Actions workflow, and once published to PyPI it will be pip install vector-sdk-py. A Vector identity is a Nostr key. bot.run takes an nsec key where discord.py takes a token. Called with no key it reuses the key stored in data_dir, which defaults to ./vector-bot-data, creating one on first run. A seed phrase works with mnemonic. Voice and Mini Apps are built by default. Speech to text (whisper), Tor and I2P are opt-in build features, and Client.features() tells you what your build has.
keyPoints: Needs Rust toolchain and cmake to build from source.
bot.run(nsec) or bot.run() to reuse the stored key.
vector.generate_nsec() mints a key; keep it secret.
invite_policy: manual, public, or whitelist=[npubs].
Whisper, Tor and I2P are opt-in features at build time.

outline.title: Events: the discord.py names plus Vector's own
outline.summary: The usual discord.py event names fire with the usual arguments: on_ready, on_message, on_message_edit, on_message_delete, on_reaction_add, on_typing, on_member_join, on_member_remove, on_member_ban, on_guild_join, on_guild_role_create and more. Vector adds events of its own: on_community_invite, on_community_change, on_member_kick, on_member_timeout, on_member_roles_update, on_overwrite_update, on_channel_keyed, on_community_dissolve, on_xdc_presence, on_xdc_session and on_slash_command. Register with bot.event or bot.listen, and use wait_for when you want to pause a command until a particular event arrives.
keyPoints: bot.event replaces a handler; bot.listen adds one.
Vector extras: on_community_invite, on_member_kick, on_member_timeout.
on_member_roles_update(member, added, removed) is finer than on_member_update.
on_slash_command(name, args, message) sees raw native commands.
Use wait_for with a check and a timeout.

outline.title: Commands: prefix and native slash at once
outline.summary: Every command you define is available as a text command and, where possible, as a native Vector slash command. The library publishes a manifest so the command appears in Vector's slash picker with typed arguments, and Vector checks the types before your code runs. Type hints decide the argument types: str is text, int is int, float is number, bool is a flag, Member or User is a user picker, Literal is a choice. Trailing arguments such as a keyword-only rest, args or Greedy become trailing text. Anything else is text, converted in Python. The default prefix is the slash. Set a prefix such as an exclamation mark to also accept text commands. Commands whose name or signature cannot be expressed natively stay prefix only.
keyPoints: command_prefix defaults to '/' (native only); '!' also accepts text.
str=text, int=int, float=number, bool=flag, Member=user, Literal=choice.
Rest, *args and Greedy become trailing text.
Names with uppercase letters or more than 8 args stay prefix only.
Groups become /name subcommand args.

outline.title: Cogs, checks, cooldowns, converters and tasks
outline.summary: Structure works as in discord.py. A Cog groups commands and listeners, and an extension module defines async def setup(bot) that adds it with bot.add_cog. Cog_check can apply a rule to every command in a cog. Checks such as has_permissions, guild_only and is_owner guard commands. Cooldowns limit how often a command can be used, per user, community, channel or other bucket. is_owner uses owner_id, which takes an npub. Converters turn text into objects: Member, Role, TextChannel, Greedy, Range, Literal and your own. tasks.loop repeats a coroutine on a schedule. Errors are classes such as MissingPermissions, BadArgument and CommandOnCooldown.
keyPoints: await bot.add_cog(Cog(bot)) inside async def setup(bot).
cog_check can guard every command in a cog.
@commands.cooldown(rate, per, BucketType.user).
has_permissions(kick_members=True), is_owner(), guild_only().
@tasks.loop(minutes=5); start with .start().

outline.title: Messages and embeds on a messenger without embeds
outline.summary: Vector has no embed objects, so vector.Embed keeps discord.py's full API but renders itself into Vector's markdown. The colour paints the title and a bar character down the left edge, inline fields sit side by side separated by a vertical line, and the timestamp is shown in each reader's own timezone. Sending works as you expect: send, reply, edit, history, purge, fetch_message, attachments with await attachment.read(), custom emoji reactions and typing indicators. delete_after sets a NIP-40 expiry that every client honours and also deletes the message after that many seconds. Other emulations are worth knowing: ephemeral replies are sent as a direct message, and deleting someone else's message hides it as a moderation action, while your own messages are really deleted.
keyPoints: Embed API is discord.py's: add_field, set_author, set_footer, set_image, to_dict.
Rendering: bar char, bold title in colour, inline fields joined with a bar.
attachment://name plus file=vector.File(...) sends a real attachment.
delete_after sets expiry and deletes; expires_in sets expiry only.
ephemeral=True sends the reply to the user's DMs.

outline.title: Views, buttons, selects and modals built from reactions
outline.summary: Vector has no message components, so vector.ui builds them from reactions. Each button or select option becomes an emoji reaction that the bot adds under the message, with a legend in the message text. Reacting clicks it, and removing your reaction clicks it again. Buttons without an emoji get regional letters A, B, C and so on. Select options get number emoji one to ten, then letters. A Modal asks its TextInput fields as a short chat conversation and then calls on_submit. ui.Paginator pages text or embeds with first, previous, next, last and stop reactions. timeout, on_timeout, interaction_check, stop, wait and interaction.response.edit_message all work as in discord.py.
keyPoints: Same decorators as discord.py: @ui.button, @ui.select, ui.View, ui.Modal.
Buttons: given emoji, else A B C. Options: 1 to 10, then letters.
Reacting clicks; removing the reaction clicks again.
ephemeral=True is sent as a DM.
Reaction limits mean views should stay small.

outline.title: Communities and moderation
outline.summary: Communities are richer than Discord guilds. You can create communities, join by invite link, preview an invite with fetch_invite, create invites with a lifetime and label, and manage roles, categories, text, voice and forum channels. Permissions work per channel with set_permissions and overwrites, and permissions_for tells you what someone may do. Moderation includes kick, ban, unban, bulk_ban for one key rotation, member.timeout, nicknames, pins, audit_logs and bans listings, and contain_raid. Recovery and operations tools include relay management with check_relays and move_relays, refound and repair_roster. leave removes the bot, and delete dissolves the community, which is irreversible and for the owner only.
keyPoints: create_community, join(invite_url), fetch_invite for a preview.
create_role, create_text_channel, create_category, create_forum.
channel.set_permissions(target, send_messages=False) locks a channel.
member.timeout(timedelta), guild.bulk_ban(members), guild.audit_logs().
guild.delete() dissolves a community; owner only, irreversible.

outline.title: Voice, Mini Apps, testing and contributing
outline.summary: Voice works like discord.py. voice_channel.connect returns a client, vc.play plays an FFmpegPCMAudio source, and bots can also listen. Audio is 48 kHz mono 16-bit PCM bytes. utterances yields one clip per speaker per pause, and a Transcriber turns a clip into text in a whisper build. Mini Apps are WebXDC apps shared in a chat. Decorate an async function with bot.xdc_app(app_id) and iterate the session for data, peer_join and peer_leave events. Sessions end after idle or quiet timeouts. For development, install maturin and pytest, run maturin develop to build the Rust extension into your virtual environment, and run pytest. The Python layer is tested against a fake native bot, so most tests need no network.
keyPoints: PCM bytes: 48000 samples per second, mono, 2 bytes per sample.
vc.play(FFmpegPCMAudio(path)); vc.say(pcm); vc.hush().
@bot.xdc_app('id') async def f(session): async for event in session.
event.type: data, peer_join, peer_leave; event.verified_sender names the sender.
maturin develop --release; pytest tests.

courses.title: Vector SDK: Private Bots on Nostr
courses.subtitle: Identity, channels, events, communities, encryption and operations for Vector bots, with Python labs
courses.author: Lilith Learning Lab
courses.description: A hands-on course based on the published vector_sdk crate, version 0.12.0 (11 November 2026, MIT, Rust 1.75+), its README, changelog and examples. Older write-ups describe 0.3.0 or 0.2.1; this course follows the current crate. Learn how a Rust bot gets an identity, sends and receives through one Channel API, handles events and history, declares typed slash commands, joins and runs communities with roles, overwrites and moderation policies, uses the optional voice, Mini App, Tor and I2P features, and is secured and troubleshot. Labs run offline and simulate the rules in Python, since Rust cannot run here.

outline.title: What the Vector SDK is: crate 0.12.0 and its parts
outline.summary: vector_sdk is a Rust crate for building bots and clients for Vector, a private encrypted messenger built on Nostr. Version 0.12.0 was published on 11 November 2026 under the MIT licence, and needs Rust 1.75 or newer. It sits on top of vector-core, which does the encryption, networking and storage. You write about a dozen lines to get a bot that sends and receives messages, files and reactions, joins communities, and survives network drops. Older write-ups are out of date. A GitBook page described version 0.3.0 and a standalone repository showed 0.2.1. This course follows the published 0.12.0 crate, its README, changelog and examples.
keyPoints: cargo add vector_sdk and cargo add tokio --features full.
0.12.0 published 2026-11-11, MIT, MSRV 1.75, edition 2021.
Features: tor, i2p, voice, whisper, xdc. None are on by default.
Depends on vector-core 0.11, nostr-sdk 0.45, tokio 1.49.
Repository: github.com/VectorPrivacy/Vector; docs: docs.rs/vector-sdk.

outline.title: Accounts and keys: identity, data directory, one bot per process
outline.summary: There are four ways to give the bot an identity. Give no key and build creates one on first run and reuses it every run after. Give an nsec, a twelve word mnemonic, or a password for keys that are encrypted at rest. VectorBot::generate_nsec mints a fresh key yourself. A keyless bot's identity is stable across restarts, so it keeps its chats and community memberships. Storage defaults to a per-OS application directory. Override it with data_dir or the VECTOR_DATA_DIR variable. Every bot on a machine needs its own data directory, and a bot owns its process while it runs, so run one bot per process.
keyPoints: No key: created on first run, reused afterwards.
.nsec(), .mnemonic(), .password(), VectorBot::generate_nsec().
.data_dir(path) or VECTOR_DATA_DIR; one directory per bot.
Run one bot per process; for more bots run more processes.
A bot on Tor or I2P must name it again on every run.

outline.title: Channels: one API for DMs and communities
outline.summary: You send through a Channel. A direct message chat and a community channel are handled identically, so you never branch on which one it is. Get one with bot.channel(id), bot.dm(npub), or msg.channel() on an incoming message. The channel methods cover send, reply, post with options, react and unreact, typing, edit, delete, send_file and send_bytes. Incoming messages also have reply and react shortcuts, and received files are in msg.message.attachments. channel.post takes PostOptions so a message can be a reply, can expire after a number of seconds, or can be addressed to one bot.
keyPoints: bot.channel(id).send(text) works for DMs and community channels.
reply(msg_id, text) threads; post(text, PostOptions) adds expiry or addressing.
send_file(path) from disk; send_bytes(bytes, name, opts) from memory.
react, unreact, react_custom; edit and delete only your own messages.
typing() shows the indicator.

outline.title: Receiving: handlers, BotEvent and history
outline.summary: bot.on_message handles every incoming chat message. bot.on_event gives the full BotEvent stream, and bot.run does the same but also exits cleanly on Ctrl-C. A slow handler will not hold up the others. BotEvent covers Ready, Message, Reaction, ReactionRemoved, Edit, Delete, MemberJoin, MemberLeave, Typing, CommunityChange, Dissolved, VoicePresence, Invite, Removed and more, each naming what changed and, where it applies, who did it. Everything sent since the bot began listening arrives once, live or through a catch-up. What came earlier is history. Read it on purpose with channel.history.
keyPoints: on_message for chat; on_event or run for everything.
Skip msg.is_mine() to avoid reply loops.
Ready fires even with zero communities.
News arrives once; old messages are history, read with channel.history(n).
The bot reconnects and catches up by itself.

outline.title: Slash commands with typed arguments
outline.summary: Do not parse message text by hand. Declare a command with bot.command(name, description), add typed arguments, and give it a handler. The SDK publishes a manifest, so every Vector client shows a slash picker with a field per argument. Argument types are string, int, number, flag, user and choice. A choice becomes a dropdown, a user becomes a member picker, and an int becomes a number field. The client validates the input before it is sent. A matched command runs its handler and never reaches on_message, so commands and free chat can live side by side.
keyPoints: bot.command(name, description).string(...).choice(...).run(handler).
Types: string, int, number, flag, user, choice.
Read values with ctx.str, ctx.int, ctx.number, ctx.flag.
Matched commands never reach on_message.
The wire format is plain text like '/roll 20', so old clients can type it.

outline.title: Communities: joining, members and invites
outline.summary: A community is a shared space with members, roles and channels. Your bot can join one by link with bot.join, preview a link first with bot.preview_link, or create its own with bot.create_community. Invites are handled by the invite policy on the builder. Manual is the default: invites wait for bot.pending_invites and bot.accept_invite. Public accepts from anyone. Whitelist accepts only listed npubs and ignores the rest. Auto-accept also picks up invites that arrived while the bot was offline. When a message arrives from a community, msg.member() gives the sender as a member you can act on: kick, ban, unban, grant or revoke admin, and check is_admin.
keyPoints: Builder: .public() or .whitelist([...]); default is Manual.
Manual: bot.pending_invites() then bot.accept_invite(id).
bot.join(link), bot.preview_link(link), bot.create_community(name, NewCommunity).
msg.member(): kick(), ban(), unban(), grant_admin(), revoke_admin(), is_admin().
Auto-accept also joins invites that arrived while offline.

outline.title: Running a community: roles, channels, permissions and policies
outline.summary: From 0.12 a bot can do what a person with admin rights can do: create roles with permissions, make categories and channels, set per-channel overwrites, time members out, set nicknames, pin messages, and read a typed audit log. Each action is checked the way every member's client will judge it, so a refusal comes back as an error rather than an edit that everyone ignores. Moderation policies add rulebooks. community.policies() writes rules such as words, links, repetition, flooding or a joining cohort, previews them against real history, and acts only when armed.
keyPoints: RoleSpec::new(name).color(..).permissions(Permissions::KICK | ...).
create_category, create_channel_with(NewChannel::default().private().in_category(id)).
channel.set_overwrite(Overwrite::role(&role).allow(...)).
member.timeout(duration), member.add_role(&role), msg.pin().
Policies start in dry-run; only arm() lets them act, and never on less than proof.

outline.title: Voice, Mini Apps and the optional networks
outline.summary: Four optional features extend a bot. Voice joins voice channels and hears 48 kHz mono audio per speaker. Whisper turns clips into text. Xdc joins Mini Apps, small shared apps in a chat. Tor and I2P route traffic through anonymity networks. Tor and I2P need the Cargo feature and a builder call, .tor() or .i2p(). The feature alone only compiles the code in. A bot on Tor or I2P must name it on every run. For web requests, such as to a language model, use vector_sdk::net::build_http_client so a bot on Tor or I2P never leaks its address with a side request.
keyPoints: Voice: channel.join_voice(); call.listen(); call.say(pcm).
Audio is 48 kHz mono PCM; a frame is 20 ms.
Mini Apps: bot.xdc(app_id).run(handler); sessions end after 3 minutes idle or 15 minutes quiet.
Tor and I2P need the feature and .tor() or .i2p().
Use vector_sdk::net::build_http_client for side requests.

outline.title: Security, privacy and troubleshooting
outline.summary: Treat the nsec and mnemonic as passwords: read them from the environment or a secret store, never commit or log them, and rotate when in doubt. Use wss relays, cap the size of files you accept, and keep logs free of message text. Be honest about limits. Relays can see metadata and can delay or withhold messages, profile information is public, and a leaked key can expose what that key could read. Voice and Mini App sessions can reveal network addresses unless the bot uses Tor or I2P. Most failures are simple: using the bot before build finishes, letting the process exit, a relative file path, or missing rights. vector-lab can test a setup against real relays before you deploy.
keyPoints: Never hardcode, commit or log keys.
Await build() before any other call.
No events: keep the process alive.
Relative file paths follow the working directory; use absolute paths in services.
Test against real relays with vector-lab before deploying.

courses.title: VQ-VAE: Discrete Latents
courses.subtitle: Codebooks, straight-through gradients and priors, with Python labs
courses.author: Lilith Learning Lab
courses.description: Neural Discrete Representation Learning (van den Oord, Vinyals, Kavukcuoglu, 2017): the codebook and nearest-neighbour quantizer, the straight-through estimator, the three-part loss, EMA and dead codes, perplexity, autoregressive priors, and extensions. Theory plus Python labs.

outline.title: What is VQ-VAE?
outline.summary: VQ-VAE, the Vector Quantised Variational AutoEncoder, is a generative model that learns discrete codes. It was introduced by Aaron van den Oord, Oriol Vinyals and Koray Kavukcuoglu in the 2017 paper Neural Discrete Representation Learning. An encoder turns the input into vectors. Each vector is replaced by the nearest entry of a learned codebook. A decoder rebuilds the input from the chosen entries. What remains between them is a grid of integer indices. A second model, an autoregressive prior such as PixelCNN, learns to generate those indices, and sampling from it plus decoding makes new data.
keyPoints: Published at NeurIPS 2017 by van den Oord, Vinyals and Kavukcuoglu.
Latents are discrete: each position holds an index into a codebook of K vectors.
The quantizer is a nearest-neighbour lookup; gradients are copied across it.
The loss has three parts: reconstruction, codebook and commitment.
Generation needs a separate prior over the code indices, such as PixelCNN or WaveNet.
The discrete bottleneck avoids the posterior collapse seen in many VAEs with powerful decoders.

outline.title: Autoencoders and bottlenecks
outline.summary: An autoencoder squeezes an input through a narrow code and tries to rebuild it. The narrowness, the bottleneck, forces the network to keep only what matters. A variational autoencoder, VAE, makes the code random and pushes it toward a simple prior. A known weakness is posterior collapse: a strong decoder learns to ignore the code. VQ-VAE avoids it, since the discrete code carries a fixed number of bits that the decoder must use. The size of the bottleneck is measurable. This chapter counts the bits and the compression.
keyPoints: An autoencoder trains encoder and decoder together to minimize reconstruction error.
A code with K possible values per position carries log2(K) bits per position.
The compression ratio is input bits over code bits.
VAEs with powerful decoders can suffer posterior collapse.
A discrete code forces the decoder to use the bits it gets.
In the paper, 128 by 128 ImageNet images were compressed to a 32 by 32 grid of discrete codes.

outline.title: The codebook and nearest-neighbour quantization
outline.summary: The codebook is a table e with K rows, each a vector of dimension D. At each position, the encoder's output vector z is compared with every row, and the closest one wins. The index of the winner is the discrete code. The looked-up row, not the original vector, goes to the decoder. How well the codebook is used matters. If only a few rows ever win, the capacity is wasted. The labs count the usage.
keyPoints: z_q(x) = e_k with k = argmin_j of the squared distance between z_e(x) and e_j.
Ties go to the lowest index in the labs.
The posterior is deterministic: one-hot on the nearest code.
The latent for an image is a grid of indices; the decoder sees the vectors, not the indices.
Codebook usage should be spread across many rows.
The paper used a codebook of 512 vectors with dimension 64 in its image experiments, and mentions K and D as the main sizes.

outline.title: The straight-through estimator
outline.summary: Training by gradient descent needs derivatives all the way back. The nearest-neighbour step is a staircase: its derivative is zero almost everywhere, and undefined at the jumps. Gradients from the decoder would never reach the encoder. The straight-through estimator ignores the staircase in the backward pass. The forward pass uses the quantized vector; the backward pass passes the gradient at z_q straight to z_e as if the quantizer were the identity. It is a biased approximation but works well in practice. The labs measure the true derivative and train a one-dimensional example with the trick.
keyPoints: The quantizer's true derivative is zero almost everywhere.
Straight-through: dL/dz_e is set equal to dL/dz_q.
Common implementation: z_q_st = z_e + sg[z_q - z_e]; the value is z_q, the gradient is that of z_e.
The decoder gradient moves the encoder output toward better codes.
The codebook gets no gradient from reconstruction, so it needs its own loss.
The estimate is biased but effective.

outline.title: The VQ-VAE loss
outline.summary: The VQ-VAE loss has three terms. The reconstruction term trains the encoder and decoder; its gradient reaches the encoder by the straight-through path. The codebook term pulls the chosen codebook vector toward the encoder's output. The commitment term pulls the encoder's output toward the chosen vector. The stop-gradient operator keeps the two pulls apart, so that each only moves one side. A weight beta, 0.25 in the paper's experiments, scales the commitment term; the authors report the results are robust to its value. The labs compute each term and the gradients that result.
keyPoints: Only the decoder and encoder see the first term (encoder via straight-through).
Only the codebook sees the second term.
Only the encoder sees the third term.
beta was 0.25 in the paper, which found results robust for values from about 0.1 to 2.
The paper's first experiments used the squared error for images and a categorical output for audio.

outline.title: Learning the codebook: k-means, EMA and dead codes
outline.summary: Updating the codebook entry toward the vectors assigned to it is the k-means algorithm. The VQ-VAE codebook loss does this by gradient descent. The paper's appendix describes an alternative with exponential moving averages: keep a running count and sum for each code and set the code to their ratio. A frequent failure is the dead code: an entry that is never nearest to anything, so it never moves. Typical repairs replace dead entries with encoder outputs from the batch. The labs write a k-means step, an EMA update and a dead-code repair.
keyPoints: The codebook loss is a gradient-descent form of k-means.
EMA update: N_i = g N_i + (1 - g) n_i; m_i = g m_i + (1 - g) sum of assigned z; e_i = m_i / N_i.
The paper's appendix suggests decay 0.99 for the EMA variant.
Dead codes never receive updates and waste capacity.
Fixes: reinitialise from data, lower codebook dimension, or normalise.
The EMA variant needs no codebook gradient and is often steadier.

outline.title: Information: rate, perplexity and usage
outline.summary: How many of the K codes does a trained model really use? Entropy and perplexity give the answer. Entropy measures the average information per code in bits. Perplexity, two to the power of the entropy, is the effective number of equally likely codes. If all K codes are used equally, perplexity is K. If one code takes everything, it is 1. Perplexity is tracked in many VQ-VAE implementations as a health check on the codebook. The labs compute entropy, perplexity and the fraction of the codebook in use.
keyPoints: H = -sum p_i log2 p_i bits; perplexity = 2^H.
Uniform usage over K codes: H = log2 K and perplexity = K.
One code used: H = 0 and perplexity = 1.
A model with perplexity far below K is wasting its codebook.
The fraction of unused codes is another simple diagnostic.
Rate is bounded by log2 K per position; the prior can code the indices in fewer bits.

outline.title: The prior: generating with PixelCNN
outline.summary: Training the autoencoder gives codes but not new data. To generate we need a model of which grids of codes are likely: a prior. The VQ-VAE paper trains an autoregressive prior after the autoencoder is fixed. An autoregressive model predicts each code from the ones before it in a fixed order, such as raster order for an image grid. Sampling goes one code at a time, then the decoder turns the grid into an image. For audio the paper uses a WaveNet. The labs build a tiny autoregressive prior, a bigram model on code sequences, with training, scoring and sampling.
keyPoints: p(z) = product of p(z_t | z_1 ... z_(t-1)) over the codes in raster order.
The paper used PixelCNN for images and WaveNet for audio.
In training the prior, the autoencoder is frozen.
Sampling: draw a code, append, repeat; then decode.
The paper's ImageNet latents are 32 by 32 grids; the prior models these 1,024 positions.
Because the prior is over a small grid, it is far cheaper than a PixelCNN on pixels.

outline.title: Extensions: hierarchies, residual and product codes
outline.summary: The VQ-VAE idea has been extended in many directions. VQ-VAE-2 uses a hierarchy: a coarse top-level code grid for global structure and finer codes conditioned on it. Residual quantization uses several codebooks in a row, each coding what the previous ones missed. Product quantization splits a vector into parts and quantizes each part with its own small codebook. All of these raise the capacity of the code: with several levels or parts, the number of distinct combinations multiplies, while each codebook stays small. These extensions are background knowledge in this course, beyond the original paper. The labs implement residual and product quantization.
keyPoints: Capacity of m codebooks of K entries each is K^m with residual or product quantization.
Residual: z_q = e1[k1] + e2[k2] + ..., where each k is chosen on the remainder.
Product: split z into parts and quantize each part with its own codebook.
VQ-VAE-2 (Razavi et al., 2019) used a top and bottom level of codes with PixelCNN priors.
Later systems for images (such as VQGAN), music (Jukebox) and audio codecs (such as SoundStream) build on discrete codes; this is background, not from the 2017 paper.
Discrete tokens let Transformers do generation over images and audio.

outline.title: Problems, comparisons and where it stands
outline.summary: VQ-VAE solved posterior collapse and gave a clean way to learn discrete representations, but it has its own weak points. Codebook collapse leaves most codes unused. The straight-through gradient is a biased approximation. The two-stage training means the prior never influences the codes. Compared with a standard VAE, the latent is discrete and the prior is learned. Compared with a GAN, VQ-VAE has an explicit encoder and likelihood-based training, but its reconstructions can be blurry, a reason later work added adversarial and perceptual losses. The labs finish with diagnostic tools: a collapse report and a quantization error summary.
keyPoints: Codebook collapse is the main training failure; diagnose it with usage and perplexity.
The straight-through gradient is biased but works if the commitment loss keeps z_e close to z_q.
The prior is trained after the autoencoder, so generation quality depends on both stages.
Squared error tends to give blurry reconstructions; later work adds adversarial and perceptual losses (background).
Alternatives: EMA codebooks, reinitialisation, lower-dimensional codes, residual codes.
The core idea, discrete learned tokens, now underpins many generative systems.
